REASONS FOR VARIATIONS / UNDER UTILIZATIONS DURING, 2022-23, 
2023-24 AND CURRENT FINANCIAL YEAR 2024-25: 
5. For 2022-23, the initial budgetary provision was ₹ 3009.05 crore, which was 
revised to ₹ 3363.07 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry incurred an expenditure of ₹ 
3284.12 crore, which is approximately 97.65% of the revised allocation. 
6. For 2023-24, the budget was set at ₹ 3399.65 crore, later increased by ₹ 60.35 
crore to ₹ 3460 crore at the RE stage. The Ministry's expenditure for the year was ₹ 
3406.90 crore, representing 98.46% of the revised estimate. 
7. For 2024-25, the budgetary provision is ₹ 3260.93 crore, including ₹ 190.01 
crore under the Capital section. Although the Ministry proposed an RE allocation of ₹ 
3756.55 crore, reflecting an increase of ₹ 495.62 crore, the RE allocation remained the 
same as the BE allocation. The Committee acknowledges that the Ministry has 
undertaken additional activities such as the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day 
tableau, which were not included in the RE stage. However, it is expected that the 

7 
 
allocated budget for 2024-25 will be utilized optimally as per the Ministry's planned 
activities. 
8. The Committee observes that there is a significant reduction in the 
Ministry's total budget from ₹ 3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 
crore (RE) in 2024-25 and an increase to ₹ 3,360.96 crore for 2025-26. The 
Committee further observes the reduction in the Ministry’s total budget from ₹ 
3,406.90 crore (actual) in 2023-24 to ₹ 3,260.93 crore (RE) in 2024-25 can be 
attributed primarily to the one-time expenditures related to the Azadi Ka Amrit 
Mahotsav (AKAM). The AKAM celebrations saw a substantial increase in 
expenditure, with a revision of the Budget Estimate (BE) from ₹ 185 crore to ₹ 
335 crore during 2023-24, resulting in an expenditure of ₹ 334.39 crore, which 
was more than 80% over and above the original BE allocation. 
9. The Committee acknowledges that the reduction in budget during the 
2024-25 fiscal year is a reflection of the conclusion of AKAM-related activities, 
which were exceptional in nature and not a recurring part of the Ministry's 
regular expenditure plans. However, the reduction in the budget allocation for 
2024-25 compared to 2023-24 highlights the need to ensure that the Ministry's 
cultural preservation and development initiatives are adequately funded, 
especially in light of long-term goals for heritage conservation.  
10. The Committee further notes that the budget formulation process for 
2024-25 did not adequately account for key national cultural commitments, 
including the Kumbh at Prayag and the Republic Day tableau, leading to an 
additional request for funds mid-year. The omission of such significant 
expenditures at the BE stage does seem to indicate deficiencies in financial 
forecasting and contingency planning. The Committee recommends the 
implementation of a comprehensive Multi-Year Budgetary Framework (MYBF) 
for the Ministry of Culture that extends beyond the annual budget cycle. This 
framework should incorporate: 

8 
 
a) A five-year rolling budget projection with annual revisions to accommodate 
changing priorities while maintaining long-term vision. 
b) Categorization of expenditures into core recurring activities, planned 
development initiatives, and special events/commemorations with separate 
budgetary provisions for each category. 
c) Establishment of a Budget Stabilization Reserve of approximately 5% of the 
total annual allocation to account for unforeseen cultural activities or 
emergencies, preventing mid-year fiscal disruptions. 
This approach would mitigate the abrupt budgetary fluctuations witnessed 
between 2023-24 and 2024-25, and provide greater stability for cultural 
institutions dependent on Government funding. 
11. The Committee further notes that although overall budget utilisation 
remains high, expenditure patterns across various cultural schemes have been 
inconsistent. Programmes such as museum development, cultural mapping, and 
global cultural engagement have experienced fluctuating levels of fund 
disbursement, with some initiatives facing under-utilisation in certain years and 
excessive allocations in other.  The Committee strongly recommends the 
development of a Cultural Calendar-Based Budgeting system that: 
a) Maintains a comprehensive five-year cultural events calendar that identifies 
recurring festivals, commemorations, and international engagements with 
historical budget requirements. 
b) Integrates cyclical cultural events (such as Kumbh Mela, which occurs every 
12 years) into long-term financial planning through a dedicated cultural events 
fund. 
c) Implements quarterly budget review mechanisms to assess expenditure 
against planned activities and make necessary adjustments before the Revised 
Estimates stage. 

9 
 
d) Develops an AI-assisted forecasting model that analyzes historical expenditure 
patterns and predicts resource requirements for upcoming cultural activities 
based on past event costs, inflation factors, and attendance projections. 
This systematic approach would ensure that cultural events of national 
importance receive appropriate financial provisions at the Budget Estimate stage 
rather than relying on mid-year adjustments 
 
12. The Committee observes a pattern wherein the Ministry relies heavily on 
mid-year budgetary adjustments, seeking substantial increases at the RE stage 
instead of ensuring that BE allocations accurately reflect financial needs. In the 
opinion of the Committee, this approach introduces uncertainty into long-term 
financial planning and may disrupt the timely execution of projects. A more 
accurate and predictive budget estimation process is required to minimise 
dependency on RE-stage adjustments. The Committee recommends that the 
Ministry strengthen its engagement with the Ministry of Finance to establish a 
more flexible, needs-based budget allocation framework, one that will ensure 
funding provisions are more effectively met with practical expenditure 
requirements. Also, the Ministry should establish a Corporate Social 
Responsibility (CSR) engagement cell within the Ministry to facilitate 
partnerships between businesses and cultural projects, capitalizing on the 100% 
tax exemption available under Section 80G(ii) of the Income Tax Act

14. The Committee recommends a more robust allocation for the conservation, 
restoration, and maintenance of protected monuments, especially the World 
Heritage Sites. Considering the increasing pressure on ASI’s existing resources, 
the allocation need to be increased to ensure timely conservation and meet global 
standards for preservation. It is recommended to create a dedicated Heritage 
Conservation Fund with a corpus of ₹ 500 crore over five years, with 
contributions from tourism revenue, CSR initiatives, and matching government 
grants through the National Culture Fund framework. This fund would 
specifically address emergency conservation needs and climate vulnerability 
mitigation measures at protected monuments.  
14.1 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) manages 3,698 centrally 
protected monuments under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites 
and Remains (AMASR) Act, 1958, encompassing temples, forts, tombs, and 
prehistoric sites. Despite recent efforts, including a 70% budget increase to ₹ 
443.53 crore in 2023–24 and the delisting of 18 untraceable monuments like 
Delhi’s Barakhamba Cemetery and Haryana’s Kos Minar No.13, challenges such 
as encroachment, climate threats, and resource gaps persist. To address these 
issues, parliamentary committees recommends a multi-pronged strategy. First, a 
GIS-based digital inventory with real-time monitoring and biennial audits 
should be prioritized to enhance accountability and prevent monuments from 
disappearing due to urbanization. Strengthening legal frameworks, including 

12 
 
stricter penalties under the AMASR Act and fast-track courts for heritage 
violations, would streamline enforcement against encroachments. 
14.2 Climate resilience measures, such as expanding Automated Weather 
Stations (AWS) and pollution monitoring labs to high-risk sites like Konark Sun 
Temple, must be scaled to mitigate environmental damage. Concurrently, 
integrating AI-driven predictive maintenance, 3D mapping, and drone 
surveillance—as seen in Tamil Nadu’s excavation projects and Mehrauli’s recent 
Supreme Court-mandated survey—can revolutionize preservation through early 
damage detection. Community engagement is equally critical; initiatives like a 
tax-incentivized “Adopt a Monument” program and training locals as heritage 
stewards would foster grassroots ownership. 
14.3 Finally, delisting protocols require reform. An independent panel should 
reassess criteria to ensure delisting occurs only after rigorous documentation and 
public consultation, paired with a relic repatriation policy for displaced artifacts. 
By combining technology, legal rigor, climate adaptation, and community 
participation, India can balance heritage conservation with developmental 
pressures, safeguarding its cultural legacy for future generations. These steps 
would align with ASI’s mandate while addressing systemic gaps in monument 
management. 
15. The Committee recommends addressing delays in ongoing Museum 
Projects like the Dholavira Museum and the Leh Museum as they have faced 
significant delays due to issues such as land allotments, extending timelines by 8–
12 months. The committee further recommends prioritizing the resolution of 
these delays, ensuring that land allotments are expedited and necessary 
clearances are streamlined. A dedicated task force or coordination mechanism 
should be set up to oversee and speed up the approval processes for critical 
infrastructure projects. 

13 
 
16. The Committee recommends comprehensive digitalization of heritage 
assets to enhance both preservation efforts and public engagement: 
a) Develop a phased implementation of "Digital Twin" technology for all 
World Heritage Sites and at least 100 nationally significant monuments by 
2028. This would involve creating precise digital replicas to monitor 
structural changes, simulate conservation interventions, and enhance 
visitor experience through augmented reality applications. 
b) Establish a centralized Heritage Monitoring System using remote sensing 
and IoT devices to provide real-time data on environmental conditions, 
structural stability, and visitor impact at critical monuments. This would 
enable predictive maintenance and early intervention, potentially reducing 
long-term conservation costs by 30-35%. 
c) Launch a Metaverse Heritage Initiative that creates immersive digital 
experiences of inaccessible or vulnerable monument areas, allowing for 
virtual tourism while reducing physical impact on fragile structures. This 
initiative should prioritize monuments facing access restrictions due to 
conservation concerns. 
d) Implement block chain technology for monument documentation and 
conservation history, creating an immutable record of interventions and 
condition assessments that ensures accountability and preservation of 
institutional knowledge across administrative transitions. 
16.1 Recommendation: Institutional Reforms for Museum Project 
Implementation: The Committee recommends fundamental reforms to the 
project implementation mechanisms: 
a) Implement a modular development approach for museum projects, enabling 
phased completion and partial operationalization while resolving issues with 
remaining components. This would allow for incremental public access and 

14 
 
revenue generation rather than complete closure during extended development 
periods. 
b) Develop a standardized pre-implementation framework for museum projects 
that mandates resolution of land acquisition, environmental clearances, and 
conceptual design before budget allocation and project announcement, 
minimizing mid-project disruptions. 
c) Create specialized project management units for each major museum 
initiative with representation from relevant stakeholders, including state 
governments, ASI, content specialists, and community representatives to ensure 
coordinated action and accountability. 
 
16.2 To address content finalization delays as observed in the Digital Museum 
project at Kanakakunnu Palace, the Committee recommends: 
 
a) Establish a permanent Museum Content Advisory Board comprising 
historians, cultural anthropologists, museologists, and digital content specialists 
to expedite content development processes across all museum projects. 
b) Implement concurrent content development alongside infrastructure creation 
rather than sequential processes, with rolling approvals for thematic sections to 
prevent complete project stagnation during content refinement. 
c) Develop a shared digital content repository for Ministry museums that enables 
efficient resource sharing and adaptation of existing content for new museums, 
reducing redundant research and development costs. 
d) Integrate emerging technologies such as AI-assisted curation, interactive 
installations, and personalized visitor journeys through mobile applications to 
enhance the museum experience and attract younger audiences. 
e) Implement a "Living Museum" approach that encourages regular content 
updates and community contributions, moving away from static permanent 

15 
 
exhibitions toward more dynamic and participatory models of heritage 
presentation. 
16.3 Recommendation: Heritage-Led Regional Development Strategy: The 
Committee recommends leveraging archaeological sites for sustainable local 
development: 
a) Implement a Heritage-Led Regeneration approach, integrating archaeological 
sites into broader regional development plans. This would involve creating 
archaeological tourism circuits with appropriate infrastructure, interpretation 
facilities, and community engagement. 
b) Establish Archaeological Heritage Zones around significant excavation sites 
with special planning regulations, economic incentives for heritage-sensitive

ENHANCING EFFORTS FOR CULTURAL REPATRIATION 
29.1 The Archaeological Survey of India, operating under the Ministry of 
Culture, is spearheading this significant cultural recovery effort, which includes 
the Kohinoor and beyond it to encompass thousands of artifacts removed during 
British colonial rule. 
29.2 To strengthen India’s campaign for cultural repatriation, the government 
should consider establishing a specialized “Heritage Recovery Task Force” 
comprised of diplomats, legal experts, archaeologists, and art historians. This 
multidisciplinary team would be dedicated exclusively to identifying, 
documenting, and pursuing claims for stolen Indian artifacts worldwide. The 
task force could develop comprehensive dossiers on priority items, including 
detailed provenance research, legal arguments for restitution, and cultural 
significance documentation to bolster India’s claims. 
29.3 India should leverage its growing economic and diplomatic influence to 
negotiate cultural property agreements with more countries, similar to the recent 
pact with the United States. These agreements should establish clear mechanisms 
for identifying looted artifacts, resolving disputes, and facilitating returns. 
Special attention should be paid to former colonial powers like the United 
Kingdom, where many significant Indian treasures remain. These agreements 

24 
 
could be tied to broader diplomatic and trade relationships, creating incentives 
for cooperation on repatriation issues. 
29.4 To strengthen legal arguments for repatriation, India should invest in 
cutting-edge technological tools for provenance research and authentication. 
Advanced imaging techniques, DNA analysis of organic materials, and AI-
powered databases could help establish the Indian origin of disputed artifacts 
and track the chain of ownership. This scientific evidence could prove invaluable 
in making compelling cases for return, particularly for items with unclear 
provenance records. 
29.5 Additionally, India should explore innovative public-private partnerships 
to support repatriation efforts. The government could establish a “Heritage 
Repatriation Fund” that accepts contributions from corporations, wealthy 
individuals, and the Indian diaspora to support legal challenges, negotiate 
purchases when necessary, and fund transportation and conservation of 
returned artifacts. This approach would expand the resources available for 
recovery efforts while engaging broader segments of society in the mission.

32.2 The Committee recommends establishing a dedicated research program

five specialized Conservation Research Laboratories focused on different 
manuscript materials (palm leaf, birch bark, paper, cloth, and metals) to develop 
non-invasive preservation techniques, research environmentally sustainable 
conservation materials, and establish evidence-based protocols for treatment of 
deteriorating manuscripts. The implementation of a "Preventive Conservation 
Network" with environmental monitoring systems at all major manuscript 
repositories would enable real-time assessment of conservation risks and 
preventive interventions, significantly reducing deterioration rates in vulnerable 
collections.

conservation institutes worldwide would facilitate knowledge exchange, joint

Committee notes that while the NMM employs various methods of preservation 
such as lamination, restoration, and de-acidification, there is a need for more

MANPOWER SHORTAGES - 
35. As per Paragraph No. 8.1 of Report No. 12 of 2017 of the C&AG Report 
(Annexure), the Ministry of Culture failed to fill up key posts in the National Gallery 
of Modern Art for over a decade resulting in failure to relocate 16,582 works of art to 
a new state of the art storage system, leading to idling of investment of ₹ 3.81 crore 
since March 2014.  Further, as per Para 3.1 of Report No.3 of 2024 of the said Report 
regarding Functioning of IGRMS, there was a shortage of staff in IGRMS as on 2024 
as out of total sanctioned strength of 118 posts in all the cadres, there was a vacancy 
of 36 posts (30.51 per cent) which included five vacancies (100 per cent) in Group A 
cadre. These vacancies will hinder in research and preservation efforts, thereby 
impacting the overall effectiveness of heritage management. 
36. The Committee recommends that the Ministry of Culture should prioritize 
the immediate recruitment of qualified personnel to fill the existing vacancies, 
especially at the National Gallery of Modern Art (NGMA) and Indira Gandhi 
Rashtriya Manav Sangrahalaya (IGRMS), in critical positions such as those in 
Group A cadres. This will ensure the effective management of cultural heritage, 
facilitate the relocation of artworks, and support research and preservation 
efforts. The Ministry should streamline the recruitment process, establish a 
dedicated task force to monitor progress, and allocate necessary resources to 
ensure timely appointments, thereby strengthening the overall functionality of 
these institutions and preventing any further delays in their operations. 
37. The Committee further observes that the integration of major monuments 
with tourism circuits through modern technological solutions, such as Artificial 
Intelligence and Augmented Reality, is increasing the demand for specialized 
manpower. This includes not only technical roles for preservation but also skilled 
personnel for the management and implementation of these advanced 

30 
 
technologies, which will require a focus on recruiting professionals with expertise 
in both heritage conservation and cutting-edge technological fields. 
38. Accordingly, the Committee recommends that ASI prioritize the 
recruitment of skilled professionals with expertise in both heritage conservation 
and modern technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality, 
to support the integration of major monuments with tourism circuits and ensure 
the effective management and preservation of cultural heritage. 
39. Further, in light of the increasing demand for specialized manpower due to 
the integration of Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality, for the 
digitization and preservation of monuments, the Committee desires to know 
whether the Ministry has made any progress in implementing the 
recommendations from the 2020 Expert Committee regarding the adoption of 
these technologies. The Committee would also like to know the steps taken to 
recruit professionals with expertise in both heritage conservation and cutting-
edge technological fields to manage and execute these initiatives effectively.

10.  The meeting resumed at 02: 40 P.M. to hear the views of the Secretary, Ministry of 
Culture on Demands for Grants (2025 -26) of the Ministry . At the outset, the Chairman opened 
the meeting by welcoming the Members of the Committee, officers and representatives from the

11.  Shri Arunish Chawla, Secretary, Ministry of Culture started his presentation by 
presenting a comprehensive overview of the Ministry’s financial allocations and key policy 
initiatives. He stated that the Ministry has been allocated Rs. 3,360 crore s for the financial year 
2025-26, reflecting a marginal increase over the previous year. The Ministry has consistently 
maintained a high expenditure rate, with 98.47% of the allocated budget utilised in the preceding 
financial year and 89% already expended  in the current fiscal cycle. He outlined the 
implementation of seven Central Sector Schemes, which include Kala Sanskriti Vikas Yojana, 
Centenaries and Anniversaries, Development of Museums, Development of Libraries and 
Archives, Gyan Bharatam Mission, Gl obal Engagement Scheme, and the National Mission on 
Cultural Mapping. The Secretary also highlighted major accomplishments, such as the successful 
organisation of the World Heritage Committee Meeting in July 2024, the repatriation of 655 
antiquities, and t he recognition of Garba of Gujarat as part of UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural 
Heritage.  
12.   The Secretary emphasised the Ministry’s ambitious vision under Rachanatmak Bharat: 
namely, the National Mission on Creative Economy, which seeks to integrate India’s cultural and 
artistic heritage with modern economic frameworks while initiatives like the Cultural Satellite 
Account, aimed at quantifying the economic contribution of cultural activities, as well as the 
integration of major monuments with tourism circui ts through modern technological solutions, 
including Artificial Intelligence and Augmented Reality. He reassured the Committee that steps 
were being taken to expedite recruitment processes for vacant positions in ASI, museums, and 
national academies.  

41 
 
 
13.  Thereafter, the Ministry elaborated on its financial strategies, explaining categorization of 
the budget under three verticals: Establishment Expenditure, covering administrative costs and 
institutional overheads; Central Sector Schemes, dedicated to the  implementation of key cultural 
programmes; and Autonomous Bodies and Grantee Institutions, which provide financial support 
to cultural academies, museums, and research institutions.  
14. The Ministry highlighted its efforts to optimize fund utilization an d streamline 
administrative processes. It emphasized the budget for cultural infrastructure and digital 
modernization, with greater investments allocated to digital repositories, archival preservation, 
and museum enhancements. It was informed that internat ional collaborations and public -private 
partnerships were actively being pursued to reduce reliance on domestic financial allocations and 
secure expertise for large -scale cultural preservation projects. The Ministry asserted that its  
approach to prudent f iscal management, strategic planning, and innovative funding mechanisms 
would significantly bolster its ability to preserve the country’s rich cultural legacy and enhance 
global cultural influence. 
15.   The Committee raised the following issues during the course of the Meeting:  
 Members queried on the reasons behind certain funds remaining underutilized  despite an 
increase in budgetary allocations and sought clarity on measures to ensure timely 
expenditure. 
 Concerns were raised regarding vacancies in key i nstitutions such as the ASI, museums, 
and national academies, and their impact on research and preservation efforts. 
 Members raised q ueries regarding the decreasing number of archaeological excavations 
compared to previous years, particularly in historical ly significant sites such as 
Balirajgarh and Harappan settlements. 
 Members sought clarification on whether tribal dances, oral traditions, and other 
indigenous cultural elements were being adequately documented and supported. 
 Members highlighted the need f or financial assistance, pension schemes, and capacity -
building programmes to safeguard the livelihoods of folk artists and craftsmen. 
 Concerns were expressed regarding the perceived inactivity of Zonal Cultural Centres 
and their engagement with local communities. 
 Members sought to know the conditions of artefacts stored in museum basements and the 
Ministry’s plan for their proper preservation and exhibition. 
 Members welcomed efforts to reclaim antiquities from the United States  and urged 
similar bilateral agreements with the United Kingdom and other nations to recover 
significant cultural artefacts.

promote awareness and appreciation among students;

livelihoods of folk artists and craftsmen; and 
 Devising of a  detailed inventory an d digitization plan for artefacts stored in museum 
basements to facilitate preservation and exhibition.

INTRODUCTION 
Maritime transport constitutes a fundamental pillar of national infrastructure, 
underpinning the economic growth, trade expansion, and social advancement of the 
country. It plays an instrumental role in shaping the pace, structure, and trajectory of 
development, ensuring India’s connectivity with global markets and reinforcing its 
position in international trade. 
2. The Ministry of Ports, Shipping, and Waterways (MoPSW) bears the paramount 
responsibility for the formulation and execution of policies and programmes aimed at 
fortifying the maritime sector. Its remit encompasses ports, shipping, inland waterways, 
shipbuilding and ship-repair services, with the overarching objective of ensuring a 
modern, efficient, and globally competitive maritime infrastructure. 
3. To address the complexities and evolving demands of the maritime sector, a 
comprehensive, strategic, and future-oriented policy framework is imperative. In 
furtherance of this objective, the Ministry is actively engaged in: 
 Augmenting port capacity by advancing infrastructure, enhancing berths, and 
modernising cargo-handling mechanisms to facilitate seamless trade and efficient 
logistics. 
 Empowering the shipping and waterways industries to assume greater 
responsibility in handling sea-borne trade through indigenous vessels, thereby 
reducing reliance on foreign carriers and reinforcing national maritime 
sovereignty. 
 Encouraging sustainable investment in port infrastructure, recognizing that the 
development of ports demands substantial capital investment, entails prolonged 
gestation periods, and is subject to multifaceted externalities. 

2 
 
4. Historically, port development has been state-driven, necessitated by the 
considerable financial outlay, uncertain returns, and strategic implications inherent in 
such large-scale projects. The Ministry’s proactive approach in navigating these 
challenges is pivotal in fortifying India’s maritime capabilities and ensuring that the 
nation remains at the forefront of global maritime trade. Through infrastructure 
modernization, progressive policy initiatives, and steadfast commitment, the Ministry of 
Ports, Shipping, and Waterways is spearheading the transformation of India’s maritime 
sector, making it a driving force for economic prosperity and global trade leadership.

GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
6. The Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF), published by the Ministry 
of Ports, Shipping, and Waterways for FY 2025-26 outlines the strategic objectives, 

4 
 
financial allocations, and expected outcomes for key maritime initiatives under the 
Ministry. The framework focuses on enhancing maritime infrastructure, promoting 
shipbuilding, strengthening research & development, and improving logistics 
connectivity. The principal objectives are as follows: 
i. Research & Development (allocated budget ₹0.71 crore): The allotted 
budget will focus on promoting studies on sediment management, tsunami-
resilient breakwaters, and dredged sediment valorisation. There is also a 
planned development of draft forecasting models for River Hooghly and 
siltation control measures for Mumbai & JNPT ports. 
ii. Sagarmala Programme (allocated budget ₹866 crore): The Sagarmala 
Programme aims at augmenting port connectivity, modernization of 
infrastructure, and promoting maritime tourism. Under this initiative, one 
major road project is set to be completed, with an anticipated reduction in 
transit time for goods by 0.5 hours, improving overall port logistics. 
Infrastructure modernization efforts include the addition of 1 MTPA cargo 
handling capacity, the construction of a new cruise terminal, and the 
development of seven Ro-Ro passenger jetties. Additionally, 20 skill 
development courses are planned, targeting the certification of 6,000 
individuals. 
iii. Shipbuilding and Research (allocated budget ₹350 crore): The aim is to 
construct and deliver 37 vessels, with the resulting generation of ₹1,837 
crore in business revenue, reflecting a 292.5% growth from the previous 
year, and create2,99,900 additional man-days of employment, marking a 
24.98% increase. Furthermore, an increase of 31,000 gross tonnages (GT) 
in ship production capacity, representing77.5% growth, is targeted.

MOVEMENT, EFFICIENCY AND COOPERATION  
8. Container Movement Timing Recommendations 
8.1 The Committee recommends immediate attention to the challenges facing 
maritime container movement schedules due to global disruptions and trade 
volatility. The Committee strongly urges the Ministry to implement comprehensive 
digital tracking platforms for real-time monitoring of container movements across 
all major ports. Furthermore, the Committee recommends establishing a dedicated 
Maritime Response Unit to address contingencies arising from geopolitical 
disruptions along key shipping routes. The Committee believes these measures are 
essential to mitigate extended lead times currently affecting Asia-Europe shipments 
and to reduce congestion at strategic port hubs. 
Port Efficiency Recommendations 
8.2 The Committee notes the ambitious targets under Maritime India Vision 2030 
and recommends accelerated implementation of mechanization initiatives at all 
major ports to achieve the sub-20-hour turnaround time goal. The Committee 
strongly advises prioritizing budget allocation for modernizing port infrastructure, 
particularly automated cargo handling systems and digital documentation 
processes. The Committee further recommends quarterly performance reviews of 
port efficiency metrics with standardized benchmarks to ensure measurable 
progress toward capacity enhancement targets. 
Inter-Ministerial Port Connectivity Recommendations 
8.3 The Committee emphasizes that inadequate multi-modal connectivity 
remains a significant bottleneck affecting port efficiency. The Committee 
recommends establishing a dedicated Inter-Ministerial Coordination Cell to 
expedite port connectivity projects under PM Gati Shakti. With reference to 

10 
 
Paradip Port, the Committee recommends immediate completion of pending 
railway linkage projects and upgradation of NH-53A to facilitate smoother cargo 
evacuation. The Committee strongly urges synchronized planning between the 
Ministries of Railways, Road Transport and Highways, and Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways to ensure infrastructure development aligns with projected cargo 
volumes. The Committee recommends that the Paradip Port development model be 
replicated across other major ports to enhance seamless connectivity and reduce 
logistics costs. 
8.4 The Committee notes that the allocation of ₹0.71 crore for Research & 
Development (R&D) in port development is strikingly low, especially considering 
the critical role that technological advancement plays in ensuring the 
competitiveness and efficiency of the country’s maritime infrastructure. The 
Committee strongly recommends a significant augmentation of R&D funding to 
bring out innovation in port infrastructure, automation, and environmental 
sustainability.

CENTRAL SECTOR SCHEMES-an analysis 
Sagarmala Programme 
15. The Sagarmala Programme, the Ministry of Ports, Shipping & Waterways' 
flagship Central Sector Scheme, promotes port-led development by harnessing 
India’s coastline, waterways, and strategic maritime position. Projects are 
implemented by Central Ministries, State Governments, State Maritime Boards, 
and Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs), with the Ministry also supporting high-
impact, low-return projects. For FY 2025-26, ₹ 810 crore has been allocated for 
port infrastructure, coastal berths, road and rail links, fishery harbours, floating 
jetties, skill development, cruise terminals, and Ro-Pax ferry services. Under the 
Sagarmala Scheme, the Ministry is developing the National Maritime Heritage 
Complex (NMHC) at Lothal, Gujarat, as a one-of-a-kind project dedicated to 
India’s maritime heritage. The Ministry is enhancing urban waterways transport 
(Ro-Pax services) to improve cargo movement, reduce travel time, ease road 
congestion, and cut pollution. It is part-funding 26 fishing harbours, with 9 
completed at ₹ 144.5 crore, and upgrading five major harbours—Kochi, Chennai, 
Visakhapatnam, Paradip, and Mallet Bunder. Additionally, 50 floating jetty 
locations have been identified in Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Puducherry, 
Karnataka, and Kerala, while ₹ 56 crore has been allocated for maritime 
infrastructure in the Andaman & Nicobar Islands and Lakshadweep.

16. The Committee, upon examination of the financial allocations and 
expenditure trends under the Sagarmala Programme, notes that while the Budget 
Estimate (BE) for 2025-26 has been set at ₹ 810 crore which is a 26.6% increase 
from the previous year’s BE of ₹ 640 crore, there are concerns regarding fund 
utilisation efficiency. In 2024-25, the Revised Estimate (RE) was marginally 
increased to ₹ 649 crore, but actual expenditure, as of date, stands at ₹ 566 crore, 
reflecting an 87.2% utilisation rate. In the opinion of the Committee, there seems to 
be delays in project execution, or administrative inefficiencies, which, if left 
unaddressed, may hinder the full realisation of the ambitious programme’s intended 
objectives. The Committee, therefore, urges the Ministry to ensure greater financial 
discipline and proactive project monitoring to facilitate timely and effective 
utilisation of allocated resources. It is recommended that a comprehensive review be 
undertaken to identify and rectify procedural impediments that have contributed to 
underutilisation in 2024-25, ensuring that the ₹ 810 crore allocated for 2025-26 is 
expended in a structured and time-bound manner. Furthermore, the Committee 
stresses the importance of accurate budget forecasting to minimise the need for mid-
year revisions and recommends that the Ministry strengthen its project 
implementation framework, including regular financial performance reviews and 
enhanced inter-agency coordination, to uphold fiscal prudence and programme 
efficacy.

18 
 
comprehensive development of NW-2 (the Brahmaputra), NW-16 (the Barak) and Indo-
Bangladesh Protocol (IBP) route at a total cost of ₹ 1010 crore for a period of 5 years 
2020-2025 to continue during the year which would boost economic development and

for creation of Capital Assets and operation and maintenance of operational National

19. Balancing Capital Expenditure and Maintenance Requirements 
The Committee observes imbalance between capital investments (₹994.33 
crore for JMVP) and maintenance expenditure (₹267 crore) which in its opinion 
reflects a critical concern in infrastructure development strategy. The Jal Marg 
Vikas Project, currently extended to 2026 with World Bank support, represents a 
substantial commitment to expanding the inland waterway infrastructure along 
National Waterway-1. While the project has demonstrated progress in creating 
multi-modal terminals at Varanasi, Sahibganj, and Haldia, evidence suggests 
implementation challenges persist, with certain tenders being cancelled due to 
significantly higher bids than estimated values. The Committee notes that 
maintenance expenditure forms the backbone of any sustainable infrastructure 
network, particularly for waterways where regular dredging and channel 
maintenance are essential for ensuring navigability. The current allocation of ₹267 
crore for maintaining existing waterways appears insufficient, especially when 
considered against the extensive network of 111 National Waterways. The 
experience from European waterway management indicates that sustained 
maintenance funding is crucial for ensuring the reliability and performance of 
inland navigation infrastructure. The Committee therefore recommends a more 

19 
 
strategic approach involving implementation of a Life-Cycle Cost Assessment 
(LCCA) framework for waterway infrastructure that balances initial capital 
expenditure with long-term maintenance requirements. This framework should 
incorporate detailed assessment of annual maintenance needs for each operational 
waterway segment, ensuring sufficient allocation for critical activities like dredging 
campaigns, navigation aids maintenance, and terminal upkeep. The Ministry should 
establish a minimum maintenance-to-capital expenditure ratio of 1:2 for mature 
waterways, gradually transitioning to 1:1 as the network stabilizes, ensuring 
sustainable operation while continuing necessary expansion. 
20. Reconsidering Debt Financing Strategy for IWT Projects 
The Committee notes the allocation of ₹76.50 crore toward interest payments on 
IWAI bonds  and raises concerns about the sustainability of debt-based financing 
for inland waterway projects. While debt instruments provide immediate access to 
capital necessary for infrastructure development, they create rigid fiscal obligations 
that constrain future budgetary flexibility. The current financing structure of the 
JMVP, with its reliance on both international loans (₹2,512 crore from IBRD) and 
government bonds, exemplifies this mixed approach. 
Debt financing offers certain advantages, including preservation of operational 
autonomy and prevention of ownership dilution. However, it also introduces 
financial covenants that may restrict operational flexibility and increases overall 
financial risk exposure. The experience from the financing survey of the inland 
waterway transport sector indicates that while loans on favorable terms remain a 
preferred financial instrument, there is growing interest in alternative financing 
approaches, particularly among larger operators. 
20.1 The Committee therefore recommends a more balanced financing strategy that 
incorporates diversified funding sources beyond traditional debt instruments. The 
Ministry should develop a Waterway Infrastructure Finance Framework that 

20 
 
includes: (1) Project-specific revenue bonds tied to direct income streams from 
waterway operations, reducing dependency on general budgetary allocations; (2) 
Dedicated Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs) specifically for waterway 
projects with stable revenue potential, allowing broader market participation; and 
(3) Blended finance models combining concessional loans, grants, and commercial 
financing to optimize the capital structure for different project components. 
21. Enhancing Effectiveness of North-Eastern Region Investments 
The Committee notes the allocation of ₹421 crore for North-Eastern Region 
infrastructure development targeting NW-2 (Brahmaputra), NW-16 (Barak), and 
the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol route which represents a significant opportunity to 
enhance regional connectivity. However, the unique geographical and logistical 
challenges of the region necessitate more nuanced implementation strategies to 
ensure these investments yield meaningful economic returns. 
In its opinion, stakeholder consultations in the North-Eastern Region reveal limited 
awareness about environmental safeguards and coordination challenges among 
different agencies involved in riverine infrastructure. Local communities prioritize 
rapid development but lack understanding of the quality standards necessary for 
sustainable waterway operations. Field observations indicate that structural 
interventions like piers, bridges, and river training works can pose navigational 
hazards when not properly coordinated among stakeholders. 
In order to maximize the effectiveness of the ₹1,010 crore five-year NER project 
(2020-2025), the Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry implements a 
Regional Waterway Development Consortium model that brings together state 
governments, local bodies, technical institutions, and private stakeholders in a 
structured governance framework. This consortium should establish a unified 
project monitoring system with standardized reporting protocols and performance 

21 
 
indicators for all NER waterway projects, enabling real-time tracking of 
implementation progress and rapid intervention where needed. 
21.1 Furthermore, the Ministry should initiate quarterly multi-stakeholder 
coordination forums in each NER state to harmonize river training works, terminal 
development, and navigation infrastructure planning. These forums should 
specifically address the coordination issues between state Water Resources 
Departments (WRD) and Inland Water Transport (IWT) authorities identified 
during stakeholder consultations. 
22. Structuring Framework for Enhancing Private Sector Participation 
The Committee further notes the limited engagement of the private sector in inland 
waterway development which in its opinion represents a missed opportunity for 
accelerating infrastructure development while reducing fiscal burden. Despite 
allocations of ₹301 crore for private participation under PPP mode within the 
JMVP framework, actual private investment has remained below expectations. The 
Ministry’s emphasis on nurturing public-private partnerships is indicative of 
governmental recognition of this gap, but systematic structural interventions are 
needed to translate this intent into action. 
22.1 The Committee therefore urges the Ministry to establish a comprehensive 
Inland Waterway Investment Framework specifically designed to attract private 
capital across multiple segments of the value chain. This framework should include 
distinct incentive structures for three categories of private participation: (1) 
Infrastructure developers focusing on terminal construction, navigation aids, and 
specialized cargo handling facilities; (2) Vessel operators and logistics providers 
offering transportation services on established waterways; and (3) Technology 
partners bringing innovations in vessel design, navigation systems, and 
environmental solutions. 

22 
 
Financial mechanisms should be calibrated to address specific barriers faced by 
different types of private investors. For infrastructure developers, enhanced 
Viability Gap Funding with coverage up to 40% for waterway projects in 
challenging geographies would reduce entry barriers. For vessel operators, 
accelerated depreciation provisions and priority sector lending status would 
stimulate fleet modernization. For technology partners, a dedicated Waterway 
Innovation Fund providing matching grants for pilot deployments would accelerate 
adoption of new solutions. 
22.2 Furthermore, the Ministry should reform the concession framework for 
waterway operations to offer more attractive risk-sharing arrangements. This 
includes implementing flexible concession periods tied to actual traffic achievement 
rather than fixed timelines, establishing minimum revenue guarantees for pioneer 
routes, and creating streamlined regulatory clearance mechanisms for waterway 
projects through a single-window system. 
  
23. Ship Building and ship repair- The Ministry informed the Committee that to 
promote indigenous shipbuilding industry in India, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and 
Waterways has brought in Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy (SBFAP) scheme for 
Indian shipyards to procure orders from domestic as well as international market and to 
be competitive in international market for securing global orders. The scheme offers 
financial assistance to Indian Shipyards for shipbuilding contracts signed between April 
1, 2016 to March 31, 2026 with rate of financial assistance starting from 20% in 2016 and 
diminishing to 11% in 2026 with a budget allocation of ₹4000Crore. Also, financial 
assistance of 30% is given for vessels where main propulsion is achieved by means of 
green fuels such as Methanol/ Ammonia / Hydrogen fuel cells and financial assistance of 
20% for vessels with electric means of propulsion or vessels fitted with hybrid propulsion 
system. An amount of ₹ 138Crore has been allocated for SBFAP for FY 2025-26. Funds 
are projected based on tentative delivery of ships by shipyards. 

23 
 
24. Current State of SBFAP Implementation and Fund Utilization 
The Committee notes the allocation of ₹138 crore for shipbuilding assistance in FY 
2025-26 which represents a modest commitment when viewed against the backdrop 
of the scheme's total allocation of ₹4,000 crore that was intended to span from 2016 
to 2026. This relatively small annual allocation however raises serious concerns 
about the pace and scale of implementation. Evidence suggests that despite the 
policy being operational for nearly nine years, barely 10% of the total corpus has 
been utilized, indicating structural impediments in policy implementation. Since its 
inception, the SBFAP has facilitated 313 vessel orders across 39 shipyards, with a 
cumulative value of approximately ₹10,500 crore. However, financial assistance 
disbursed stands at only ₹337 crore for 135 completed vessels. This significant gap 
between allocated funds and actual disbursement suggests systemic issues in fund 
absorption capacity within the industry. The progressive reduction in financial 
assistance percentages—from 20% in 2016 to the current 11%—appears to have 
contributed to diminishing industry interest in the scheme, particularly as 
competing shipbuilding nations like China and South Korea continue to provide 20-
30% subsidies to their shipyards. 
24.1 The Committee therefore suggests that the Ministry undertakes a 
comprehensive performance audit of the SBFAP to identify specific bottlenecks 
preventing optimal fund utilization. The audit should examine whether procedural 
complexities in application processing, unrealistic valuation mechanisms, or lack of 
shipyard capacity are inhibiting fund absorption. The web application for 
processing applications, despite improvements made after industry feedback, may 
require further streamlining to facilitate easier access to financial assistance. 
25. Strategic Realignment for Green Shipbuilding Technologies 
The Committee observes the current SBFAP framework includes provisions for 
enhanced incentives—30% for vessels powered by green fuels (methanol, ammonia, 

24 
 
hydrogen) and 20% for those with electric or hybrid propulsion systems. However, 
without a dedicated allocation specifically earmarked for these sustainable 
technologies within the ₹138 crore budget for FY 2025-26, there remains a serious 
risk that traditional shipbuilding might continue to dominate fund utilization. As 
global shipping increasingly focuses on decarbonization, India risks falling behind 
in developing indigenous capabilities for green vessel construction. The implications 
extend beyond environmental considerations to encompass future market 
competitiveness, as regulatory pressures and market demands increasingly favor 
low-emission vessels. The shipping ministry's recognition of green vessels in its 
policy framework indicates awareness of this shift, but implementation requires 
more targeted financial commitment. 
25.1 The Committee further notes the upcoming SBFAP 2.0, with its proposed 
allocation of ₹18,000 crore and enhanced subsidies of 25% for specialized vessels 
and 30% for green vessels, represents a significant step forward. However, this 
policy requires immediate operationalisation with a clear timeline for 
implementation and specific allocations for different vessel categories. The Ministry 
should establish immediate ring-fencing of at least 40% of the current year's 
allocation (approximately ₹55 crore) exclusively for green vessel construction, 
creating a dedicated funding stream that ensures India builds capacity in this 
emerging technology area. 
25.2 Implementation of Milestone-Based Disbursement Mechanism 
The Committee notes that the current practice of projecting SBFAP funds based on 
tentative ship delivery schedules introduces significant inefficiencies in fund 
utilization. Shipbuilding projects, particularly those involving complex vessels, are 
vulnerable to production delays, supply chain disruptions, and technical challenges 
that can extend timelines considerably. This creates a mismatch between projected 
fund requirements and actual disbursement schedules, contributing to the observed 

25 
 
pattern of underutilization. The construction of specialized and green vessels, which 
involve more complex technologies and often require sourcing components from 
global supply chains, are particularly susceptible to such delays. This problem is 
likely to be exacerbated as Indian shipyards expand their capabilities to build more 
sophisticated vessels with lower emission profiles. 
The Committee feels implementing a milestone-based fund release mechanism 
would fundamentally transform how financial assistance is distributed. Under this 
approach, shipyards would receive predetermined percentages of the total 
assistance amount upon completion of defined construction milestones, such as steel 
cutting, keel laying, launching, and final delivery. This approach would provide 
shipyards with steady cash flow throughout the construction process, rather than 
concentrating financial support at project completion. 
 
25.3 The Committee therefore urges the Ministry develops a standardized set of 
verifiable milestones for different vessel categories, with appropriate weightage 
assigned to each stage. For instance, the steel cutting stage might trigger release of 
15% of the total assistance, keel laying another 25%, launching 30%, and final 
delivery the remaining 30%. This structured approach would maintain financial 
pressure on shipyards to progress systematically while providing them with the 
liquidity needed to finance ongoing construction. 
26. Comprehensive Recommendations for Policy Enhancement 
Based on the analysis of current SBFAP implementation and the proposed 
transition to SBFAP 2.0, the following recommendations are provided to enhance 
the effectiveness of India's shipbuilding assistance framework: 
26.1 Immediate Fund Reallocation and Optimization 

26 
 
The Ministry should conduct an urgent review of anticipated fund requirements for 
the remainder of FY 2025-26, identifying shipyards with confirmed orders that can 
demonstrate clear progress toward delivery milestones. Unutilized funds from the 
broader ₹4,000 crore allocation should be systematically redistributed to support 
these viable projects, ensuring maximum resource utilization before the current 
scheme expires in 2026. 
This reallocation should prioritize yards that have demonstrated consistent delivery 
performance and those engaged in constructing specialized or green vessels that 
align with future maritime needs. The experience gained from the previous 
shipbuilding financial assistance scheme, which has supported 135 delivered vessels, 
provides sufficient data to identify high-performing shipyards that can effectively 
utilize additional funding. 
26.2 Establishment of Green Shipbuilding Innovation Fund 
Beyond simply allocating a portion of existing funds to green vessel construction, the 
Ministry should establish a dedicated Green Shipbuilding Innovation Fund within 
the SBFAP framework. This fund would finance not only vessel construction but 
also research and development activities focused on adapting international green 
shipping technologies to Indian conditions. 
The proposed SBFAP 2.0, with its enhanced subsidies for green vessels, creates an 
opportunity to institutionalize this approach. The fund should support collaborative 
projects between shipyards, research institutions, and technology providers to 
develop standardized designs for green vessels suited to Indian operational contexts. 
This would create a pipeline of technically validated vessel designs that Indian 
shipyards could offer to domestic and international clients at competitive prices. 
26.3 Development of Integrated Monitoring Framework 

27 
 
To address the persistent challenges in fund disbursement and project tracking, the 
Ministry should implement an integrated digital monitoring framework that 
provides real-time visibility into project progress across all SBFAP-supported 
shipbuilding activities. This system should incorporate automated milestone 
verification through digital documentation, physical inspections, and timestamped 
visual evidence of construction progress. 
The framework should include a quarterly performance dashboard accessible to all 
stakeholders, including the Ministry, shipyards, and oversight bodies. This 
dashboard would track key performance indicators such as funds allocated, 
milestones achieved, disbursements made, and potential bottlenecks. Regular 
performance reviews based on this data would enable proactive intervention where 
projects show signs of delay. 
 
27. Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL)- The Directorate 
General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL) is the national agency on Marine Aids to 
Navigation. It is a self-sustaining organization and meets its expenditure through the 
revenue collected by it. The organization collects its revenue by levying marine aids to 
navigation dues on all the foreign going ships arriving at or departing from any port in 
India as per the provisions of the Marine Aids to Navigation Act, 2021. Accordingly, 
Budget allocation 2025-26 of₹ 565 Crore to DGLL under Capital Outlay and Revenue 
Expenditure has been made.

28. The Ministry further informed that the Budget Estimate for the Directorate 
General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL) for the FY 2025-26 has been planned to 
support both ongoing and new initiatives aimed at enhancing maritime safety and 
efficiency. The capital outlay of Rs. 90 Crores is earmarked for the execution of key 
projects, including the development of new lighthouses, implementation of remote 
monitoring systems for aids to navigation, establishment of a new Vessel Traffic Service 
(VTS) at Port Blair, and integration of Vessel Traffic Management Systems (VTMS) 
across major ports to ensure seamless maritime traffic management. On the other hand, 
the revenue outlay is structured to meet the expenditure requirements for the general 
administration of DGLL, as well as the operation and maintenance of essential maritime 
infrastructure. This includes aids to navigation, the VTS at Gulf of Kachchh (VTS-GOK), 
and lighthouse tender vessels. The allocation also supports the continuous improvement 
of navigational services, reinforcing India's commitment to safe navigation. 
29. The Committee has undertaken an assessment of the budgetary allocation for 
the Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL) for FY 2025-26, 
amounting to ₹ 565 crore. It notes that as the DGLL operates as a self-sustaining 
entity, funding its revenue expenditure (₹ 475 crore) through navigation dues 

29 
 
collected (₹ 475 crore) and meeting its capital expenditure (₹ 90 crore) from reserve 
funds, it also makes DGLL highly dependent on stable maritime traffic for revenue 
generation. Any decline in international shipping activity could adversely impact its 
financial sustainability and restrict future capital investments.The Committee 
recommends that DGLL adopts a more diversified financial approach to secure 
resilience and ensure uninterrupted modernisation of India’s marine navigation 
infrastructure. It may conduct a comprehensive risk assessment to evaluate 
potential fluctuations in revenue collection due to global shipping trends, economic 
downturns, or geopolitical disruptions; explore alternative revenue-generation 
mechanisms, including collaborations with private maritime stakeholders and 
leveraging DGLL’s expertise for international consultancy services, and should 
consider establishing a contingency reserve fund to mitigate financial instability 
during periods of reduced revenue collection. 
30. The Committee further notes that the ₹ 90 crore capital outlay is mainly 
allocated towards development of new lighthouses, implementation of remote 
monitoring systems for navigation aids, establishment of a new Vessel Traffic 
Service (VTS) at Port Blair, and Integration of Vessel Traffic Management Systems 
(VTMS) across major ports. However, there is limited clarity on project timelines, 
cost efficiency, and expected impact. The Committee therefore recommends the 
Ministry to provide detailed project implementation roadmaps with timelines, 
performance benchmarks, projected outcomes for capital projects, and see to a 
timely completion of VTMS integration. 
31. The Committee observes that ₹ 475 crore revenue outlay is directed towards 
general administration of DGLL, operation and maintenance of maritime 
navigation aids, management of the Vessel Traffic Service at Gulf of Kachchh (VTS-
GOK), and upkeep of lighthouse tender vessels. It acknowledges that though these 
allocations support day-to-day functionality, there is a need for increased 

30 
 
investment in technological upgrades and human resource capacity-building to 
bring the country’s marine navigation systems at par with international best 
practices. The Committee recommends that the Ministry allocate a greater 
proportion of revenue towards technological modernisation, particularly in 
automation of aids to navigation and regular training and capacity-building 
programmes for DGLL personnel to ensure efficient utilisation of advanced 
maritime technologies.

31 
 
KEY HIGHLIGHTS OF THE COMMITTEE'S 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS 
1.   Budgetary Allocation and Utilization 
The Committee observes that the Ministry's Budget Estimates (BE) and 
Revised Estimates (RE) for FY 2024-25 indicate underutilization of allocated 
funds, particularly in key projects such as Sagarmala and port modernization 
initiatives. It recommends that the Ministry ensure timely utilization of funds 
to avoid lapses and enhance project execution efficiency. 
2.  Focus on Sagarmala Projects 
The Committee emphasizes the importance of Sagarmala as a flagship 
program for port-led development and recommends prioritizing its 
implementation by addressing delays in project approvals and execution. 
Adequate funding and monitoring mechanisms should be ensured to achieve 
the envisaged objectives. 
3.  Strengthening Inland Waterways Infrastructure 
Recognizing the potential of inland waterways for reducing logistics costs, the 
Committee recommends expediting the development of National Waterways 
by ensuring sufficient budgetary support for infrastructure creation. 
4.  Enhancing Coastal Shipping 
To promote coastal shipping as an economical and environment-friendly 
mode of transport, the Committee recommends targeted incentives for 
stakeholders, including subsidies for vessel acquisition, and improved 
regulatory frameworks to attract private investment. 
5.  Green Ports Initiative 
The Committee notes the Ministry’s efforts toward sustainable port operations 
through renewable energy adoption and waste management systems. It 
recommends scaling up these initiatives with dedicated funding to achieve 
carbon neutrality targets across all major ports. 
6.  Skill Development in Maritime Sector 
The Committee highlights the need for skill development programs to cater to 
the growing demand for trained manpower in the maritime sector. It 

32 
 
recommends collaboration with educational institutions and industry 
stakeholders to design specialized courses and ensure adequate funding for 
training initiatives. 
7.  Digitalization of Port Operations 
Observing delays in implementing digital solutions at ports, the Committee 
recommends fast-tracking digitalization projects like port community systems 
and cargo tracking mechanisms to improve efficiency and transparency. 
8.  Promotion of Cruise Tourism 
Given the potential of cruise tourism to boost revenue and employment, the 
Committee recommends focused efforts on developing cruise terminals, 
marketing strategies, and partnerships with global operators while ensuring 
adequate budgetary allocations. 
9.  Monitoring Mechanisms for PPP Projects 
The Committee observes challenges in Public-Private Partnership (PPP) 
projects related to ports and waterways due to contractual disputes and delays. 
It recommends establishing robust monitoring frameworks to address these 
issues promptly and ensure accountability. 
10.  Research & Development in Maritime Technology 
To foster innovation in maritime technology, the Committee recommends 
increased funding for R&D activities focused on automation, alternative fuels, 
and vessel design improvements while encouraging private sector 
participation. 
11. Periodic Review of Policies 
The Committee advises periodic reviews of policies governing ports, 
shipping, and waterways to ensure alignment with global standards and 
emerging trends in maritime trade.

10.  The meeting resumed at 02:25 P.M. to hear the views of the Secretary, Ministry of Ports,

Chairman opened the meeting by welcoming the Members of the Committee, officers and

11. Secretary, Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways started the presentation by 
providing a detailed account of the Ministry’s budgetary allocations, financial performan ce, and 
strategic objectives. The Ministry informed that the budget for 2025 -26 stands at Rs. 3,470 
crores, supplemented by Rs. 7,123 crores from internal resources. The Ministry’s financial 
strategy prioritises self -reliance through Internal Extra Budgeta ry Resources, reducing 
dependence on Gross Budgetary Support while key priorities include port modernisation, 
maritime digitalisation, inland waterways expansion, and green energy adoption. It was alsp 
informd that the country has 229 ports, of which 79 ha ndle cargo, supported by legislative 
reforms such as the Major Port Authorities Act and Harit Sagar Guidelines for sustainable 
operations. Other innitives include the India -Middle East -Europe Economic Corridor and 
Chabahar Port expansion aim to boost trade  connectivity. Beside, the Ministry is promoting 
hydrogen fuel cell vessels, electric ferries, and solar -powered ships, while the Shipbuilding 
Financial Assistance Policy 2.0 is under revision to give a boost to domestic shipbuilding. For 
inland waterways,  the Minstry informed that the cargo movement has increased on National 
Waterway 1 under the Jal Marg Vikas Project, and initiatives such as the Harit Nauka Scheme 
are accelerating the shift to green fuels. It is also working towards expanding the number o f 
operational National Waterways from 26 to 50 by 2030. The Coastal Shipping Bill and Indian 
Ports Bill are key legislative initiatives under review to streamline maritime governance and 
encourage private sector participation. 
12.  The Ministry apprised th e Committee about the growing role of digitization in maritime 
logistics, noting that the Sagarmala Maritime Digital Centre of Excellence is being established to 
drive automation, blockchain integration, and real-time monitoring of cargo movement. Also, the 
Integrated Vessel Traffic Management System is being implemented to enhance real -time 
coordination and navigation safety across major ports and inland waterways.

13.   The Committee raised the following issues during the course of the Meeting:  
 Members sought clarification on the progress of pending projects under the Sagarmala 
Programme, particularly those that have seen repeated delays despite funding allocations;  
 Members sought specific timelines for the conversion of lighthouses into tourism  sites, 
calling into question the progress of infrastructure upgrades, visitor amenities, and safety 
measures; 
 Members sought details on the adoption rate of electric and hybrid vessels  and also 
sought to know whether  regulatory and financial frameworks ha d been finalised to 
support a transition to green shipping; 
 Members expressed dissatisfaction  with the limited growth in cargo movement on 
National Waterways  and sought explanations for why  freight traffic remain ed 
significantly below target projections despite substantial investments; 
 Members raised concerns over the ecological impact of dredging operations and the steps 
taken to implement green port initiatives and reduce carbon emissions; 
 Members enquired about t he preparedness of Indian ports and shipping infrastructure to 
meet international maritime safety standards , particularly in oil spill response 
mechanisms, vessel monitoring, and compliance with global shipping regulations; 
 Members questioned the effective ness of public-private partnership (PPP) initiatives and 
sought to determine whether such initiatives were yielding the expected results, Members 
also expressed  concerns that certain port projects under the National Monetization 
Pipeline (NMP) had failed to attract sufficient private sector interest; and 
 Concerns were raised regarding insufficient last -mile connectivity for coastal shipping 
operations and the slower-than-expected growth of cruise tourism was also questioned. 
 
14.  To address these concerns effectively, the Committee made the following actionable 
recommendations: 
 Streamlining the project implementation process by way of setting up a monitoring 
mechanism so as to ensure timely completion of ongoing works, and strengthening inter -
agency coordination to eliminate procedural delays; 
 Conducting a comprehensive assessment of operational bottlenecks in National 
Waterways and corrective measures to enhance freight movement efficiency; 
 Incorporation of stringent environmental safeguards in all port expansion and inland 
waterway development projects; 
 Prioritising up -gradation of vessel tracking, oil spill response systems, and maritime 
security protocols; 
 Evaluation of the challenges in attracting private investment under the National 
Monetisation Pipeline and introduc tion of  policy measures that will enhance investor 
confidence and participation in port infrastructure projects; and 
 Improving last-mile connectivity for coastal shipping operations, enhance passenger 
terminal infrastructure, and expan d policy support for cruise tourism to attract greater 
private investment in the sector.

INTRODUCTION 
A well-structured road network is crucial for economic growth and social 
connectivity. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) plays a 
pivotal role in developing and maintaining this infrastructure. 
2. The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways (MoRTH) is responsible for 
the construction and maintenance of National Highways, the administration of key 
legislative frameworks, including the National Highways Act, 1956, and the Motor 
Vehicles Act, 1988, as well as the formulation of broad policies on road transport, 
automotive standards, and cross-border vehicular movement. The Ministry plays a 
pivotal role in ensuring an efficient, sustainable, and well-regulated road transport 
system, underpinning national economic growth and connectivity. 
3. Associated Offices under the Ministry are: 
⮚ National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) 
⮚ National Highways & Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. 
(NHIDCL) 
⮚ Indian Roads Congress (IRC) 
 
GOALS AND OBJECTIVES 
4. The Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) is a performance 
measurement tool to assess the effectiveness of various schemes and projects. 
Outputs refer to the immediate, measurable deliverables of a project, such as the 
number of highways constructed or the number of safety audits conducted. 
Outcomes, on the other hand, represent the long-term impact and effectiveness of 
these outputs, such as improved mobility, reduced accidents, or increased private 
sector investment. The OOMF ensures transparency, accountability, and efficiency 
 

2 
 
in infrastructure development and policy implementation. The OOMF of the 
Ministry sets out the following objectives- 
⮚ National Highway Development (allocated budget ₹2,76,475. 09 crore)-  
To achieve this objective, with an allocated budget of ₹2,76,475.09 crore, it 
sets forth a target of 10,000 km of new highways to be constructed in the 
financial year 2025-26 including the development of 1,100 km of highways in 
the North-Eastern States and 750 km in tribal areas. Also, a high-speed corridor 
network covering 5,800 km is also planned to be operationalised. 
⮚ Private Investment and Public-Private Partnerships (PPP)-  
The Ministry aims to secure ₹35,000 crore in private investment for highway 
projects during the FY 2025-26 year. Furthermore, 30% of the total awarded 
highway projects is being targeted to be executed under the Public-Private 
Partnership (PPP) model. 
⮚ Asset Monetisation and Resource Mobilisation- 
The Government has set a target of ₹30,000 crore to be raised from the 
monetisation of developed highway stretches, utilising existing infrastructure to 
generate revenue. 10% of total budgetary resources are expected to be sourced 
from asset monetisation efforts. 
⮚ Road Safety and Accident Reduction- 
The framework outlines the removal of 1,000 identified black spots on 
national highways. Furthermore, 40,000 km of highways will undergo 
comprehensive road safety audits. 
⮚ Vehicle Scrapping, Inspection, and Certification (allocated budget of 
₹595.02 crore)- 
The plan includes the establishment of 130 Automated Testing Stations 
(ATSs) to improve vehicle inspection standards across various States and Union 
Territories. Additionally, 15 Registered Vehicle Scrapping Facilities (RVSFs) 
are planned to be developed to phase out obsolete and polluting vehicles, 
promoting cleaner and more fuel-efficient transport systems. 

3 
 
⮚ Training and Capacity Building- 
The Government plans to set up four Institutes of Driving Training and 
Research (IDTRs) and seven Regional Driving Training Centres (RDTCs). 
Moreover, 25 small driving training centres will be established to improve 
access to professional driver training. Also, five training programmes for road 
safety auditors will be conducted to develop expertise in accident prevention 
and highway safety measures. 
⮚ Emergency Care and Cashless Treatment for Road Accident Victims-  
Under this objective, it aims for the implementation of cashless treatment 
facilities for road accident victims across all 36 States and Union Territories.
