Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee observes that the Capital Outlay for BE 2025-26 has a distinct 
imbalance in the allocation of funds across key aviation bodies. The Directorate General of 
Civil Aviation (DGCA), entrusted with regulatory oversight, commands the largest share of 
₹30 crore—nearly half of the total budget. While its role in ensuring compliance with 
aviation standards is indisputable, the justification for such a significant allocation must be 
carefully examined to ensure efficiency and accountability. The discrepancy in funding 
raises important questions about the prioritization of regulatory compliance over security 
infrastructure and accident investigation capabilities.  
(Para 8)    
Reply of the Ministry     
1.1 With the growth in aviation sector, role of Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) 
is also growing. DGCA has digitized its operations (like eGCA portal and recent launch of 
electronic licenses for pilots), which requires constant upgradation and investments. These 
changes are designed to simplify processes, improve accessibility, and create a more effective 
system for managing aviation regulations.  
The Budgetary allocation is made on the basis of requirement of each organization and within 
the total allocated budget ceiling.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. In contrast, the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) and the Aircraft Accident 
Investigation Bureau (AAIB) receive ₹15 crore and ₹20 crore, respectively. While 
regulatory compliance remains essential, the rapid expansion of aviation infrastructure - 
with airports increasing from 74 in 2014 to 147 in 2022 and a target of 220 by 2024-25 - 
necessitates proportional growth in security capabilities and accident investigation 
resources. In view of the growing complexity of aviation security threats and the critical 

18 
 
nature of accident investigations, the Committee finds these allocations relatively modest. 
The UDAN scheme, which has enabled 1.5 crore passengers to access air travel and is 
planned to connect 120 new destinations in the coming decade, has seen its allocation 
reduced by 32 percent to Rs 540 crore in the current budget. This reduction, coupled with 
the announcement to expand the scheme significantly, creates potential resource 
constraints that could affect implementation. The government has committed to expanding 
the UDAN scheme to 120 new destinations with a target of carrying 4 crore passengers in 
the next decade. This ambitious goal, coupled with the establishment of new airports and 
helipads in hilly, aspirational, and North Eastern regions, will require enhanced security 
protocols and accident response mechanisms that appear underfunded in the current 
allocation structure. In its view, it is imperative to assess whether these funds are adequate 
to strengthen security infrastructure and enhance investigative capabilities. As aviation 
expands to tier II and III cities under the modified UDAN scheme, security infrastructure 
and capabilities must be extended proportionally.  
(Para 9)   
Reply of the Ministry     
2.1 The Aircraft Accident Investigation Bureau (AAIB) is an attached office under Ministry 
of Civil Aviation for investigating aircraft accidents in India. It is responsible for independently 
investigating aircraft accidents in line with International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) 
guidelines. The capital allocation to AAIB is utilized for procurement of assets and lab 
equipment to meet the operational requirements of the office.  
 "The Bureau of Civil Aviation Security (BCAS) is the regulatory body for civil aviation 
security in India. It is responsible for aviation security regulation in line with International Civil 
Aviation Organization (ICAO) guidelines. The capital allocation to BCAS is primarily meant for 
procurement of assets for day-to-day operational requirements and construction of office 
premises. The provision of security infrastructure at Airports is taken care of by the Airports 
Operator concerned."

aviation regulatory bodies, linking allocations to specific performance indicators and 
outcomes. This approach would enhance accountability and ensure that funds are utilized 
efficiently to address the most pressing challenges within each domain. Regular 
performance audits should be conducted to assess the effectiveness of allocated resources 
and inform future budgeting decisions.

9. The Committee has taken cognizant of reports concerning premature deterioration 
of seating materials, ergonomic failures, and technological obsolescence plaguing multiple 
airlines. This urgent disparity demands ministerial intervention through a standardized 
regulatory framework to ensure Indian aviation maintains competitive parity with global 
leaders. The Committee proposes establishing the Aviation Interior Quality Commission 
with immediate effect to implement rigorous testing protocols, sustainability guidelines, 
and accessibility standards across all domestic carriers. The situation is particularly 
concerning given the considerable fleet expansion underway. With Air India alone having 
ordered 570 new aircraft—including the recent addition of 100 more Airbus aircraft 
comprising 10 wide-body A350s and 90 narrow-body A320 family planes—the potential 
scale of interior quality issues demands immediate ministerial attention. Sustainability 
must become a central consideration in interior design and material selection. The 
Commission would establish progressive environmental standards for cabin interiors, 
including recyclability requirements, VOC emissions limits, and lifecycle assessment 
obligations. These standards would align with India’s broader environmental commitments 
while positioning Indian aviation as a leader in sustainable cabin design.  
(Para 13.1)   

29 
 
Reply of the Ministry     
9.1 Regulatory Framework for Aircraft Seating and Cabin Fabrics in India  
  
In India, all aircraft seats and cabin interior fabrics (including carpets, rugs, and other textile 
materials) used by airlines must comply with pre-defined standards. These include:  
1. Flammability Standards  
 All cabin materials must meet fire resistance requirements in line with TSO (Technical 
Standard Order) criteria.  
 Tests include vertical Bunsen burner, oil burner, and heat release/smoke density 
evaluations to ensure safety during fire incidents.  
 
2. Toxicity & Smoke Emission  
 Materials are tested for:  
 Smoke density  
 Toxic gas emissions (e.g., carbon monoxide, hydrogen cyanide)  
 Compliance with internationally recognized protocols like Boeing BSS 7239 or Airbus 
ABD 0031 is standard practice.  
 
3. Durability & Wear Resistance  
 Materials must pass: 
 Abrasion resistance tests (e.g., Martindale)  
 Colorfastness to light and rubbing  
 Tear strength  
 These ensure longevity, passenger comfort, and aesthetic integrity.  

30 
 
9.2 Role of TSO/ITSO and DGCA Oversight  
 These standards are enforced through the Technical Standard Order (TSO), which defines 
minimum performance requirements for specific materials, parts, processes, and 
appliances used in civil aircraft.  
 The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA), India, accepts these standards as part 
of the Type Certification process for aircraft operating in Indian airspace.  
 DGCA also approves Indian Technical Standard Orders (ITSOs) for seats designed and 
manufactured domestically.  
 
9.3 Operational Compliance and Maintenance  
 Aircraft seats and interior elements are maintained to minimum airworthiness standards 
throughout their operational life.  
 Seat manufacturers may issue mid-life Service Bulletins (SBs) to improve or rectify 
existing components.  
 Airline personnel, along with DGCA inspectors, conduct regular inspections to ensure 
ongoing compliance. Any component found below standard is declared unserviceable.  
 
9.4 Interior Design and Maintenance Protocols  
 
 Aircraft interiors are designed by manufacturers following stringent requirements for:  
 Safety 
 Security  
 Ergonomics  
 Emergency responsiveness 
 
 Airlines must maintain interiors in accordance with the manufacturer's certified design 
and standards accepted by DGCA.  
 Any cabin defects encountered during operations are recorded in the Cabin Defect 
Logbook (CDL) by the cabin crew.  
 These defects are addressed by qualified engineers post-flight.  
 Seats or cabin components found non-compliant are:  
 Clearly marked as unserviceable  
 Not assigned to passengers  
 Note: DGCA may constitute a committee comprising of officers from different 
Directorates for reviewing and revising the Aviation Interior Quality system and standardisation 
of cabin interiors, including ergonomic, recyclability requirements, VOC emissions limits, and 
lifecycle assessment obligation.

AIR INDIA-RELATED EXPENDITURE 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee, while examining the Demand for Grants of the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
for 2025-26, recommends the establishment of a stringent airfare pricing regulation mechanism 
under the framework of an AI-powered predictive monitoring system, tentatively named 
"AirPrice Guardian." This system should aim to address consumer grievances related to 
unpredictable and exorbitant airfare surges, particularly during peak travel periods and 
emergencies, while ensuring transparency and fairness in pricing practices. The Committee 
notes that the current regulatory framework under DGCA lacks the capacity to proactively 
monitor and regulate airfare trends, necessitating a transformative approach leveraging 
advanced technology. 
(Para 12.1)   
Reply of the Ministry     
1.1 Airfares are not subject to government regulation, and airlines have the flexibility to 
determine their fares based on operational needs, adhering to Rule 135 of the Aircraft Rules, 
1937.  
Globally, most countries have deregulated their aviation sector, i.e., removing government 
imposed entry and price restrictions on airlines. Deregulation has led to increased competition 
between airline carriers, leading to decrease in airfare. As a result of deregulation, entry into the 
airlines industry for a potential new airline has become easier, resulting in many new airlines 
entering the market, thus increasing competition. The direct impact of deregulation is that a 
passenger in a lower income group can afford to travel by air.  
Given the complex dynamics of the Indian aviation industry, Government is playing the role of a 
facilitator by way of creating enabling environment to support the growth of the sector. 
However, while the government generally refrains from regulating airfares to maintain market 
competitiveness, however, it remains vigilant, and the Government intervenes to shift capacity 
from one sector to another to prevent exorbitant pricing to ensure passenger comfort and welfare. 
Further, Government also encourages Airlines to induct new aircrafts and increase their fleet so 
as to improve connectivity and as a result reduction in airfares. Airlines have placed orders of 
more than 1500 aircrafts which will further improve connectivity and reduce airfare. 

49 
 
With the enhancement of capacity by induction of more aircraft fleet, modernization of airports 
and development of new airports, domestic passenger traffic has increased to 153,674,310 in 
2023-24 as compared to 136,028,656 in the year 2022-23. In the current financial year 2024-25, 
the domestic passenger traffic has surpassed the volume during the corresponding period in the 
year 2023-24, reflecting an impressive growth rate. 
Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has setup a Tariff Monitoring Unit (TMU) that 
monitors airfares on select domestic sectors on random basis by using airlines' websites on 
monthly basis to ensure that the airlines do not charge airfares outside the range declared by 
them. These selected sectors represent almost 20% of the passenger traffic in 2024. 
The analysis of TMU reveals that the airfare per kilometre offered by Indian carrier is low in 
India when compared globally. Furthermore, TMU is being strengthened and concerted efforts 
are being made towards the digitisation of TMU. 
1.2  Regular consultations are held with airlines who are also being sensitized to exercise 
moderation in pricing and to keep passengers' interest in mind. The airlines have committed to 
ensure that airfares do not surge during events such as natural disasters, calamities, Mahakhumb, 
National emergent situations, etc. 
To address concerns over high airfares to Prayagraj during Maha Kumbh 2025, the Ministry held 
a meeting with airline operators on 29.01.2025. Key issues discussed included air connectivity 
and fare rationalization. Following the Ministry’s intervention, airlines increased weekly flights 
from 51 to 533, connecting Prayagraj with 18 cities and accommodating around 70,000 
passengers weekly. As a result, airfares dropped by nearly 50%. 
In the wake of the tragic terror attack in Kashmir, Ministry moved swiftly to ensure the safety 
and well-being of affected tourists and victims. As part of immediate relief measures, four 
special flights from Srinagar – two to Delhi and two to Mumbai, were arranged, with additional 
flights kept on standby to cater to further evacuation needs. 
DGCA issued an advisory to increase the number of flights in response to heightened demand 
and also to ensure uninterrupted connectivity from Srinagar to various destinations across India, 
facilitating evacuation of stranded tourists. Meetings with all airline operators was held and a 
strong advisory was issued against surge pricing. Airlines were directed to maintain regular fare 
levels, ensuring that no passenger is burdened during this sensitive time. 
Additionally, all airlines were asked to extend full cooperation for the transportation of deceased 
individuals to their respective home states, working in sync with state governments and local 
authorities. 
The airlines were sensitised to consider waiving cancellation and rescheduling fees and provide 
all necessary assistance to tourists facing unexpected circumstances and challenges during this 
difficult time. 

50 
 
DGCA also issued an advisory to airlines on passenger handling measures in view of Airspace 
Restrictions Resulting in Extended Flight Durations and Technical Stops. 
1.3  To ensure prompt and effective resolution of grievances from passengers and other 
stakeholders, Ministry of Civil Aviation (MoCA) launched Air Sewa portal on November, 2016. 
It provides a common platform for air travellers to submit grievances related to air travel and 
seek information about flight status. The platform is accessible through both a web portal and a 
mobile app available on Android and iOS platform. 
Airsewa aims to offer a convenient and hassle-free air travel experience by addressing traveller 
concerns and providing real time updates on flight status, schedules and airport information. 
The system offers interactive grievance management, enabling two-way communication between 
stakeholders and complainants. It includes enhanced flight information and real-time tracking 
capabilities. A mobile app is available for nodal officers, allowing them to log in and receive 
notifications. The system can integrate with airport AODB systems to fetch live flight status 
data. Additionally, grievances can be escalated if resolutions are unsatisfactory or delayed, and 
they can be transferred to other relevant nodal authorities when needed. 
 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
1.4 The Committee appreciates the acknowledgement of the need to strengthen the 
TMU and efforts towards its digitization. However, the proposed "AirPrice Guardian" 
system goes beyond mere monitoring. It envisions an AI-powered predictive mechanism. 
To truly address consumer grievances, the Committee recommends that the DGCA, 
through "AirPrice Guardian," be empowered with quasi-judicial authority. This authority 
should enable the DGCA to: 
 Impose temporary price caps or penalties on airlines found to be engaging in 
exploitative pricing practices, especially when the AI system flags significant 
deviations from predicted fair price bands. 
 Establish dynamic fare bands for each route, updated periodically (e.g., quarterly) 
through the predictive models of "AirPrice Guardian." These fare bands would 
serve as a transparent benchmark for consumers and a clear guideline for airlines, 
allowing for market-driven pricing within reasonable parameters. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The proposed “AirPrice Guardian” system will utilize machine learning algorithms and 
predictive analytics to forecast airfare trends based on historical data, demand patterns, fuel 

51 
 
costs, seasonal fluctuations, and external factors such as festivals or emergencies. By 
establishing dynamic fare bands for each route, updated quarterly through predictive models, 
this system will empower regulators to monitor deviations in real-time and take 10 preemptive 
action against excessive pricing. The Committee recommends that DGCA be empowered with 
quasi-judicial authority to impose temporary price caps or penalties on airlines engaging in 
exploitative practices. Additionally, a Pricing Transparency Index should be developed to rate 
airlines on their adherence to fair pricing norms, with this information made publicly available 
through a consumer-facing portal. 
(Para 12.2)

Recommendation/Observation  
4. The budget for aero sports and allied activities was initially planned for Rs. 1 crore in 
the year 2022-23 but no expenditure was made. The following year 2023-24 the budget was 
reduced to Rs. 0.10 crore. Subsequent for the year 2024-25 has been kept to Rs. 0.10 crore. The 
committee takes note of the fact that the Government of India has formed the National Aero 
Sports Guidelines (NASG) to develop a robust aero sports ecosystem, which has a global 
potential to partner in $30 billion industry across the world. The government has consciously 
taken a call to create a strong ecosystem for aero sports, which includes Ballooning, 
Aeromodelling, Amateur Built and Experimental Aircraft, Drones, Gliding, Microlights, Para 
Motors, Parachuting and Rotorcraft. The Aero Club of India has been designated as the 
National Airsports Control (NAC) by the government for promotion of aero sports across all the 
states. In order to implement the policy in letter and spirit, ACI requires a hand holding through 
a budgetary support to create an ecosystem for aero sports. The Committee recommends that 
budgetary allocation as per the requirement of the Aero Club of India may be enhanced as to 
support Flying Training Organizations and aero sports across the country. The committee also 
notes that the Aero Club of India has been one of the oldest autonomous organization of the 
Ministry of Civil Aviation working to support development for flying training and has 
successfully established an ecosystem of flying training for last 50 years. The Aero Club of India 
headquartered at the Safdarjung Airport area, Sri Aurobindo Marg, New Delhi and it was 
managed and run as an autonomous organization to conduct aero sports and flying training by 
assets created by the budgetary funding of the Government which intern created an ecosystem 
for pilots training in India. The Aero Club of India was dispossessed of its office building some 
years ago, which requires restorations as the office building constructed through its own 
resources which now has been turned into a Directorate of Licensing for Air Traffic Services 
(ATS) under Airports Authority of India (AAI). The Committee recommends that the Ministry 

56 
 
prioritize spending on aero sports and allocate budgetary support, including restoring the 
administrative infrastructure of the Aero Club of India (ACI), to facilitate the fulfillment of the 
National Aero Sports Guidelines (NASG) issued by the Government. The Committee further 
recommends enhancing budgetary support for the ACI will strengthen India’s aero sports sector 
and Flight Training Organizations (FTOs), ensuring the sustainable growth of the sector.  
(Para 40)

4.1 In this context, as per Para 10(b) of NASG “The Central/State government /ASFI may

token amount to accommodate any initiation of providing budgetary support in future. It may be 
noted that the Ministry has sanctioned a grant of ₹35 lakh to the Aero Club of India (ACI) for 
organizing the FAI-CIA Plenary Meeting from 12-15 March 2025 in New Delhi in FY 2024-25.”  
 
Further Recommendations/Observations 
4.2 The Committee strongly urges the Ministry to reassess the budgetary allocation for

* Objective identification of abnormal pricing: Moving beyond subjective "sensitization" 
to airlines, the system will provide data-driven evidence of price gouging by flagging 
deviations from dynamically calculated "fair price bands." This objective evidence is 
crucial for any regulatory action.  
* Targeted and timely intervention: Instead of broad advisories, the system will pinpoint 
specific routes, dates, and airlines exhibiting problematic pricing, allowing for precise and 
timely intervention, such as capacity re-allocation or direct engagement with specific 
carriers, as already demonstrated during the Maha Kumbh and Kashmir incident.  
 
* Long-term market stability: By consistently identifying and addressing extreme price 
volatility, the system can contribute to greater transparency and predictability in the 
market, benefiting both consumers and responsible airlines. 
The Committee stresses that the development of "AirPrice Guardian" should be 
prioritized, with a clear roadmap for its technological development, data integration with 
airlines, and a robust framework for its operationalization within the DGCA. 

60 
 
(Para 2.4) 
  
The Committee appreciates that RCS-UDAN is dynamic, but the "modular approval 
approach" aims to provide structural flexibility beyond just recalibration. The Committee 
recommends: 
 Principal Scheme Approval with Component Flexibility: The core framework and 
long-term vision of the UDAN scheme should receive a principal, overarching 
approval. However, specific elements, such as the inclusion of new 
unserved/underserved destinations, changes in VGF parameters for specific regions, 
or modifications to route types (e.g., seaplanes, heliports), should be adaptable 
through a streamlined modification protocol. This would prevent the need for re-
approving the entire scheme for minor adjustments, which can indeed lead to 
perceived "paralysis" at the operational level. 
 Pre-approved Frameworks for Hilly, Aspirational, and North-Eastern Regions: 
Given the specific focus on these regions, the Ministry should develop pre-approved 
frameworks or templates for route identification, infrastructure development, and 
VGF allocation for these areas. This would expedite approvals for proposals falling 
within these defined parameters. 
(Para 3.2) 
 
The Committee strongly urges the Ministry to reassess the budgetary allocation for aero 
sports and significantly enhance it, moving beyond a "token amount" to a sum 
commensurate with the aspirations of the National Aero Sports Guidelines and the 
potential of India's aero sports sector. This enhanced budget should not be merely for 
event-specific grants but for: 
 Long-term ecosystem development: Funding for the establishment and upgrading of 
aero sports infrastructure, procurement of modern equipment for various aero 
sports disciplines (Ballooning, Aeromodelling, Gliding, Microlights, etc.), and the 
development of dedicated aero sports facilities across states. 
 Support for Flying Training Organizations (FTOs): Financial assistance to FTOs 
affiliated with ACI to upgrade their fleets, enhance training infrastructure, and 
provide affordable training, thereby increasing the pool of skilled pilots and aero 
sports enthusiasts. 

61 
 
 Capacity building and skill development: Funds for training programs, workshops, 
and certification courses for instructors, ground staff, and participants, ensuring 
adherence to international safety standards. 
 Promotional activities and outreach: Budget for national and regional aero sports 
events, awareness campaigns, and initiatives to encourage greater participation, 
especially among youth and in remote areas. 
(Para 4.2)

the recommendations/observations as contained in its 376th Report on ‘Demands for Grants 
(2025-26) of the Ministry of Culture which was presented to both the Houses of Parliament.

categorized as follows:-

2 
 
CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee further notes that although overall budget utilisation remains high, 
expenditure patterns across various cultural schemes have been inconsistent. Programmes 
such as museum development, cultural mapping, and global cultural engagement have 
experienced fluctuating levels of fund disbursement, with some initiatives facing under-
utilisation in certain years and excessive allocations in other. The Committee strongly 
recommends the development of a Cultural Calendar-Based Budgeting system that: 
a. Maintains a comprehensive five-year cultural events calendar that identifies 
recurring festivals, commemorations, and international engagements with historical 
budget requirements. 
b. Integrates cyclical cultural events (such as Kumbh Mela, which occurs every 12 
years) into long-term financial planning through a dedicated cultural events fund. 
c. Implements quarterly budget review mechanisms to assess expenditure against 
planned activities and make necessary adjustments before the Revised Estimates 
stage. 
d. Develops an AI-assisted forecasting model that analyzes historical expenditure 
patterns and predicts resource requirements for upcoming cultural activities based 
on past event costs, inflation factors, and attendance projections. 
This systematic approach would ensure that cultural events of national importance receive 
appropriate financial provisions at the Budget Estimate stage rather than relying on mid-
year adjustments 
 (Para 11)   
 
 
Reply of the Ministry   
1.1 For comprehensive Budget planning, a calendar of events for the entire Ministry is being 
prepared. Expenditure on special events which have not been envisaged at the time of 
submission stage of BE/RE is taken care of by seeking extra budgetary support. Review of 

3 
 
budget/expenditure is a continuous exercise in the Ministry. Efforts shall be made to link budget 
with cultural calendar and integration of cyclical events in long term planning.  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee recommends addressing delays in ongoing Museum Projects like the 
Dholavira Museum and the Leh Museum as they have faced significant delays due to issues 
such as land allotments, extending timelines by 8– 12 months. The committee further 
recommends prioritizing the resolution of these delays, ensuring that land allotments are 
expedited and necessary clearances are streamlined. A dedicated task force or coordination 
mechanism should be set up to oversee and speed up the approval processes for critical 
infrastructure projects. 
 (Para 15)   
 
Reply of the Ministry   
 
2.1 Dholavira Museum: The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has made significant 
advanced efforts towards the development of the Dholavira Archaeological Museum. In this 
regard 10.5 Acres of land has been acquired by ASI and the same has been secured through a 
boundary wall. ASI is exploring the engagement of implementation partner for execution. 
Further detailed site visits have been conducted by subject/domain experts to assess and develop 
the mechanism for construction and development of the site museum. These measures are aimed 
at expediting the project while maintaining the highest standards of quality and coordination. 
Leh Museum: At present, there is no proposal for the development of a specific museum facility 
at Leh. However, to ensure meaningful engagement with the region’s rich history and culture, an 
interpretative display along with an audio-visual room with seating capacity of approximately 
30-40 pax has already been established at the historic Leh Palace as a museum showcasing the 
history and cultural heritage of the Ladakh and the Indus river valley. 
To showcase India’s archaeological excellence to the world, the Ministry is proposing to launch 
a new scheme to develop archaeological sites—including Dholavira, and Leh Palace —into 
vibrant, experiential cultural destinations. This scheme proposes to boost cultural tourism, 
generate local livelihoods, and reaffirm India’s global leadership in heritage management. 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee recommends comprehensive digitalization of heritage assets to 
enhance both preservation efforts and public engagement: 

4 
 
a. Develop a phased implementation of "Digital Twin" technology for all World 
Heritage Sites and at least 100 nationally significant monuments by 2028. This 
would involve creating precise digital replicas to monitor structural changes, 
simulate conservation interventions, and enhance visitor experience through 
augmented reality applications. 
b. Establish a centralized Heritage Monitoring System using remote sensing and IoT 
devices to provide real-time data on environmental conditions, structural stability, 
and visitor impact at critical monuments. This would enable predictive maintenance 
and early intervention, potentially reducing long-term conservation costs by 30-
35%. 
c. Launch a Metaverse Heritage Initiative that creates immersive digital experiences of 
inaccessible or vulnerable monument areas, allowing for virtual tourism while 
reducing physical impact on fragile structures. This initiative should prioritize 
monuments facing access restrictions due to conservation concerns. 
d. Implement block chain technology for monument documentation and conservation 
history, creating an immutable record of interventions and condition assessments 
that ensures accountability and preservation of institutional knowledge across 
administrative transitions. 
 (Para 16)   
 
Reply of the Ministry   
 The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is currently engaged in various IT-related 
initiatives. In addition, we are using the latest digital technologies to enhance the digital 
experience at various monuments and museums. Internally, ASI has introduced several digital 
advancements to support the above-mentioned initiatives and archaeological research. 
(i)   Website Revamp: ASI revamped its official website in February 2024. 
(ii)  Monuments and Sites: ASI has launched new applications and websites such as the Adopt 
a Heritage portal and the Heritage Atlas application. These initiatives aim to provide visitors 
with up-to-date information about centrally protected monuments and enable corporate bodies to 
contribute towards development of these monuments under the Adopt a Heritage program. ASI 
has also created 360-degree views and drone footage for various monuments. 
(iii)  Museums: Augmented Reality (AR) and Virtual Reality (VR) experiences have been 
developed at various museums to enhance visitor engagement. The virtual experiential museum 
(VEM) was inaugurated at Sarnath in 2019. Digital upgradation of the Hampi museum and the 
DPR for the Nalanda has also been prepared. 

5 
 
(iv)  Antiquities: Under the National Mission for Monuments and Antiquities, 17.2 lakh approx. 
antiquities and 11 thousand “Biodiversity Heritage Sites” (BHS) (both protected and 
unprotected, located across the country) have been digitised. The website is proposed to be 
enhanced with new features soon. 
(v) Archives & Archival Data Digitisation: Around 22,000 glass negatives digitised and 
30,000 photographs have been digitised and are being prepared for public access, so that revenue 
can be generated from this archive. The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) is actively 
engaged in the digitisation of archival materials, which have been systematically sorted, 
identified, arranged, and documented. These materials include photographs, glass negatives, 
drawings, plans, elevation maps, and old files from various ASI circles, with the aim of 
preserving and enhancing access to historical records. 
(vi)  Library: The Central Archaeological Library in the ASI is one of the largest libraries on the 
subject in the country. Currently, a part of its collection has been digitised and is in the process 
of going online through the library management system KOHA. 
(vii) Permission Portal: ASI is developing an online portal to facilitate easy access for citizens 
seeking permissions related to filming, videography, cultural events, and archival materials. This 
portal will be live soon. Internally, ASI is also revamping its e-Governance portal for better 
usability. 
(viii)  Digital technology is evolving rapidly, and ASI is committed to adopt the latest 
technologies across its activities. We remain dedicated to support all future-oriented IT 
developments in the field of heritage conservation. 
  
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. Institutional Reforms for Museum Project Implementation: The Committee 
recommends fundamental reforms to the project implementation mechanisms: 
a. Implement a modular development approach for museum projects, enabling phased 
completion and partial operationalization while resolving issues with remaining 
components. This would allow for incremental public access and revenue generation 
rather than complete closure during extended development periods. 
b. Develop a standardized pre-implementation framework for museum projects that 
mandates resolution of land acquisition, environmental clearances, and conceptual 
design before budget allocation and project announcement, minimizing mid-project 
disruptions. 

6 
 
c. Create specialized project management units for each major museum initiative with 
representation from relevant stakeholders, including state governments, ASI, 
content specialists, and community representatives to ensure coordinated action and 
accountability. 
 (Para 16.1)   
Reply of the Ministry:-  
4.1 The Committee’s recommendations on institutional reforms for museum project 
implementation broadly align with the evolving practices being adopted by major national 
museums. The Ministry has already initiated measures that reflect these principles, as evidenced 
by ongoing modernization and governance reforms in Museums under the Ministry of Culture. 
 a) Modular and Phased Development of Museum Projects 
 The Indian Museum, Kolkata, has undertaken a major modernization initiative involving the 
phased re-curation of nine galleries, with four key galleries targeted for completion initially.  An 
Implementation Committee has been constituted to facilitate the effective planning and seamless 
execution of the ongoing re-curation project at the Indian Museum.  
 The National Council of Science Museum (NCSM) also employs modular development 
strategies to facilitate phased implementation in Science Cities/Centres projects. 
 b) Strengthening Pre-Implementation Planning Frameworks 
The Committee’s recommendation for a standardized pre-implementation framework is 
acknowledged as critical for minimizing mid-project disruptions. The Indian Museum 
modernization project reflects this approach, with clearly defined galleries, content themes, and 
implementation timelines established before execution. 
 Land acquisition and environmental clearances are prerequisite conditions that must be fulfilled 
by the State Government prior to signing of the MoU under SPoCS (Scheme for Promotion of 
Culture of Science). 
 c) Dedicated Project Management and Governance Structures 
 NCSM deploys dedicated project management units for its projects and engages proactively 
with State Governments to facilitate seamless project completion. 
 A Task Force has been constituted to develop a comprehensive roadmap for transforming 
Victoria Memorial Hall (VMH) into a vibrant national hub of cultural activities. 

7 
 
The Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) has adopted a modular and scalable approach for the 
development of both new and ongoing museum projects, enabling phased execution with greater 
flexibility and efficiency. In collaboration with concerned state authorities, ASI now ensures that 
critical statutory and logistical clearances-such as land acquisition and environmental approvals-
are secured prior to budgetary allocations, thereby minimizing delays and facilitating seamless 
project implementation. Effective coordination, timely decision-making, and alignment among 
all stakeholders throughout the project lifecycle shall be ensured through proper project 
management. 
The Ministry of Culture is also proposing a new scheme for creation of cultural infrastructure, 
including Museums with better project implementation provisions. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. To address content finalization delays as observed in the Digital Museum project at 
Kanakakunnu Palace, the Committee recommends: 
a. Establish a permanent Museum Content Advisory Board comprising historians, 
cultural anthropologists, museologists, and digital content specialists to expedite 
content development processes across all museum projects. 
b. Implement concurrent content development alongside infrastructure creation 
rather than sequential processes, with rolling approvals for thematic sections to 
prevent complete project stagnation during content refinement. 
c. Develop a shared digital content repository for Ministry museums that enables 
efficient resource sharing and adaptation of existing content for new museums, 
reducing redundant research and development costs. 
d. Integrate emerging technologies such as AI-assisted curation, interactive 
installations, and personalized visitor journeys through mobile applications to 
enhance the museum experience and attract younger audiences. 
e. Implement a "Living Museum" approach that encourages regular content updates 
and community contributions, moving away from static permanent exhibitions 
toward more dynamic and participatory models of heritage presentation. 
 
(Para 16.2)   
 

8 
 
Reply of the Ministry:-  
5.1 Museums being narrative-based institutions, established mechanisms already exist for content 
conceptualization, vetting, and finalization. Museum projects are supported through Content Advisory 
Committees, comprising subject experts such as historians, museologists, domain specialists, and other 
scholars as required. These committees guide thematic development, review narratives, and finalize 
exhibition content at various stages of project implementation. In Museums, exhibit design and content 
development are already undertaken in parallel with building construction, in rolling and phased manner 
for thematic sections. This ensures optimal time utilization and prevents project delays or stagnation 
during content finalization. 
 Regarding the emerging technologies NCSM has been actively leveraging advanced technologies such as 
augmented reality (AR), virtual reality (VR) and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance visitor engagement 
and create immersive interactive museum experiences. NCSM is also developing digital content 
repositories to optimize costs and ensure sustainability.  
 Indian Museum, Kolkata has also taken initiatives to digitally reconstruct significant portions of damaged 
archeological artifacts especially those from Gandhara period, utilizing advanced deep learning based AI 
models for 3D point cloud processing.  
 Museums under the control of Central Government are actively undertaking the digitization of their 
artefacts and collections, making digital content accessible through national and institutional online 
platforms, e.g. ‘Museums of India’ portal. This collective effort supports the creation of shared digital 
repositories, improves preservation, and significantly enhances public outreach, research access, and 
cultural engagement. 
 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. Heritage-Led Regional Development Strategy: The Committee recommends 
leveraging archaeological sites for sustainable local development: 
a. Implement a Heritage-Led Regeneration approach, integrating archaeological sites 
into broader regional development plans. This would involve creating 
archaeological tourism circuits with appropriate infrastructure, interpretation 
facilities, and community engagement. 
b. Establish Archaeological Heritage Zones around significant excavation sites with 
special planning regulations, economic incentives for heritage-sensitive 
development, and community stewardship programs. 

9 
 
c. Develop skills training centres in proximity to major archaeological sites to train 
local communities in conservation techniques, heritage interpretation, and 
traditional crafts associated with the archaeological context. 
d. Create Archaeological Research Stations with permanent facilities at key excavation 
sites, enabling continuous research, conservation, and public education activities 
rather than intermittent excavation campaigns. 
(Para 16.3)   
Reply of the Ministry of the Ministry     
6.1 Recommendations of the Committee are noted. ASI is running Institute of Archaeology 
to provide extensive training in Archaeological field work, conservation and chemical 
preservation. Short term training programmes, workshops and exhibitions are organized to 
extend the subject knowledge for the interested persons and citizens. A new scheme is also being 
proposed to showcase India’s archaeological excellence to the world and to boost cultural 
tourism, generate local livelihoods, and reaffirm India’s global leadership in heritage 
management. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry not only focus on the 
immediate budget allocation but also develops a long-term plan for the sustainability and 
legacy of the commemorative events, like integrating such events into school curriculums 
or creating lasting cultural installations (e.g., monuments, museums) that serve as 
reminders of the achievements of these figures for generations to come. 
 (Para 19)   
 
Reply of the Ministry  
6.1 The Ministry has incorporated a legacy-oriented approach within the proposed revamped 
scheme architecture— ensuring that commemorations are not limited to one-time events but are 
embedded into long-term cultural and educational outcomes. 
  
 
 

10 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
7. The committee further recommends that the ministry actively pursue international 
collaborations and public-private partnerships to reduce reliance on domestic financial 
allocations. By securing expertise and additional funding through these collaborations, the 
ministry can ensure the successful implementation and sustainability of large-scale cultural 
preservation projects, thereby enhancing their impact and reach. 
 (Para 26)   
Reply of the Ministry     
7.1 In furtherance of the Committee’s recommendation to actively pursue international 
collaborations and public–private partnerships (PPPs), the Ministry has demonstrated a 
successful model through the recent repatriation and exhibition of the sacred Piprahwa relics. 
These revered Buddhist relics- comprising reliquaries, gemstone offerings and associated 
remains linked to the life of Lord Buddha were secured and brought back to India through a 
strategic partnership with the Godrej Industries Group, which facilitated their recovery and 
return. The Ministry subsequently curated and presented the international exhibition “The Light 
and the Lotus: Relics of the Awakened One”, which combined the repatriated artefacts with 
national collections to enable wide public access, deepen civilizational understanding, and 
advance India’s cultural diplomacy. This initiative illustrates how PPPs can mobilize private 
expertise and resources to achieve high-value heritage outcomes that might otherwise be difficult 
to realize through public funding alone. 
 The Ministry is also strengthening PPP frameworks to expand India’s global cultural footprint 
by leveraging the expertise, resources and managerial capacities of leading private institutions 
and patrons. A key illustration is the National Pavilion of India at the 61st International Art 
Exhibition of La Biennale di Venezia (2026) only the third Indian national pavilion in the 
Biennale’s 125-year history presented by the Ministry of Culture and commissioned by the 
National Gallery of Modern Art, in partnership with the Nita Mukesh Ambani Cultural Centre 
and the Serendipity Arts Foundation,  and supported by a distinguished list of patrons. Through 
this PPP model, the Government provides curatorial oversight and national representation, while 
private partners contribute sponsorship, institutional capacity, and international outreach, 
ensuring efficient execution and enhanced global visibility for India’s contemporary art and 
cultural diversity at the Venice Art Biennale 2026.  Together, these initiatives demonstrate a 
coherent, scalable approach to PPP-led cultural engagement that directly responds to the 
Committee’s guidance on reducing fiscal reliance while amplifying impact and reach. 
 

11 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
8. The Committee recommends establishing a dedicated research program for 
developing advanced conservation technologies. This should include creating five 
specialized Conservation Research Laboratories focused on different manuscript materials 
(palm leaf, birch bark, paper, cloth, and metals) to develop non-invasive preservation 
techniques, research environmentally sustainable conservation materials, and establish 
evidence-based protocols for treatment of deteriorating manuscripts. The implementation 
of a "Preventive Conservation Network" with environmental monitoring systems at all 
major manuscript repositories would enable real-time assessment of conservation risks and 
preventive interventions, significantly reducing deterioration rates in vulnerable 
collections.                     
8.1    Developing specialized training modules in conservation science for Manuscript 
Conservation Centres (MCCs) would incorporate latest international practices with 
traditional knowledge systems, creating a uniquely Indian approach to conservation that 
respects both scientific principles and cultural heritage. Establishing international research 
partnerships with leading conservation institutes worldwide would facilitate knowledge 
exchange, joint research projects, and capacity building for Indian conservation specialists. 
The Committee notes that while the NMM employs various methods of preservation such 
as lamination, restoration, and de-acidification, there is a need for more systematic 
research into conservation technologies specific to Indian manuscript materials and 
environmental conditions, especially considering the diverse climatic zones across the 
country and their distinct conservation challenges. 
8.2    Building on the existing digitization guidelines, the Committee recommends 
developing an advanced knowledge extraction framework. This should include creating an 
AI-assisted transcription and translation platform that automates the conversion of 
manuscript images to searchable text, provides provisional translations across major 
Indian languages, and allows scholarly review and refinement of automated outputs. The 
establishment of a "Manuscript Knowledge Portal" would contextualize manuscript 
content with related historical information, create thematic collections across manuscripts 
from different repositories, and develop educational modules for various age groups and 
knowledge levels, democratizing access to manuscript knowledge beyond specialized 
academic circles. 
8.3    The implementation of a "Digital Humanities Incubator" program would provide 
grants and technical support for innovative projects utilizing digitized manuscript 
collections for interdisciplinary research, stimulating new scholarly approaches to 
manuscript studies.  Developing mobile and immersive applications would bring 
manuscript content to wider audiences through virtual reality experiences, interactive 
storytelling, and gamified learning environments, particularly engaging younger 

12 
 
generations with India's manuscript heritage. The Committee believes that mere 
digitization without knowledge extraction and meaningful access would significantly limit 
the cultural and scholarly impact of the NMM's work. This recommendation addresses

examined by an independent multidisciplinary expert panel prior to final approval.

₹ 21.61 crore in the RE 2024-25 and ₹ 53.19 crore has been proposed for BE 2025-26. The 
actual expenditure in 2023-24 is significantly lower at ₹ 4.69 crore, which is drastically below 
both the revised estimates for 2024-25 and the proposed budget for 2025-26. Further, the actual 
expenditure in 2023-24 is only ₹ 4.69 crore, which is significantly lower than both the revised 
estimates for 2024-25 and the proposed allocation for 2025-26. In view of underutilization of 
funds in 2023-24 (₹ 4.69 crore out of a higher allocation), the Committee recommends that the 
ministry strengthens the management and monitoring mechanisms to ensure efficient use of 
allocated resources. The Committee further recommends the Ministry to adopt quarterly reviews 
of fund utilization and take corrective action where necessary to prevent underutilization or 
misallocation. 
(Para 20)

2.1  The National Mission on Libraries (NML) operates in coordination with the State/UT 
library authorities for the implementation of the NML Model Library Scheme for the 
development of public libraries. 
 Sanction of proposals under the NML Model Library Scheme is subject to submission of 
complete and duly approved proposals by the respective State/UT library authorities. Payments 

30 
 
are released by NML strictly on the basis of certified claims accompanied by requisite 
documents, as per the conditions laid down in the sanction order. 
 It is clarified that the execution of approved projects under the NML Model Library Scheme is 
directly managed and controlled by the respective State/UT Library Authorities. It is further

CHAPTER-I 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE 
MINISTRY 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
1. The Committee recommends immediate attention to the challenges facing maritime 
container movement schedules due to global disruptions and trade volatility. The 
Committee strongly urges the Ministry to implement comprehensive digital tracking 
platforms for real-time monitoring of container movements across all major ports. 
Furthermore, the Committee recommends establishing a dedicated Maritime Response 
Unit to address contingencies arising from geopolitical disruptions along key shipping 
routes. The Committee believes these measures are essential to mitigate extended lead 
times currently affecting Asia-Europe shipments and to reduce congestion at strategic port 
hubs.  
(Para 8.1)   
Reply of the Ministry   
1.1 In alignment with the Committee’s recommendations, the Ministry is actively assessing 
the implementation of comprehensive digital tracking platforms to enhance real-time monitoring 
of container movements across all major ports. These efforts align with our broader objective of 
leveraging technology to improve supply chain efficiency and transparency.  
Furthermore, the Ministry acknowledges the strategic significance of establishing a 
dedicated Maritime Response Unit to ensure timely and coordinated responses to geopolitical 
disruptions along key shipping routes. As part of this initiative, the Ministry is evaluating 
potential frameworks for enhancing resilience in maritime logistics and optimizing trade routes 
to safeguard India’s shipping interests. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
2. The Committee notes the ambitious targets under Maritime India Vision 2030 and 
recommends accelerated implementation of mechanization initiatives at all major ports to 
achieve the sub-20-hour turnaround time goal. The Committee strongly advises prioritizing 
budget allocation for modernizing port infrastructure, particularly automated cargo 
handling systems and digital documentation processes. The Committee further 

3 
 
recommends quarterly performance reviews of port efficiency metrics with standardized 
benchmarks to ensure measurable progress toward capacity enhancement targets. 
(Para 8.2)   
 
Reply of the Ministry   
 
2.1 The Ministry acknowledges the Committee’s recommendation for the accelerated 
implementation of mechanisation initiatives across all major ports. In FY 2024–25, the median 
container turnaround time at major ports was recorded at 26.2 hours. Over the past five years, 
major ports in India have undertaken capital expenditure amounting to ₹14,080 crore through 
Internal and Extra Budgetary Resources (IEBR) and Gross Budgetary Support (GBS), along with 
an additional ₹8,898 crore through Public-Private Partnership (PPP) projects. These investments 
have been directed towards comprehensive port modernisation, capacity enhancement for 
handling large volumes of cargo, and the development of port-led industrialisation initiatives 
aimed at streamlining operations and improving overall efficiency. The Ministry also conducts 
regular monthly reviews of key port efficiency parameters to ensure continuous performance 
monitoring and improvement. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
3. The Committee emphasizes that inadequate multi-modal connectivity remains a 
significant bottleneck affecting port efficiency. The Committee recommends establishing a 
dedicated Inter-Ministerial Coordination Cell to expedite port connectivity projects under 
PM Gati Shakti. With reference to 10 Paradip Port, the Committee recommends 
immediate completion of pending railway linkage projects and upgradation of NH-53A to 
facilitate smoother cargo evacuation. The Committee strongly urges synchronized planning 
between the Ministries of Railways, Road Transport and Highways, and Ports, Shipping 
and Waterways to ensure infrastructure development aligns with projected cargo volumes. 
The Committee recommends that the Paradip Port development model be replicated across 
other major ports to enhance seamless connectivity and reduce logistics costs. 
(Para 8.3)   
 
 

4 
 
Reply of the Ministry   
3.1 The Ministry acknowledges the Committee’s observations regarding multi-modal 
connectivity challenges affecting port efficiency. Strengthening infrastructure linkages remains a 
key priority, particularly under the PM Gati Shakti initiative, which is designed to facilitate 
synchronized planning across multiple sectors, ensuring seamless cargo movement and reduced 
logistics costs. 
In alignment with the Committee’s recommendations, the Department for Promotion of Industry 
and Internal Trade (DPIIT) is leading inter-ministerial coordination efforts to expedite 
connectivity projects and ensure alignment with projected cargo volumes. Through DPIIT’s 
leadership, coordination among the Ministries of Railways, Road Transport and Highways, and 
Ports, Shipping and Waterways has been streamlined to accelerate infrastructure development 
and optimize multimodal logistics solutions. 
Regarding Paradip Port, the Ministry remains committed to the timely completion of pending 
railway linkage projects and the upgradation of NH-53A, recognizing their strategic importance 
in facilitating efficient cargo evacuation. These initiatives are being fast-tracked to enhance 
operational capacity, improve trade facilitation, and bolster India’s maritime connectivity 
framework. 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
4. The Committee appreciates the Government’s continued emphasis on portled 
economic development which is reflected in the budgetary outlay of ₹866 crore for the 
Sagarmala Programme, inclusive of ₹30 crores for Community Development and ₹24.10 
crore for administrative expenditure. At the same time, however, it recommends that a 
comprehensive impact assessment of Sagarmala projects be conducted, to ensure that 
investments are directly correlated with economic growth, employment generation, and 
infrastructural improvements. Future funding for Sagarmala Programme should be tied to 
performance-based outcomes, with a clear roadmap for project execution timelines and 
transparent reporting mechanisms.  
(Para 9)   
Reply of the Ministry:-  
4.1 The recommendations of the Hon’ble Committee have been duly noted. 
 

5 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
5. The Committee observes that the allocation of ₹ 15 crore for the Inland Water 
Transport - North Eastern Region (IWT-NER) appears disproportionately low given the 
vast potential of inland waterways as a cost-effective and environmentally sustainable 
mode of transport. It did note the investment of ₹ 1,752.31 crore in inland water transport 
infrastructure which would go a long way in strengthening the waterway connectivity. The 
Committee, therefore recommends that a dedicated Inland Waterway Corridor 
Development Plan be instituted, which will ensure that investments extend beyond mere 
infrastructural augmentation to include operational efficiency, multimodal logistics 
integration, and cargo handling capabilities. A periodic review mechanism must be 
established to assess the effectiveness of these investments in enhancing inland navigability 
and economic viability. 
 (Para 10)   
Reply of the Ministry of the Ministry     
5.1 The allocation of ₹ 15 crore is for the Central Sector Schemes for Inland Water Transport 
- North Eastern Region (IWT-NER) under which works are being executed by the concerned 
States on their inland waterways. For the development of cost-effective and environmentally 
sustainable mode of transport on National Waterways (NWs) of NER through Inland Waterways 
Authority of India (IWAI), an investment of Rs. 421 cr. is proposed under BE 2025-26 under 
Capital outlay in North Eastern Areas- Inland Waterways Authority of India. 
In line with the recommendations of the Committee, for the development of a regional 
waterways network integrated with road and rail, the Regional Waterway Grid (RWG) project is 
proposed. The broad objective of the RWG project is to enhance economic activity in the region 
by facilitating trade and commerce via efficient movement of goods and passengers by 
augmenting waterways, putting in place connectivity in a manner that is socially, 
environmentally, and economically sustainable. 
A robust weekly/fortnightly/monthly review mechanism has been established at regional/ 
organizational /ministerial level for effective implementation of works being executed by IWAI 
for close monitoring and targeted progress. 
 
 

6 
 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
6. The Committee is happy to note the allocation of ₹100.62 crore to the Indian 
Maritime University (IMU) which it believes reflects a commendable commitment on the 
part of the Government to maritime education and workforce development. However, the 
Committee notes with concerns the relatively modest provision of crore for the Tariff 
Authority for Major Ports (TAMP), as it may affect its ability to effectively regulate port

10. The Committee notes the allocation of ₹138 crore for shipbuilding assistance in FY 
2025-26 which represents a modest commitment when viewed against the backdrop of the 
scheme's total allocation of ₹4,000 crore that was intended to span from 2016 to 2026. This 
relatively small annual allocation however raises serious concerns about the pace and scale 
of implementation. Evidence suggests that despite the policy being operational for nearly 
nine years, barely 10% of the total corpus has been utilized, indicating structural 
impediments in policy implementation. Since its inception, the SBFAP has facilitated 313 
vessel orders across 39 shipyards, with a cumulative value of approximately ₹10,500 crore. 
However, financial assistance disbursed stands at only ₹337 crore for 135 completed 
vessels. This significant gap between allocated funds and actual disbursement suggests 
systemic issues in fund absorption capacity within the industry. The progressive reduction 
in financial assistance percentages—from 20% in 2016 to the current 11%—appears to 
have contributed to diminishing industry interest in the scheme, particularly as competing 
shipbuilding nations like China and South Korea continue to provide 20-30% subsidies to 
their shipyards. 
10.1 The Committee therefore suggests that the Ministry undertakes a comprehensive 
performance audit of the SBFAP to identify specific bottlenecks preventing optimal fund 
utilization. The audit should examine whether procedural complexities in application 
processing, unrealistic valuation mechanisms, or lack of shipyard capacity are inhibiting 
fund absorption. The web application for processing applications, despite improvements 
made after industry feedback, may require further streamlining to facilitate easier access 
to financial assistance. 
(Para 24 & 24.1)    
Reply of the Ministry     
10.2 It is informed that the funds allocated for SBFAP for FY 2025-26 is Rs. 350 crores. 
(I) The reasons for lower disbursement till date are as under: 

18 
 
(a) At the time of drafting the Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy, several major shipyards 
such as Reliance Naval and Engineering Limited, ABG Shipyard, Bharati Shipyard, and Tebma 
Shipyard Limited were operational, with numerous vessels under construction. These shipyards 
represented the bulk of India’s commercial shipbuilding capacity. However, due to multiple 
challenges—including the absence of a shipbuilding subsidy between September 2007 and 
March 2016 —many of these shipyards entered insolvency proceedings under the National 
Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). This led to a substantial decline in India’s shipbuilding 
capacity, reducing it by more than half, and significantly impacting the country’s overall 
shipbuilding capability. 
(b) In addition to the above, the COVID-19 pandemic and its aftermath further affected the 
sector, causing high lead times and extremely low production volumes during the period 2020–
2022. This severely constrained shipbuilding operations nationwide. 
(c) It may also be noted that ship construction is a long-gestation process. Hence, though the 
current policy was introduced in 2016, the first application for financial assistance was received 
only in January 2018. As a result, no disbursements occurred during the initial 1.5 years of 
policy implementation. 
(d) Under the present Shipbuilding Financial Assistance Policy, approvals are granted in two 
stages. First, an in-principle approval is accorded at the time of signing of the shipbuilding 
contract. Second, the actual disbursement of financial assistance takes place upon the successful 
delivery of the vessel. Accordingly, the applicability and timeline of the policy must be 
interpreted in this framework. While in-principle approvals will be granted until March 31, 2026, 
fund disbursement under these approvals will necessarily extend beyond this date. For instance: 
For regular vessels, which are allowed three year construction period, disbursement may extend 
until March 2029, if the contract is signed in Mar 2026. For specialized vessels, which are 
allowed a six-year construction period, disbursement may extend until Mar 2032, if the contract 
is signed in Mar 2026. 
(e) In this context, it is important to highlight that a significant number of shipbuilding contracts 
were signed in the post-COVID period, reflecting a revival of market confidence and renewed 
interest in domestic shipbuilding. As a result, while the actual disbursement under the policy 
currently stands at approximately 
Rs. 464.15 crore, the committed liability under approved contracts is already estimated at around 
Rs. 2,700 crore. These further underscores the necessity for continued and predictable policy 
support to ensure the long-term sustainability and growth of the shipbuilding sector in India. 
(f) Considering the capital intensive and long gestation nature of shipbuilding, initiatives to boost 
shipbuilding need a stable, long-term perspective to alter the existing market dynamics. 
Accordingly, the impact of the shipbuilding financial assistance policy has taken some time to 
reflect in the increased shipbuilding contracts being signed. 

19 
 
(II) Web Application and processing of fund release applications: 
For the Financial Year 2024–2025, the average time taken for release of funds under the scheme 
has been approximately 60 days. This includes a 30-day window provided to applicant shipyards 
to address any deficiencies or to furnish required clarifications. The current fund disbursement 
process is end-to-end electronic workflow with no manual intervention from the shipyards. 
Nevertheless, to enhance user experience, operational efficiency and a shift to an upgraded 
reporting module, a new and improved digital portal is currently under development. The 
upgraded portal is expected to go live by June 2026. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
11. The Committee observes the current SBFAP framework includes provisions for 
enhanced incentives—30% for vessels powered by green fuels (methanol, ammonia, 
hydrogen) and 20% for those with electric or hybrid propulsion systems. However, without 
a dedicated allocation specifically earmarked for these sustainable technologies within the 
₹138 crore budget for FY 2025-26, there remains a serious risk that traditional 
shipbuilding might continue to dominate fund utilization. As global shipping increasingly 
focuses on decarbonization, India risks falling behind in developing indigenous capabilities 
for green vessel construction. The implications extend beyond environmental 
considerations to encompass future market competitiveness, as regulatory pressures and 
market demands increasingly favor low-emission vessels. The shipping ministry's 
recognition of green vessels in its policy framework indicates awareness of this shift, but 
implementation requires more targeted financial commitment.  
11.1 The Committee further notes the upcoming SBFAP 2.0, with its proposed allocation 
of ₹18,000 crore and enhanced subsidies of 25% for specialized vessels and 30% for green 
vessels, represents a significant step forward. However, this policy requires immediate 
operationalisation with a clear timeline for implementation and specific allocations for 
different vessel categories. The Ministry should establish immediate ring-fencing of at least 
40% of the current year's allocation (approximately ₹55 crore) exclusively for green vessel 
construction, creating a dedicated funding stream that ensures India builds capacity in this 
emerging technology area. 
11.2 The Committee notes that the current practice of projecting SBFAP funds based on 
tentative ship delivery schedules introduces significant inefficiencies in fund utilization. 
Shipbuilding projects, particularly those involving complex vessels, are vulnerable to 
production delays, supply chain disruptions, and technical challenges that can extend 
timelines considerably. This creates a mismatch between projected fund requirements and 

20 
 
actual disbursement schedules, contributing to the observed pattern of underutilization. 
The construction of specialized and green vessels, which involve more complex technologies 
and often require sourcing components from global supply chains, are particularly 
susceptible to such delays. This problem is likely to be exacerbated as Indian shipyards 
expand their capabilities to build more sophisticated vessels with lower emission profiles. 
The Committee feels implementing a milestone-based fund release mechanism would 
fundamentally transform how financial assistance is distributed. Under this approach, 
shipyards would receive predetermined percentages of the total assistance amount upon 
completion of defined construction milestones, such as steel cutting, keel laying, launching, 
and final delivery. This approach would provide shipyards with steady cash flow 
throughout the construction process, rather than concentrating financial support at project 
completion. 
11.3 The Committee therefore urges the Ministry develops a standardized set of 
verifiable milestones for different vessel categories, with appropriate weightage assigned to 
each stage. For instance, the steel cutting stage might trigger release of 15% of the total 
assistance, keel laying another 25%, launching 30%, and final delivery the remaining 30%. 
This structured approach would maintain financial pressure on shipyards to progress 
systematically while providing them with the liquidity needed to finance ongoing 
construction. 
(Para 25, 25.1, 25.2 & 25.3)

for the public to view. Also, Sagarmanthan data is being regularly updated to provide real time 
performance review by MoPSW. Further, the new portal being developed by DGS for the 
implementation of the SBFAP policy will also provide separate access to MoPSW with specific 
screen to monitor real time progress including quarterly performance dashboard and visibility on 
funds disbursed to shipyards in their respective login. Further, PFMS integration is envisaged in 
the development of the new portal, which will show the real time updates on disbursal of funds 
without necessitating manual interventions. 
 
Recommendation/Observation  
13. The Committee has undertaken an assessment of the budgetary allocation for the 
Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships (DGLL) for FY 2025-26, amounting to 
₹ 565 crore. It notes that as the DGLL operates as a self-sustaining entity, funding its 
revenue expenditure (₹ 475 crore) through navigation dues 29 collected (₹ 475 crore) and 
meeting its capital expenditure (₹ 90 crore) from reserve funds, it also makes DGLL highly 
dependent on stable maritime traffic for revenue generation. Any decline in international 
shipping activity could adversely impact its financial sustainability and restrict future 
capital investments.The Committee recommends that DGLL adopts a more diversified 
financial approach to secure resilience and ensure uninterrupted modernisation of India’s 

22 
 
marine navigation infrastructure. It may conduct a comprehensive risk assessment to 
evaluate potential fluctuations in revenue collection due to global shipping trends, 
economic downturns, or geopolitical disruptions; explore alternative revenue-generation 
mechanisms, including collaborations with private maritime stakeholders and leveraging 
DGLL’s expertise for international consultancy services, and should consider establishing a 
contingency reserve fund to mitigate financial instability during periods of reduced 
revenue collection.  
(Para 29)   
 
Reply of the Ministry     
13.1 The observations of the committee are noted and the following details are submitted for 
kind consideration: 
• DGLL is a self-sustaining organization, and its revenue expenditures are met from the 
receipts of Marine Aids to Navigation Dues and its capital expenditures are met from its own 
Reserve Funds.  
• DGLL being an organization under the Government of India, its receipts are deposited 
with the Consolidated Fund of India (CFI) and expenditures are being met from the allocated 
budget through Gross Budgetary Support (GBS) of Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways. 
• A comparative statement of revenue receipts for the last 5 years and % of variation with 
respect to previous year may be seen in Annexure-I. 
• From the data given in Annexure-I, it is evident that a stable and largely upward trend is 
evident in the revenue generation for DGLL over the years, even recovering positively after 
occasional short-term declines due to exceptional circumstances (e.g., COVID-19 pandemic). 
The recent consistent growth reflects a robust and resilient revenue model. 
• DGLL is maintaining 02 reserve funds namely “General Reserve Fund“ and 
“Depreciation Reserve Fund”. Annual contribution to these reserve funds is strategically planned 
to meet the long-term capital investment in future projects and financial sustainability. 
• The operational and financial performance, including revenue status of DGLL are 
periodically reviewed by the Central Advisory Committee for Marine Aids to Navigation 
(CACAtoN) which is a consultative body constituted under the provision of the Marine Aids to 
Navigation Act, 2021. This committee is headed by Secretary (MoPSW) and comprises of 

23 
 
Hon’ble Members of Parliament, Senior officials from Government of India and maritime 
stakeholders including private associations.  
• Additionally, provisions under the Marine Aids to Navigation Act, 2021 empowers the 
Central Government, in consultation with CACAtoN, to revise and increase the Marine Aids to 
Navigation Dues if any revenue shortfall is anticipated. This mechanism ensures financial 
resilience against any unexpected economic downturns.
