THE MINISTRY 
  
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS (2025-26) 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. The Committee acknowledges the Ministry's commitment to infrastructure 
development but emphasizes the necessity for enhanced financial oversight, timely 
project execution, and rigorous quality control standards. It recommends establishing a 
comprehensive and independent monitoring framework, supported by advanced project 
management technologies and regular audits, to proactively address delays in land 
acquisition, regulatory approvals, and contractor inefficiencies. Additionally, the 
Committee advises careful and strategic management of asset monetization initiatives to 
safeguard long-term revenue sustainability without compromising future income 
streams.  
 (Para 7) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 MoRTH has institutionalized independent online monitoring framework for addressing 
the delay in Land Acquisition, Environment & Forest Clearance and GAD for ROBs/RUBs 
approval.  
1.2 The complete Land acquisition process has been made online through Bhoomi Rashi 
Portal by leveraging the technology.3,200+ projects have been facilitated, covering over 
145,000 hectares of land and issuing 13,500+ gazette notifications. This has enabled direct 
transfer of Rs. 19,500 Cr to landowners, reducing leakages and also eliminating the need for 
Rs. 27,000 Cr. of float funds in CALA accounts. Overall, LA process has been shortened by 
~3 months, thus significantly improving efficiency and transparency. 
1.3 MoEF&CC has developed the Parivesh Portal 2.0 and customized for MoRT&H 
providing a single-window system for monitoring and managing environmental, forest, 
wildlife, and CRZ clearances. This enabled tracking the online status of clearances which 
helps in early Forest and Wildlife clearances. With real-time dashboards, color-coded alerts 
for delays, and a three-tier oversight structure, it ensures faster, transparent and accountable 
clearance processes while reducing bottlenecks. Analysis of delay shows that 75% of the 
delay is at State level and 25% is at central level. 
1.4 Similarly, MoRTH and the Ministry of Railways jointly launched RoB/RUB Portal, in 
July 2025, to centralize approvals for Road Over Bridges and Road Under Bridges. The 
portal sets fixed timelines for approvals, reducing the time for GADs from 70 to 50 days, 

- 3 - 
 
structural drawings to 11 days (plus 7 after compliance), and launching schemes and 
QAP/WPSS approvals within 30 days. With role-based access, dashboards, and auto-
notifications, the portal ensures predictable, time-bound approvals and closer coordination 
between highway and railway agencies. 
1.5 Data Lake MIS is MoRT&H’s in-house project and contract management system that 
enables continuous project monitoring, payment tracking and dispute resolution. Provides 
real-time project monitoring through GIS-enabled dashboards and customized reports for 
senior management. Accountability is ensured at all levels, from concessionaires and 
consultants to PIUs, regional offices, and headquarters, with automated alerts highlighting 
pending actions. Includes a dispute resolution module to ensure timely redressal of contractor 
and stakeholder issues.  
1.6 Together, these platforms form a cohesive digital stack that supports MoRTH’s vision 
for efficient National Highway development. By digitizing key processes across the lifecycle 
from land acquisition and clearances to implementation and monitoring, MoRTH has 
significantly improved project delivery and stakeholder coordination. 
1.7 Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs authorized MoRTH / NHAI to monetize 
public funded NH projects which are operational and are generating toll revenues for at least 
two years (which was later reduced to one year) after the Commercial Operations Date 
(COD) subject to approval of the Competent Authority in MoRTH/NHAI. Cabinet also 
approved the proposal to authorize MoRTH / NHAI to set up Infrastructure Investment Trust 
(InvIT) and monetize completed and operational NH projects. NHAI is also authorized to 
raise long term finance from banks by securitizing user fee receipts from toll plazas as an 
alternate mode of asset monetization.  
1.8 Accordingly, MoRTH through NHAI monetizes assets through three modes – Toll 
Operate & Transfer (ToT), InvIT, and Securitization [Project based Financing through 
Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV)]. Under ToT and InvIT, operational assets with stable cash 
flow are offered to investors, freeing them from pre-construction and construction risks. The 
concessionaires are exposed to revenue risk and operations and maintenance obligations. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2. The relatively small reduction in maintenance funding (Rs.4,595 crore allocated 
against Rs.4,695 crore projected) may seem insignificant but requires deeper analysis. 
Research indicates that when agencies attend to routine maintenance (filling potholes, 
maintaining pavement edges) but neglect periodic maintenance and rehabilitation, they 
may save money in the short term but eventually face expensive reconstruction costs. 
(Para 16) 

- 4 - 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Ministry should transform its approach to maintenance by implementing a 
comprehensive 10-step maintenance planning process that includes facility audits, task 
definition, prioritization, scheduling, resource allocation, implementation, safety 
protocols, performance metrics, emergency preparedness, and documentation. This 
structured approach would ensure that maintenance budgets, though slightly reduced, 
deliver optimal outcomes through strategic targeting and efficient execution. 
(Para 16.1) 
Recommendation/Observation 
4. For effective implementation, the Ministry should develop a digitized asset 
management system that tracks the condition of all national highways and predicts 
maintenance needs based on traffic patterns, climate conditions, and construction 
materials. This system should prioritize maintenance based on safety concerns, 
economic importance, and cost-effectiveness rather than simply responding to visible 
deterioration. Furthermore, maintenance contracts should incorporate performance-
based incentives that reward contractors for maintaining high-quality road conditions 
rather than merely completing specified activities. 
(Para 16.2) 
Reply of the Ministry (2 to 4, above) 
4.1 Maintenance expenditure in the ongoing works which are ongoing and during Defect 
Libility Period / Concession period of Projects under EPC/HAM/BOT/TOT/INvIT are taken 
up the respective Contractor and Concessionaire. Such expenditure are not included in the 
MoRTH expenditure statement as these expenditure are not being done through Government 
Budget 
 
4.2 For all remaining sections of NHs stretches, where DLP has ended or is not under any 
concession period of BOT/HAM/TOT/InvIT project, Government has taken a policy decision 
to undertake maintenance works through Performance Based Maintenance Contract (PBMC) 
or Short Term Maintenance Contract (STMC). While STMC works are generally undertaken 
for a contract period of 1-2 year, PBMC works are undertaken for a contract period of about 
5-7 years. The maintenance work on PBMC mode is in line with the recommendation of the 
committee which ensures minimum performance standards in maintenance with time bound 
defect rectification. Any delay in account of defect rectification attracts automatic penal 
provisions.

2014-15 onwards is as under:-

Training and Research (IDTR) for every 2.5 crore Population, one Regional Driving Training 
Centre (RDTC) for every 1 crore population (with at least one RDTC in each state, regardless

State Transport Authorities, as applicable. DO letters are issued on 27 May,2025 to the Chief

the outcome of the study, the scheme shall be re-designed and submitted for kind approval

(IDTRs) based on district and population criteria, as well as the current sanction of 67

- 51 - 
 
road safety by focusing on critical areas such as fatigue management, defensive driving

CHAPTER-I 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY 
THE MINISTRY 
  
Comparative Analysis between Budgetary Allocation for Financial Year 2023-24, 2024-
25 and 2025-26 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
1. To address the chronic underutilization of funds, the Committee recommends 
implementing a three-tier monitoring mechanism for Swadesh Darshan and PRASHAD 
schemes, comprising central oversight, state-level coordination committees, and destination-
specific implementation teams with defined quarterly milestones and real-time digital 
tracking systems. Furthermore, the Ministry should strategically leverage the Public-Private 
Partnership (PPP) model to enhance operational efficiency and attract additional investment 
for tourism infrastructure development. Specific tourism circuits could benefit from private 
sector involvement in not just construction but also in management and innovation of visitor 
experiences, bringing entrepreneurial dynamism to heritage and spiritual tourism 
destinations. The Committee also recommends establishing a dedicated Project Management 
Unit within the Ministry with tourism infrastructure Specialists and financial experts to 
conduct pre-feasibility assessments and ensure project viability before fund disbursement.  
(Para 10) 
Reply of the Ministry 
1.1 The suggestion of the Committee is noted. 
 
1.2 The Ministry of Tourism under Swadesh Darshan 2.0 and PRASHAD Schemes 
follow the 2-3 tier system for execution of scheme.  As per the guidelines of the above 
mentioned Schemes, the Ministry centrally monitors the progress through Mission 
Directorate (chaired by Joint Secretary/Additional Secretary level officer and Central 
Sanctioning and Monitoring Committee (CSMC), constituted under the chairmanship of 
Secretary (Tourism).  Further, SD 2.0 provisions for State Steering Committee (SSC) under 
the chairmanship of Chief Secretary and State Mission Director at State level and 
Destination Management Committee under the chairmanship of District Collector has been 
constituted. Ministry of Tourism has also set up a National Programme Management Unit 
(NPMU) to oversee programme implementation.  The scope of work of NPMU primarily 
includes the following:  
(i) Provide program management support 
(ii) Preparation of Detailed Perspective Plan (DPP) for the identified themes, benchmarks 
and standards 
(iii) Preparation of toolkits and SOPs 

3 
 
(iv) Preparation of model RFP/ EOI / agreements 
(v) Support in processing the Project Concept and Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) 
(vi) Provide MIS support in monitoring the scheme 
(vii) Provide support for O&M and PPP 
(viii) Provide capacity-building support, documentation of best practices 
(ix) Impact Assessment 
(x) Provide any other related support as may be required 
  
1.3 The Ministry of Tourism is also advising States to prepare Destination Master Plans 
for identified destinations.   
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2 The Committee expresses serious concern over the sharp decline in allocation for the 
Restructured Overseas Promotion and Publicity Scheme, which has been reduced to an 
inadequate ₹3.07 crore in 2025-26. This drastic reduction threatens India's competitiveness 
in the global tourism market where competing destinations are substantially increasing their 
marketing investments. The Committee recommends establishing an Integrated Global 
Tourism Marketing Framework that leverages digital platforms and artificial intelligence to 
deliver personalized, targeted international campaigns. The Incredible India Digital 
Platform (IIDP) should be enhanced with AI-driven personalization capabilities, virtual 
tourism experiences, and seamless booking interfaces to provide potential international 
visitors with immersive pre-visit experiences of India's diverse destinations.  
(Para 11) 
Reply of the Ministry 
2.1 Recommendation of the Committee is duly noted. 
  
2.2 The Ministry is working on revamping the existing Overseas Promotion and Publicity 
Scheme to make it more targeted and  result oriented. The objective of revamping the scheme 
is to leverage user generated content creation for targeted promotional campaigns through 
digital platforms to re-position Incredible India in targeted global markets. 
  
2.3 It is submitted that the revamped Incredible India website has personalization features 
and seamless booking interfaces.  
Recommendation/Observation 
3. The Committee strongly recommends allocation specifically for a comprehensive 
digital marketing campaign targeting key international source markets. This initiative should 
incorporate advanced data analytics to identify high-potential visitor segments, create 
personalized digital experiences, and measure campaign effectiveness with precision. The 

4 
 
Ministry should collaborate with leading technology partners to develop virtual reality tours 
of India's iconic destinations, interactive cultural experiences, and AI-powered trip planners 
that can be accessed through mobile applications and the Incredible India website. 
Implementing a 360-degree digital presence strategy across social media platforms, travel 
forums, and international digital publications would ensure maximum visibility with efficient 
resource utilization. 
(Para 12) 
Reply of the Ministry 
3.1 The recommendations of the Committee are duly noted.  
  
3.2 The Ministry is undertaking data driven policy decision to formulate market specific 
action plans and strategies, including digital promotion strategies. A comprehensive plan will 
be undertaken including various digital platforms and social media channels. 
 
Utilisation of Budgetary Allocations 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4 The Committee notes with serious concern the chronic pattern of fund 
underutilization by the Ministry of Tourism, which represents not merely an administrative 
challenge but a fundamental impediment to the growth of India's tourism potential. The 
alarming statistics of only 33.4% utilization of allocated funds in 2023-24 (₹801.81 crore out 
of ₹2400 crore) and the continuation of this trend in 2024-25 (only ₹396.82 crore utilized 
thus far out of ₹2479.62 crore) indicates deep-rooted systemic inefficiencies that require 
comprehensive structural reforms. While the Ministry has attributed this underperformance 
to administrative bottlenecks, procedural delays, and coordination challenges with 
implementing agencies, the Committee finds these explanations inadequate and reflective of 
entrenched operational weaknesses that demand immediate redressal. 
(Para 19) 
Reply of the Ministry 
4.1 The observation of the Committee is noted.  In this regard, it is to mention that the 
Ministry of Tourism under Swadesh Darshan scheme sanctioned projects till 2018-19, after 
which the scheme was reviewed. Thereafter, the scheme of Swadesh Darshan was revamped 
as Swadesh Darshan 2.0 with the focus on Destination Centric Approach.  Accordingly, the 
Ministry of Tourism till now has sanctioned 48 projects under SD 2.0 for Rs. 1930.31 Crore.  
Further, 36 projects have been sanctioned under Challenge Based Destination Development 
(CBDD), a sub-scheme of Swadesh Darshan for Rs. 623.13 Crore.  Since a robust pipeline of 
sanctioned projects has now been recreated under SD 2.0, Ministry of Tourism is hopeful of 
achievingits financial targets from FY 2025-26 onwards.   
  

5 
 
4.2 It is submitted that for financial year 2024-25 under DPPH scheme, in Revised 
Estimate Rs. 92.95 Crores was allocated out of which 89.69 Crores were utilized. 
  
4.3  It is also submitted that for the FY 2024-25, an amount of Rs. 30 crore was allocated 
under Overseas Promotion and Publicity (OPP) Scheme. Out of this, Rs. 29.26 crore was 
utilized during the last FY which is more than 97% of the total Budget Estimate allocated 
under the Scheme. It is further submitted that the existing Scheme is being revamped to 
tackle deficiencies in the existing scheme and to make it more relevant due to the changing 
times. 
  
4.4 The Ministry of Tourism does regular monitoring of funds through the CNA model, 
as the information is updated in the CNA modules on day to day basis. Under the scheme of 
Assistance to IHMs/FCI/IITTM/NCHMCT, budget provision of Rs.37.50 Crore was kept at 
RE for FY 2023-24, of which an amount of Rs.31.71 Cr was utilized during the financial 
year. Whereas, budget provision of Rs.32.00 Crore was kept at RE stage for FY 2024-25, of 
which an amount of Rs.24.40 Cr was utilized during the financial year. The reason for 
underutilization of funds is lack of timely receipt of Utilization Certificate and pegging of 
funds to a particular project. The concern of pegging of funds to a particular project has now 
been addressed and optimum utilization of funds is expected to be achieved. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
5 The Committee recommends establishing Regional Tourism Coordination Councils 
(RTCCs) that bring together clusters of states with similar tourism characteristics for 
quarterly coordination meetings to address regional implementation challenges. These 
councils would facilitate peer learning, regional tourism circuit development, and coordinated 
infrastructure planning while creating a forum for regular interaction between the Ministry 
and state implementation agencies. Additionally, the Ministry should develop Standard 
Operating Procedures (SOPs) for all critical processes including fund requests, utilization 
certificate submission, and project closure documentation, eliminating ambiguities that 
frequently cause delays. Further, the Committee recommends creating a Tourism 
Implementation Support Cell (TISC) in each state tourism department with dedicated 
officials trained specifically in Ministry of Tourism scheme implementation protocols. These 
structural enhancements to state coordination would address the root causes of 
implementation delays while creating sustainable mechanisms for ongoing collaboration. 
(Para 21) 
Reply of the Ministry 
5.1 The observation of the Committee regarding Regional Tourism Coordination 
Councils (RTCCs) is noted. 
  
5.2 The Ministry of Tourism actively engages and collaborates with all stakeholders, 
including State Governments and Union Territory Administrations, for the development and 

6 
 
promotion of tourism across the country. Meetings are conducted with State 
Governments/UTs on regular basis to deliberate on sectoral issues and address challenges, 
ensuring coordinated tourism development on a pan-India scale. In addition to these 
interactions, National and Regional Conferences of State Tourism Ministers are periodically 
organized to review the sector, discuss ongoing schemes and policies, and share initiatives 
aimed at fostering holistic tourism growth in collaboration with States, UTs, and other 
stakeholders.  
 
New Tourism Hubs nearby National Highways 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
6 The Committee recommends the development of tourism hubs along national 
highways, showcasing the unique regional heritage, cuisine, and offering world-class 
facilities. As a model, the Committee suggests the Ministry consider the Mithila Haat, located 
along National Highway-57 in Madhubani, Bihar. This hub beautifully reflects the rich 
traditions, flavors, and creative spirit of Mithila, offering visitors an immersive cultural 
experience. In line with this, the Committee recommends targeting 100 such sites in the 
coming year to refocus efforts on developing the local cuisine, art, culture, and heritage of 
each state. This initiative aims to attract tourists from around the world while also promoting 
and popularizing local brands and identities. 
(Para 33) 
Reply of the Ministry 
6.1 The recommendation of the Committee is noted.

recommend the eligible projects for funding to Ministry of Finance by 15th November, 
2024.   
  
12.2 Further, an evaluation criteria was formulated   for assessment of the project 
proposals received.  Accordingly, in line with the criteria and as per the scheme guidelines, 
the Ministry of Tourism recommended the projects to Department of Expenditure which 
further sanctioned 40 projects under SASCI initiatives across 23 States for Rs. 3295.76 
Crore.  

21 
 
  
12.3 The projects are to be implemented immediately by the State Implementing 
Agencies. As of now, there is no proposal before the Ministry of Tourism for continuation of 
SASCI scheme for sanctioning of new tourism projects during the current Financial Year. 
 
Integrating Digital Transformation Across Infrastructure Initiatives 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
13 The Committee recommends leveraging the framework of the emerging National 
Digital Tourism Mission to create an integrated digital ecosystem across all tourism 
infrastructure development schemes. This would involve establishing unified digital 
standards for project proposal submission, implementation tracking, and outcome 
measurement across all schemes, eliminating the siloed approach that currently impedes 
cross-scheme learning and coordination. The Ministry should develop a Unified Tourism 
Infrastructure Interface that provides real-time visibility into project status, fund utilization, 
and implementation challenges across all schemes, enabling data-driven decision making 
and timely interventions. Additionally, the Committee recommends implementing AI-driven 
predictive analytics to identify potential implementation bottlenecks before they emerge, 
allowing for pre-emptive resolution of common challenges that typically cause delays. This 
digital transformation would fundamentally enhance the efficiency of all tourism 
infrastructure development initiatives while creating unprecedented transparency and 
accountability throughout the implementation cycle. 
(Para 30) 
Reply of the Ministry 
13.1 The observation of the committee is noted.   
 
13.2 While deliberating on the implementation of National Digital Tourism Mission 
(NDTM), it has been noted that the Incredible India portal has recently been revamped and 
made live as a comprehensive digital platform to cater to all tourism-related information and 
service needs. Since both NDTM and the Incredible India 2.0 website aim to achieve the 
same objectives, it has been decided, in orderto avoid duplication of efforts,that NDTM may 
be discontinued and all digital requirements of the tourism sector will be addressed through 
the Incredible India 2.0 website. 
 
Promotion & Marketing 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
14 The Committee has examined the Ministry of Tourism’s promotional initiatives, 
including the Domestic Promotion and Publicity including Hospitality (DPPH) Scheme and 
the Overseas Promotion and Publicity including Marketing Development Assistance 

22 
 
(OPMD) Scheme, the latter currently under review. While the Ministry’s efforts to enhance 
domestic and international tourism visibility are acknowledged, the Committee notes 
persisting concerns regarding fund utilisation, programme effectiveness, and strategic 
planning. The sharp reduction in Revised Estimates for 2024-25, from ₹176.97 crore to 
₹92.95 crore is especially noted which seems to indicate delays in fund disbursal or 
underperformance in implementation. Frequent budget cuts highlight inefficiencies in 
planning and execution, and delays in the OPMD review may weaken India's international 
tourism outreach. The Committee also notes that delays in overseas engagement may reduce 
India’s global market share. It is, therefore, recommended that the Ministry ensures full 
utilisation of allocated funds, expedites the OPMD review, introduces measurable impact 
assessments, enhances domestic outreach, and expands global partnerships through 
collaboration with Indian Missions and international stakeholders. The Committee urges the 
Ministry to promptly address these inefficiencies and improve accountability in tourism 
promotion. 
(Para 32) 
Reply of the Ministry 
14.1 The recommendations of the Committee are duly noted. The Overseas Promotion and 
Publicity Scheme for tourism is currently under review, and work is already underway to 
improve the existing guidelines in order to align with the prevailing market conditions and 
demands. The Ministry has been collaborating more strategically and intensively with 
selected Indian Missions abroad. A country specific action plan aimed at promoting India as 
a preferred tourist destination has been prepared and shared with the Ministry of External 
Affairs for their feedback and suggestions. 
 
Analysis of Foreign Tourist Arrivals 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
15 The Committee has conducted a comprehensive assessment of India's tourism 
performance metrics, including foreign tourist arrivals (FTAs), international tourist arrivals 
(ITAs), foreign exchange earnings (FEEs), and the overall contribution of tourism to GDP. 
While acknowledging the Ministry's various promotional initiatives such as participation in 
international trade fairs, roadshows, and the innovative Chalo India Global Diaspora 
Campaign, the Committee observes that despite post-pandemic recovery, significant 
challenges persist in establishing India as a premier global tourism destination. Current 
data indicates that India ranks 39th in the global travel and tourism competitiveness index 
despite possessing extraordinary potential through its rich cultural heritage, diverse 
landscapes, and emerging global influence. This positioning represents a substantial gap 
between India's tourism capabilities and its actual market performance, necessitating 
transformative strategies to enhance competitiveness and sustain long-term growth in the 
international tourism sector. 
(Para 36) 
 

23 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
15.1 The Ministry of Tourism has been continuously monitoring various indicators of 
tourism metrics (Foreign Tourist Arrivals, International Tourist Arrivals, Foreign Exchange 
Earnings) along with the Travel and Tourism Development Index (TTDI). Multiple 
measures/ steps are being taken for the improvement of these matrix. 
  
15.2 The steps taken / are being taken towards improving the rank of India in TTDI are 
mentioned in the reply to recommendation No. 36.1. 
 
Implementing a Multi-Dimensional Competitiveness Enhancement Strategy 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
16 The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a comprehensive Tourism 
Competitiveness Enhancement Framework based on a thorough analysis of India's strengths 
and weaknesses in the global tourism ecosystem. This framework should leverage India's 
significant advantages in natural resources (scoring 5.88 out of 7), cultural resources (5.62), 
and non-leisure resources (5.05), while systematically addressing areas of 
underperformance. The Ministry should establish a dedicated Tourism Competitiveness Task 
Force comprising industry leaders, academic experts, and government representatives to 
identify specific barriers to India's advancement in global rankings and develop targeted 
interventions. Furthermore, the framework should incorporate innovative benchmarking 
mechanisms that regularly compare India's performance against rapidly advancing tourism 
destinations, particularly in emerging markets with similar tourism profiles. Beyond 
conventional tourism metrics, the framework should incorporate sustainability parameters, 
digital readiness indicators, and visitor satisfaction indices to ensure a holistic approach to 
competitiveness enhancement. This structured approach would transform India's 
competitiveness strategy from reactive to proactive, positioning the country to advance 
significantly from its current 39th position toward the top 20 global destinations by 2030. 
(Para 36.1) 
Reply of the Ministry 
16.1 Ministry of Tourism is continuously monitoring India’s Rank in Travel and Tourism 
Development Index (TTDI).  
16.2 The steps undertaken/ are being taken are as follows:  
a) Monitoring of India’s Rank in every publication (2019, 2021, 2024). 
b) Analysis and evaluation of all the indicators under every dimension and pillar of 
TTDI. 
c) Constitution of Coordination Committee for timely monitoring of progress and 
status. 
d)  Mapping of all the indicators to relevant line ministries and departments for their 
comments and appropriate measures towards further improvement. 

24 
 
e) Identifying and rectifying the gaps in the data-based indicators and indicators which 
are perception based. 
f) Coordinating with Publishing agency and data agencies to highlight the identified 
issues and solutions to rectify same. 
g) Further, Ministry is in the process of developing the State Assessment Framework 
(SAF) to assess the tourism ecosystem of States/Union Territories based on 55 
indicators which have been converged from TTDI. 
  
16.3 SAF is based on the following objective – 
a) Competitive model of assessment for States/ UT travel and tourism sector. 
b) Identification of weaknesses, strengths, and improvements. 
c) Comprehensive picture of States/ UT travel and tourism sector. 
d)  
Implementing Next-Generation Visa Facilitation Programs 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
17 Recognizing visa complexity as a significant barrier to tourism growth, the 
Committee recommends implementing a Progressive Visa Liberalization Roadmap that 
systematically expands visa-free access based on strategic tourism priorities rather than 
conventional diplomatic reciprocity. The Ministry, in coordination with the Ministry of 
External Affairs, should develop data-driven criteria for identifying and prioritizing high-
potential source markets for visa liberalization, considering factors beyond current arrival 
numbers to include average spending patterns, length of stay, and potential for market 
growth. Furthermore, the Committee recommends implementing a Digital Nomad Visa 
Program specifically designed to attract long-term international visitors who can work 
remotely while experiencing India's diverse destinations, effectively creating a new category 
of extended- stay tourism that generates sustained economic impact. For markets where 
visa-free access is not immediately feasible, the Ministry should implement an Advanced 
Traveler Authorization System enabling simplified entry for pre- approved visitors from key 
tourism markets. These innovations would significantly reduce barriers to entry while 
maintaining necessary security protocols, positioning India as a leader in intelligent border 
facilitation for tourism growth. 
(Para 37) 
Reply of the Ministry 
17.1 The Ministry of Tourism has been regularly engaging with tourism 
associations/hospitality stakeholders, Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry of External 
Affairs with regard to matters related to Visa. 
 
17.2 It has been conveyed by Ministry of Home Affairs that: -  

25 
 
“lndia has a robust visa regime in place to enable lawful inward movement of foreigners 
including foreign tourists, professionals and skilled workforce, business persons, students, 
etc. Government has taken a number of initiatives over the last few years to liberalize, 
streamline and simplify visa regime with a view to facilitate the legitimate foreign travellers 
while simultaneously ramping up the technological infrastructure to enhance internal 
security. Liberalization and simplification of the visa regime, including the visa for foreign 
tourists is an ongoing process which is done after taking into consideration the issues of 
security, inbound tourism and investments, bi-lateral relations etc.” 
  
17.3 The matter regarding Progressive Visa Liberalization Roadmap, implementing a 
Digital Nomad Visa Program have been taken with Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry 
of External Affairs. 
 
17.4 Ministry of Tourism, in association with MHA and MEA, is currently trying to 
simplify the e-visa regime along with streamlining the e-visa form. A stakeholders meeting 
was organized by the Ministry in April 2025 to take inputs and feedback from the tour 
operators and various interlinked associations while applying for the e-tourist visa. Ministry 
of Tourism has been working with both these in-line Ministries (MHA & MEA) to 
streamline the system, which will reduce the waiting time as well as be able to simplify the 
procedures involved. 
 
Growth in Domestic Tourists Footfalls 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
18 The Committee notes that the success of pilgrimage and heritage tourism demands a 
need for greater investment in cultural circuits and historical site preservation. The 
Committee urges the Ministry to extend financial support to State Governments for the 
upkeep and enhancement of such sites. 
(Para 44) 
Reply of the Ministry 
18.1 While the Ministry of Tourism provides financial assistance for development of 
tourism infrastructure to provide better facilities and amenities to the tourists, maintenance 
and operation of the created assets is the responsibility of the concerned State Government/ 
UT Administration. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
19 The Committee observes the uneven distribution of domestic tourist visits and flags it 
as a matter of concern, as some States remain underrepresented in national tourism circuits. 
It is recommended that the Ministry target emerging destinations through regional 
promotional strategies and incentives for eco-tourism, rural tourism, and adventure tourism. 

26 
 
(Para 45) 
Reply of the Ministry 
19.1 The Ministry of Tourism promotes India in a holistic manner, through various 
initiatives. As part of on-going activities, promotion of various tourism destinations and 
products of India including eco-tourism, rural tourism and adventure tourism are taken up. 
 
19.2 The Ministry organized Best Tourism Village Competition to honour and encourage 
villages that best exemplify a tourism destination which preserves cultural and natural assets, 
promotes community-based values and lifestyles and has a clear commitment to 
sustainability in all its aspects - economic, social, and environmental. The competition 
recognized villages excelling in various tourism activities including adventure tourism. 
 
Strategic Expansion of Hospitality Education Infrastructure 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
20 The Committee, while acknowledging the expansion efforts in hospitality training 
institutes, identifies critical geographical disparities that severely limit access to quality 
tourism education in several high-potential tourism regions. This education infrastructure 
gap creates persistent workforce challenges and hinders the development of local tourism 
ecosystems. The Committee recommends implementing a Tiered Hospitality Education 
Framework that strategically distributes training facilities based on tourism potential and 
workforce needs rather than conventional administrative considerations. This framework 
would establish three distinct institutional models: Comprehensive Institutes of Hotel 
Management (IHMs) in regional hubs, specialized Focused Culinary Institutes (FCIs) 
aligned with distinct culinary heritage zones, and flexible Community Tourism Skill Centers 
in emerging tourism destinations. The Ministry should prioritize establishing at least one 
specialized hospitality training institute in each North Eastern State by 2027, with particular 
focus on developing centers of excellence that align with each region's unique tourism 
attributes—adventure tourism in Arunachal Pradesh, cultural tourism in Assam, and 
ecological tourism in Meghalaya. Additionally, the Committee recommends introducing the 
Tourism Satellite Campus model, wherein established IHMs develop extension facilities in 
underserved regions, leveraging existing administrative infrastructure while expanding 
geographical reach cost-effectively. This transformative approach would systematically 
address geographical disparities while ensuring that educational infrastructure aligns 
precisely with each region's specific tourism development trajectory. 
(Para 48) 
Reply of the Ministry 
20.1 Ministry of Tourism is in agreement with the recommendations of the Committee 
that addressing geographical disparities through strategically located IHMs, FCIs, and 
Community Tourism Skill Centers will not only expand access to quality hospitality 
education but also create localized talent pools aligned with regional tourism profiles.  

27 
 
  
20.2 It is submitted that Central IHMs in Guwahati (Assam) and Shillong (Meghalaya); 
State IHM in Gangtok (Sikkim); State IHMs being run in PPP mode at Dimapur (Nagaland) 
and Agartala (Tripura); FCI at Tura (Meghalaya) have come-up with the support of Ministry 
of Tourism, Govt. of India. In addition, 3 State IHMs at Imphal (Manipur), Aizawl 
(Mizoram) and Itanagar (Arunachal Pradesh), including 1 FCI at Namchi (Sikkim) are in 
pipeline. IITTM is also exploring proposals for setting up Community Tourism Skill Centers 
and extension campuses in underserved regions. 
 
Elevating Specialized Tourism Training through Centers of Excellence 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
21 The Committee acknowledges the critical importance of specialized tourism training 
exemplified by the National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS), while noting significant 
limitations in both geographical reach and integration with mainstream tourism education. 
The Committee recommends transforming NIWS into the National Center for Adventure 
Tourism Excellence with expanded scope encompassing all adventure tourism segments 
including mountaineering, trekking, wildlife tourism, and desert expeditions, creating a 
comprehensive ecosystem for adventure tourism human resource development. The Center 
should establish Regional Adventure Tourism Training Hubs in five strategic locations—
Uttarakhand (mountaineering), Goa (water sports), Rajasthan (desert tourism), Madhya 
Pradesh (wildlife tourism), and Sikkim (eco-adventure tourism)—ensuring specialized 
training reaches diverse geographical areas with distinct adventure tourism potential. 
Furthermore, the Committee recommends implementing an Integrated Adventure Tourism 
Certification System aligned with international standards that creates clearly defined career 
pathways for professionals across different adventure tourism segments. Additionally, the 
Ministry should develop the Adventure Tourism Digital Knowledge Repository, a 
comprehensive online platform providing training resources, safety protocols, and best 
practices accessible to adventure tourism operators nationwide. These transformative 
initiatives would elevate specialized tourism training from isolated programs to a 
comprehensive national framework that develops world-class human resources across the 
adventure tourism ecosystem. 
(Para 51) 
 
Reply of the Ministry 
21.1 National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS)-Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel 
Management (IITTM) Goa is an autonomous Organisation under Ministry of Tourism, 
Government of India. The Organisation is responsible for the following activities: 
a) To develop the skill and train the manpower in water sports and lifesaving skills.  
b) Research and Consultancy in waterbodies consisting of both Inland and Sea front 
zones that includes: 

28 
 
i. Feasibility study for the waterbodies. 
ii. Risk Assessment for new developed activities in water sports. 
iii. Safety Audit/ Physical Inspection of Parasailing Operations, Scuba Diving 
Centers, sea-walk and underwater submersible scooter, etc.  
c) Develop safety benchmarking protocol for water sports operations. 
d) To Develop Guidelines and SOPs for Water sports activities and also assisting State 
Governments for proper implementation. 
e) NIWS is working with Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) for developing of Scuba 
Diving and Water sports operations and Training Standards.  
f) NIWS provides the technical inputs to State Governments in terms of guidelines, 
SOPs and equipment specifications.  
 
21.2 As of now the Organisation has trained around 40,000 youth of the Nation and out of 
this 90% are employed in the sector. NIWS is also acting as a bridge between the 
stakeholders/ operators and the State Governments by providing the technical norms to both 
the sides. The Organisation is also providing consultancy services to State Governments of 
around 25 States of India.  
 
21.3 The Organisation has signed the MoU’s with the following bodies: 
a) Directorate General of Resettlement (under Ministry of Defence). 
b) Indian Naval Physical Training School (INPT- under Ministry of Defence). 
c) National Adventure Foundation (NAF- under Ministry of Sports and Youth 
Affairs). 
d) Andaman & Nicobar Administration. 
e) Uttarakhand Tourism Development Board (UTDB), Uttarakhand. 
f) Madhya Pradesh Tourism Development Corporation. 
g) Tourism Corporation of Gujarat Limited (TCGL). 
h) Odisha Tourism  
i) Tamil Nadu Tourism Development Corporation (TTDC). 
j) Jharkhand Tourism Development Corporation (JTDC) 
 
21.4 Along with courses in water sports, the institution is also providing higher education 
courses in Tourism Management (MBA-TTM, BBA-TT and PhD in tourism in collaboration 
with Jawaharlal Nehru University).  
 

29 
 
21.5 Further, it may be informed that Nehru Institute of Mountaineering (NIM) at 
Uttarkashi, Uttarakhand is among the best mountaineering institutes in India and also 
considered as the most prestigious mountaineering institute in Asia. 
 
21.6 At Namchi, Sikkim, the Indian Himalayan Centre for Adventure and Ecotourism 
(IHCAE) provides high standard eco-tourism and adventure related training courses. 
 
Capacity Building for Service Providers 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
22 The Committee acknowledges the importance of skill development in improving 
India’s tourism competitiveness but notes that the CBSP scheme has not yet achieved uniform 
accessibility. Many rural and emerging tourism hubs lack structured training facilities, 
limiting opportunities for communities that would benefit most from employment in the 
sector. It therefore urges the Ministry to imbibe a more balanced regional approach by 
increasing training coverage in underserved areas. 
(Para 52) 
Reply of the Ministry 
22.1 In order to augment the manpower to the hospitality sector, Ministry of Tourism has 
undertaken intensive training programme involving skilling and up-skilling and re-skilling 
under CBSP scheme. During the Financial Year 2024-25, Ministry decided to scale up the 
training level by roping in private sector and also coordinate with Ministry of Skill 
Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE). Further, during the Financial Year 2025-26, 
Ministry of Tourism has collaborated with Ministry of Skill Development and 
Entrepreneurship (MSDE) under Pradhan MantriKaushalVikasYojana (PMKVY)and have 
identified jointly about 57 destinations to undertake training programme. Ministry of Tourism 
has provided them the various job roles under tourism sector which should be taken on 
priority basis for training the manpower. MSDE has initiated the process in consultation with 
tourism and hospitality partners.

Recommendation/Observation

implementation framework to address the specific challenges of brownfield projects, which

implementation approach for complex projects, breaking them into smaller, more

interventions would address the specific challenges that have hindered the PRASHAD 
Scheme's implementation while ensuring that its critical objectives of enhancing spiritual 
tourism infrastructure are achieved.

under PRASHAD Scheme.

throughout the implementation lifecycle.

with Indian diplomatic missions abroad, leveraging their presence and local knowledge for

Drive (Prashad) Scheme

under the Assistance to Central Agencies for Tourism Infrastructure Development Scheme 
have reached completion, creating substantial risk of asset deterioration and visitor 
dissatisfaction at key tourism destinations. To catalyze project execution, the Committee

agency leadership, establishing clear consequences for persistent delays including

develop a specialized Project Acceleration Task Force deployable to stalled projects to

overcome implementation barriers. Furthermore, the Committee recommends establishing a 
Tourism Infrastructure Excellence Program wherein Central Agencies achieving exceptional 
implementation efficiency receive recognition, performance incentives, and priority 
consideration for future projects, creating positive reinforcement for operational excellence.

mechanisms to accelerate project completion rates across all implementing agencies.

4.2 A National Programme Management Unit (NPMU) has been on-boarded by Ministry

Assessment of the Central Sector Schemes of the Ministry by IIM. Based on the 
recommendations of the report submitted by IIM, necessary improvements will be made to

status and timeline of the ongoing Impact Assessment of the PRASHAD Scheme,

Introduction 
 I, the Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on
 Transport,  Tourism and Culture, having been authorised by the 
 Committee, to present on its behalf this Three Hundred  and  Eighty-Sixth 
 Report on the subject “Holistic Development  of India’s Tourism Sector 
 through  Formal  Skill  Development  University- Level Courses 
 and Professional  Training  for Guides, Hospitality and Eco-Tourism.” 
 
2. The Committee selected this subject in view of the growing strategic importance of 
tourism as a pillar of economic growth, employment generation, cultural preservation, 
and India’s global engagement. Tourism is uniquely positioned as a sector that 
integrates infrastructure, services, heritage, livelihoods, and soft power. The 
Committee notes that while physical infrastructure and destination promotion have 
received sustained policy attention in recent years, the human dimension of tourism 
has not evolved at a commensurate pace. 
 
3. The Committee is of the considered view that the future trajectory of India’s tourism 
sector will be determined not merely by the creation of assets, but by the quality, 
integrity, and professionalism of the human interfaces through which tourists 
experience the country. Guides, hospitality professionals, destination managers, 
cultural interpreters, and facilitators collectively shape visitor perception. Deficiencies 
in training, ethical conduct, and career structures in these roles directly erode trust and 
suppress tourism’s economic potential. 
 
4. Recent policy initiatives announced by the Government, including the creation of a 
National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid and the institutional upgradation of the 
National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology into a National 
Institute of Hospitality, represent significant structural interventions. The Committee, 
however, observes that such initiatives can yield sustained outcomes only when 
anchored in a comprehensive framework for formal education, professional 
certification, continuous skill upgradation, and institutional accountability. 
 
5. In the course of examination of the subject, the Committee held multiple oral 
evidence sessions with the Secretary and senior officials from the Ministry of 
Tourism. The Committee also received detailed presentations from academic and 
training institutions, including the National Council for Hotel Management and 
Catering Technology, Indian Institute of Tourism and Travel Management, Indian 
Culinary Institute, Jamia Millia Islamia, State Institute of Hotel Management 
Faridabad, Banarsidas Chandiwala Institute of Hotel Management, Madurai Kamaraj 
University, the Central University of Tamil Nadu, FHRAI,IATO, Hotel Association 
of India (HAI), and ATOAI. The Committee places on record its sincere appreciation 
for the comprehensive presentations and inputs received during the examination of 
this subject. During its sitting on 4 February 2026 with the Secretary, Ministry of 
Tourism, the Committee examined in detail the Ministry’s three‑pillar skill 
development framework, institutional presentations from NCHMCT, IITTM, ICI, 
universities and industry associations, and the alignment of tourism skilling with the 
Union Budget 2026‑27 priorities of employment generation and local economic 
development. 
 

iii 
 
 
6. To examine implementation at the regional and institutional level, the Committee 
undertook a study visit to Chennai on 21 January 2026. During this visit, the 
Committee interacted with officials of the Ministry of Tourism, representatives of the 
Government of Tamil Nadu, and faculty members of Central and State universities. 
These interactions provided valuable insights into decentralised models of tourism 
education, university-community partnerships, and the integration of heritage, 
research, and livelihood development. An oral evidence was again held in New Delhi 
on 4th February, 2026 with the Ministry of Tourism and other industry stakeholders. 
 
7. This Report synthesises evidence received from the ministry of Tourism, institutions, 
industry stakeholders, and academic experts. It places human capital at the centre of 
tourism policy and emphasises the need for standardisation, ethical conduct, digital 
capability, and coordination between the Ministry and other industry stakeholders. 
The Committee expects that the recommendations contained in this Report will 
contribute to professionalising the tourism sector, restoring visitor trust, and 
positioning India as a globally competitive tourism destination. 
 
8. The Committee places on record its appreciation of the assistance rendered by the 
officers of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat and the cooperation extended by the Ministry 
of Tourism, institutions, and stakeholders who contributed to this examination. 
9. The Committee considered and adopted the Report in its meeting held on the 11th 
February, 2026.

Executive Summary 
1. This Report presents a comprehensive assessment of the present state of tourism in 
India, with particular reference to formal skill development, university‑level education 
and professional training frameworks. The Committee notes that the Union Budget 
2026‑27 explicitly identifies tourism as a significant employer and a key driver of 
local economic development, which in turn underscores the need for a structured 
human capital framework rather than a series of project‑centric interventions. 
 
2. The Committee observes that tourism has emerged as one of the most 
employment‑intensive sectors of the Indian economy, with strong multiplier effects 
across agriculture, handicrafts, transport, construction and allied services. The sector 
currently contributes approximately five to six and a half per cent of national GDP 
and sustains nearly twelve to thirteen per cent of total employment. 
 
3. The Committee notes that India’s distinctive cultural, historical, spiritual and natural 
endowments provide a robust foundation for expanding India’s share of global 
tourism. Comparative analysis placed before the Committee, however, shows that 
countries with far fewer attractions record higher international tourist arrivals and 
tourism receipts, indicating that India’s under‑performance is not primarily on account 
of infrastructure gaps or under‑promotion. 
 
4. The Committee’s review points instead to systemic weaknesses in service delivery 
and human engagement as key constraints. Evidence received highlights a persistent 
trust deficit at several tourist destinations, arising from untrained or inadequately 
trained human interfaces, inconsistent service standards and unethical practices such 
as touting, harassment and extortion, which not only deter repeat visits but also create 
negative digital narratives that undermine national tourism branding. 
 
5. The Committee also notes a structural paradox. While tourism is projected to generate 
employment at scale, there is declining student interest in traditional hospitality and 
tourism courses, high vacancy levels in training institutions and significant attrition at 
entry level. Stakeholders attributed this trend to low starting wages, unclear career 
progression, limited professional recognition and the perception of tourism as an 
informal vocation rather than a structured profession. 
 
6. Oral evidence indicated that current formal tourism and hospitality training pipelines 
together reach only tens of thousands of learners annually, whereas the projected 
workforce requirement for a target of 100 million foreign tourists by 2047, along with 
associated domestic growth, is in the range of many millions. The Committee notes 
with concern that only about one per cent of the current tourism workforce is 
estimated to be formally skilled. 
 
7. The Committee therefore regards human capital not as an ancillary input but as the 
defining asset of the tourism economy. The Report accordingly advocates a shift from 
fragmented skilling schemes to a nationally coherent professional framework, centred 
on structured career pathways supported by formal education, mandatory institutional 
attachments, continuous professional development, and periodic certification and 
re‑certification. 
 
8. The Committee places particular emphasis on alignment of tourism education with the 
National Education Policy 2020. Flexibility through multiple entry and exit options, 
credit linkage via the Academic Bank of Credits, and a strong focus on experiential 
learning are viewed as essential to attract diverse learners and reduce drop‑outs, with 

v 
 
Central Universities envisaged as hubs for research and specialised training and State 
Universities and affiliated colleges as spokes for mass skilling and regional delivery. 
 
9. Ethical conduct and trust restoration form a core pillar of the Report. The Committee 
recommends embedding ethical training across all tourism education programmes, 
instituting enforceable licensure regimes, strengthening grievance redress mechanisms 
and linking professional certification to digital reputation and feedback systems, so 
that visitors can rely on transparent, accountable and respectful engagement at 
destinations. 
 
10. Recognising the rapid transformation of global tourism through technology, the 
Committee underlines the need to build digital and creative capabilities within the 
tourism workforce, including competencies in artificial intelligence, immersive 
technologies and digital storytelling, so that India develops the capacity to design, and 
not merely consume, tourism technology and content. The Report also flags emerging 
and under‑served segments such as border tourism, spiritual tourism, medical tourism, 
ecological circuits, cruise tourism and sites of historical trauma, each of which 
requires specialised skills, regulatory oversight and ethical sensitivity; without 
targeted human capital development, infrastructure‑led efforts in these segments risk 
significant under‑performance. The Committee is of the view that the 
outcome‑oriented and implementation‑focused recommendations contained in this 
Report, taken together, can professionalise tourism, strengthen visitor trust, generate 
dignified employment and position India as a global hub for tourism education and 
expertise in alignment with the national vision of Viksit Bharat 2047.

1 
 
REPORT 
1 Context and Rationale 
1.1 Tourism as an Economic System 
1.1.1 The Committee observes that tourism is not a standalone sector but a complex economic system 
that integrates multiple industries, services, and livelihoods. The tourism economy encompasses direct 
expenditure by visitors on accommodation, food, transport, attractions, and shopping; indirect economic 
activity generated through supply chains serving tourism establishments; induced effects arising from 
expenditure by tourism workers in local economies; and catalytic impacts on infrastructure development, 
entrepreneurship, and regional investment. 
1.1.2 Unlike manufacturing or extractive industries, tourism distributes economic benefits across a 
wide geographic and social spectrum. Expenditure by tourists flows directly into local communities, 
including artisans, farmers, transport operators, guides, and small entrepreneurs. The Committee notes 
that this decentralised multiplier effect makes tourism uniquely suited for inclusive growth, particularly in 
regions with limited industrial alternatives, and aligns with recommendations for high-value spiritual and 
cultural tourism pathways (Recommendation 21) and targeted skilling for underrepresented groups 
(Recommendation 28). 
1.1.3 The Committee further notes that tourism has one of the lowest capital-to-labour ratios among 
major economic sectors. This characteristic enables large-scale employment generation with relatively 
modest capital investment, making tourism particularly relevant for absorbing India’s young workforce 
and addressing regional employment imbalances through knowledge-based roles for humanities graduates 
(Recommendation 23) and national apprenticeship programmes (Recommendation 20). 
1.2 Employment and Demographic Relevance 
1.2.1 Evidence placed before the Committee indicates that the tourism sector currently supports 
approximately twelve to thirteen per cent of total employment in the country. Employment opportunities 
span the full skill spectrum, from entry-level service roles to highly specialised positions in heritage 
interpretation, destination management, digital content creation, and tourism technology, supported by a 
dedicated Knowledge and Interpretation Stream within a National Tourism Professional Cadre 
(Recommendation 5). 
1.2.2 The Committee notes that tourism offers significant opportunities for women, youth, and rural 
populations. Many roles in tourism leverage local knowledge, cultural familiarity, and interpersonal skills 
rather than formal technical training alone. This makes tourism an important pathway for integrating 
traditionally underrepresented groups into the formal economy, as emphasized in recommendations for 
women and inclusion (Recommendation 28) and local community capacity building (Recommendation 
26). 
1.2.3 The Committee also observes that tourism employment has strong linkages with informal and 
micro-enterprise activity. While this flexibility provides livelihood opportunities, it has also resulted in 
fragmented skill development, inconsistent service quality, and limited professional recognition. 
Addressing this imbalance between accessibility and professionalism is central to the Committee’s 
examination, through Recognition of Prior Learning (Recommendation 15) and continuous upskilling 
(Recommendation 29). 

2 
 
1.3 Global Tourism Context and India’s Position 
1.3.1 The Committee notes that global tourism contributes approximately ten per cent of world GDP 
and supports one in ten jobs worldwide. International tourist arrivals have rebounded strongly following 
the pandemic, demonstrating the sector’s resilience and adaptability. 
1.3.2 Despite possessing a civilisational heritage, cultural diversity, and natural endowments 
unmatched by most destinations, India’s share of global tourism remains comparatively modest. 
Countries with far fewer historical and cultural assets attract substantially higher numbers of international 
visitors and generate greater tourism receipts. 
1.3.3 The Committee examined multiple explanations for this gap, including infrastructure, 
connectivity, marketing, and visa facilitation. While acknowledging that challenges remain in these areas, 
the Committee is of the view that the most persistent constraint lies in the quality of on-ground experience 
delivery, which is fundamentally a function of human capability, addressed through redesigning tourism 
curricula (Recommendation 7) and international collaboration (Recommendation 31). 
1.4 The Centrality of Human Interfaces 
1.4.1 The Committee observes that tourism is experienced through people. Guides, hotel staff, transport 
providers, site managers, and facilitators constitute the human interface between the visitor and the 
destination. Even the most iconic monument or pristine landscape can fail to deliver value if mediated 
through untrained, indifferent, or unethical human engagement. 
1.4.2 Evidence presented to the Committee highlighted recurring issues at tourist destinations, 
including misinformation, lack of interpretative depth, inconsistent service standards, and unethical 
practices such as touting and coercive selling. These experiences erode visitor trust and generate 
reputational damage that far exceeds the immediate transaction, mitigated by ethical guardrails 
(Recommendation 13) and linking ethical evaluation to certification (Recommendation 14). 
1.4.3 The Committee notes that digital platforms amplify both positive and negative visitor 
experiences. A single adverse interaction can influence thousands of potential visitors through online 
reviews and social media. Human capital deficiencies therefore have systemic consequences for national 
tourism performance, supported by national digital platforms for guide matching (Recommendation 17). 
1.5 Trust Deficit as a Structural Constraint 
1.5.1 The Committee identifies the trust deficit as one of the most damaging structural constraints 
facing India’s tourism sector. Trust encompasses safety, transparency, professionalism, and respect. 
Tourists gravitate towards destinations where they feel protected and valued, regardless of price or 
distance. 
1.5.2 The Committee observes that trust deficits arise not only from criminal or unethical behaviour but 
also from inadequate training, poor communication skills, and lack of accountability. In many cases, 
individuals operating at tourist sites are neither formally trained nor institutionally supported, leading to 
inconsistent behaviour and outcomes, addressed via destination-level narrative teams (Recommendation 
3). 
1.5.3 The Committee is of the view that restoring trust requires systemic intervention rather than 
isolated enforcement measures. Professionalisation through education, certification, ethical training, and 
institutional oversight is essential for sustainable trust restoration, including a national tourism 
professionals database (Recommendation 16). 

3 
 
1.6 Tourism Education: From Vocation to Profession 
1.6.1 The Committee notes that tourism in India has historically been treated as a vocational activity 
learned informally or on the job. While this approach enabled rapid workforce expansion, it has not kept 
pace with the increasing complexity of tourism as an experience-driven and technology-enabled sector. 
1.6.2 Contemporary tourism requires competencies in history, culture, communication, digital tools, 
sustainability, crisis management, and ethics. These competencies cannot be reliably developed through 
ad-hoc training alone. The Committee therefore emphasises the need to reposition tourism as a formal 
profession grounded in structured education, continuous learning, and research, through curriculum 
redesign (Recommendation 7) and long-duration field residencies (Recommendation 8). 
1.6.3 The Committee also observes that the absence of clear career pathways and professional 
recognition has contributed to declining student interest in tourism and hospitality courses. Elevating 
tourism education within the higher education ecosystem is essential to attract talent and retain skilled 
professionals, via clear career pathways (Recommendation 6) and early education integration 
(Recommendation 33). 
1.7 Rationale for Parliamentary Intervention 
1.7.1 The Committee considers that tourism’s multi-sectoral nature necessitates parliamentary 
oversight and coordinated policy direction. Human capital development in tourism intersects with 
education, culture, skill development, technology, internal security, and external engagement. 
1.7.2 Individual institutional or ministerial measures can deliver local gains, but a joined-up approach 
is required to tackle systemic challenges at scale. A coherent national framework, guided by 
parliamentary recommendations, is required to align institutional roles, standardise outcomes, and ensure 
accountability, through inter-ministerial coordination (Recommendation 10). 
1.7.3 This Report is therefore anchored in the Committee’s mandate to examine policy coherence, 
institutional effectiveness, and long-term national interest. The recommendations that follow seek to 
establish a sustainable human capital architecture for tourism that supports economic growth, social 
inclusion, cultural preservation, and global engagement, avoiding new apex bodies (Recommendation 9) 
and declaring narrative leadership as India’s advantage (Recommendation 25). 
2 The Tourism Workforce Landscape 
2.1 Overview of the Tourism Workforce 
2.1.1 The Committee observes that the tourism workforce in India is diverse, decentralised, and 
heterogeneous in nature. It spans multiple sub-sectors, including hospitality, travel and transport services, 
heritage and cultural interpretation, destination management, adventure and eco-tourism, spiritual 
tourism, medical tourism, and emerging digital tourism services. This diversity reflects the breadth of 
India’s tourism assets but also poses challenges for standardisation, quality assurance, and professional 
recognition. 
2.1.2 The tourism workforce comprises both organised and unorganised segments. While a portion of 
the workforce is employed in formal establishments such as hotels, airlines, and travel companies, a 
substantial proportion operates in informal or semi-formal arrangements. Guides, facilitators, small 
transport operators, homestay owners, and local cultural practitioners often function outside structured 
employment frameworks, with limited access to training, certification, or social security, integrated 
through Recognition of Prior Learning (Recommendation 15). 

4 
 
2.1.3 The Committee notes that this fragmented structure has enabled rapid expansion of tourism-
related livelihoods but has also resulted in uneven service quality, weak accountability, and limited career 
mobility. Addressing these structural limitations requires a comprehensive understanding of the 
workforce landscape and its underlying dynamics, via a national tourism professionals database 
(Recommendation 16). 
2.2 Skill Spectrum and Occupational Diversity 
2.2.1 Evidence placed before the Committee indicates that tourism employment spans the full skill 
spectrum. Entry-level roles include frontline service staff, site attendants, junior guides, and basic 
hospitality workers. Mid-level roles encompass supervisors, destination coordinators, senior guides, tour 
managers, and operations executives. Senior roles include destination strategists, policy advisors, 
institutional leaders, educators, and technology specialists. 
2.2.2 The Committee observes that many tourism roles require a combination of technical, cognitive, 
and interpersonal skills. Knowledge of history, culture, and geography must be complemented by 
communication ability, emotional intelligence, problem-solving capacity, and ethical judgement. 
Increasingly, digital literacy and familiarity with technology platforms are also becoming essential across 
roles, enhanced by digital training platforms (Recommendation 11). 
2.2.3 The Committee further notes that traditional training frameworks have focused predominantly on 
operational competencies, often neglecting higher-order skills such as interpretation, narrative building, 
leadership, and strategic planning. This imbalance constrains the sector’s ability to move up the value 
chain and deliver premium experiences, addressed by anchoring tourism knowledge in universities 
(Recommendation 4). 
2.3 Organised Workforce: Institutions and Outcomes 
2.3.1 The organised segment of the tourism workforce is primarily supplied by institutions under the 
Ministry of Tourism and allied Ministries. These include Institutes of Hotel Management, Indian Institute 
of Tourism and Travel Management, Indian Culinary Institute, and affiliated universities and private 
institutions. 
2.3.2 The Committee acknowledges the historical contribution of these institutions in creating a skilled 
hospitality workforce and establishing India’s reputation in global hospitality markets. Alumni from these 
institutions occupy leadership positions in domestic and international organisations, demonstrating the 
foundational strength of the system. 
2.3.3 At the same time, the Committee notes emerging challenges. Several institutions report declining 
enrolment, vacant seats, and reduced student interest in traditional programmes. Stakeholders attributed 
this trend to wage compression at entry levels, long working hours, limited work-life balance, and unclear 
career progression pathways, mitigated by CSR-linked internships (Recommendation 19). 
2.3.4 The Committee is of the view that without structural reforms in curriculum design, professional 
recognition, and career architecture, the organised training system risks losing relevance among younger 
cohorts, through industry-academia linkages (Recommendation 30). The Committee acknowledges the 
inputs received from industry associations including FHRAI, IATO, Hotel Association of India (HAI), 
and ATOAI on workforce challenges, skill gaps, attrition patterns, and industry expectations. The 
evidence on entry-level wage structures, career progression bottlenecks, and changing operational 
requirements informed the Committee's recommendations on professional cadre structures, career 
pathways, and mid-career training frameworks.The Committee is concerned that existing institutional 
capacity, estimated at around 25,000 learners at a given time across MoT‑linked institutions, is not 
commensurate with projected employment needs and therefore cannot on its own shift the sector from 

5 
 
informality to professionalism. 
2.4 Unorganised Workforce and Informality 
2.4.1 A significant proportion of tourism-related human interfaces operate in the unorganised sector. 
These include informal guides, seasonal facilitators, local transport providers, community elders, artisans, 
and gig-based tourism workers. 
2.4.2 The Committee recognises that many individuals in the unorganised segment possess deep local 
knowledge, linguistic ability, and cultural familiarity. Their exclusion from formal frameworks is not due 
to lack of capability but due to structural barriers such as educational prerequisites, geographic distance 
from training centres, cost of certification, and limited access to information, formalised via national 
online platforms for micro-guides (Recommendation 18). 
2.4.3 The persistence of informality has multiple consequences. It creates income instability for 
workers, limits accountability, and exposes tourists to inconsistent or unethical practices. The Committee 
emphasises that informality should be addressed through inclusion and professionalisation rather than 
punitive measures, including incentives for training investment (Recommendation 34). 
2.5 Wage Structures and Career Progression 
2.5.1 The Committee notes that wage structures in the tourism sector remain a critical area of concern. 
Entry-level wages are often low relative to working hours and job demands. In the absence of transparent 
career ladders, many skilled workers exit the sector within a few years, leading to high attrition and loss 
of institutional memory. 
2.5.2 Evidence indicates that the absence of formal mid-career training and leadership development 
contributes significantly to stagnation. Workers often remain confined to operational roles without 
opportunities to transition into supervisory or strategic positions. 
2.5.3 The Committee is of the view that tourism must be restructured as a career, not merely a job. This 
requires defined progression pathways, recognition of experience through certification, and access to 
periodic skill upgradation linked to promotion and remuneration, as in clear career pathways 
(Recommendation 6). 
2.6 Proposal for a Structured Professional Cadre 
2.6.1 In view of the above, the Committee proposes structuring the tourism workforce into a formal 
National Tourism Professional Cadre, comprising multiple functional streams including a specialised 
Knowledge and Interpretation Stream. This framework is intended to provide clarity of roles, standardise 
competencies, and create transparent progression pathways across the sector, per Recommendation 5. 
2.6.2 The proposed cadre structure includes three broad levels: 
● Entry Level: Professionals equipped with foundational education in tourism, hospitality, or 
heritage, combined with mandatory institutional attachments and site-based training. 
● Mid-Career Level: Experienced professionals responsible for team leadership, destination 
coordination, and complex operations, supported by structured management training and 
certification. 
● Senior Leadership Level: Strategists, policy contributors, institutional leaders, and mentors 
responsible for destination planning, policy formulation, and international engagement. 
2.6.3 Progression between levels is envisaged to be competency-based rather than time-bound. Periodic 
assessment, refresher training, and evaluation through practical assignments are considered essential to 

6 
 
maintain professional standards, aligned with continuous upskilling (Recommendation 29). 
2.7 Mid-Career Training and Continuous Learning 
2.7.1 The Committee observes that continuous learning is critical in a sector characterised by changing 
visitor expectations, technological evolution, and regulatory frameworks. Mid-career training must 
therefore be institutionalised rather than left to individual initiative, via national apprenticeship 
programmes (Recommendation 20). 
2.7.2 The Committee supports the development of structured mid-career management programmes in 
partnership with reputed institutions. Such programmes should focus on leadership, crisis management, 
sustainability, digital transformation, and ethical decision-making. 
2.7.3 Mandatory refresher courses at defined intervals are considered necessary to ensure that certified 
professionals remain updated with new developments, including archaeological discoveries, regulatory 
changes, and emerging technologies. 
2.8 Addressing Geographic and Demand Mismatch 
2.8.1 The Committee notes a mismatch between the geographic distribution of trained professionals 
and areas of tourism demand. High-potential destinations often face shortages of trained personnel, while 
some regions with limited tourism activity produce surplus graduates. 
2.8.2 The Committee emphasises the need for national-level placement coordination, mobility 
incentives, and region-specific training programmes to address this imbalance. Decentralised training 
delivery combined with centralised standards is considered the optimal approach, including border-area 
tourism skills (Recommendation 27). 
2.9 Observations 
2.9.1 The Committee observes that the tourism workforce landscape reflects both opportunity and 
vulnerability. While tourism has the capacity to generate large-scale employment, its human capital 
framework remains fragmented and under-institutionalised. 
2.9.2 Professionalisation of the workforce through structured education, certification, career pathways, 
and continuous learning is essential to enhance service quality, restore trust, and improve economic 
outcomes. 
2.9.3 The Committee is of the view that reforms in the workforce landscape form the foundation upon 
which institutional, technological, and ethical interventions discussed in subsequent chapters must be 
built. 
3 Unorganised Guides and Informal Human Interfaces 
3.1 Significance and Nature of Informal Human Interfaces 
3.1.1 The Committee observes that informal human interfaces constitute a substantial and visible 
component of India’s tourism ecosystem. At many destinations, particularly heritage sites, religious 
centres, rural circuits, and emerging tourist locations, the first point of contact for visitors is often an 
individual operating outside formal institutional frameworks. 
3.1.2 These informal actors include site‑based guides, seasonal facilitators, community elders, local 
language interpreters, transport intermediaries, and gig‑based tourism workers. Their modes of 

7 
 
engagement vary, but collectively they shape visitor experience, perception, and trust. 
3.1.3 The Committee is of the considered view that such interfaces should not be approached solely as 
a regulatory challenge. They represent a reservoir of local knowledge, cultural familiarity, and lived 
experience that formal systems have not fully harnessed. Exclusion of this workforce from structured 
frameworks has resulted in both economic inefficiency and reputational risk, which the Committee seeks 
to address through systematic integration of informal knowledge holders (Recommendation 15). 
3.2 Typology of Unorganised Guides and Facilitators 
3.2.1 Based on evidence received, the Committee identifies multiple categories within the unorganised 
guiding and facilitation ecosystem: 
3.2.2 Site‑based informal guides operate at specific monuments, temples, museums, and natural 
attractions. Many possess inherited or self‑acquired knowledge but lack formal certification. 
3.2.3 Seasonal and event‑based facilitators emerge during festivals, pilgrimage seasons, and peak 
tourist periods. Their engagement is demand‑driven and often temporary. 
3.2.4 Community custodians and cultural practitioners, including village elders, tribal leaders, artisans, 
and performers, provide authentic insights into local traditions, folklore, and intangible heritage. 
3.2.5 Language facilitators assist visitors in multilingual regions, particularly where formal guides with 
requisite language skills are unavailable. 
3.2.6 Gig‑based tourism workers, often using digital platforms or informal networks, provide sporadic 
services such as walking tours, food trails, and experiential activities. 
3.2.7 The Committee notes that this diversity reflects the organic evolution of tourism livelihoods. Any 
formalisation strategy must therefore be flexible and context‑sensitive, including through national online 
platforms for micro‑guides (Recommendation 18). 
3.3 Structural Causes of Persisting Informality 
3.3.1 The Committee examined the reasons underlying the persistence of informality in tourism 
guiding and facilitation. 
3.3.2 High barriers to entry, including rigid educational prerequisites and centralised training 
requirements, exclude individuals with substantial practical knowledge but limited formal schooling. 
3.3.3 Language and literacy constraints further limit participation, as many certification programmes 
are delivered primarily in English or Hindi without adequate regional language support. 
3.3.4 Geographic concentration of training institutions creates access challenges for individuals in 
remote, border, or rural areas. Travel and accommodation costs act as deterrents. 
3.3.5 In some locations, informal monopolies and exclusionary practices restrict entry into formal 
guiding systems, perpetuating parallel informal arrangements, which can be reduced through national 
digital platforms for tourist–guide matching (Recommendation 17). 
3.3.6 The Committee also notes that the absence of clear pathways from informal engagement to 
formal recognition discourages voluntary participation in certification processes. 
 

8 
 
3.4 Consequences of Informality 
3.4.1 The Committee observes that persistent informality has multiple adverse consequences. Members
