CHAPTER 6 
Detailed Observations and Recommendations 
The Committee, having scrutinised the Demands for Grants (2026-27), the Ministry's 
written submission to the Committee's questionnaire, the Ministry's depositional notes, the 
Annual Report (2025-26), the Annual Action Plan, the Output-Outcome Monitoring 
Framework, and the oral evidence of the representatives of the Ministry, place on record the 
following observations and recommendations. 
6.1 Financial Management and Budgetary Discipline 
6.1.1 Observation 1 — Overall Budgetary Architecture and Absorptive Capacity: 
The Committee scrutinised the Detailed Demands for Grants and note that the net allocation 
of          Rs. 5,164.80 crore represents a 78 per cent increase over the RE of Rs. 2,899.11 crore 
for 2025-26. Rs. 1,765 crore (34 per cent of net GBS) is directed towards SBFAS, SbDS, and 
MDF, schemes approved by Cabinet on 24th September 2025, with operational guidelines 
released only on 26th December 2025. The combined corpus of these three schemes over the 
decade to 2036 is approximately Rs. 69,725 crore. The Ministry's written submission 
discloses that actual expenditure in 2025-26 stood at Rs. 2,329.86 crore as on 31st January 
2026 against  BE of Rs. 3,470.58 crore. The Committee further note from the Output-
Outcome Monitoring Framework that the OOMF designates 'Target not amenable' for 
virtually all quantitative indicators under SbDS and SBFAS, raising the question of how 
absorption will be monitored in the absence of measurable output benchmarks. 
6.1.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a phased 
disbursement plan for the first year of SBFAS, SbDS, and MDF operations, with quarterly 
milestones tied to specific operational readiness benchmarks including scheme portal 
operationalisation, application pipeline development, appraisal infrastructure, and fund 
release triggers. An inter-divisional Task Force may be constituted to monitor the roll-out of 
these schemes and identify absorptive capacity gaps in real time rather than at year-end. 
6.1.3 Observation 2 — Realism of Budget Estimates and Expenditure Pattern: As 
examined from the documents received from the Ministry, the depository statement for 
2025–26 reveals that the 2025-26 BE was contracted by 16.5 per cent at RE, with only 71 per 
cent of RE expended by 31st December 2025 (updated to 80.4 per cent as at 31st January 
2026). In the two preceding years, the BE was revised upward by 7.9 per cent and 20.2 per 
cent respectively. In Sagarmala, Actuals of Rs. 658.29 crore fell short of RE by Rs. 50.71 
crore. Such oscillation between over-estimation and under-utilisation points to systemic 
deficiencies in the Ministry's internal budget estimation methodology. The Committee 
further note that the Ministry furnished no analysis of the reasons for variation in its 
statement, with multiple entries showing, suggesting inadequate quality control in the 
preparation of budgetary documentation itself. 

 
16 
 
6.1.4 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry institute a 
structured monthly expenditure tracking mechanism for each major head, consonant with 
the Modified Cash Management System of the Department of Expenditure. The internal 
estimation process may be redesigned as a bottom-up exercise drawing on implementing 
agencies' quarterly fund absorption plans, rather than a top-down normative allocation 
model, so as to produce estimates that are realistic at inception rather than requiring 
substantial mid-year correction. 
6.1.5 Observation 3 — Revenue-Capital Composition and Subsidy-to-Asset 
Conversion: The Committee note that the Revenue Section constitutes 77.5 per cent of the 
gross Demand, a structural feature driven by the subsidy character of SBFAS. The Ministry's 
written submission furnished that SBFAS provides financial assistance of 15-25 per cent per 
vessel to make construction viable. The Ministry's depositional notes further record that the 
shipbreaking credit note provides 40 per cent of fair scrap value. The Committee observes 
that the predominance of revenue expenditure in a sector requiring massive infrastructure 
creation warrants systematic tracking of whether each tranche of revenue subsidy is 
generating verifiable capital-asset creation in the form of delivered gross tonnage. 
6.1.6 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a Subsidy-to-Asset Conversion Index for the SBFAS programme, tracking 
the relationship between each tranche of financial assistance disbursed and the 
corresponding shipbuilding capacity commissioned, measured in gross tonnage. Such an 
index, published annually alongside the OOMF, would strengthen expenditure-outcome 
accountability for the single largest revenue head in the Demand and provide the Committee 
with a structured basis for future scrutiny. 
6.1.7 Observation 4 — IEBR Monitoring and Port Authority Financial Health: 
The IEBR of Rs. 12,702.94 crore is approximately 2.5 times the GBS. The Ports and 
Lighthouses sector relies on IEBR of Rs. 11,944.07 crore against GBS of Rs. 841.74 crore. 
While this leveraging model reduces the fiscal burden on the Consolidated Fund, the 
Committee observes that it creates a structural gap in parliamentary oversight, since the 
IEBR does not form part of the Demand and is not subjected to the same degree of scrutiny 
as GBS allocations. 
6.1.8 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to include a comprehensive annexure on the IEBR of Major Port Authorities in future 
Demands for Grants documentation, furnishing project-wise allocations, expenditure, and 
outcome indicators, so as to provide Parliament with a complete picture of public and quasi-
public investment in maritime infrastructure. 
6.1.9 Observation 5 — Settlement of Audit Observations: Fifteen CAG paras were 
settled and 14 remain pending as on 31st January 2026. All 10 PAC paras were settled. The 
continued pendency of 14 CAG paras warrants sustained institutional attention, particularly 
given the transformative scale of new schemes being operationalised. 

 
17 
 
6.1.10 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry constitute a 
dedicated Audit Para Settlement Cell with monthly progress reviews, establishing a 
structured workflow for each pending para with clear internal accountability assigned to the 
concerned Division. 
6.2 Port Infrastructure, Connectivity and Capacity Utilisation 
6.2.1 Observation 6 — Port Capacity Utilisation and the Capacity-Throughput 
Disparity: The Committee scrutinised the Ministry's written submission and the Annual 
Report and note that 145 out of 283 berths at Major Ports are fully mechanised, handling 
approximately 78 per cent of total cargo, with a mechanisation target of 93 per cent by 2030. 
The written submission discloses that cargo handling capacity at Major Ports has increased 
from 800.52 MTPA in 2013-14 to 1,681 MTPA in 2024-25 (an increase of 110 per cent) and 
berth productivity has risen from 12,468 tonnes in 2013-14 to 18,304 tonnes in 2024-25 (47 
per cent increase). Total national port handling capacity, including other-than-major ports, 
has risen from 1,400 MTPA to 2,771 MTPA. Notwithstanding these gains, aggregate cargo 
throughput of 854.86 MMT at Major Ports in 2024-25, when juxtaposed against 57 PPP 
projects contributing approximately 660 MTPA of additional capacity, indicates that a 
significant proportion of installed capacity remains dormant. The Chairman of Paradip Port 
Authority confirmed during oral evidence that capacity utilisation at Major Ports is 
approximately 50-60 per cent. This structural under-utilisation represents both an 
opportunity cost and a challenge to the investment rationale underlying further large-scale 
capacity additions such as Vadhvan (Rs. 76,220 crore) and ICTP Great Nicobar (Rs. 99,000 
crore). 
6.2.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry commission a 
comprehensive Port Capacity Utilisation Audit across all 12 Major Ports, disaggregated by 
berth type, cargo category, and connectivity modality, to identify the specific bottlenecks 
that account for the under-utilisation. Such an audit, if integrated with the Port Master 
Planning process, would enable targeted interventions that improve throughput on existing 
infrastructure before committing to further capacity creation. 
6.2.3 Observation 7 — Last-mile Road and Rail Connectivity and Logistics Cost 
Reduction: The Committee noted from the Annual Report that the Sagarmala Port 
Connectivity pillar encompasses last-mile rail and road enhancements for faster evacuation. 
The Haridaspur-Paradip Railway Company Ltd., an SPV, is operational and yielding 
dividends. IPRCL provides rail evacuation at several Major Ports. The Committee also 
observed that a consolidated assessment of port-wise connectivity status, classifying each 
Major Port's road and rail linkage as adequate, under construction, or deficient, was not 
placed before the Committee. During oral evidence, the Ministry was unable to state the 
number of Major Ports with 100 per cent modular ship-to-rail transfer connectivity and 
committed to furnish the details in writing. The absence of such an assessment impedes a 
systematic evaluation of whether the single largest structural impediment to port utilisation, 
namely evacuation infrastructure, is being addressed with adequate priority and 

 
18 
 
coordination with the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and the Ministry of 
Railways. 
6.2.4 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry should prepare a 
comprehensive Port Connectivity Scorecard for each Major Port, benchmarking road (lane 
count, NHAI status), rail (last-mile connectivity, DFC linkage), and waterway access against 
a defined adequacy standard. The Ministry may further wish to explore modular ship-to-rail 
transfer facilities at high-volume ports as a mechanism for reducing container dwell time 
and transshipment costs, directly addressing the logistics cost imperative. 
6.2.5 Observation 8 — JNPA-Dedicated Freight Corridor Connectivity: The 
Committee noted from the oral evidence that JNPA, India's largest container port handling 
approximately 10 million TEUs, has not yet been connected to the Dedicated Freight 
Corridor. The Ministry's Additional Secretary submitted that JNPA has completed its yard 
infrastructure but that the Railway portion has been delayed due to land issues, with a 
revised timeline of April 2026. A Member noted that the DFC was connected to Mundra in 
Gujarat, contributing to Mundra's rising market share relative to JNPA. The Committee 
observes that the absence of DFC connectivity to JNPA over a prolonged period has had 
significant implications for the port's competitiveness and for logistics costs on the western 
corridor. 
6.2.6 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry pursue the JNPA-
DFC connection as a matter of the highest priority and furnish a status report to the 
Committee. The Committee further recommend that the Ministry undertake a logistic cost-
impact assessment of the DFC connectivity delay on JNPA's competitive position vis-a-vis 
other western coast ports. 
6.2.7 Observation 9 — Vessel Turnaround Time and Operational Efficiency: The 
Ministry, in its written submission, records that average turnaround time at Major Ports has 
improved from 93.6 hours in 2013-14 to 49.5 hours in 2024-25, a reduction of 47 per cent. 
The Committee note from the oral evidence that the Special Secretary cited an average of 
28.5 hours, which appears to use a different measurement methodology. Nevertheless, the 
Annual Report discloses that turnaround times continue to vary widely across ports, from 
approximately 26.35 hours at JNPA to over 81.73 hours at SMP Kolkata, and that the 
container vessel turnaround time was 41.76 hours. SMP Kolkata has commenced night 
navigation in the upper Hooghly to reduce turnaround and pre-berthing delays. The 
Committee observes that turnaround time is a composite indicator encompassing berth 
availability, crane productivity, documentation clearance, pilotage, and evacuation 
infrastructure, and that the wide variance across ports suggests that best practices are not 
being systematically disseminated. 
6.2.8 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry establish Port 
Turnaround Time Reduction Targets for each Major Port, benchmarked against 
international comparators, with specific interventions mapped to each component of the 
turnaround cycle. The Ministry may further wish to standardise the measurement 
methodology for turnaround time across all reporting platforms. The ONOP initiative, by 

 
19 
 
standardising documentation and reducing transaction volumes, provides a strong platform; 
turnaround time tracking may be integrated into the ONOP digital architecture so as to 
generate real-time port performance dashboards. 
6.2.9 Observation 10 — Berth Mechanisation and PPP Award Rates: The 
Committee note that 49 PPP projects worth Rs. 51,093 crore have been approved since 2019-
20, of which only 25 projects valued at Rs. 13,355 crore (26 per cent of investment value) 
have been awarded. The 24 unawarded projects, representing Rs. 37,738 crore, constitute a 
significant pipeline blockage. The Committee observes that where berth mechanisation is the 
binding constraint on throughput, a finding consistent with the wide turnaround time 
variance noted in Observation 9, the pace of PPP award directly constrains the capacity 
utilisation improvement. 
6.2.10 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to conduct a diagnostic review of the 24 approved-but-unawarded PPP projects, 
identifying patterns in bidding failures, investor reluctance, or concession design 
shortcomings. A Berth Modernisation Programme that sequences PPP awards by 
productivity impact, prioritising ports where mechanisation would yield the greatest 
improvement in berth-day output, would constitute a structured response. 
6.2.11 Observation 11 — Sagarmala Programme Implementation Pace: As 
examined from the ministries documents, 839 Sagarmala projects with estimated 
investment of Rs. 5.79 lakh crore, 277 (33 per cent) have been completed after 
approximately a decade. The 353 projects (Rs. 2.75 lakh crore) still at the planning stage 
constitute 47 per cent of total investment. The Ministry's written submission further records 
that of 272 port connectivity projects (144 road and 128 rail), only 17 road projects worth Rs. 
8,947 crore (adding 473 km) and 57 rail projects worth Rs. 40,329 crore (adding 2,771 km) 
have been completed, while 91 road projects (Rs. 56,824 crore) and 41 rail projects (Rs. 
23,199 crore) remain at the planning stage. The completion rate requires substantial 
acceleration if the Programme's 2035 objectives are to be realised. 
6.2.12 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry conduct a 
comprehensive mid-term review of the Sagarmala Programme, categorising projects by 
implementation stage, sector, and region, and identifying systemic bottlenecks in the 
transition from planning to implementation. A differentiated project acceleration strategy 
may be adopted, fast-tracking connectivity and port modernisation projects that bear 
directly on logistics cost reduction and port utilisation. The Committee further recommend 
that the Ministry furnish a State-wise status of Sagarmala project implementation and fund 
release. 
6.2.13 Observation 12 — Vadhvan Port and ICTP Great Nicobar: Inter-
ministerial Coordination: Vadhvan Port (Rs. 76,220 crore) received Cabinet approval on 
19th June 2024; pre-construction has commenced but the breakwater tender awaits security 
clearance. ICTP Great Nicobar (Rs. 99,000 crore) received Environmental Clearance in 
November 2022 but the PPPAC proposal was forwarded to DEA only on 31st December 
2025. The Committee observes that these two mega-projects, representing combined 

 
20 
 
investment of approximately Rs. 1.75 lakh crore, are critically dependent on the pace of 
inter-ministerial clearances. 
6.2.14 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to establish dedicated Project Management Units for each mega-project, with 
fortnightly progress reviews, so that inter-ministerial requirements are resolved on a 
concurrent rather than sequential basis. 
6.3 Shipbuilding, Ship Repair, Recycling, and Dredging 
6.3.1 Observation 13 — Shipbuilding Capacity Gap and Indian Ownership 
Deficit: The Committee scrutinised the Ministry's depositional notes and noted that India's 
annual shipbuilding output of 0.1 million GT constitutes less than 1 per cent of global 
capacity. Only 5 per cent of India's EXIM cargo is carried by Indian-owned or Indian-flagged 
vessels, and Indian-built ships account for merely 7.63 per cent of Indian-owned ships. 
Against comparators such as China (33 million GT), Korea (25 million GT), and Japan (16 
million GT), India's position is marginal. The Ministry's written submission confirms that 
Indian shipyards face a 25-30 per cent cost disadvantage due to higher financing costs, 
limited economies of scale, and gaps in advanced technology. The employment multiplier of 
6.4 and the investment multiplier of 1.82 underscore the sector's economic significance, yet 
the forty-five-fold expansion required to achieve the MAKV 2047 target of 4.5 million GT 
represents a challenge of unprecedented magnitude. 
6.3.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry may develop a 
transparent order-flow projection framework under SBFAS that provides a region-wise and 
capacity-wise assessment of shipbuilding opportunities, including the anticipated share of 
eastern India's shipyards (GRSE, Hooghly-CSL) and the southern facilities (CSL, Goa 
Shipyard). The National Shipbuilding Mission, once constituted, may design a dedicated 
MSME Vendor Development Programme to map supply chain ecosystems around major 
yards, identify gaps, and create a searchable digital registry of qualified vendors to facilitate 
local sourcing and employment generation. 
6.3.3 Observation 14 — National Shipbuilding Mission: Constitution and 
Mandate: The NSbM, designated as the institutional response to coordinate SBFAS 
implementation, has not yet been formally constituted despite Rs. 515 crore having been 
allocated for SBFAS and NSbM in 2026-27. The OOMF designates 'Target not amenable' for 
all indicators. The Ministry's written submission records that the India Ship Technology 
Centre is to be established under IMU with a proposed financial outlay of Rs. 305 crore to 
serve as the apex body for indigenous design capabilities, shared ship-design tools, 
specialised software, high-end computing, and R&D support. ISTC is similarly at the 
conceptual stage. The Committee observes that the absence of the nodal coordinating body 
creates a governance vacuum at precisely the moment when the three largest new schemes 
in the Demand are seeking to commence operations. 

 
21 
 
6.3.4 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry expedite the 
constitution of the NSbM with a mandate encompassing not only scheme implementation 
but also long-term demand forecasting, so that the Mission serves as a market intelligence 
and coordination body. The ISTC may be designed as a centre of excellence for ship design 
innovation, with formal collaboration agreements with international classification societies 
and research institutions. 
6.3.5 Observation 15 — Container Manufacturing Scheme and Coastal Cargo 
Promotion: The Committee note from the oral evidence that the Budget 2026-27 
announced a Rs. 10,000 crore Container Manufacturing Scheme over five years to scale 
domestic container production capacity from approximately 70,000 to 7 lakh containers 
annually, and a Coastal Cargo Promotion Scheme targeting an increase in the modal share of 
IWT and coastal shipping from 6 per cent to 12 per cent by 2047. The Ministry confirmed 
that the Container Manufacturing Scheme is at the development stage and will provide 
financial assistance to incentivise private sector manufacturing. The Committee observes 
that both schemes address critical supply-side gaps and warrant timely formulation and roll-
out. 
6.3.6 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry finalise and 
operationalise both the Container Manufacturing Scheme and the Coastal Cargo Promotion 
Scheme within the current financial year. For the Container Manufacturing Scheme, the 
Ministry may develop clear eligibility criteria, a transparent incentive structure, and 
measurable annual targets for domestic container production. For the Coastal Cargo 
Promotion Scheme, a baseline measurement of the current 6 per cent modal share and 
intermediate annual targets leading to 12 per cent by 2047 may be established to enable 
structured monitoring. 
6.3.7 Observation 16 — Dredger Procurement and Deployment: The Committee 
note from the Annual Report that the DCI is procuring 11 dredgers at Rs. 3,775 crore. 
Dredging is a critical prerequisite for both cargo operations and cruise navigation in the 
Hooghly River system. SMP Kolkata's initiation of night navigation in the upper Hooghly 
underscores the operational pressure on this waterway. The Committee also observe that the 
documentation does not specify the port-wise or waterway-wise deployment plan for the 11 
new dredgers. During oral evidence,  Members raised concerns about DCI's accountability 
for river dredging, questioning how dredging outcomes are measured and verified, 
particularly in rivers with high sedimentation loads where annual silt replenishment may 
negate dredging efforts. 
6.3.8 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a 
Dredger Deployment Strategy specifying the allocation of the 11 new dredgers by port and 
waterway, accounting for silting characteristics, cargo growth projections, and navigational 
requirements. The Committee further recommend that the DCI develop a measurable 
dredging performance framework specifying depth targets, maintenance schedules, and 
outcome verification mechanisms. For the Hooghly-Haldia channel system, the feasibility of 
a dedicated Dredger Maintenance Hub at Kolkata, leveraging the marine engineering 

 
22 
 
ecosystem at GRSE and Hooghly-CSL, may be evaluated so as to reduce dredger downtime 
and enhance operational availability. 
6.3.9 Observation 17 — Ship Repair Ecosystem at Varanasi and Patna: As 
examined from the Ministry's depositional notes record plans for inland vessel repair 
facilities at Varanasi and Patna, prompted by the increase in NW-1 cruise vessels from 1 to 
14. The IWAI Chairman clarified during oral evidence that these are inland vessel repair 
facilities and not ocean-going ship repair yards. The existing facility at Pandu (Assam) is 
operational. The Committee observes that the absence of upstream repair infrastructure on 
NW-1 compels vessels to travel downstream for maintenance, increasing downtime and 
operating costs. 
6.3.10 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to expedite establishment of the vessel repair ecosystems at Varanasi and Patna, 
designing them as integrated vessel lifecycle support centres capable of servicing electric 
catamarans, hydrogen fuel-cell vessels, and cruise vessels. The selection of sites may take 
into account the requirement for year-round water availability, as flagged during oral 
evidence. A public-private partnership model may attract private repair operators while 
ensuring compliance with the Inland Vessels Act, 2021. 
6.3.11 Observation 18 — Ship Recycling and the Circular Maritime Economy: 
The Ministry's depositional notes state that SBFAS intends to create a circular economy by 
leveraging India's ship recycling ecosystem and providing a 40 per cent shipbreaking credit 
note. The Annual Report records that the Alang-Sosiya Safety Training Institute has trained 
over 1.5 lakh workers in hazardous material handling. The Committee observes that the 
formal integration of ship recycling into the shipbuilding value chain, where recycled steel 
and components feed into new construction, has transformative potential for India's 
maritime industrial base but requires explicit policy architecture beyond the credit note 
mechanism. 
6.3.12 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a Circular Maritime Economy Strategy that links the Alang recycling 
ecosystem with greenfield and brownfield shipbuilding clusters under SbDS. The strategy 
may map material flows between recycling and construction, establish quality certification 
standards for recycled marine-grade steel, and create incentive mechanisms for builders who 
source a minimum percentage of materials domestically, simultaneously strengthening 
India's global recycling position and reducing input costs. 
6.3.13 Observation 19 — Container Fleet Expansion and Funding Architecture: 
The Committee noted from the Ministry's written submission that the Maritime 
Development Fund comprises two distinct components: the Maritime Investment Fund (Rs. 
20,000 crore) and the Interest Incentivization Fund (Rs. 5,000 crore). A high-level 
Governing Council under the Chairmanship of Secretary (MoPSW) has been constituted, 
SMFCL appointed as the implementation agency for the IIF, and the RFP for selection of the 
MIF Fund Manager is under preparation. India's container fleet remains undersized relative 
to EXIM volumes, and the Committee observes that the distinction between VGF-supported 

 
23 
 
acquisition, MDF equity participation, and private commercial investment has implications 
for fiscal strategy, private sector investment appetite, and India's strategic interest in 
reducing dependence on foreign-flag container tonnage. 
6.3.14 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a Container Fleet Expansion Framework specifying the respective roles of 
budgetary support, VGF, MDF financing, and private equity across different vessel 
categories. The framework, designed in consultation with SCI and private operators, would 
provide investment clarity and de-risk private participation. 
6.4 Inland Waterways, Cruise Tourism, and NW Development 
6.4.1 Observation 20 — IWT Cargo Concentration and Diversification 
Imperative: The Committee scrutinised the Annual Report and note that approximately 85 
per cent of IWT cargo is concentrated on five NWs, NW-100, NW-91, NW-10, NW-1, and 
NW-4. The Ministry's depositional notes record that coal leads commodity share at 20 per 
cent. The Ministry's written submission states that 32 National Waterways are now 
operational with a combined length of 5,155 km. While concentration on high-volume 
waterways is a natural feature of network development, the Committee observes that the 
sustainability and scalability of the 500 MMT target for 2047 requires activation of a 
broader network beyond the five dominant waterways. 
6.4.2 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a tiered waterway development strategy that classifies operational 
waterways by cargo potential and investment readiness, directing concentrated investment 
towards high-potential waterways while ensuring lower-tier waterways receive foundational 
infrastructure for future commercial activation. 
6.4.3 Observation 21 — JMVP, Kalughat Terminal, and the NW-1 Corridor: The 
Ministry's written submission records that the entire 1,390 km stretch of NW-1 from 
Varanasi to Haldia is being developed under JMVP with 2.2/3 metres Least Available Depth 
and 45-metre bottom width, and that 60 community jetties have been installed and 
commissioned. The Annual Report records that the JMVP (Rs. 4,600.58 crore) targets 
completion by June 2026. Major terminals at Varanasi (1.26 MMTPA), Sahibganj (3.03 
MMTPA), Haldia (3.08 MMTPA), and Kalughat (77,000 TEU) are reported. The Farakka 
lock has reduced transit time from 2 hours to 23 minutes; cruise vessels have grown from 1 
to 14. However, as discussed in Chapter 3, the Kalughat Intermodal Terminal has not been 
operationalised despite significant investment, raising questions about the adequacy of pre-
construction hydrological assessment. The Committee further note from the oral evidence 
that a Member observed that vessel movements between Varanasi and Kolkata are 
infrequent, and that the stretch lacks the kind of regular commercial traffic that would 
characterise a functioning waterway corridor. 
6.4.4 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry may develop an 
integrated NW-1 Corridor Management Plan that brings together fairway maintenance, 

 
24 
 
terminal operationalisation (including a specific action plan for the Kalughat Terminal), 
cruise terminal development, ship repair ecosystems, cross-border protocol coordination, 
and multimodal connectivity into a single operational framework. The Committee further 
recommend that the Ministry furnish vessel movement frequency data on the Varanasi-
Kolkata stretch for each month of the current financial year, so as to enable the Committee 
to assess whether the NW-1 corridor is functioning as a commercial waterway or remains 
primarily a project-based intervention. 
6.4.5 Observation 22 — NW-5 Development and Industrial Waterway Corridor 
Model: NW-5 in Odisha (Rs. 13,865 crore; 588 km) connects the mineral-rich Talcher-
Angul-Kalinga Nagar belt to Paradip and Dhamra ports. The design specifications represent 
the most ambitious NW development outside NW-1. The Committee observes from the oral 
evidence that the integration of the historic East Coast Canal system with NW-5 could 
reduce capital costs, though the IWAI Chairman noted cross-structures and encroachments 
as current impediments. 
6.4.6 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry commission a 
dedicated feasibility study on the integration of the East Coast Canal system with the NW-5 
configuration, assessing structural condition, hydraulic compatibility, and the engineering 
requirements for commercial navigation. NW-5 may be developed as a model industrial 
waterway corridor with barge specifications and terminal designs optimised for the eastern 
corridor's cargo mix. 
6.4.7 Observation 23 — North-Eastern Waterways: Brahmaputra Tributaries 
and Over-Dimensional Cargo: During the  oral evidence, the Members submitted that 
the major tributaries of the Brahmaputra in Arunachal Pradesh should be considered for 
waterway development to facilitate over-dimensional cargo transport for hydropower 
projects of unprecedented scale. The Committee observes that the North-Eastern region 
receives Rs. 265 crore (5.1 per cent of net GBS), and that the current waterway development 
focus beyond Dibrugarh does not address the transport requirements generated by major 
infrastructure projects on the Brahmaputra tributaries. 
6.4.8 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry commission 
navigability feasibility studies for the Kameng, Subansiri, Siang, Dibang, Lohit, and Tirap 
rivers, with priority given to rivers where large hydropower projects are under construction 
or planned. The feasibility studies may assess the potential for over-dimensional cargo 
transport, seasonal navigability, and the infrastructure requirements for commercial 
activation. The Committee further recommend that the Ministry examine the Barak Valley 
route via Myanmar for its potential as an alternative connectivity corridor for the North-
Eastern region, and take steps to fulfil the commitment to establish a jetty at Pasighat. 
6.4.9 Observation 24 — River Cruise Tourism: Corridor Expansion and Cross-
border Operations: The Ministry's written submission records that 17 river cruise circuits 
are currently operational across 15 National Waterways, with flagship projects proposed for 
cruise terminals at Varanasi, Bishwanath Ghat, Patna, and Neamati Ghat. The Ministry's 
depositional notes further record 443 cruise voyages in 2024-25 across 9 States, with 

 
25 
 
operations extending to the Indo-Bangladesh Protocol route. NW-73 (Narmada) is 
operational with two concrete jetties sanctioned. The Committee note that Cochin Shipyard 
is constructing vessels for Heritage and Viking cruise operators, indicating growing 
commercial demand. 
6.4.10 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a National River Cruise Tourism Policy in coordination with the Ministry of 
Tourism and the Ministry of External Affairs, addressing: (a) the operational protocol for 
Indo-Bangladesh cross-border cruise movements including customs clearance and dredging 
coordination; (b) the development of NW-73 (Narmada) as a dedicated cruise corridor with 
jetty infrastructure at identified locations; and (c) the regulatory and safety framework for 
night-cruise and marina operations, which represent a high-value tourism product currently 
constrained by the absence of navigational lighting, anchorage protocols, and on-water 
hospitality standards. 
6.4.11 Observation 25 — Jalvahak Scheme and Modal Shift Effectiveness: The 
Ministry's written submission records that the Jalvahak scheme, launched on 15th December 
2024, provides a 35 per cent incentive to promote utilisation of IWT by cargo owners. Under 
the scheme, 12.50 million tonnes of cargo has been moved through 21 scheduled voyages, 
and scheduled waterway cargo services have commenced between Kolkata and 
Varanasi/Pandu. The OOMF targets 3,12,000 tonnes of modal-shift cargo for 2026-27. The 
Committee observes that the scheme is at an early stage and that the relationship between 
the 35 per cent incentive rate and the actual cost differential between IWT and road/rail 
transport has not been empirically established before the Committee. 
6.4.12 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to commission an independent evaluation of the Jalvahak scheme's cost-effectiveness, 
measuring the per-TKM subsidy cost against the per-TKM savings in logistics costs, carbon 
emissions, and road congestion achieved by modal shift. 
6.4.13 Observation 26 — Community Jetty Utilisation on NW-1: As noted from the 
Ministry depository documents, the 60 community jetties on NW-1, including 21 in Bihar, 
were the subject of concern during the oral evidence, regarding their actual utilisation and 
condition. The IWAI committed to furnish utilisation details in writing. 
6.4.14 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry may furnish the 
utilisation data, current condition, and GPS coordinates of all 60 community jetties on NW-
1, along with a classification of each jetty by type (HDPE, concrete floating, or steel) and by 
functional status (fully operational, partially operational, or non-functional). 
6.5 Sector Reforms and Regulatory Architecture 
6.5.1 Observation 27 — Merchant Shipping Act, 2025: Institutional 
Preparedness: The Merchant Shipping Act, 2025 reduces provisions from 560 to 325. The 
Ministry's written submission confirms that the Directorate General of Shipping is to be 
reconstituted as the Directorate General of Maritime Affairs. The Ministry submitted during 

 
26 
 
oral evidence that 46 technical rules are being framed and that the Act, along with the 
Coastal Shipping Act, was targeted for enforcement by 15th March 2026. The Committee 
observes that this transition requires institutional restructuring, subordinate rule-framing, 
capacity building, and stakeholder orientation on a significant scale. 
6.5.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a detailed 
Implementation Roadmap for the Merchant Shipping Act, 2025, specifying the sequencing 
of subordinate rules, DGMA establishment, staffing requirements, and stakeholder 
engagement. A Transition Management Committee under the Additional Secretary may 
ensure that the Act's reforms are not diluted by implementation delays. 
6.5.3 Observation 28 — Coastal Shipping Act, 2025 and Indian Ports Act, 2025: 
The Coastal Shipping Act removes licensing for Indian-flag coastal trade. The Indian Ports 
Act establishes the MSDC. The Committee observes that these Acts provide a framework for 
reducing logistics costs and improving port governance, but their efficacy depends on the 
pace and quality of subordinate legislation and institutional operationalisation. 
6.5.4 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop implementation plans for both Acts. A dedicated coastal cargo modal share 
index, measuring whether the removal of licensing translates into measurable modal shift 
from road to coastal shipping, would provide an empirical test of the reform's impact. 
6.5.5 Observation 29 — SMFCL: NBFC Transition: The Committee note that SMFCL 
was registered as an NBFC on 19th June 2025, with a borrowing limit of Rs. 25,000 crore 
and Rs. 8,000 crore approved for the current year. Lending of Rs. 4,198.10 crore has been 
sanctioned. SMFCL also received dividend income of Rs. 24.81 crore from VPRCL and 
Haridaspur-Paradip Railway Company Ltd. 
6.5.6 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop a framework for periodic parliamentary reporting on SMFCL's NBFC 
operations, including the sectoral composition of its lending portfolio, asset quality 
indicators, and developmental outcomes. 
6.5.7 Observation 30 — IIMDRC and Private Sector Engagement Architecture: 
The planned IIMDRC in Mumbai, and the PPP pipeline (48 projects, Rs. 23,000 crore) with 
PPP operators projected to handle 80 per cent of Major Port cargo by 2030, together 
indicate the Ministry's deepening reliance on private participation. 
6.5.8 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to design a structured annual Private Sector Engagement Forum and develop the 
IIMDRC drawing on international models such as the London Maritime Arbitrators 
Association and the Singapore Chamber of Maritime Arbitration. 
 
 

 
27 
 
6.6 Technology, Digital Governance, and Green Transition 
6.6.1 Observation 31 — ONOP/ONOD and MSW-Sagar Setu: The Ministry's written 
submission provides a comprehensive account of the digital governance reforms. The ONOD 
component has standardised transactions with port authorities (39 per cent reduction), port 
health organisations (77 per cent reduction), and immigration authorities (77 per cent 
reduction). As of January 2026, over 90 per cent compliance has been achieved, with 9 of 12 
Major Ports fully compliant and the remaining three expected to comply by April 2026. 
MSW-Sagar Setu covers over 60 ports and handles more than Rs. 1,000 crore in monthly 
transactions. MSW 2.0, under development, is expected to reduce data entry by 85 per cent 
and documentation by 65 per cent. 
6.6.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry may achieve 100 
per cent ONOD compliance across all 12 Major Ports and extend the framework to the top 
20 non-major ports by traffic volume. The Ministry may further measure the reform's 
impact on vessel turnaround time through a controlled before-and-after analysis at early-
adopter ports. 
6.6.3 Observation 32 — Enterprise Business System: The Ministry's depositional 
notes record that the EBS implementation reduces processes from over 1,800 to 
approximately 160 across five Major Ports. Go-Live has been achieved at Chennai Port, 
Mumbai Port, Deendayal Port, and Paradip Port. 
6.6.4 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to commission an independent assessment of efficiency gains at Chennai and Mumbai 
post Go-Live, quantifying process reduction, time savings, error rates, and user satisfaction. 
6.6.5 Observation 33 — IWT Digital Platform Integration: The Ministry's written 
submission describes the Jalyan and Navic portal as a single-window digital platform for all 
functions related to inland vessels and crews, with the registry covering over 9,000 vessels 
across 16 States. Additional platforms include Naudarshika, CarD, PANI, and LADIS. The 
Committee observes that the multiplicity of platforms creates risks of data fragmentation 
and interoperability challenges. 
6.6.6 Recommendation: He Committeeis of theconsidered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop an Integrated Digital Architecture for IWT, consolidating existing platforms 
into a unified data layer with common APIs. 
6.6.7 Observation 34 — Green Port Performance Index and Green Transition: 
The GPPI Framework was launched in October 2025. The GTTP envisages 16 green harbour 
tugs in Phase-I. Green power procurement targets 275 MW Solar PV with 1,000 MWh BESS 
via port SPVs. Green Hydrogen Hubs are at Deendayal (5 MMTPA by 2031; 1 MW plant 
commissioned July 2025), Paradip (Rs. 800 crore jetty), and VOC (2 MMTPA). India's first 
hydrogen fuel-cell vessel was launched at Varanasi on 11th December 2025, and four electric 
catamarans are operational. The Special Secretary submitted during oral evidence that 

 
28 
 
renewable energy currently accounts for 26 per cent of port power consumption, with targets 
of 60 per cent by 2030 and 90 per cent by 2047. 
6.6.8 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry publish the first 
annual GPPI rankings with port-wise improvement plans, establishing a competitive 
dynamic among Major Ports. A Green IWT Fleet Transition Roadmap with deployment 
targets for electric and hydrogen vessels by 2030 and terminal-level charging and refuelling 
specifications would complete the green transition architecture. 
6.7 Workforce Development, International Connectivity, and Heritage 
6.7.1 Observation 35 — Maritime Workforce Readiness for Shipbuilding 
Expansion: The Ministry's written submission states that the training ecosystem comprises 
IMU (6 campuses, 17 affiliated institutes), 167 MTIs approved by DGS, CEMS, DGLL, and 
NINI, and that the target for 2026-27 is to train, skill, or upskill over 38,000 candidates. 
DGS plans to train 18,700 candidates in officer and rating courses. The Ministry's 
depositional notes additionally note that under DDU-GKY through Sagarmala, 7,000 
candidates have been trained with 3,000 placed, and that GRSE has initiated training in four 
marine trade roles. The Committee observes that the forty-five-fold expansion in 
shipbuilding capacity will require an order-of-magnitude increase in skilled personnel that 
the current training infrastructure cannot support. 
6.7.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry commission a 
comprehensive Maritime Workforce Assessment quantifying skill requirements across the 
value chain arising from SBFAS, SbDS, IWT expansion, and port modernisation over the 
next decade. Shipyard-specific training academies co-located with greenfield clusters under 
SbDS would ensure that workforce development is concurrent with infrastructure creation. 
6.7.3 Observation 36 — IWT Cargo Connectivity to Nepal and Customs 
Framework: The Committee note that the development of NW-1 creates a natural corridor 
for transit cargo to Nepal. The operationalisation of this corridor requires coordinated action 
between the Ministry, the CBIC, and the Ministry of External Affairs. The IWAI Chairman 
submitted during oral evidence that a customs notification under Sections 7 and 8 is 
awaited. 
6.7.4 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry constitute an 
inter-ministerial working group with the CBIC and the Ministry of External Affairs to 
develop the operational protocol for IWT cargo to Nepal, addressing the designation of 
specific NW-1 terminals as transit cargo points. 
6.7.5 Observation 37 — National Maritime Heritage Complex at Lothal: The 
Committee note that Rs. 100.88 crore has been earmarked for NMHC at Lothal, approved by 
Cabinet on 9th October 2024. The Ministry's depositional notes describe the project as 
dedicated to showcasing India's maritime heritage, located at the site of the world's oldest 
known man-made dockyard. 

 
29 
 
6.7.6 Recommendation: He Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry may 
wish to develop the NMHC as a world-class interpretive centre combining archaeological 
preservation with interactive maritime education, drawing on international best practices. 
The NMHC may be integrated with the broader maritime tourism ecosystem, including 
lighthouse tourism (18.64 lakh visitors in 2024-25) and river cruise circuits, creating a 
national maritime heritage trail. 
6.8 Maritime Resilience and Trade Diversification 
6.8.1 Observation 38 — Maritime Chokepoint Vulnerability and India’s Trade 
Resilience Architecture: The Committee note that the escalation of security risks in the 
Red Sea, Gulf of Aden, and Strait of Hormuz since 28 February 2026 has tested the 
resilience of India’s maritime trade and energy supply architecture. India, as the world’s 
third-largest crude oil importer with an import dependency of approximately 88 per cent, is 
among the nations most exposed to chokepoint disruptions. A substantial proportion of 
India’s crude oil, LPG, and LNG imports originate from Gulf suppliers whose shipments 
transit the Strait of Hormuz. The disruption has resulted in vessel rerouting via the Cape of 
Good Hope, adding 10 to 14 days to transit times, elevating freight and insurance costs, and 
placing pressure on export competitiveness, particularly for low-margin merchandise. The 
Committee observe, however, that India’s proactive diversification strategy has yielded 
demonstrable results: approximately 70 per cent of crude imports are now routed from 
sources outside the Strait of Hormuz, up from 55 per cent previously, and India now imports 
crude from approximately 40 countries. Domestic refineries continue to operate at high 
utilisation levels. The Directorate General of Shipping has established a 24-hour control 
room to monitor Indian-flagged vessels operating in the Persian Gulf region. India’s 
combined petroleum storage capacity, including Strategic Petroleum Reserves and 
commercial stocks held by Oil Marketing Companies, provides a buffer of approximately 74 
days. While these measures demonstrate institutional preparedness, he Committeeis of 
theconsidered view that the structural exposure of India’s maritime trade to chokepoint risks 
warrants a systematic, forward-looking framework that converts crisis-response measures 
into permanent resilience architecture. 
6.8.2 Recommendation: He Committee recommends that the Ministry of Ports, Shipping 
and Waterways, in coordination with the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, the Ministry 
of Petroleum and Natural Gas, the Ministry of External Affairs, and the Directorate General 
of Shipping, develop and institutionalise a Maritime Resilience and Trade Diversification 
Framework (MRTDF) as a permanent component of India’s maritime policy architecture. 
The Committee note with appreciation the Government’s decisive measures in diversifying 
crude sourcing and securing alternative supply chains. Building upon these gains, the 
Framework may encompass the following pillars: 
(a) Targeted Cost Relief and Trade Facilitation: He Committee recommends 
calibrated and time-bound support measures to shield exporters from transient cost 
escalation. These may include partial underwriting of war-risk premiums for Indian-flagged 
vessels through a dedicated Maritime Risk Pool operated by SMFCL; extension of export 

 
30 
 
obligation compliance timelines for EPCG and Advance Authorisation holders affected by 
rerouting delays; facilitation of enhanced working capital limits through coordination with 
trade finance institutions; and a structured relief framework for port-related charges on 
delayed cargo, including demurrage waivers and container detention fee adjustments at 
Major Ports. 
(b) Structural Rerouting and Alternative Maritime Corridors: He Committee 
recommends that the Ministry facilitate a structured alternate routing preparedness protocol 
for Indian shipping operators and port authorities. This may include pre-negotiated berthing 
and bunkering arrangements at key transshipment hubs including Colombo, Singapore, and 
Cape Town; bilateral maritime logistics agreements with strategic partner nations to ensure 
priority access during disruptions; and capacity assessment of India’s own transshipment-
capable ports, particularly Vizhinjam (under commissioning), Vadhvan, and ICTP Great 
Nicobar, to reduce dependence on foreign transshipment hubs in the medium term. The 
Committee further note that multimodal alternatives such as the International North-South 
Transport Corridor (INSTC) and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) 
could partly de-risk maritime chokepoint concentration, and recommend that the Ministry 
coordinate with the Ministry of External Affairs on the expeditious operationalisation of 
these corridors. 
(c) Energy Supply Resilience: He Committee recommends that the Ministry, in 
coordination with the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas, support the strengthening of 
India’s energy supply resilience. The approved Phase-II expansion of Strategic Petroleum 
Reserves at Chandikhol (Odisha) and Padur (Karnataka) under Public-Private Partnership 
merits accelerated execution. The Committee further recommend that port infrastructure at 
Major Ports be assessed and, where necessary, augmented to handle increased volumes 
arising from rerouted supply chains. India’s ongoing diversification of crude sourcing to 
approximately 40 countries represents a significant strategic gain that merits continued 
policy support. Logistical preparedness for extended maritime routes, including pre-
positioning of bunkering capacity at Indian ports, may be developed as a standing 
contingency measure. 
(d) Maritime Coordination and Risk Management Mechanism: He Committee 
recommends the establishment of a coordinated mechanism under the proposed Directorate 
General of Maritime Affairs for real-time monitoring of maritime risks, integrating vessel 
tracking, coordination with the Indian Navy’s Information Fusion Centre for the Indian 
Ocean Region (IFC-IOR), and advisory dissemination to shipowners and port authorities. 
The Committee further recommend that the Ministry examine the feasibility of a dedicated 
Marine War Risk Insurance Pool for Indian-flagged vessels. Given that only 5 per cent of 
India’s EXIM cargo is currently carried on Indian-flagged ships, the Committee observes 
that expanding the Indian-flag fleet through the SBFAS and MDF programmes acquires 
additional strategic significance in the context of chokepoint vulnerability, as dependence on 
foreign-flag tonnage during maritime disruptions exposes Indian trade to the routing 
decisions and insurance constraints of foreign operators. 

 
31 
 
Expected outcomes: The proposed Framework is expected to ensure continuity of 
essential trade flows during maritime disruptions, moderate cost pressures on exporters, 
strengthen energy supply resilience through expanded petroleum reserves and diversified 
sourcing, develop India’s own transshipment capacity, and embed maritime chokepoint risk 
management as a permanent institutional capability within the Ministry’s operational 
architecture.

recommendations contained in Chapter 6 of this Report.

INTRODUCTION 
            I, the Chairman, Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism, having been authorised by the Committee to
 present on their behalf, present this Thirty-ninth Report on the Demands for Grants 1999-2000 of the Ministry of
 Surface Transport.           
2.         The Committee at its meeting held on 26
th & 30th March,1999, considered the Demands for Grants 1999-2000
 of the Ministry of Surface Transport (Demand Nos. 78, 79 and 80) and heard the Secretary, the Ministry of Surface
 Transport on the subject. 
3.         The Committee expresses its thanks to the officers of the Ministry for placing before the Committee, the material
 and information desired in connection with the examination of the Demands for Grants of the Ministry and for giving
 evidence before the Committee. 
4.         The Committee considered and adopted the Report at its meeting held on the 8
th April, 1999.
 
 
New Delhi                                                                                                    
 PROF. VIJAY KUMAR MALHOTRA
8TH April,1999                                                                                                                 Chairman
Chaitra 18,1921(Saka)                                                                               Committee on Transport &Tourism
           
 
REPORT 
 
The Ministry of Surface Transport is responsible for the development, formulation and implementation of policies on
 road transport and inland water transport, development and modernisation of major ports, lighthouses and lightships,
 shipbuilding industries, Central Sector Road Schemes, administration of Central Road Fund and Co-ordination of
 research pertaining to road works.  Besides, the Ministry is responsible for making necessary shipment arrangements by
 chartering ships at economic and competitive rates in respect of Government owned/controlled bulk carriers.  
2.         The Ministry is administratively divided into different wings, namely roads, Ports, shipping, Road Transport,
 Chartering development and finance.
3.         The following are the subordinate offices, public sector undertakings and autonomous bodies functioning under
 the administrative control of this Ministry:-
 
SUBORDINATE OFFICES: 
1.         Directorate General of Shipping
2.         Directorate General of Lighthouses and Lightships
3.         Andaman and Lakshadweep Harbour Works
4.         Minor Ports Survey Organisations.
 
AUTONOMOUS  BODIES:
 
1.         Port Trust at Mumbai, Calcutta, Cochin, Kandla, Madras, Murmugao, New Mangalore, Jawaharlal Nehru Port
 Trust, Paradip, Tuticorin and Vishakhapatnam.
2.         Inland Waterways Authority of India
3.         National Highways Authority of India
4.         National Ship Design and Research Centre at Vishakhapatnam
5.         Dock Labour Boards at Mumbai, Calcutta, Cochin, Kandla, Madras, Murmugao and Vishakhapatnam
6.         National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers.
 
PUBLIC SECTOR UNDERTAKINGS
 
1.         Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Limited
2.         Shipping Corporation of India Limited

3.         Hindustan Shipyard Limited
4.         Cochin Shipyard Limited
5.         Hooghly Dock and Ports Engineers Limited
6.         Dredging Corporation of India Limited
7.         Indian Roads Construction Corporation Limited.
            The following three demands pertain to the Ministry of Surface Transport:
(a)        Demand No. 78: Surface Transport
(b)        Demand No. 79: Roads and
(c)        Demand No. 80: Ports, Light houses and shipping.
 
DEMAND No. 78: SURFACE TRANSORT
 
4.         This demand covers the activities related to the surface transport sector i.e. (I) road transport sector for 
 formulation of broad policies concerning road transport, motor vehicle legislation, legislation related to State Road
 Transport Corporations and movement of vehicular traffic with neighboring countries and (ii) inland water transport
 sector. Under this demand a provision of Rs. 86.39 crores has been kept for the year 1999-2000 as against Rs. 121.40
 crores at the B.E. and Rs. 100.62 crores at the R.E. stages for the year 1998-99.
 
(i)         Road Transport Sector
5.         The 8
th plan outlay for road transport sector was Rs. 264 crores. However the 9th plan outlay for this sector is
 only Rs. 77.15 crores.    The Committee was informed the reasons for this huge gap is that the working group on VIII
 plan recommended Rs. 766 crores for road transport sector.  However, allocation was made to the tune of Rs. 264
 crores only which included an allocation of Rs. 140 crores for DTC.  The working group on road transport for the 9th 
 plan recommended an outlay of Rs. 328 crores for this sector, however, the planning commission has approved an
 outlay of Rs. 77 crores. The annual plan for 1999-2000 provides for Rs. 9 crores.
 
6.         The Committee was very much surprised to know that the budgetary allocation for this important sector
 relating to road transport, which covers matters relating to road safety, control of vehicular pollution, accidents
 on roads etc., which directly effects public life, has not only been reduced for the year 1998-99 but a lesser
 amount provided during 1999=2000. The total 9th plan allocation is only Rs. 77.15 crores against Rs. 378 crores
 recommended by the working group on road transport sector as compared to Rs. 264 crores during 8th plan.
 The Committee is of the opinion that keeping in view the high rate of accidents on Indian roads and the existing
 levels of pollution especially in the metropolitan cities, this sector deserves higher allocations which would go a
 long way in making the driving safer on the Indian roads as well as for providing clean environment in the cities.
 
ROAD SAFETY AND VEHICULAR POLLUTION 
7.         The Committee was informed that there are miscellaneous schemes pertaining to road transport sector.  These
 basically comprise of Road safety programmes.  The assistance is provided in the form of grants-in-aid to various State
 Governments.  The grants-in-aid is given for taking up proposals relating  to National Highways Patrolling scheme and
 scheme for Pollution Testing Equipments.
 
8.         During the year 1998-99 a total provision of Rs. 13.00 crores was made for taking up various road safety
 programmes.  Out of these Rs. 13 crores, Rs. 4 crores was for grants-in-aid to State governments and Rs. 9 crores for
 other road safety programmes such as publicity measures on road safety.  Training of drivers in unorganised sector,
 study on transport industry, strengthening of Central Institute of Road Transport (CIRT), Pune and Research &
 Development Schemes etc.  At R.E. stage, these provisions have been reduced to Rs. 2.77 crores and Rs. 2.73 crores
 respectively.
 
9.         For 1999-2000 a provisions of Rs. 9 crores has been made in the plan budget.  Out of this Rs. 4.00 crores
 provisions has been made for grant-in-aid to State governments and two schemes viz. National Highway patrolling
 schemes an amount of Rs. 3 crores and Pollution Testing Equipments an amount of Rs. 1 crore have been kept Rs. 4.00
 crores has been provided for other road safety programmes such as publicity measures on Road Safety, Training of 
 Drivers in unorganised sector, study on Transport Industry, strengthening of CIRT Pune and R & D scheme etc.

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/39threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:02]
 
10.       The Committee was unhappy to note that despite its recommendation as contained in its 33rd Report for
 enhanced budgetary allocation for road safety measures, no action appears to have been taken by the Ministry
 to increase the amount for the said purpose and instead only Rs. 1 Crore has been provided whereas Rs. 2.5
 crores was the budgetary allocation during the year 1998-99.  The Committee further observed that with this
 meager allocation it would not be possible for the Ministry to cover all the States. The Committee, therefore,
 reiterates its earlier recommendation that amount for the purpose should be increased in order to give wide
 publicity to various road safety measures, so that the number of road accidents which are increasing day by day
 could be reduced.  The Committee further recommends that a Centrally sponsored scheme should be introduced
 for this purpose so that more and more States could enjoy the benefits of it in order to make transport system of
 their States more safer and pollution free.
 
STATE ROAD TRANSPORT CORPORATIONS
11.       The 9
th plan outlay for capital contribution to the SRTCs is Rs. 20 crores.  This scheme was dispensed with from
 the year 1993-94.  Provisions in the budget were being made to liquidate the arrears.
 
12.       The annual plan outlay under this head during 1998-99 was Rs. 3.00 crores which was reduced to Rs. 1.6 crores
 at R.E. stage.  Out of this Rs. 1.517 crores has been released to Gujarat SRTC.  The Committee was informed that many
 of the State Governments have requested for the revival of the scheme.  Realizing the need for revival of this scheme,
 the matter was taken up by the Ministry of Surface Transport with Planning Commission.  The working group on road
 transport has suggested the following criteria for granting capital contribution to SRTCs. The share of capital
 contribution for purchase of buses should be kept in the ratio of 1:2. Wherein one part i.e. 33% would be provided by
 the Central  Government and the balance 67% will have be provided for by State Governments.  In case the SRTCs
 were able to raise funds from the financing agencies, the need for getting the financial support from the State
 Government could be dispensed with.
 
13.       The Committee was informed that the above formulation which was referred to Planning Commission for
 concurrence has been rejected by it. The Committee, however, realises the need for revival of this scheme as assistance
 to SRTC’s is essential in view of the fact that their services are largely used by common man. The Committee desires
 that reasons for discontinuing the scheme may be furnished to it. However, the Committee observed that many
 States have requested for revival of the scheme, it would be appropriate if such a scheme may be revived
 especially  for the benefit of those States which are totally dependent on road transport. The Committee also
 desires that funds should be provided to those corporations, which could improve their performance if financial
 support is extended to them.
 
 (ii)       INLAND WATER TRANSPORT SECTOR
14.       The 9
th plan outlay for the Inland Water Transport sector is Rs. 408 crores.  During 1999-2000, the plan outlay
 for IWT sector is Rs. 26.04 crores consisting of Rs. 6.04 crores for Central Inland Water Transport Corporation
 (CIWTC), Rs. 20.00 crores for Inland Waterway Authority of India (IWAI) which includes Grants to Inland Waterways
 Authority of India and for other schemes such as Technical studies, research and development schemes for IWT
 personnel, interest subsidy to bank/financial institutions for loans to IWT entrepreneurs and other incentive schemes.
 
15.       During 1998-99 Ministry of Surface Transport projected fund requirement of Rs. 143.70 crores against which
 budgetary allocation made was Rs. 45.00 crores at B.E. stage which was reduced to Rs. 33.91 crores at R.E. state.  The
 amount allocated at R.E. stage was utilised fully.
 
16.       The Committee was informed that for the year 1999-2000 the Ministry of Surface Transport has projected fund
 requirement of Rs. 129.37 crores, but the budgetary allocation has been made only for Rs. 20 crores for IWAI.  This
 drastic reduction is not sufficient even to meet the requirement for the schemes which are under execution.  The IWAI
 has requested for enhancement in B.E. 1999-2000.  The Ministry of Surface Transport requested Planning Commission
 to consider enhanced allocation because in case the allocations during 1999-2000 are not increased, it  will result in set
 back in achieving the target set for the 9
th plan by the Government for IWT sector. The three waterways which are
 covered under this sector are:-

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/39threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:02]
 
(A)    National Waterways No.1
17.       Ganga-Bhagirathi-Hooghly river system from Allahabad to Haldia ( 1620 kms.) was declared as National
 Waterway  in 1986.  The waterway  is being developed for shipping and navigation and infrastructure facilities such as
 fairway terminals and Navigational aids are provided.  Loading/unloading/terminal facilities are existing at Haldia,
 Calcutta, Pakur, Farakka, Bhagalpur,Munger , Patna, Ballia and Varanasi. Public sector CIWTC and private operators
 operate vessels between Haldia and Varanasi. A provision of Rs. 5 crores has been made  during 9
th plan for setting up
 of terminals, Rs.15 crores for terminal at Gaighat, at Patna and  Rs. 3 crores for infrastructural facilities  between Patna
 and Allahabad, apart from other miscellaneous works.
 
(B)       National Waterway NO.2
18.       The river Brahmaputra from Dhubri to Sadiya (891 Kms) was declared as National waterway No. 2 in 1988.
 This  waterways runs through  Bangaladesh and Sunderbans and  links North-East part of the country with the ports of
 Calcutta and Haldia and is a very important traditional IWT route. Under an agreement with the Government of
 Bangaladesh , the CIWTC and other Indian  vessels operators ply cargo between Assam and Calcutta region making
 use of IWT transit facilities through Bangaladesh. Floating terminal facilities have been provided at Dhubri , Jogighopa
 ,Pandu, Tejpur, and Neamati and at Sadiya and Saikhowoa similar facilities would be provided during 1999-2000. A
 provision Rs.  5 crores exists for terminals during 9
th plan, Rs. 10 crores for 24 hours navigational aids, Rs. 10 crores
 for fairway improvement/conservancy  works, Rs. 4 crores for terminal maintenance, 15 crores for acquisition of
 dredgers and allied vessels and Rs. 4 crores for acquisition/replacement of survey vessels, apart from other
 miscellaneous works. 
 
(C)       National waterway No.3
19.       The West-Coast canal from Kottapuram to Kollam alongwith Champakara and Udyogamandal canals (205 Kms)
 was declared as National waterway No. 3 in 1993. The waterway composes of natural lakes, back-waters, river sections
 and manmade canal sections. The cargo handling terminal exist at Kochi port, Udyogamandal, Ambalamugal, and
 Edapallikota etc. A provision of Rs. 2 crores exists for construction and maintenance of locks, Rs. 8 crores for land
 acquisition for construction of terminals, Rs. 27 crores for capital dredging ,Rs. 1 crores for acquisition survey vessels
 and Rs. 3.21 crores for 24 hours navigational aids, apart from other miscellaneous works exists for 9
th plan period.
 
20.       A provision of Rs. 10 crores exist for development of new waterways under 9
th plan. Such waterways are,
 Sunderbans, Godavari river, Goa rivers, Bangladesh protocal routes, East Coast canal, Mahanadi and Brahmani rivers,
 Narmada river, extension of NW-3 in North and South sides, DVC canal, river Yamuna in Delhi region, Kakinada,
 Mercunam canal and Barak river.
 
21.       The Committee was informed that during first two years of 9
th plan there were drastic reductions both at BE and
 RE stages which have led to slowing down of development works for IWT sector. However, many important schemes
 for infrastructure development on three national water ways have been initiated during the first two years of 9
th plan.
 Some of these schemes are capital dredging including land acquisition for widening for narrow sections of canal in
 NW-3, procurement of hydraulic surface dredges for NW-1 and 2 and land acquisition for construction of terminal on
 NW-3, provision of 24  hrs navigational aids on certain stretches of NW-1 and NW-2, acquisition of survey launches
 for NW-2 and NW-3, permanent RCC hardware and software for hydrographic survey system etc.
 
22.       The Committee noted with concern the less budgetary allocations made in respect of IWT sector despite its
 earlier recommendations in previous reports to increase budgetary allocations to this sector. The reduced allocations
 are  inadequate to meet the targets for the development of IWT. The Committee feels that the development of
 waterways in the country which were contemplated to the share some of the load from the road/rail sector, is very slow
 due to shortage of funds and improper planning. The Committee was informed that this mode of transport is more cost-
effective than road sector. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Public Sector Undertakings may be asked to
 earmark some percentage of their Cargo for water transport sector. The Committee, further, recommends that the
 Ministry should take up the matter with regard to less allocation of grants to this sector  with the Planning Commission
 more seriously and it should be specifically underlined to the Planning Commission the significance of this important

PARLIAMENT OF INDIA
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/39threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:02]
 transport sector,  which would, if developed in time, not only lessen the burden on the road/rail sectors but also is a
 much cleaner and less polluting mode of transportation.  They may also be apprised that  the projects under IWT sector
 are moving at a snail’s pace and in order to ensure that these are completed in time without further cost overruns,  it is
 necessary that adequate allocations should be made for water transport sector.  The Committee also observed that in our
 country the IWT sector has been neglected for a long time and if the same attitude continues towards such a nature
 friendly transportation system, definitely the IWT sector will not survive. The Committee also desired that a total
 review of the IWT sector is required and suggests that both the Ministry of Surface Transport and Planning
 Commission take a realistic view and prepare such a plan so as to make a better use of this mode of transportation.
 
 
CENTRAL INLAND WATER TRANSPORT CORPORATION
23.       In 9
th five year plan, a tentative allocation of Rs. 100 crores has been made for various schemes of CIWTC.
 Budget allocation of Rs. 15.04 crores for plan schemes was provided in the financial year 1998-99 which was reduced
 to Rs. 7.30 crores at RE stage. For the financial year 1999-2000, against a demand of Rs. 10.16 crores, only Rs. 6.04
 crores has been provided. It was pointed out to the Committee  that  sufficient allocation in favour of CIWTC for its
 various schemes including repair/replacement of overage vessels, capital repair of minor terminals, modernisation of
 handling facilities of minor terminals etc., has not been provided. The Committee was also informed that CIWTC has
 incurred accumulated losses amounting for Rs. 140 crores till date.   
 
24.       The non-plan provision in BE for the year 1999-2000 for CIWTC was Rs. 8 crores. However, due to the fact that
 the deficit of the company was increasing and statutory payments had to be made, the non-plan support to CIWTC was
 increased from Rs. 8 crores to Rs. 12.05 crores in RE stage during last year. But for BE 1999-2000 a provisions of Rs.
 9.56 crores only has been made but in view of the precarious financial position of the company a minimum support of
 atleast Rs.16 crores is required. The revival package of the company is under consideration of the Cabinet. Thus non-
plan outlay of Rs. 9.56 crores for first 6 month has been acquired pending cabinet decision.
 
25.       The Committee finds that no serious attempt is being made by the Ministry of Surface Transport to turn around
 CIWTC which has been incurring losses since its inception despite its earlier recommendation as contained in its 33
rd
 report for early restructuring of the Company to that fact. The Committee, therefore, impresses upon the Ministry of
 Surface Transport to take an early decision with regard to the restructuring of CIWTC which would also give
 boost to the growth and development of IWT sector in the country.
 
DEMAND NO.79
26.       This demand covers the activities related to the construction, development and maintenance of National
 Highways, strategic and border roads, inter state roads, permanent bridges and roads of economic importance, schemes
 financed under the Central Road Fund, Bridges fees fund etc. The total amount allocated under this demand for 1999-
2000 is Rs. 3,709.54 crores against Rs. 3,431.12 crores at BE stage which was reduced to Rs. 2865.11 crores at R.E.
 stage for the year 1998-99.
 
NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
27.       National Highways consisting of 35610 Kms. constituted about 1.7% of the length of entire road net work in the
 country but carry about 40% of total road traffic. In the 8
th plan, the provision for roads sector was Rs. 2600 crores,
 against the projected requirements of about Rs. 23,000 crores, the 9th plan outlay is restricted to Rs. 7929.04 crores. An
 estimated amount of Rs. 52,000 crores is needed only for removal of various existing deficiencies.
 
28.       During the first year of 9th plan total plan expenditure was Rs. 1565.31 crores. During 1999-2000 planning

mandate vested in the Committee under Rule 270 and related provisions of the Rules of 
Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States. 
 
2. The Committee has examined the Demands for Grants of the Ministry in view of the 
central and catalytic role that Road Transport and Highway Infrastructure occupies in India's 
economic architecture. With a National Highway network exceeding 1,46,000 km and an 
annual capital outlay of Rs.  2,94,167.45 crore proposed for 2026 -27, the Ministry of Road 
Transport and Highways administers one of the largest infrastructure programmes in the world. 
The quality, pace and efficiency of its expenditure has a direct bearing on logistics costs, 
industrial competitiveness, agricultural market access, regional integration and the living 
standards of communities traversed by the national highway network. 
 
3. The Committee is of the considered view that the future trajectory of India's highway 
programme will be determined not merely by the quantum of capital mobilised but by the 
rigour with which it is planned, targeted and executed. The transition from a phase of rapid 
network expansion to one that prioritises quality assurance, long -term asset preserva tion, 
logistical efficiency and road safety represents a maturing of infrastructure policy. The 
Committee's scrutiny has accordingly been directed not only at the adequacy of financial 
allocations, but at the alignment between budgetary intent and ground -level outcomes with 
particular attention to recurring patterns of under -utilization in maintenance and research, the 
pace of completion of ongoing projects and the equity of regional distribution of infrastructure 
investment. 
4. The present Demands for Gran ts reflect several significant policy transitions. The 
introduction of Performance Based Maintenance Contracts (PBMC) as a distinct capital head, 
the closure of new project awards under Bharatmala Pariyojana in favour of need -based 
development under Nation al Highways (Original), the impending transition to cashless tolling 
through GNSS and ANPR technologies from April 2026 and the notification of the Cashless 
Treatment of Road Accident Victims Scheme, 2025 are among the substantive shifts that have 
informed the Committee's examination. The Committee has sought to assess whether these 
policy innovations are accompanied by the institutional capacity, budgetary provisioning and 
monitoring frameworks necessary for effective implementation. 
 
5. During the course of its examination, the Committee held oral evidence sessions with 
the Secretary and senior officials of the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. The 
Committee scrutinized the Detailed Demands for Grants (Demand No.86), the Annual Report 
(2025-26), the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (OOMF) 2026-27, the Salient Features 
of the Budget 2026 -27 and the Statement of Budget Estimates along with accompanying 
Remarks and Explanatory Notes furnished by the Ministry. The Committee also received 
written respo nses to a detailed questionnaire covering financial performance, scheme -wise 

iii 
 
progress and policy implementation. The Committee places on record its appreciation for the 
comprehensive documentation and oral submissions provided by the Ministry during this 
examination. 
 
6. The Committee's examination encompassed five principal thematic areas : the overall 
financial structure of the Demands and its alignment with stated policy objectives; scheme -
wise scrutiny of major programmes including National Highways (Ori ginal), NHAI 
investment, Bharatmala Pariyojana, SARDP -NE, Externally Aided Projects, Parvatmala 
Pariyojana and Multi-Modal Logistics Parks, a review of past demand versus fulfilment across 
three financial years, cross -cutting tests of budget realism, regio nal equity, efficiency of 
outcome linkage and institutional governance and a focused assessment of transport sector 
reforms including vehicle scrapping, the BH Series registration, Advanced Driver Assistance 
Systems and digital enforcement. The Committee's  observations and recommendations across 
these areas are detailed in this Report. 
 
7. This Report synthesizes evidence received from the Ministry, the detailed budgetary 
documentation and the Committee's own analysis of multi -year financial trends. It places fiscal 
prudence, outcome accountability and equitable regional development at the centre of its 
assessment. The Committee's recommendations are framed in a spirit of constructive 
engagement and are intended to support the Ministry in strengthening the p lanning, execution 
and monitoring of its programmes. The Committee expects that the Ministry will give careful 
and sympathetic consideration to these recommendations and that appropriate action taken 
notes will be communicated to the Committee in a timely manner. 
 
8. The Committee places on record its sincere appreciation of the assistance rendered by 
the officers of the Rajya Sabha Secretariat in facilitating the examination of the Demands for 
Grants and of the cooperation extended by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and 
the National Highways Authority of India in providing detailed documentation, responses to 
the Committee's questionnaire and oral submissions during the evidence sessions. The 
diligence of the Ministry's officials in placing comp rehensive data before the Committee has 
materially contributed to the depth of this examination.
