            Inland Waterways is an important mode of transport having potential for future development at places where
 Inland Traffic originate and terminates from the water front. At a time when the pollution caused by the vehicular
 traffic is playing havoc with the environment in India, the eco friendly inland waterways mode of transport can be of
 some help.  Unfortunately this important mode of transport have played little and negligible role in transportation of
 goods in India. The Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. is the only public sector undertaking, which has
 been engaged in the activity of transportation of cargo through inland Waterways in the country.  Besides it, the
 CIWTC has also been engaged in construction and repair of vessels. 
2.         The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport & Tourism, in order to have a view of
 the problems of cargo transportation by Inland Waterways, decided to examine the functioning of the CIWTC.           
 The Committee heard the Secretary, Department of Shipping, Ministry of Surface Transport and the representatives of
 Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. (CIWTC), at its meeting held on 6
th July 2000, on the “Functioning
 and Revival of Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd.” 
3.         The Committee was apprised that the Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd., was set up as a
 Government of India Undertaking on 22
nd February, 1967 after taking over the assets and certain liabilities of the
 erstwhile River Steam Navigation Company Ltd. Under the orders of Calcutta High Court on 3rd May, 1967, the
 Corporation started functioning as an independent Company under the administrative control of the Ministry of Surface
 Transport from May 1967 and commenced its business from 5
th June 1967. The Corporation, which has 2626
 employees (as on 01.04.2000) on its pay roll, is headed by a full-time Chairman-cum-Managing Director, who is
 assisted by the Board of Directors. The principal activities of the Corporation includes:
Transportation by Inland Waterways from Calcutta to Bangladesh and to Assam (NW-II) and lighterage operations on
 the river Hooghly. 
Transportation by Inland Waterways from Calcutta to Allahabad    (NW-I) 
Construction and repair of small and medium sized vessels.
 Repair of ocean – going vessels. 
Ferry and Charter, General Engineering etc.
 4.         The Corporation has its Head Office at Calcutta.  There are three main divisions viz Rivers Service Division
 (RSD), Rajabagan Dock Yard (RBD) and Deep Sea Ship Repairs Division (DSSR).
RIVER SERVICES DIVISION (RSD) 
5.         It is the main earning division of the Corporation and engaged in riverine operations in Eastern (NW-I) and in
 the North Eastern (NW-II) regions of the country through Bangladesh.  The total number of employees in this division
 is 1300. 
6.            CIWTC is presently the principal IWT operator in the country with a fleet of 19 tugs (each capable of towing 2
 nos. 750 Tonnes capacity Dumb Barges), 16 nos. (600 Tonnes capacity each) self-propelled general cargo carriers, 3
 nos. self-propelled POL Tankers having average carrying capacity of 1350 Tonnes, 58 nos. (750 Tonnes capacity each)
 Dumb Barges and 5 nos.   Over Dimensional Cargo (ODC) carriers with average capacity of 500 Tonnes. 
The fleet of the company has been deployed for operation in the following routes:
 
Calcutta – Pandu – Guwahati – Calcutta on National Waterway-II serving Dhubri – Jogigopa – Pandu river stations. 
Calcutta – Karimganj – Calcutta serving Karimganj – Badarpur river stations. 
Calcutta – Bangladesh – Calcutta serving Khulna, Mongla and Narayanganj river stations in Bangladesh. 
Haldia – Calcutta – Patna – Varanasi – Allahabad on National Waterway No.1 route serving Farakka – Bhagalpur –
 Munger – Barauni Patna and Allahabad river stations.
 Sauger, Haldia, Diamond Harbour, Calcutta for lighterage operations. 
8.         The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport & Tourism undertook the study visit
 to Calcutta and inter-alia held discussions with the representatives of the CIWTC on its functioning and performance in
 the month of June 2000. In the course of discussion the Committee was informed about the main reasons/constraints for
 poor performance and operating losses of the Corporation. The representatives of CIWTC submitted that the River
 Services Division is facing the following Operational Constraints in Inland Water Transportation sector: -
 

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/45threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:50:07]
 (1)       Lack of proper navigational aids:
 
  (a)  Channel marking: No marking in the rivers indicating the draft. 
      (b)  Draft: Absence of fair way having required draft (2 meters. LAD) to achieve further capacity utilisation of IWT
 vessels round the year. 
Night Navigational facilities: No night navigation facilities exist along NW 1 From Haldia to Allahabad. However,
 night navigation facilities, which are available for ocean going vessels from Haldia to Calcutta, cannot be used for
 movement of IWT vessels. 
 Mooring facilities: Mooring buoys are absent which are very much required during high Tides.
 Communication facilities: Vessels of the Corporation are of very old models.  No Modern Communication
 facility/technology is provided to the vessels.
 
(2) Development of Rail and Road modes of transportation: Freight charges of road & rail modes of transportation
 are cheaper than the Inland water transport. Inland Water Transport is available only for few months i.e. 6-7 months
 where as Rail & Road Transport is available through out the year. 
(3) Slower speed of movement of Vessels. 
(4) In most of the routes, cargo availability is only on one side. 
(5) Seasonal character of Rivers: Many rivers are of seasonal character and are fit for vessel movement for a few
 months of the year. 
(6) Financial constraints for development. 
(7)            Availability of special product vessels: Corporation has only two to three types of vessels. These vessels are
 not fit to transport perishable item like fish due to absence of   refrigerated rooms/cabins. Neither do they have tankers
 to carry oil/crude etc. 
(8)            Allocation of Cargo: Central Government and State Governments have not earmarked the minimum
 percentage of their cargo to Inland water transport, in spite of, many requests made by the Corporation. 
(9)        Lack of infrastructural facilities required at river terminals: Permanent jetties with mechanical handling
 arrangements, back-up space and godown, weighbridge and proper approach roads are not available at river terminals. 
9.         The continuous poor performance on account of the above factors has resulted into regular drain of scarce
 resources available with the Corporation.  As a result, the Corporation has defaulted in payment of statutory dues and
 has been dependent on non-plan support from the Government.  Various remedial measures adopted by the Corporation
 to improve its financial performance such as reduction of manpower through VRS, increased cargo handling, enhanced
 profitable lighterage operations etc., have not yet yielded the desired result.
 10.       River Services Division had also a chronic problem of contract – labour militancy, which has been successfully
 addressed to in end 1998.  Since January 1999, it has shown a consistent and sustainable level of growth.  It has
 operating offices in Calcutta and Haldia in West Bengal, Dhubri/Pandu/Guwahati/Karimganj/Badarpur in Assam, Patna
 in Bihar and Allahabad in U.P. Besides, the traditional route between Calcutta-Bangladesh-Assam,  it has opened up a
 new route in Calcutta-Allahabad stretch of river Ganga for effective exploitation of the potential of Inland Water
 Transport across Bihar and U.P. In line with the demand for survival, it has developed alternative cargo like molasses,
 stone-slabs, etc.  It is expected to handle large volume of export cargo to Bangladesh in tune with the thrust, of the 1999
 renewal of Indo-Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade, towards expansion of Bilateral trade.  This is
 expected to increase significantly IWT movement in the country. 
11.       The Committee was apprised about the Steps being Taken for better Navigation in National Waterways and
 submitted that the funds to the tune of Rs.42 crores have been made available to the Inland Waterways Authority of
 India for proper up keep of National Waterways.  The Inland Waterways Authority of India will be focusing its
 attention in maintaining 2 meter LAD from Allahabad to Haldia.  Vessels of 600 tonnes capacity can be run from
 Allahabad to Haldia for at least 330 days in a year.  
12.       The Committee is constrained to note that even after lapse of more than thirty years the Government has not
 taken adequate steps to provide proper navigational aids, which has not only affected the efficiency of River Services
 Division of the Corporation but also led to under utilization of such a cheap and eco friendly mode of transportation for
 cargo.  The Channel marking in rivers, provision of required draft of 2 meters LAD, night navigational facilities and
 mooring buoys are the main functions of Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) which is also under the
 administrative control of Ministry of Surface Transport and is responsible for regulation and development of Inland
 waterways for the purposes of shipping and navigation.  The Committee is surprised to know that after having well
 recognised the Inland Waterways as an important mode of Transport, Ministry of Surface Transport has not bothered to

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/45threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:50:07]
 provide even basic navigational facilities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Surface Transport
 should take concrete steps in this regard and instruct Inland Waterways Authority of India to provide basic needs of
 navigation in National Waterways. As the adequate funds have been made available to Inland Waterways Authority of
 India (IWAI) this year, the Committee hopes that the route from Allahabad to Haldia will be navigable and CIWTC
 will be able to establish its credibility and attract private and other agencies to put in more vessels, which will not only
 enhance utilisation of all the waterways but also the traffic of Inland Waterways will go up. The Committee further
 recommends that for providing facilities i.e. terminal facilities, handling facilities, which are not being used regularly,
 private investment should be encouraged.  The dredging handling and channel marking need be intensified to increase
 the availability of draft throughout the year.    If night navigation of the vessels of Corporation becomes possible, then
 the functioning   and performance of the Corporation will definitely go up and will make the Organisation profitable. 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that early steps be taken to provide the requisite navigational facilities.
 
VESSELS OF THE CORPORATION
 
13.       The Committee was also informed that Corporation has vessels of very old models.  No modern communication
 facility/technology has been provided to these vessels.  The Corporation also does not have sufficient number of special
 product vessels.  It has only two to three types of special product vessels. These vessels are also not fit for transport of
 perishables items like fish due to the absence of refrigerated rooms/cabins.  The Corporation does not have sufficient
 number of tankers to carry petroleum products i.e. crude oil etc. 
14.       Giving details of the fleet utilisation, the representatives of the Corporation submitted before the Committee that
 presently 58 vessels out of 143 are in operation and earning revenue.  The vessels are required to undergo statutory
 repairs over 4 years cycle. However, non-availability of adequate funds and capital repair of more than 7-8 vessels per
 year could not be undertaken for the last few years.  There is now a huge backlog of such repairs.  In view of four
 yearly statutory docking repair and maintenance, about 80 vessels could not be employed for cargo transportation. 
 Considering the future growth potential, the changes in economic prospects of Eastern Region of the Country,
 importance of Indo-Bangladesh trade vis-à-vis movement in inland water route through both the countries and in
 consideration of the primary objective of reaching Break – Even point within next 5 years, one time grant of Rs.13
 crores is considered necessary.  
15.       The Committee is of the view that the paucity of modern technology and communication facilities in the
 vessels has severely affected the functioning of the River Service Division, which is the nodal working
 establishment of the Corporation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the vessels of the Corporation
 should be equipped with modern technology and communication facilities.  The Committee also recommends
 that the adequate number of special product vessels and tankers should be made available to the Corporation so
 as to increase its expertise in transportation of perishable items and petroleum products. 
16.       The Committee is surprised to note that the out of 143 vessels, only 58 vessels of the Corporation are in
 operation.  The Ministry of Surface Transport has not provided even minimum funds required for statutory
 repairs of vessels, which resulted in non-utilisation of 80 vessels.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that for
 the maintenance and repair of vessels, the Ministry of Surface Transport should provide adequate funds, which
 will enable the Corporation to improve fleet utilisation and therefore, the Corporation should be granted, as
 requested, one time grant of Rs.13 crores for repairing work of its vessels.
 
INDO-BANGLADESH PROTOCOL ON INLAND WATER TRANSIT & TRADE

rd October, 2001.  The following are the main routes under the existing Protocol:-

20.       The Committee was informed that the Numaligarh Refinery of Assam would reach optimum production level in
 early 2001.  Considering the usage of POL in North–East, and maximum available capacity of the Railway and road
 transportation, at least half a million Ton of POL will have to be transported from the refinery to Bangladesh and West
 Bengal by river.  To achieve the same, the following steps are required: 
The refinery has to lay pipeline of approximately of 26 kms. from its premises to the river front. 
About 25 tankers of 1000 Ton capacity each have to be acquired to carry the refinery products to Bangladesh. 
 Alternatively 45 similar tankers will be required to carry the refinery products to Calcutta/Haldia. 
21.       It is the well-known fact that CIWTC is the only Indian operator engaged in inter – country traffic between India
 and Bangladesh.  Calcutta - Bangladesh – Calcutta route is navigable round the year but this also lacks night
 navigation.  However, there are some major difficulties standing in the way of optimal capacity utilization for
 movement of inter – country traffic as mentioned below: - 
As per stipulation of Indo-Bangladesh Protocol on Transit & Trade Narayanganj, Khulna, Mongla and Sirajganj are
 designated Ports of call in Bangladesh.  Ashuganj may be included in that list to increase the cargo movement to North
 – Eastern region specially Tripura for movement of foodgrain including general/containerized cargo. 
Non-availability of godown facilities adjacent to the above Ports of  call for better movement of cargo. 
Non-availability of mechanical cargo handling facilities in almost all designated ports of call in Bangladesh. 
22.       The Committee noted the value of bilateral relations with the neighbouring countries and appreciates the CIWTC
 for maintaining Indo – Bangladesh Protocol on Inland Water Transit and Trade, despite incurring loss in each voyage
 made there under to Bangladesh.  However, the Committee feels that while honouring the Indo-Bangla protocol, the
 losses of CIWTC can be reduced if the facilities of godown and mechanical cargo handling are improved.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should initiate dialogue with Bangladesh for
 providing godown and mechanical cargo handling facilities at all the designated Ports of Call in Bangladesh.  The
 matter may be taken up with Bangladesh to have Ashuganj as an additional Port of Call to facilitate the transportation
 of food grains.  The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Surface Transport should provide sufficient
 funds for acquisition of oil tankers by the Corporation as projected by it, for carrying POL products from Numaligarh
 Refinery of Assam to Bangladesh and West Bengal.  The Committee also recommends that Ministry of Petroleum &
 Natural Gas may also be approached for laying of pipeline from premises of the refinery to the river front, so that the
 potential of Corporation in POL cargo handling may be utilised.
 
CARGO AVAILABILITY TO THE CORPORATION
 
23.       It was submitted before the Committee that one of the major constraints for its development is the availability of
 single route cargo.  In all the major routes where CIWTC operates IWT vessels, only one-way cargo is available.  The
 Committee was informed that there is hardly any cargo available from Pandughat to Calcutta, Karimganj to Calcutta

B)            RAJABAGAN DOCKYARD (RBD) 
27.            Rajabagan Dockyard, the main factory establishment in Calcutta is engaged in shipbuilding and ship-repair
 activities.  Rajabagan Dockyard with around 1050 employees has a chequered history of ship-building/repair of more
 than 150 years. It has now been languishing due to extremely low orderbook position and huge fixed overhead.  It now
 only builds and repairs vessels of its sister unit RSD.  
28.       The Committee was apprised that due to lack of maintenance for years together and pending implementation of
 the proposal for modernisation of Rajabagan Dockyard under Indo-Dutch Bilateral Cooperation Programme, the
 condition of the existing facilities at RBD viz. Dry Dock, Shipways, Cranes etc. have become extremely dilapidated. 
 Considering the immediate and continuous requirement of dry-docking of a large number of vessels belonging to River
 Services Division certain minimum facilities need to be modernised at RBD. With the projected growth of RSD and its
 increasing demand for operational vessels, RBD expects to do more repairs of vessels of RSD.  It, however, is
 exploring various other sources of revenue and new customers.  Recently, it has successfully repaired a vessel of Coast
 Guard Authority.

 selling the surplus land available to it.  In this connection reduction of facilities, approximately 17.00 acres of land

33.       The Committee was informed that the principal function of this division is to undertake all types of repair work
 for ocean – going vessels belonging to SCI, DCI, various port authorities and other Government Departments.  It is a
 small division of around 100 employees with a very low asset base.  The existing DSSR division is located on CPT land
 and building.  It does not have any cost by machinery/equipment.  This unit works with only some portable machines
 and hand tools.  Due to decline in number of vessels calling at the Port of Calcutta, its traditional business of repairing
 the ocean-gong vessels has suffered.  It has now been diversifying into repair of RSD vessels and other activities.

 merged with Rajabagan Dock Yard.

 Ship Repair Division (DSSR) as a separate Division.  This can serve at the most as an extended arm of the RBD of the
 Corporation.  However, for locational advantage and to cater to vessels under repair at Calcutta Dock System, this may
 be designated as an outdoor unit of the RBD.  It will however remain under the administrative control of River Services
 Division.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the DSSR division should be merged with the Raja Bagan Dock
 Yard Division and be designated as out door unit of RBD.

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
                       
RIVER SERVICES DIVISION (RSD)
 
The Committee is constrained to note that even after lapse of more than thirty years the Government has not taken
 adequate steps to provide proper navigational aids, which has not only affected the efficiency of River Services
 Division of the Corporation but also led to under utilization of such a cheap and eco friendly mode of transportation for
 cargo.  The Channel marking in rivers, provision of required draft of 2 meters LAD, night navigational facilities and
 mooring buoys are the main functions of Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) which is also under the
 administrative control of Ministry of Surface Transport and is responsible for regulation and development of Inland
 waterways for the purposes of shipping and navigation.  The Committee is surprised to know that after having well
 recognised the Inland Waterways as an important mode of Transport, Ministry of Surface Transport has not bothered to
 provide even basic navigational facilities. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Surface Transport
 should take concrete steps in this regard and instruct Inland Waterways Authority of India to provide basic needs of
 navigation in National Waterways. As the adequate funds have been made available to Inland Waterways Authority of
 India (IWAI) this year, the Committee hopes that the route from Allahabad to Haldia will be navigable and CIWTC
 will be able to establish its credibility and attract private and other agencies to put in more vessels, which will not only
 enhance utilisation of all the waterways but also the traffic of Inland Waterways will go up. The Committee further
 recommends that for providing facilities i.e. terminal facilities, handling facilities, which are not being used regularly,
 private investment should be encouraged.  The dredging handling and channel marking need be intensified to increase
 the availability of draft throughout the year.    If night navigation of the vessels of Corporation becomes possible, then
 the functioning   and performance of the Corporation will definitely go up and will make the Organisation profitable. 
 The Committee, therefore, recommends that early steps be taken to provide the requisite navigational facilities.
(Para 12)
VESSELS OF THE CORPORATION
 
The Committee is of the view that the paucity of modern technology and communication facilities in the vessels has
 severely affected the functioning of the River Service Division, which is the nodal working establishment of the
 Corporation.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the vessels of the Corporation should be equipped with
 modern technology and communication facilities.  The Committee also recommends that the adequate number of
 special product vessels and tankers should be made available to the Corporation so as to increase its expertise in
 transportation of perishable items and petroleum products.
 
The Committee is surprised to note that the out of 143 vessels, only 58 vessels of the Corporation are in operation.  The
 Ministry of Surface Transport has not provided even minimum funds required for statutory repairs of vessels, which
 resulted in non-utilisation of 80 vessels.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that for the maintenance and repair of
 vessels, the Ministry of Surface Transport should provide adequate funds, which will enable the Corporation to improve

CHARTERING AND MANAGEMENT OF FLIGHTS FOR HAJ PILGRIMS
            India is a multilingual, multicultural and multi-religious country.  A large number of people visit religious places
 within and outside the country.  Haj pilgrimage is also one such important annual event and every year a large number
 of people from India and all over the world visit Jeddah for Haj pilgrimage.  As per Government estimates, nearly
 72,000 people from India performed Haj pilgrimage in 2000 through the arrangement of the Central Haj Committee. 
2.         Before 1995, the transportation of Haj pilgrims to Jeddah and back was undertaken by air and sea.  The sea
 transportation was through Mugal Line Limited till June 1986, after which the Shipping Corporation of India Limited
 took over.  Some difficulties were faced in the provisioning of ships for Haj operations since this caused the diversion
 of the regular ships from the mainland-island services.  As the subsidy by sea passage was more than the subsidy for air
 passage, it was considered to continue Haj operations by air alone and stop sea travel altogether and since 1995 Haj
 pilgrims are being transported to Jeddah by air only. 
3.         The Ministry of Civil Aviation, while giving the details of history of Haj operations, informed the Committee
 that as a policy, the Government of India has been subsidizing the Haj charter operations to facilitate performance of
 Haj pilgrimage even by socio-economically weaker sections of Society.  The amount charged as airfare from the
 pilgrims has more or less remained the same in the last ten years whereas the Government’s subsidy has shown a
 tremendous increase.  The information regarding the number of pilgrims, number of flights, fares and the subsidy per
 pilgrim since 1991 is as under:-

4.            However, since the last few years, there have been a lot of complaints regarding the chartering of flights,
 condition of aircraft deployed and the gross mismanagement in the facilities provided to the Haj pilgrims.  Keeping in
 view the enormity of the event and the fact that the most of the Hajis are senior citizens and that there had been a lot of
 discontentment among the pilgrims who had undertaken the pilgrimage in Haj-2000, the Committee took up the subject
 for examination and report and held discussions with the various agencies involved in the organisation of Haj
 pilgrimage.  The Committee also undertook study visits to Calcutta, Mumbai, Cochin, Chennai and other places to
 gather first hand information and interacted with the representatives of the Ministries of Civil Aviation, External
 Affairs, Air India, Airports Authority of India, Central Haj Committee, various State Haj Committees and NGOs
 working to help in organizing the Haj pilgrimage.
5.         During its deliberations with the various agencies involved with the Haj operations, State Haj Committees/NGOs
 etc. informed the Committee about the problems faced by the Haj pilgrims since the last few years.  Some of these are
 condition of aircraft, delay/dislocation of flights, lack of information to the Hajis, lack of basic amenities at airports,
 loss/mishandling of baggage, language communication problems, behaviour of cabin crew of the aircraft, late receipt of
 visa from the Saudi Arabian Embassy, communication gap between the Central Haj Committee and the State Haj
 Committees, lack of accommodation for pilgrims due to delay/cancellation of flights etc. 
6.            Regarding the management of Haj operations, the Committee was informed that the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 was handling the movement of Haj pilgrims to/from Saudi Arabia upto 1995.  However, in 1996, the Government took
 a decision enabling the Central Haj Committee to take over the function of wet leasing of aircraft from outside charter
 operators.  But the Central Haj Committee was unsuccessful in procuring aircraft for Haj operations in time and,

8.         Haj operation is not a new event.  However, it appears that the Government is still experimenting with the Haj
 operations in so far as its operation is concerned.  Allocating the management of Haj operations to the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation and then to the Central Haj Committee and again to the Ministry of Civil Aviation shows adhocism on the part
 of the Government.  The Committee feels that by now the Government agencies involved in the management of Haj
 operations must have achieved expertise to handle these operations efficiently and taking benefit thereof, sincere efforts
 are required to make the Haj operations smooth and successful.  Therefore, instead of adhoc arrangements, there should
 be some regular arrangements for undertaking Haj operations.
9.         In a reply to a point regarding evolution of chartering of aircraft for Haj operations, the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation informed the Committee that prior to 1993, Air India/Indian Airlines undertook the Haj operations by
 deploying their own aircraft.  This resulted in innumerable cancellations of the scheduled flights, badly affecting the
 image of the airline with regard to operational reliability and resulting in loss of revenue and goodwill.  Therefore, from
 1993 onwards (except 1997), the arrangements for Haj operations were made by Air India with wet leased aircraft from
 charter companies.  The following are the reasons for chartering of aircraft for undertaking Haj operations: -
The entire Haj travel operations involve a heavy volume of traffic in a limited space of time every year.  Therefore, it is
 not economical to have dedicated aircraft devoted only to Haj operations.  The aircraft are very costly equipment and
 their economic viability depends on their optimal utilization.  If aircraft are purchased and kept specifically for the
 purpose of undertaking a time limited operation, it will prove to be much more expensive exercise as compared to the
 cost of chartering.
The current requirement is approximately 2400 seats a day.  Air India cannot deploy this capacity owing to its small
 fleet size.  Further, the whole fleet is optimally deployed for economic considerations.  However, in 1997, Haj
 operations had to be undertaken by Air India with its own aircraft.  This led to massive cancellation/reduction of its
 services to various stations.  This disruption in Air India’s scheduled flights because of the Haj movement invited
 criticism from all quarters and also caused a loss of reputation/image of the Airline, which it can ill-afford. 
 Consequently, it was decided that in future, the disruption of Air India’s scheduled flights be avoided and Haj
 operations be undertaken with chartered aircraft.
The deployment of Air India’s own aircraft for Haj may also entail the modification of seat configuration of Air India’s
 aircraft to suit these operations and this modification, both costs a lot of money and also needs a sufficient time period
 of around a month.  This would imply withdrawal of Air India’s aircraft not only for the period of Haj operations, but
 also for the modification period before and after these operations.
In high tourist seasons around the world, the extra passenger loads are carried on tourist charters.  Accordingly, the
 Central Haj Committee is organizing charter operations for the Haj traffic.
10.       The Committee also had the opportunity to peruse relevant para of C&AG Report on Haj operations.  Audit

 supposed to be conducted on no-profit-no-loss basis, substantial expenditure on these operations was absorbed by Air

CHARTERING OF AIRCRAFT
12.       In a reply to a question regarding the procedure for chartering of aircraft, the Committee was informed that each
 year the Government of India constitutes the Haj Tender Committee comprising of representatives from the Central Haj
 Committee, Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of External Affairs, Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Air
 India.  The Haj Tender Committee meets to decide on the arrangements for the Haj operation and to review the
 previous performance so as to bring about improvement.  The Tender process/procedure involves inviting of tender
 offers from airlines/charter operator for wet-lease capacity to transport the Haj pilgrims by means of Tender
 Enquiry/Notice, advertisement in Flight International magazine and insertion on Air India’s web-site.
13.       The Tender offers are required to be submitted within the stipulated deadline for both the financial aspects and
 the technical aspects.  The Haj Tender Committee meets to review the tender offers received.  The offers containing
 technical bids are opened and evaluated by a team of DGCA/Air India officials.  The financial offers of only those
 parties who are found to be technically suitable are opened and the operator selected for the Haj operation is as per the
 standard tender procedures.  In case the aircraft offered by the operator are more than 15 years old, the DGCA carries
 out inspection of the aircraft with the assistance of Air India Engineering personnel to establish the airworthiness of
 these aircraft.
14.       The Committee feels that the delay in the finalisation of the tender process is one of the major factors
 responsible for the delay in finalisation of flight schedule of the Haj pilgrims.  Haj operation is a planned annual event
 and the delay in award of contract for charter operations can certainly be avoided.  The Committee recommends that
 tenders for aircraft for Haj operations should be invited in advance and agreement signed with the operator at least three
 months prior to the commencement of operations so as to avoid the consequent delays and mismanagement.
 
DELAY/DISLOCATION OF FLIGHTS
15.       The Haj movement has been in operation for a long time but till now a large number of complaints with regard
 to the various aspects of management of Haj operations keep occurring.  In this connection, the Committee enquired
 about the dislocation/delay of flights during Haj 2000.  Giving the details in this regard, the representatives of Air India
 informed the Committee that the number of pilgrims transported from India to Jeddah and back for the Haj operations
 has increased substantially from approximately 10,000 in the year 1991 to around 72,000 in the year 2000.  Thus the
 entire Haj travel operations involve a heavy volume of traffic in a limited space of time every year.  Air India has
 claimed that the transportation of over 70000 pilgrims within a limited period of around 30 days on a no-profit-no-loss
 basis tantamount to a major operation where some delays etc. on account of technical snags etc. are inherent inspite of
 maximum planning.  For Haj movement 2000, the Ministry of Civil Aviation had earlier decided to give the contract to
 the same operator as per provision contained in the agreement for 1999 Haj operation.  Subsequently, the Ministry
 decided to go in for fresh tenders in order to inject transparency in the deal.  However, after a series of deliberations,
 M/s MIDO Aviation Group, UK, the same operator who had undertaken the Haj movement-1999, was selected for
 undertaking Haj movement-2000.  The operator deployed six wide-bodied aircraft for Haj movement. 
16.       Air India have also informed that during phase-I of Haj operation 2000, there had been certain problems.  Two
 aircraft were supposed to report at Delhi reported late by two days.  As for the remedial action, Air India aircraft were
 pressed into service and operations were not allowed to delay.  The collision to one of the 747 aircraft at IGI Airport,
 Delhi had also caused delay.  Further, two aircraft collided while taxing at Jeddah, which led to dislocation of the
 service.  Again there was another dislocation, which occurred on 14.4.2000, and it was a major engine trouble after it
 landed at Cochin and for three days the Engineers of MIDO Aviation group had to work on it.  This led to four days of
 dislocation of services of aircraft meant for Haj operations from Cochin. 
17.       As regards the airworthiness of aircraft, Air India has claimed that the question of selection of any aircraft whose
 performance is even remotely suspected does not arise.  It was also informed that the Management Committee for Haj
 2001 has decided to go in for younger aircraft.  In the first tender, Air India had asked for aircraft below 15 years age,
 but they did not get any response.  In the second tender, Air India has asked for aircraft below 20 years age.  Air India
 have stated that if aircraft below 15 years age do not become available, then they would go in for aircraft below 20

18.       Air India has informed that private aircraft are chartered on ACMI (Aircraft, Crew, Maintenance and Insurance)

 The cabin crew of the aircraft was also not familiar with the language spoken by the Hajis, which also led to

 airport and wide-bodied aircraft can be operated only after the runway expansion work is over.
23.       The Committee also pointed out that nearly 3000 pilgrim from Nagpur have to go all the way to Mumbai and put

 the difficulties being faced by Haj pilgrims from Jammu & Kashmir.  The Hajis have to go Delhi to take the flights to
 Jeddah.  But there are problems for Hajis from Kashmir, which is a snowbound area.  They have to travel by road for
 about 12 hours to Jammu and then halt there for three days.  Kashmir being a snowbound area, they are required to be
 in possession of blanket and other woollen clothing and after their flights from Jammu to Delhi, they have to leave all
 the clothing brought by them.

24.       The Committee is surprised to note that selection of airports for the Haj flights is done merely on the basis of the

 recommending any centre for operation of Haj flights.  The Haj pilgrims, who are mostly senior citizens, have to travel

 airports selected are not very far off from the native places of the Hajis so that, in case of delay, they could go back to
 their homes.  The Committee feels that it will go a long way in reducing the hardships of the Haj pilgrims in case of

 operations.  There should be Haj flights from Thiruvananthapuram and Nagpur and the frequency of flights should be

 Haj House and a Musafirkhana are already in existence near the Calicut airport.  Efforts should also be made to explore
 the possibility of direct flights from Jammu and Srinagar to Delhi separately. 
 
BAGGAGE PROBLEMS
25.       One of the major problems faced by the pilgrims during the Haj 2000 was of return of baggage.  The problem of
 return of baggage has also been faced during the last few years and this problem is compounding every year.  During
 Haj 2000, on the return flights the baggage of several persons was missing and necessary information was not
 available.  As a result, the pilgrims had to wait at the airport for getting their baggage before they could start return
 journey for their hometown.  It has been informed that every Haj pilgrim is permitted to take 30 kg luggage to Jeddah. 
 On return journey, the quantum of luggage goes up.  Air India has suggested that standard bags should be provided to
 the pilgrims which will restrict the weight of the baggage on the return flights.  The Committee was informed that the
 Saudi Airlines have given permission for 50 kg luggage, 15 kg for hand baggage and 35 kg for check in and 10 kg for
 ‘zum-zum’ water. 
26.       In response to a suggestion of the Committee that the Airlines should bring the ‘zum-zum’ water and distribute it
 at the airport itself, it was informed that Indian Mission in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia has made arrangements for
 procuring ‘zum-zum’ water, which will be transported to India on the Phase I return flights.  Such ‘zum-zum’ water
 will be handed over to the local Haj Authorities for distribution to the returning pilgrims.  Air India has also informed
 that Airports Authority of India is making the necessary arrangements to provide the storage space for the ‘zum-zum’
 water.
27.       The Committee feels that with the arrangement for storage and distribution of ‘zum-zum’ water having been
 made at Indian airports, the problem of distribution of ‘zum-zum’ water would be solved.  The Committee notes with
 concern the problem of missing/delayed arrival of baggage on return journey. The Committee feels that proper attention
 has not been paid at all to this aspect more so since Air India, which has been in this business for so long, should have
 anticipated this problem and taken appropriate measures.  The problem with regard to return baggage also worsened
 due to the fact that the Hajis were totally in the dark about the fate of their baggage.  The Committee hopes that
 henceforth Air India and other agencies involved in the Haj operations would be more careful and would take
 corrective measures to ensure that this does not recur.  As regards the excess baggage, the Committee is of the view that
 it is not expected that while coming back a pilgrim will have the same luggage which he was having while going.  The
 restriction on the weight of the baggage while coming back from Jeddah has also created a lot of problems.  The
 Committee understands the constraints of the airlines in allowing excess baggage.  But keeping in view the sentiments
 of the Haj pilgrims, the Committee recommends that the Haj pilgrims may be permitted to bring back a reasonable
 amount of excess baggage, thereby reducing the hardships faced by the Haj pilgrims.  
 
LACK OF INFORMATION
28.            Another major area in Haj operations where the authorities completely failed was the utter lack of
 information regarding flight schedule to Haj pilgrims at Jeddah and their relatives in India.  There has been delay and
 the consequent dislocation in the operation of both outward/inward flights.  Even the local authorities were helpless in
 coordinating mechanism at control room set up at Air India headquarters and at Jeddah.  Lack of information about
 departure/arrival of flights aggravated the problem.  The officials of Air India stated that a large number of problems
 were from Jeddah on the return leg of the operations due to inadequate infrastructural facilities such as aircraft
 departure bays, check in counters etc.   It was informed that some of the aircraft collided in the darkness at Jeddah
 airport as the bays were not even lit up.  That also caused some delay.  Air India have also desired that additional bay
 should be provided to Air India at Jeddah and the matter may be taken up with the Saudi Arabian authorities through
 Ministry of External Affairs.  The Committee has also been informed that due to the congregation of people from all

 there shall be no problem of Visa.  That will help a lot in managing ground handling at Jeddah.  The Committee was
 also informed by Air India that during Haj 2001, they would be appointing a ground handling agent who is supposed to

 operations.  Moreover, the Jeddah Airport Authority has also informed that this time checking of baggage of pilgrims
 will be carried out at a spacious place and the baggage checking would be done in 6 to 8 hours.  The benefit of this will
 be that the Hajis will be allowed to check in with the hand baggage only. With the hand baggage alone, the checking
 will be much faster and the flights would operate within one and a half hours instead of 5 to 6 hours.  
31.       In Haj 2000, Air India was not having a control room at Madina.  The Hajis leave Madina 24 hours before the
 departure from Jeddah.  However, next year they shall be having control room in Madina and Jeddah and there will be
 close connectivity between Mecca, Madina, Jeddah and the 8 airports in 8 cities in India. 
32.       The flight schedules are prepared on the basis of station-wise breakup of pilgrims to be carried, which is advised
 by the Central Haj Committee/Ministry of External Affairs and the type of aircraft/capacity offered by the operator. 
 The schedules are filed with Presidency of Civil Aviation (PCA) in Saudi Arabia.  The necessary arrangements for
 handling of these flights are made by Traffic Services Division of Air India for smooth operation of Haj flights. 
 However, It has been brought to the notice of the Committee that flight schedule for the departing Haj pilgrims is
 intimated to them at a very late stage.  Even the State Haj Committees are not aware of the departure schedule of the
 Hajis.  The inconvenience to the Hajis is multiplied due to the frequent change of flight timings.  The Committee feels
 that the flight schedule for the Hajis should be State Haj Committee friendly and Hajis friendly.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that finalisation of flight schedule should be done in consultation with the Central and State Haj
 Committees.  Any unavoidable change in the flight schedules should be intimated in advance to respective Haj
 Committee Headquarters and the Airports Authority of India at the airports by Air India.  At airports, necessary
 arrangements should be made to display the change in time on Flight Information Display (FID) system and there
 should be repetitive announcements in different languages on Public Address System.  The Committee also feels that
 the reporting time of 48 hours both from Indian airports and from Jeddah is on the higher side.  The Committee
 recommends that efforts should be made to reasonably reduce the reporting time at the airports. 
33.       The Committee recommends that before a flight takes off from Saudi Arabia, the relevant information regarding
 the passengers on board a flight should be available at Indian airports.  The Central Haj Committee and the State Haj
 Committee should also be involved in the process and they should coordinate for passing on the necessary information
 to the Hajis/their near & dear ones in India.
34.       The Committee is surprised to know that Air India employees could not get Visa from Saudi Arabian authorities
 due to some bureaucratic problems and feels that such incidents can be avoided.  The Committee feels that information
 dissemination should be such that all disembarkation points are in a position to know in advance the flight timings. The
 Committee recommends that the resource requirement to handle this operation should be assessed in advance and the
 necessary arrangements should be made to ensure the smooth and effective handling of the Haj flights.  Haj House, Air
 India booking offices, all the disembarkation airports and Air India headquarters should be linked electronically to
 provide instant information to the pilgrims.  Control rooms should be set up at Jeddah, Mecca and Madina and these
 rooms should be manned round the clock to enable the pilgrims and their relatives to access latest and current
 information with regard to the flight movement.  Also, there should be improvement in coordination level.

 Minister of Finance and Minister of Civil Aviation should review the advisability of continuing the present practice of

 available, the fare and subsidy to be applicable for Haj-2001 and the policy to be followed thereafter.  The process of

 privatized Air India may undertake Haj operations only if there is a profit margin and commercial viability.  They may
 procure wet-lease aircraft on their own and quote all-inclusive per pilgrim price keeping in mind the profit element.

 various agencies concerned with the Haj operation since lack of coordination gives a bad impression not only of

 paying for their journey and, in some cases, even higher than what is being charged by some private agencies.  So many
 Government agencies with able officers from External Affairs, Civil Aviation, Air India and Airport Authority of India
 are engaged in these operations but the Hajis are not provided with satisfactory services.

 professional and world-class airline.  Its ability to provide satisfactory services to the Hajis can earn it a big name
 internationally, since the Hajis come across millions of people from all over the world and the event can be used as an
 instrument to publicise, at no cost, the services provided by Air India in a big way.  Haj is an international event and the
 Hajis are the cultural ambassadors of the nation.  Ministry of External Affairs and Air India combined together, by
 successfully organizing the Haj pilgrimage and providing good facilities, can exploit this opportunity for creating
 goodwill among the muslim population all over the world and attracting foreign tourist arrival.  The Committee hopes
 and expects that Haj-2001 will be smoother and better in comparison to previous operations.

 Aviation and then to the Central Haj Committee and again to the Ministry of Civil Aviation shows adhocism on the part
 of the Government.  The Committee feels that by now the Government agencies involved in the management of Haj
 operations must have achieved expertise to handle these operations efficiently and taking benefit thereof, sincere efforts

 agencies without pursuing the matter as to whether any action has been taken/initiated against those who fail to provide
 satisfactory services.  The Committee feels that the Central Haj Committee should not merely act as a passive spectator
 of the events but has an important role to play in successful organisation of Haj flights in coordination with other
 concerned agencies.  The Committee recommends that Central Haj Committee should take notice of the problems being
 faced by the Haj pilgrims and set up control rooms at various disembarkation centres for Haj pilgrims so that in case
 any help is required, they can be contacted. Ministry of External Affairs, being the nodal agency for the Haj operations,
 should define the responsibilities of the various organisations concerned with the Haj operations such as who will
 manage ground operations, who will be in-charge of the control rooms etc. and the guidelines in this context should be
 circulated in black and white.  All the organisations should take collective responsibility and accountability should be
 fixed individually. Ministry of External Affairs should take the responsibility for coordination among the various
 agencies concerned with the Haj operation since lack of coordination gives a bad impression not only of
 agencies/individuals involved but also of the whole country.
 
Although there are several agencies working together for operation of Haj flights, yet the hardships and problems of the
 Haj pilgrims have been increasing since the last few years.  Since Haj is a regular annual phenomenon, instead of an
 adhoc arrangement there should be some regular arrangements for Haj pilgrims.  The Haj pilgrims are paying for their
 journey and, in some cases, even higher than what is being charged by some private agencies.  So many Government
 agencies with able officers from External Affairs, Civil Aviation, Air India and Airport Authority of India are engaged
 in these operations but the Hajis are not provided with satisfactory services. 
 
The Committee feels that the annual Haj operation is an occasion for Air India to establish its credentials as a
 professional and world-class airline.  Its ability to provide satisfactory services to the Hajis can earn it a big name
 internationally, since the Hajis come across millions of people from all over the world and the event can be used as an
 instrument to publicise, at no cost, the services provided by Air India in a big way.  Haj is an international event and the
 Hajis are the cultural ambassadors of the nation.  Ministry of External Affairs and Air India combined together, by
 successfully organizing the Haj pilgrimage and providing good facilities, can exploit this opportunity for creating
 goodwill among the muslim population all over the world and attracting foreign tourist arrival.  The Committee hopes
 and expects that Haj-2001 will be smoother and better in comparison to previous operations.

            Lighthouse is a real guide of the mariners in vast ocean.  Lighthouses play an important role in guiding the
 mariners and fixing their position in the sea.  The term “Lighthouse” represents all aids to navigation, including light
 vessels, sound signals, buoys, beacons for any mark, sign or apparatus, radio aids such as Differential Global
 Positioning System Racons, Loran – C, Radio Beacons etc.  The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is premier
 agency in India and provides all aids to marine navigation during harbour phase for mariners in Indian waters. 
2.         The Lighthouses are defined as ‘General’ and ‘Local’.  The lighthouses under the Central Government and
 notified in the Official Gazette are the ‘General Lighthouses’ which come under the authority of the Department of
 Lighthouses and Lightships.  The responsibility of establishment, operation and maintenance of the lighthouses lies
 with the Department.  The ‘Local’ Lighthouses are those which are under the State Governments or the Port Trusts for
 guiding the ships while entering/leaving the Ports.  However as per the Lighthouse Act, the Department is empowered
 to inspect a local lighthouse and advise the concerned authority for its improvement. 
3.         The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships consisting of 167 Lighthouses, 12 Deep Sea Buoys, 10
 Differential Global Positioning Systems, 4 Decca Navigator Chain Stations, 6 LORAN –C Stations and 29 Racons
 covering the coastal length of over 7000 kms.  The Department would be adding 5 major Lighthouses-2 along the
 Andhra Coast and 3 in the Palk Bay.    Apart from the new Lighthouses and Radio Aids to navigation, the Department
 has up graded the old and pre-independent equipments with the latest state-of-art equipments.  
4.         The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is a subordinate office under the Ministry of Shipping and
 headed by the Director General of Lighthouses and Lightships.  The Headquarters of the Department of Lighthouses
 and Lightships is situated at Noida. 
5.         The Indian coast has been divided into six regions known as Lighthouse Districts.  The area covered and
 facilities available at Regional Headquarters are as under: - 
(i)            Jamnagar -      is the regional headquarters of Saurashtra & Kachchh Lighthouse District stretching from
 Jakhau Lighthouse near Pakistan border to Bhavnagar.  The region caters to the ‘Aids to Navigation’ requirements of
 two peninsulas, namely the Gulf of Kachchh and the Gulf of Khamabat.  The vessels approaching Kandla Port and a
 number of minor ports under the aegis of Gujarat Maritime Board take the help of various Aids established in this
 region. 
(ii)            Mumbai - is the regional headquarter for Mumbai Lighthouses District stretching from Hazira Lighthouses to
 Suratkal Lighthouses near Mangalore.  The region meets the navigational requirements of Major Ports at Mumbai,
 JNPT, Mormugao and new Mangalore.  In addition the various aids established by this region also caters to the needs of
 minor ports of Gujarat Maritime Board established on the eastern bank of the Gulf of Khambat and Maharashtra
 Maritime Board. 
(iii)       Cochin - is the regional headquarter for the Cochin Lighthouse District stretching from Kasaragod to
 Manakodam and all the Lighthouses in the Lakshadweep Island.  The region meets the navigational requirements of the
 Major Port of Kochi and number of minor ports of Karnataka and Kerala. 
(iv)            Chennai - is the regional headquarters for the Chennai Lighthouse District stretching from Alleppey on the
 west coast to Kanyakumari and Kanyakumari to Machhlipatnam on the east coast.  The region meets the navigational
 requirement of a number of ports under Maritimes Boards of  Tamilnadu and  Andhra Pradesh and the ship breaking
 yard to Vodarevu. 
(v)            Kolkata - is the regional headquarters of the Kolkata Lighthouses District stretching from Antervedi
 (Narsapur) to Saugar Island.  The District caters to the need of the shipping traffic for Vishakhapatnam Port, Hoogly
 Dock and Port and a number of ports under Andhra Pradesh Martime Board and West Bengal Maritime Board. 
(vi)            Andaman & Nicobar Islands:- Port Blair is the regional headquarters of Andaman & Nicobar groups of
 Islands Lighthouse District stretching from East Island to Indira Point in the Bay of Bengal covering nearly 540
 islands/islets.  In these island shipping services is the lifeline.  The region is also situated in the international
 navigational route in the Indian Ocean and thus has been given a special significance to this Lighthouse District.  In this
 region, the Department since its inception, has established number of lighthouses, electronic navigational aids and local
 aids to navigation on agency-basis for Andaman Port Trust.  It maintains and operates all the Aids to marine navigation
 in A&N group of Islands and caters to the needs of all minor ports and international traffic. 
6.         Owing to rapid increase in the lighthouse service, the Central Advisory Committee for Lighthouses, in its 74
th
 meeting held in April 2000, has approved to have a separate Lighthouse District, the seventh District with its
 headquarters at Kakinada to provide safe navigation to mariners sailing along the Andhra Coast.

7.         Each Lighthouse District is headed by a Director (Regional) who reports on the technical matters to the Deputy
 Director General and he in turn to the Director General Lighthouses and Lightships.  A team of qualified Engineers and
 Ministerial staff assist the Director at Regional Headquarters.  
8.         The Department also undertakes construction of new Lighthouse tower and its allied buildings including
 installation and testing of Lighthouse equipment with the help of Departmental Engineers.  In addition to this, they also
 carry out the installation and testing of captive power plants, racons, high power parabolic transmission systems, the
 latest satellite-based Differential Global Positioning System etc. 
9.         The Department also undertakes foreign jobs for Maritime State for construction/ development/ maintenance of
 the Local Lighthouses on agency basis.  Most of the spares required for lighting equipment are fabricated/
 manufactured in its laboratories/workshops. 
10.       There is a statutory body called Central Advisory Committee for Lighthouses. It is appointed for a period of two
 years to advise the Government for erection, alteration, removal and examination of new proposals pertaining to
 Lighthouses. It also advises activities i.e. aids to navigation such as light vessel, Fog Signal, Buoy, Beacon or any sign
 and mark exhibited for guidance of ship.  The Central Advisory Committee for Lighthouses (CACL) meets at least
 once in a year under the Chairmanship of the Secretary,  Ministry of Shipping.  There are 16 official and non-official
 members of the   Central Advisory Committee for Lighthouses (CACL) representing various sectors of shipping and
 the Chambers of Commerce. 
11.       The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism undertook the study
 visits to Regional Headquarters at Calcutta, Cochin, Mumbai and Andaman & Nicobar Islands and held discussions
 with the representatives of the Department of Lighthouse and Lightships on the ‘Functioning of Lighthouses’.  In the
 course of discussion at various places, the Committee was informed about the functioning of the Regional Headquarters
 under the Department and maintenance of the Lighthouses. 
12.       On the basis of feedback received from the Regional Headquarters of various Lighthouses Districts, the
 Committee heard the representatives of the  Ministry of Shipping and the Department of Lighthouses & Lightships, at
 its meeting held on 13
th February 2001 at the Headquarters of the Department at  Noida.
 
RELAVANCY OF HAVING HEADQUARTER OF THE DEPARTMENT OF LIGHTHOUSES AND LIGHTSHIPS AT
 NOIDA
 
13.       The Lighthouses are operating at coast line and therefore all the schemes are executed by the Department along
 the coast line.  However, the Headquarters of the Director-General of Lighthouses and Lightships is situated at Noida.
 The Committee wanted to know the justification for keeping DGLL’s Headquarters at Noida.. 
14.       The Committee was informed that in 1929,  the Central Government took over the general control and
 supervision of Lighthouse in accordance with the provisions of Indian Lighthouse Act enacted in 1927.  A Central
 Organisation was set-up to deal with Lighthouses and its Headquarters was located at Delhi/Shimla.  This position
 continued till 1949 when this Organisation was merged with the then newly established office of Directorate General of
 Shipping at Mumbai.  Soon there after, it became apparent that there was little or no advantage in attaching the
 Lighthouse Department to the DG Shipping and that its location was away from the headquarters of the Government
 that militated against its efficient functioning.  Therefore  the Headquarters of the Lighthouse Department was moved
 back to Delhi in 1953-54. 
15.         In 1962, the shifting of the offices from Delhi was considered by the Cabinet Committee, which decided that
 Lighthouse Department should be shifted from Delhi to Calcutta.  And that time the members of the staff represented to
 the Government not to uproot them from Delhi.  The proposal of  shifting of Department to Calcutta did not materlise. 
16.       The question of de-centralisation of Government offices was considered by the Government in 1971 and   it was
 decided that the Department be shifted to Ghaziabad.  Due to certain administrative reasons, the Ministry of Surface
 Transport had finally decided to locate the office of Department of Lighthouse and Lightships at Noida. The proposal
 for shifting of the office of Department of Lighthouse from Delhi to Noida was approved by the Cabinet Committee in
 its meeting held on 7
th May, 1987.  The Department acquired plot of land for construction of office building complex at
 a cost of Rs.1.40 crores.  Simultaneously, a proposal for acquisition of ready built flats under housing scheme of Noida
 Authority was also approved and Department acquired 154 nos. ready built flats.  The establishment of DGLL was
 finally shifted from New Delhi to Noida in August 1999.   In reply to a question, it was submitted before the Committee
 that the Ministry of Shipping and the Department had no objections in shifting of Headquarters of the Department to
 any of coastal towns or centrally located place.

 Department of Lighthouses and Lightships should be provided with more functional autonomy so that they should take

BASIC FACILITIES TO THE STAFF POSTED AT REMOTE/ISLAND LIGHTHOUSES
 
25.       To provide navigational aids to the mariners, some of the operational staff members are working at
 remote/Island lighthouses .The Committee wanted to know as to what facilities i.e. educational, medical and
 accommodation, the Department has provided to staff members who are working at such isolated /remote areas. 
26.       The Committee was informed by the representatives of the Department that the Department was not having
 sufficient quarters at its disposal to provide to the operational staff at landing points of Island Lighthouses.  Most of the
 lighthouses are located in the remote areas where basic facilities like medical, schooling, transportation etc. are the
 barest minimum.  The operational staff have to keep their families at other places for the purpose of accommodation
 and  education of their children.  However 100% semi furnished  accommodation was available at the Light stations
 and the Department was contemplating to provide some quarters at landing point and hostel accommodation to the
 children of staff for better education facilities and also free ration to staff serving at Remote/Island Lighthouses. 
27.       The Committee is not satisfied with the welfare measures taken by the Department in respect of staff posted at
 landing points of Island Lighthouses.  The Committee is of the view that insufficient facilities at these locations will
 affect motivation and morale of the operational staff who are isolated from their family and society.  Therefore, the
 Committee recommends that for the operational staff posted at island/remote stations, the possibility be explored to
 provide family accommodations at mainland nearby the landing area, in addition to the accommodation already
 provided at duty place. This additional accommodation would enable the employees to avail of better educational
 facilities and social environment for their family members, wherever such facilities are not available.  The Committee
 also recommends that hostel facility in the vicinity of Regional Directorate be provided to enable the children of
 employees to avail of higher education.  Efforts also be made to provide periodical transport,  recreational facilities for
 the staff posted at remote sites and free ration to those who are not getting any special remote area allowance. 
STREAMLINING OF LIGHTDUES COLLECTION
 
28.       In India the Lightdues are charged on the basis of “Foreign Going Vessels”.  Foreign Going Vessels are defined
 in Merchant Shipping Act, 1958 as the vessels having 3000 G.R.T. and above tonnage irrespective of the origin of
 vessels.  If the G.R.T. of the vessels is 3000 or more, they fall under the purview of Lightdues. The Committee wanted
 to know the details of the Lightdues Collection and that whether it has any effect on the movement of the vessels.  
29.       The Committee was informed that the details of lightdues collection, revenue expenditure and amount
 transferred to General Reserve Fund (GRF) for the last few years are as under: -

 as an incentive to the coastal shipping, the Government of India has proposed to exempt the coastal vessels and other

31.       The Committee enquired about the procedure followed for collection of Lightdues.  In their reply the
 Department informed the Committee that the collection of Lightdues is done by the Central Customs Department on a
 commission basis (present rate ½ percent) and credited to the General Revenue of the Govt. India.  The balance 99 ½
 percent of Lightdues is remitted to the Pay and Accounts Officer, Lighthouses and Lightships, through PAO Customs. 
 A separate account is maintained by way of collection of light-dues, expenses, cost and all expenditure for maintenance
 of navigational aids in the form of Proforma Accounts.  This account is laid before the CACL after the close of each
 financial year.  Any surplus over the expenditure is credited to the General Reserve Fund (GRF) of the Department. 
 Expenditure on plan schemes is met out of the  internal resources to the extent of amount available in the GRF. 
 However, uncovered balance, if any, is met out of the general revenue of the Government as a loan to be repaid in
 subsequent years.  Therefore, no budgetary support is required though necessary provisions for plan allocations are left
 to the scrutiny and approval of the Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance and Parliament.  All expenditure of
 management and development (both plan and non-plan) are to be managed within the revenue collected by way of
 light-dues.  Thus, there is no budgetary support to the Department. 
32.       The Committee wanted to know whether the Department have any mechanism to know the quantum of
 Lightdues collected by the Customs authorities.  The Committee was apprised that the Lightdues are collected by the
 Customs authorities on behalf of the department on ½ percent commission basis   The Department of Lighthouses and
 Lightships is completely dependent upon the Customs Department for collection of Lightdues and it does not have any
 mechanism of its own either to collect Lightdues or monitor the collection. The representatives of the Department
 submitted that the Department of Lighthouse and Lightships is satisfied with the present system of collection of
 lightdues by Customs Authorities. Throwing the light on the steps being taken by the Department with regard to
 collection of lightdues, the representatives informed that in view of the fluctuations on the collection of the light dues,
 emphasis have been placed on streamlining certain important issues relating to Department’s GRF, DRF, proper
 assessment of collection of light dues in BE/RE stages etc.  Accordingly, to streamline the collection of Lightdues and
 projection of estimates, a committee has been constituted by the Ministry of Shipping under the Chairmanship of Chief
 Controller of Accounts for furnishing the recommendations.  The Report of the committee is expected soon.              
 
33.       The Committee is surprised to note that the Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is having no system of
 checking the quantum of lightdues collected by the Customs authorities and whatever amount is given by the Customs
 authorities is simply accepted by the Pay and Accounts Officer, Lighthouses.  The Committee therefore recommends
 that in order to have transparency in the system of collection of lightdues, the Department of Lighthouses and
 Lightships should have some sort of its own credible mechanism to know the amount of lightdues collected by the
 Customs authorities.   The Committee is aware that Ministry of Shipping have constituted a panel under the
 Chairmanship of Chief Controller of Accounts and hope that it will submit its report in time and efforts will be made by
 the Government    to streamline procedure of collection of the lightdues in pursuance of the recommendations of the
 panel.
 34.      The Committee appreciates the performance of the Department which has been self-sustaining and do not
 depend upon the Govt. of India for budgetary support including plan and non-plan expenditure.  The Committee
 observes that the large amount of funds are transferred to the General Reserve Fund (GRF) which are lying unutilised.  
 The Committee is unhappy to note that despite  the fact that large reserve  funds are available with the Department no
 serious efforts have been made to frame schemes for modernisation of Lighthouses.  Therefore, the Committee
 recommends that the Department should plan schemes for modernisation of Lighthouses by way of introducing modern
 technique so that the large reserve of funds available with it could be utilised. The Government should also have no
 hesitation in approving the schemes/projects of Department of Lighthouses and Lightships and rather encourage the
 Department to chalk out schemes for modernisation of Lighthouses. The Committee also recommends that the
 Department should also dedicate a part of fund for implementing such schemes which are for the welfare of
 staff/employees who are posted at difficult Remote/Island Lighthouses.
 
INADEQUATE AND UNQUALIFIED STAFF AT OPTICAL RESEARCH LABORATORY AND TRAINING
 CENTRE AT KOLKATA
 
35.       The Department of Lighthouse and Lightship has its own Optical Research Laboratory and Training Centre at
 Kolkata, which is headed by Director.  The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) has approved and
 certified the laboratory. In the laboratory all aids to navigation procured by various maritime boards are tested and
 certified before putting into the service and also experiments on lighting equipment are carried out.  Regular Refresher

file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/47threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:09]
 Courses all imparted to all technical and the operational staff of the Department to keep them abreast with the latest
 technical developments in the field of aids to maritime navigation. 
36.       The Committee was  informed that the Training Centre  is not having sufficient number of qualified staff except
 the Director (Training) as the other staff viz. two Assistant Engineers (one each Mech. And Elec.) are diploma holders
 or low  qualified staff.  The Committee was informed that when the Training Centre was established, no qualified
 faculty was envisaged, as most of the navigational aids were kerosene/gas- operated lights and the mechanism was
 based on operation of petromax light.  The technology in the field of Aids to Navigation has now evolved very fast in
 the last two decades with satellite navigation as mainstay, necessiating the improvement of the quality of training,
 which is possible only through adequate qualified faculty.  As such, the Training Centre needs adequate number of 
 qualified personnel for imparting training as well as for preparing materials for training in order to bring the quality of
 the operational staff at par with International standard.  Presently the requirement of training is being met by pooling
 engineers from the Lighthouse Districts, which adversely affects the works there.  Moreover the faculty thus pooled is
 not at home as they are not dedicated staff for training.
 
37.       The Committee observes that from the beginning itself , there is a lack of pro-active approach on the part of  the
 Department of Lighthouses and Lightships with regard to training of its staff.  The Committee is at a loss to understand
 as to how the Department had ensured effective use of modern technology in Lighthouses in absence of proper training
 to its staff.  The Committee is also of the view that before adopting latest technology and equipments in functioning of
 the Lighthouses, the Department should have ensured the adequate number of qualified staff at Training Centre. The
 Committee recommends that the Department should establish qualified, adequate and dedicated faculty at the Training
 Centre – Kolkata which will make possible not only to impart training to staff of the Department but also be able to
 train the staff of Martime States and lightkeepers from neighbouring countries. The Committee also takes strong
 exception to the fact that instead of faculty members of the Training Institute, some officials from the administrative
 side are being deputed abroad who on their return impart training to the staff of the Department.  The Committee feels
 that this affects the functioning of the Department where large number of posts are lying vacant.  The Committee
 therefore recommends that only the faculty members of the Training Centre should be sent for training in latest
 technology and modern equipment abroad so that their expertise may be better utilised  in the Department.

 candidates for promotion etc. 
40.       The Committee was further apprised that the Department has taken measures to tide over this problem by
 inducting the officials in the grade of Executive Officer on deputation which helped the Department to a certain extent
 to streamline the matters related to the recruitment and promotion from January 1999 onwards.  The recent ban of
 Ministry of Finance in filling-up the vacant posts either through promotion or through direct recruitment prohibits the
 Department to fill-up the vacancies.  The recent directives of the Govt. of India regarding abolition of promotional

 posts due to delay in filling/direct recruitment, the filling of post has become time consuming which is affecting the

 of navigational aids.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that  to achieve the very objective of providing safe
 navigation of the Department, it is very essential to fill-up the vacant posts, as early as possible, in the Organisation for
 ensuring smooth functioning of Lighthouses.   Immediate efforts should also be made to fill up the post of
 Administrator who after all is the incharge of the entire administration and in his absence, administrative machinery is
 not able to take decisions. The Committee also recommends that the Govt. of India should lift its ban on the operational
 vacant posts in the Department. 
43.       The Committee further recommends that Deputy Director General of the Department should also be provided
 with sufficient and proper functional staff, so that they can perform their duty properly.
 
EXECUTION OF CONSTRUCTION WORK OF LIGHTHOUSES
 
44.       The Department of Lighthouses and Lightships is purely an engineering department having qualified engineers
 and technicians from all the major disciplines of engineering.  The works related to construction and maintenance of
 Lighthouses towers, buildings, internal roads, etc. are taken up by the Department at remote locations where responses
 are not received from contractors.  The Department has executed all the construction works pertaining to Lighthouses
 by engaging labourers on muster roll and by procuring building materials through local suppliers.  The Lighthouses
 towers etc. built by the Department withstood the wrath of nature like cyclone.  The Committee was informed that the
 recent earthquake in Gujarat, the Lighthouses constructed by the Department also withstood the strain of earthquake
 without any major damage. 
45.       The Committee was further informed that due to restrictions on engaging labourers on muster roll and associated
 labour problems such as demand for permanent absorption, continued employment etc., the Department switched over
 during latter part of 80’s to the execution of construction work on contract basis by inviting tenders for the complete
 work including supply of materials and labourers. 
46.       The Committee appreciates the civil work done by the Department in respect of Lighthouses, as most of the
 construction work done by the Department have remained safe from the cyclone and no major damages have been
 caused to the Lighthouses even during the recent earthquake in Gujarat. Now the Department  have switched over to
 contract basis for executing their civil work.  The Committee is of the view that the Department should ensure that
 there is no compromise as far as quality of work is concerned and if the Department find the quality of construction of
 civil work not up to the standard, the Department should not hesitate to switch over to its earlier pattern. To ensure the
 quality of the construction work, the Committee recommends that the Government should give, the Department which
 has been the master in the field, freedom to adopt pattern for executing the civil work.
 
BEAUTIFICATION OF LIGHTHOUSES
 
47.       Today, tourism has taken the shape of industry and day-by-day it is gaining the importance.  Importance of
 tourism reflects the identity of the country on the world map.  The Lighthouses are situated in coastal line of the
 country. These Lighthouses can play some role in the tourism sector where tourists can enjoy and view the scenic
 beauty of mainland and sea. On being asked whether any steps have been taken to beautify the Lighthouses to attract
 the tourists, the representatives of the Department submitted that very little has been done in that area.   The

 Lightstations and Lighthouses are located in coastal area, many of which are sensitive and subject to terrorist threats. 
 Keeping in this view visitors/tourists entry to some of the Lighthouses have been stopped. 
48.         The Committee recommends that the Department of Lighthouse and Lightships should explore the possibility
 of development of Lighthouses with a view to attract tourist thereby beautifying them and take initiative to beautify the
 Lighthouses keeping tourism in the mind, without compromising the safety and security of Lighthouses so that the
 Department can earn some revenue.
