 NOIDA
 
The Committee observes that no proper thought have been given to the matter of having Headquarters of the
 Department. The Committee is not satisfied with the justification given by the Department of Lighthouse & Lightships
 for having its Headquarters at Noida just for keeping better co-ordination and liaisoning with the Ministry of Shipping
 in connection with the various matters concerning administration and development works and to avoid the procedural
 delays. The Committee is of the view that area of operation of the Department lies along the coastal line and all the
 Regional Headquarters are located along the coastal line of the country and are at a distance from DELHI/ NOIDA and
 therefore the officials of the Department sitting there and  involved in the planning and supervision of the schemes may
 not be able to do justice to their work.
The Committee is of the view that in view of latest developments and changes, which has totally revolutionised the
 information technology, the same should be used to the maximum possible extent.  It is, therefore, really not necessary
 to maintain large set up at Headquarters in Delhi for liaison work with the Ministry.  The Committee, therefore, feels
 that the present size of the headquarter of Department of Lighthouses and Lightships should be reduced to the level as
 is really required for the liaison work.  Instead regional offices may be strengthened and made more effective.  This will
 ensure better coordination between the headquarters of Department of Lighthouses and Lightships and regional
 headquarters.
(Paras 17 and 18)

The Committee appreciates the better coordination and relationship existing   between the Department of Lighthouses
 and Lightships and Ministry of Shipping. The Committee is however not satisfied with the present set up of delegation
 of financial powers to the Department.   The Committee is of view that if more financial powers are delegated   to the
 Department in respect of capital and revenue expenses, it will not only reduce the time taken  in decision making
 process but also ensure the faster implementation of the schemes of the Department.
 
The Committee observes that the Department is totally dependent on the Ministry of Shipping on its functional matters,
 which causes undue delays and affects the functioning of lighthouses.   The Committee is of the view that Ministry of
 Shipping should take into consideration the track record of the Department and ensure speedy approval of  its schemes
 by doing away the routine bureaucratic hurdles.   Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department of
 Lighthouses and Lightships should be provided with more functional autonomy so that they should take their own
 decision and do not have to depend on the Ministry even for small matters.
(Paras 23 and 24)

            Tourism has emerged as one of the world’s most important activities.  It is the world’s largest export industry. 
 According to the World Tourism Organisation, about 663 million tourists travelled internationally in 1999 and spent
 about US$ 453 billion.  The figures indicate that tourism has certainly become a major social phenomenon of the
 modern society with enormous economic consequences.  Its importance as an instrument for economic development
 and employment generation, particularly in remote and backward areas, has been now well recognized the world over. 
2.         Travel and tourism related jobs/employment are not only generated at a relatively low cost and concentrated in
 small business and local community but also provide significant opportunities for women and young people, offer
 educational training and skill development and protect and revitalize traditional arts and crafts. 
3.         India is a country of continental dimensions with a fascinating kaleidoscope of diverse races, languages,
 religions, customs and traditions.  The tourist attractions of India include historical monuments, places of religious
 importance, mountain and beach resorts, wildlife and interesting eco-systems etc.  Tourism is presently India’s third
 largest export industry-after readymade garments and gem and jewellery.  The international tourist traffic to the country
 during 1951 was just 16,829. Over a period of about 50 years, the arrivals increased to 264 million in 2000 and
 registered a compounded annual rate of growth of about 11 percent.  The foreign tourist arrivals to India and the
 estimated foreign exchange earnings through tourism along with growth rate for the year 1997 to 2000 are as under: -
Growth Rate (%)
It is, therefore, evident that the rate of growth in foreign exchange earning from tourism is exceptionally high and is
 expected to become even higher in the coming years.
 
4.         The Ministry of Tourism has been declared as Ministry of Tourism and Culture, Department of Tourism w.e.f.
 27
th May 2000.  The Department of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and
 programmes and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government Agencies, State Governments/UTs
 and the Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The role of the Department of
 Tourism has been to coordinate and supplement the efforts of the State/U.T. Governments in development of tourism
 through Central financial assistance, to catalyze private investment, strengthen promotional and marketing efforts and
 to provide trained manpower resources.  The administrative head of the Department is the Secretary (Tourism).  The
 Department is assisted by an attached office headed by the Director General.  The office of the Director General of
 Tourism provides executive directions for the implementation of various policies and programmes.  Directorate General
 of Tourism has a field formation of 21 offices within the country and 18 offices abroad.  The overseas offices are
 primarily responsible for tourism promotion and marketing in their respective areas and the field offices in India are
 responsible for providing information service to tourists and to monitor the progress of field projects. 
5.         The Department of Tourism has the following public sector undertaking/autonomous institutions under its
 administrative control:-  
India Tourism Development Corporation Limited (ITDC);
National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology and the Institutes under its control (NCHMCT)
Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management (IITTM);
Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering (IISM);
National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS).
 
6.         As per the Department of Tourism, the basic strategy during the Ninth Plan was to establish effective
 coordination with all the relevant agencies so as to achieve synergy in the development of tourism.  The development
 activities during the Plan would give necessary emphasis to environment protection and cultural preservation.  The
 thrust areas during Ninth Plan period are:- 
Infrastructure development

COORDINATION BETWEEN THE DEPARTMENT OF TOURISM AND DEPARTMENT OF CULTURE
 
12.       The Committee enquired from the representatives of Department of Tourism the nature of coordination between
 the Department of Tourism & Department of Culture and whether any institutional mechanism has been developed for
 achieving the same.  The Committee was informed that the institutional arrangements between the two departments
 existed at the Committee of Secretaries & Group of Ministers level.  Apart from these, there is informal interaction
 between the two departments.  Department of Tourism also informed that they have advised the Department of Culture
 to take up certain projects such as refurbishing all the monuments, interpretation at the historical sites, providing toilet
 facilities at the monuments, beautification of monuments etc. and that Department of Tourism is also helping
 Department of Culture in taking up these projects. 
13.       The Committee feels that one of the important aspects of Indian tourism is the cultural tourism around the
 magnificent monuments and heritage centres located in different parts of the country.  Both foreign and domestic
 tourists visit these monuments and derive intense pleasure by experiencing the journey back to the ages. 
14.       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Department of Tourism and the Department of Culture should
 develop some institutional mechanism with regard to the formulation of their policies and execution of projects.  The
 coordination between the two departments will certainly have a positive impact on the development of tourism in the
 country.

scale employment opportunities. Also, the vast number of domestic tourists visiting different parts of the country every

 Committee recommends that allocation for funds for domestic campaign should be adequately distributed between the

IMPACT OF SUSPENSION OF LTC ON DOMESTIC TOURISM 
23.       The attention of the Department of Tourism was brought to the recent decision of the Central Government to
 suspend LTC facility for 2 years for the Central Government employees.  When asked about the likely impact of this
 decision on the domestic tourism, the Department of Tourism admitted that the decision is likely to have an adverse
 affect on the domestic tourism in the country.  The Department of Tourism were asked whether the department have
 carried out any assessment of the adverse impact of the Government’s decision. The Committee was informed that they
 have not done any such study as yet. However, the Department of Tourism intends to convene a meeting on the subject
 with the State Tourism Secretaries and the tour operators after the Budget Session of the Parliament. The Department of
 Tourism also informed that the Ministry of Finance took the decision regarding suspension of LTC for 2 years without
 consulting the Department of Tourism.  After making an objective assessment of the impact of the suspension of LTC
 facility in consultation with the State Governments, Department of Tourism intend to take up the matter with the
 Ministry of Finance and Department of Personnel & Training. 
24.       The Committee is of the view that the Government’s decision to suspend LTC for 2 years for the Government
 employees will definitely have an adverse impact on the domestic tourism in the country whereas the exchequer may
 not be benefited since the LTC involves simply the transfer of money from one head to the other.  The Committee is
 constrained to note the slow pace of the Department of Tourism in making any realistic assessment of the negative
 impact of the decision on domestic tourism or take up the issue with the Ministries concerned.   The Committee feels
 that international tourism, by its very nature, is rather unpredictable and that the foreign tourist traffic is affected by the
 events in the country.  In such a scenario, domestic tourism, which has increased with improved economy and
 encouragement by various establishments by way of paid holidays and leave travel concessions, has been gaining
 popularity.   The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry of Finance should have consulted the Department of
 Tourism before taking any decision on such an important matter. The Committee recommends that after making early
 assessment of the adverse impact of the suspension of LTC facility, the Department of Tourism should take up the
 matter with the Ministry of Finance and Department of Personnel and Training.  The Committee hopes that the
 Department of Tourism would be able to convince the Government of its stand and the LTC facility to the Government
 employees will be restored to sustain the growth of domestic tourism in the country.

st report on Demands for Grants (2000-2001) of the Ministry of Tourism, observed
 that in order to encourage the involvement of private sector in the development of tourism, the Ministry of Tourism
 should take steps to remove the infrastructural and procedural hurdles which the private sector has to face and ensure

 Assistance is given to States/UTs to enable them to put up infrastructural facilities and procurement of equipment for
 activities such as trekking, rock climbing, mountaineering, winter-water and adventure related sports, tents,

 watercrafts etc.

 Manali region and the  Government of Himachal Pradesh and the organizers were extended the required assistance.

GULMARG WINTER SPORTS PROJECT
 
40.       The Gulmarg Winter Sports Projects (GWSP) was established in 1968 to popularise Kashmir as a tourist
 destination and develop winter sports with a view to attracting tourists during the lean winter season and to provide
 gainful employment to the local people.  It was set up to impart training to selected candidates to work as Ski
 Instructors and Mountaineering guides.  Later Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering (IIS&M) was added on to
 conduct courses on Mountaineering, Ski Courses and training etc.  The Committee enquired from the Department of
 Tourism about the current status the GWSP/IIS&M.  The Committee was informed that in the post-militancy situation,
 the Department of Tourism explored the possibility of transferring the project to Jawahar Institute of Mountaineering
 (JIM), Batot under the control of Ministry of Defence as well as Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP) under Ministry of
 Home Affairs.  Both the organisations have expressed their inability to take over the project.  The Department of
 Tourism has now taken a decision to wind up the WSP/IIS&M and transfer the project with assets and staff to the
 Government of Jammu and Kashmir for effectively utilizing the facilities so created. 
The Committee does not agree with the decision of the Department of Tourism to wind up Gulmarg Winter Sports
 Projects/Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering.  On the one hand the Government is taking about the promotion
 of adventure and sport tourism and on the other hand it is thinking in terms of winding up a sports institute.  The
 Committee is of the view that the Government must take steps towards the revival of the GWSP/IIS&M.

The Committee feels that domestic tourism is the mainstay of Indian Tourism. The Committee has been constrained to

 any other sector for every rupee invested.  It also creates the jobs at the local level, dispensing with the need of
 migration to distant places for earning of livelihood.  In fact, tourism plays a major role in promoting large-scale
 employment opportunities. Also, the vast number of domestic tourists visiting different parts of the country every year
 return with a better understanding of the people living in the different regions of the country and the geographical,
 biological and cultural diversity of India.

 observes that India is a country of continental dimensions that includes diverse races, languages and religions.  The
 Committee recommends that allocation for funds for domestic campaign should be adequately distributed between the
 English/regional print media so that people belonging to the various languages and the different sections/segments of
 the society become aware of the campaign launched by the Department of Tourism.

The Committee is of the view that the Government’s decision to suspend LTC for 2 years for the Government
 employees will definitely have an adverse impact on the domestic tourism in the country whereas the exchequer may
 not be benefited since the LTC involves simply the transfer of money from one head to the other.  The Committee is
 constrained to note the slow pace of the Department of Tourism in making any realistic assessment of the negative
 impact of the decision on domestic tourism or take up the issue with the Ministries concerned.   The Committee feels
 that international tourism, by its very nature, is rather unpredictable and that the foreign tourist traffic is affected by the
 events in the country.  In such a scenario, domestic tourism, which has increased with improved economy and
 encouragement by various establishments by way of paid holidays and leave travel concessions, has been gaining
 popularity.   The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry of Finance should have consulted the Department of
 Tourism before taking any decision on such an important matter. The Committee recommends that after making early
 assessment of the adverse impact of the suspension of LTC facility, the Department of Tourism should take up the
 matter with the Ministry of Finance and Department of Personnel and Training.  The Committee hopes that the
 Department of Tourism would be able to convince the Government of its stand and the LTC facility to the Government
 employees will be restored to sustain the growth of domestic tourism in the country.

 oriented in the context of foreign tourists arrival in the country.  The Committee also recommends that the Department
 of Tourism should coordinate with the Air India and find out if they could offer them some space in their offices to
 accommodate tourist offices.  This will certainly help the Department of Tourism in reducing its overhead costs.
(Para 44)
TOURISM DEVELOPMENT IN NORTH EASTERN REGION
The Committee is not convinced with the arguments advanced by the Department of Tourism for not making available
 the information regarding projects actually taken up last year or proposed to be taken up this year for development of
 tourism in the North East region.  In absence of any such information, the Committee is unable to make an assessment
 of the progress made in the tourism projects taken up in the North East Region.  The Committee agrees that at the time

 of BE allocation, a lump sum allocation is made for the North East region. But the Committee feels that this 10%
 allocation for North East is over and above the other budgetary allocations. The Committee feels the tourist
 developmental work undertaken in the North East region should be given the highest priority and recommends that the
 funds allocated for the North East region should be optimally utilised in that region only.  The Committee also
 recommends that the Government should withdraw the restriction of RAP for domestic tourists in order to enable these
 tourists to visit these places without any problem.
(Para 48)
INDIA TOURISM DEVELOPMENT CORPORATION (ITDC)
The Committee expresses its serious concern at the way the uncertain disinvestment scenario has affected the financial
 performance of ITDC.  For the first time, the ITDC posted net loss of Rs.24.04 crores during 1999-2000 and during
 2000-2001, its performance is likely to be even more dismal.  ITDC is in a fix even about the renovation/up-gradation
 of its properties.  The proposal for appointing a regular Chairman of ITDC has also been hanging since the last three
 and a half years.  The Committee recommends that a decision with respect to the disinvestment of ITDC and the time
 frame in which it is to be achieved should be taken at the earliest to put on end to this uncertainty.  The Committee also
 recommends that the Hotel properties of ITDC should not be allowed to decay and that necessary renovation work
 should be carried out at the earliest so that the commercial value of these properties does not go down.  Sufficient funds
 may also be earmarked for the purpose in the budget of the Department.
(Para 55)
GENERAL OBSERVATION
The Committee, after going through the budget performance of the Department of Tourism for the last five years, has
 come to the conclusion that so many schemes are announced, guidelines are issued and budget allocations are made but
 everything remains on paper only.  When the actual implementation part of all the schemes comes, the Department of
 Tourism gives all sorts of explanations.  The Committee feels that most of the schemes mooted by the Department are
 still pending due to the lack of pro-active approach on the part of the Department of Tourism.  This is despite the fact
 that the Committee has been repeatedly recommending in its earlier reports that, in order to avoid delay in the
 implementation of the various schemes, all related problems should be sorted out in advance.   As intimated by the
 Department of Tourism, many of the proposals based on the recommendations of the Committee are pending with the
 Ministry of Finance, Planning Commission & Ministry of Home Affairs etc. who are paying little attention thereon.  
 The Committee is of the view that development of the tourism sector is of great significance for the Indian economy
 and hence all the concerned agencies should make concerted efforts to ensure that the decisions taken in this direction
 are expedited.

            The Department of Culture primarily deals with the tangible and intangible heritage.  In a larger perspective, it
 also addresses the issues relating to the history, values and beliefs in conjunction with several other Ministries and
 Departments.  Culture being considered one of the keys to Human Resource Development, in the Five Year Plans,
 suitable emphasis was laid on development of Culture from the grass roots.  Relentless efforts made in various fields of
 Culture have started bearing fruit.  A number of institutions have been actively associated with the promotion,
 preservation and dissemination of the rich cultural heritage of India. 
2.         The Department of Culture was set up in 1985 through the 174
th Amendment of the Government of India
 (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961.  It was part of the Ministry of Human Resource Development before its transfer
 to the Ministry of Culture, Youth Affairs and Sport.  Since 27th May 2000, it forms part of the Ministry of Tourism and
 Culture and is known as the Department of Culture.  The Department is responsible to promote art and cultural mutual
 understanding and goodwill and foster closer relations with foreign countries.  Preservation of ancient and historic
 monuments and records, exploration and excavation of archaeological sites and remains, maintenance and expansion of
 libraries and museums of national importance and observance of centenaries and anniversaries of eminent personalities
 are among its other responsibilities. 
3.         The main functions/activities of the Department can be broadly classified under the following heads:- 
Maintenance and Conservation of heritage, ancient monuments and historic sites.
Administration of Museums and Libraries.
Observing Centenaries and anniversaries of important national personalities and events.
Promoting institutions and organisations of Buddhist and Tibetan Studies.
Entering into cultural agreements with foreign countries and holding of Festival of India abroad.
Anthropology and Ethnology.
Archives and Archival Libraries.
Academies and National School of Drama.
Promotion and dissemination of Culture.
Memorials.
 
4.         The Committee was also informed that while full attention will be given to all the above mentioned sectors,
 activities of the department will be particularly focused on:- 
Conservation and preservation of cultural heritage;
Schemes of the National Cultural fund;
Linkage between education and culture;
Development of a public library movement;
Strengthening of Museums and Art Galleries; and
Promotion of Culture and dissemination. 
5.         The Committee appreciates the decision of the Government to bring Department of Tourism and Culture within
 the purview of one Ministry.    The Committee feels that Culture and Tourism are interdependent and interrelated
 subjects.  India is having enormous monuments, museums, historical spots, and palaces etc., which need to be exploited
 from the tourism point of view.  The Government should have considered to keep both the Departments together very
 long back, so that synergy between the two Departments would have been achieved. Sooner or later now Government
 have realized and brought the two Departments under one Ministry. Most of the cultural sites, monuments, etc. are
 attractive spots of the tourist interest.  The Committee also feels that the coordination between Department of Culture
 and Tourism is very important for proper utilisation of the tourist value of the Cultural spots/monuments. A number of
 times, the Committee has observed that there has been contradiction in the approach of the two departments.  The
 Department of Tourism is interested in having more and more tourists whereas the Department of Culture, particularly
 ASI, discourages the tourists with a view to preserve/protect the monuments.  The Committee recommends that the two
 departments should try to achieve equilibrium between the approaches of preservation/ protection of monuments and
 arrival of tourists to these monuments.  Since the Departments of Tourism and Culture are now the parts of the same
 Ministry, the Committee hopes that a higher level of synergy will be achieved by doing away their differences.  
6.         During 2001-2002, the outlay for the Department of Culture for plan and non-plan is proposed to be Rs.430.75
 crores.  The budget outlays during the last five years has been as follows:

12.       The Committee was also informed by the Department of Culture that the ASI generates an annual revenue
 collection of Rs. 85.00 crores by way of charging fee from the visitors to these monuments. The revenue collected by
 ASI directly goes to consolidated fund of India.  The ASI is not only an expenditure-incurring organisation but also
 earning handsome amount annually.  
13.       The Committee is of the view that conservation of our heritage is important, both for domestic tourists as well as
 for attracting overseas tourists.  However the meagre plan budget of the department does not allow it to achieve its
 targets.  The Committee observes that in comparison to the amount proposed for this financial year also, the ASI has
 been allocated a meagre amount for its plan projects. The Committee expresses its concern over the shortage of
 Monument Attendants/Security guards for so many centrally protected Monuments in the country. The Committee also
 noted that in some cases the conservation and protection of monuments are in the hands of low paid security guards
 who are not trained for the purpose. Despite being recommended to this affect by the Parliamentary Committee on
 Human Resource Development for the last two/three years, no sincere effort has been made by the Department to solve
 this problem.  Last year it was informed to the Committee that the Planning commission has asked the Department to
 identify the monuments for de-protection and transfer them to the State Archaeology Departments for maintenance in
 order to reduce its own liability.  This time the Department has informed that the creation of posts is subject to approval
 of the Finance Ministry.  However, in view of the order of the Ministry of Finance imposing a ban on creation of new
 posts, it has not been possible to proceed further in the matter. The Committee feels that the delay in proper manning of
 the historical monuments by the ASI will definitely affect the preservation/ conservation of the monuments and will
 defeat the very purpose of the Department.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that serious efforts should be
 made towards regular appointment of monument attendants/security guards who are well trained to take care of the
 monuments. 
14.       The Committee was informed that severe paucity of funds is one of the main reasons why the ASI has not been
 able to carry out large-scale intensive projects.  This necessitated a step towards finding some alternative
 arrangements.  The Government has setup Cultural Fund during the year 1996 in order to facilitate the infusion of
 private and public sector funds into the field of heritage preservation and also to enable institutions and individuals to
 perform their rightful role in promoting and preserving India’s cultural heritage. Keeping in view this in the mind the
 ASI has also invited private sector participation for the upkeep and maintenance of the old monuments, the ASI has
 signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with Apeejay Group of Hotels through National Cultural Fund for
 environment upgradation and for the illumination of the monument.  Following public/private parties have approached
 Archaeological Survey of India for developing better environs of the monuments, making the monuments visitors
 friendly, providing basic facility like better toilets, better information system, interpretation centre and also audio sets
 in Delhi.

 years in spite of the fact that these reports are mandatory.  The Committee enquired from the representatives of the
 Department of Culture/ASI so to why the reports in respect of these excavations had not been published so far. While
 replying in affirmative, the ASI informed the Committee that over the years, the practice of excavating something and
 not publishing the reports had become a chronic malaise.  It was explained to the Committee that sometimes a person
 excavates something and then he goes away to some other place and somebody else takes his place.  This new person
 does not have as much interest in writing the reports on the excavation.  The Committee was also informed that the
 Department was contemplating to devise a programme whereby if some archaeologists have retired, they should be
 asked to submit the reports within three to six months and if there are some serving archaeologists, they should also
 submit it at the earliest.

 excavation works undertaken by the archaeologists so as to add transparency in the functioning of the ASI and the
 utilisation of funds in the excavations works.

SYNERGY BETWEEN DEPARTMENTS OF CULTURE & TOURISM
The Committee appreciates the decision of the Government to bring Department of Tourism and Culture within the
 purview of one Ministry.    The Committee feels that Culture and Tourism are interdependent and interrelated subjects. 
 India is having enormous monuments, museums, historical spots, and palaces etc., which need to be exploited from the
 tourism point of view.  The Government should have considered to keeping both the Departments together very long
 back, so that synergy between the two Departments would have been achieved. Sooner or later now Government have
 realized and brought the two Departments under one Ministry. Most of the cultural sites, monuments, etc. are attractive
 spots of the tourist interest.  The Committee also feels that the coordination between Department of Culture and
 Tourism is very important for proper utilisation of the tourist value of the Cultural spots/monuments. A number of
 times, the Committee has observed that there has been contradiction in the approach of the two departments.  The
 Department of Tourism is interested in having more and more tourists whereas the Department of Culture, particularly
 ASI, discourages the tourists with a view to preserve/protect the monuments.  The Committee recommends that the two
 departments should try to achieve equilibrium between the approaches of preservation/ protection of monuments and
 arrival of tourists to these monuments.  Since the Departments of Tourism and Culture are now the parts of the same
 Ministry, the Committee hopes that a higher level of synergy will be achieved by doing away their differences.

 in some cases the conservation and protection of monuments are in the hands of low paid security guards who are not
 trained for the purpose. Despite being recommended to this affect by the Parliamentary Committee on Human Resource
 Development for the last two/three years, no sincere effort has been made by the Department to solve this problem.

 monuments for de-protection and transfer them to the State Archaeology Departments for maintenance in order to

REPORT
 
 
            The Ministry of Civil Aviation is responsible for the formulation and implementation of national policies and
 programmes in the civil aviation sector.  The Ministry oversees the development and regulation of civil aviation in the
 country including inter-alia establishment of new aerodromes, maintenance and upgradation of the existing
 aerodromes, regulation of carriage of traffic by air and ensuring civil aviation security.  Railway Safety, including
 enquiries into serious railway accidents also constitutes one of the allied functions of the Ministry. 
2.         The civil aviation sector is monitored and regulated by two separate organisations under the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation i.e. Directorate General of Civil Aviation and Bureau of Civil Aviation Security.  The functions pertaining to
 Railway Safety are entrusted to a Commission.  The Ministry of Civil Aviation has the following Public Sector
 Undertakings/Companies/Autonomous Bodies under its administrative control:- 
Air India Limited and its wholly owned subsidiaries viz. Hotel Corporation of India Limited and Air India Charters
 Limited.
Indian Airlines Limited and its wholly owned subsidiary viz. Airlines Allied Services Limited.
Airports Authority of India.
Pawan Hans Helicopters Limited.
Indira Gandhi Rashtriya Uran Akademi. 
3.         The details of the budget allocations of the Ministry of Civil Aviation for the financial year 2001-2002 contained
 in the Demand No.7 were considered by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport &
 Tourism at its meeting held on the 4
th April 2001. 
4.         The Annual Plan outlay of the Ministry of Civil Aviation for the year 2001-2002 is Rs.1641.31 crores out of
 which Internal and External budgetary resources (IEBR) component is Rs.1578.31 crores and the gross budgetary
 support is Rs.63.00 crores.

Includes Rs.39.15 crores for projects in North Eastern regions, Sikkim and other priority areas; Rs.10.79 crores for
 Amritsar Airport and Rs.0.90 crores as assistance from OECF for Aurangabad Airport.

AIR INDIA LIMITED
 
6.         During the year 2000-2001, as against the approved outlay of Rs.675.30, the actual expenditure is estimated at
 Rs.699.57 crores.  The increase of Rs.24.27 crores is mainly due to increase in aircraft project loan repayment
 consequent to weakening of the Indian rupees vis-à-vis US Dollar, increase in end of term purchase price of one B747-
300 Combi, leased in November 1998 due to exchange rate variation and contribution of Rs.1.00 crore to Indira Gandhi
 Rashtriya Uran Akademi (IGRUA).  The entire expenditure was incurred out of the Internal and Extra Budgetary
 Resources of Air India Limited. 
7.         The Annual Plan Outlay of Air India for the year 2001-2002 has been estimated at Rs.445.44 crores, which
 mainly comprises of Aircraft Loan Repayments of Rs.285.44 crores and Capital Expenditure of Rs.150.00 crores.  A
 token provision for advance payment of Rs.10.00 crores has been made for new aircraft (type yet to be identified) to be
 inducted by Air India Limited.
 
8.         Air India’s present fleet consists of the following aircraft: -
AIRCRAFT NUMBER
1.  Boeing B747-200 4
2.  Boeing B747-400 6
3.  Boeing B747-300 (Combi) 2
4.  Airbus A300-B4 3
5.  Airbus A310-300 10 (including two dry leased aircraft)
 
9.         In addition, two more A310-300 aircraft are likely to be inducted on dry lease basis by the end of April 2001 or
 the first week of May 2001.  
10.       The Committee observed that a token provision of Rs.10.00 crores has been made for advance payment for new
 aircraft to be inducted by Air India Ltd.  The Committee desired to know how many aircraft do Air India intend to
 procure and what is the current status with regard to the procurement of the aircraft. 
11.       In reply, the Committee was informed that since Air India is going to be disinvested shortly, they have decided
 not to purchase any new aircraft at present.  Air India had taken up an aircraft evaluation study on the understanding
 that Government would inject funds for aircraft acquisition.  Subsequently it was decided that the Government would
 not be in a position to infuse requisite funds and Air India, therefore, discontinued the aircraft evaluation study. 
12.            Meanwhile, Air India has drawn up a 10 year Business Plan (2001-2002 to 2010-2011) which proposes the
 induction of 18 Small Capacity Long Range (SCLR) and 28 Small Capacity Short Range (SCSR) aircraft.  Aircraft
 induction begins from 2003-2004, after the induction of the Strategic Partner. 
13.       The Government is presently processing the disinvestment of part of its stake in Air India.  The strategic partner
 proposed to be inducted would be expected to finance and support the aircraft acquisition process and for these reasons,
 the aircraft selection process and purchase decisions are being deferred till the completion of the disinvestment process.
14.       Only a token provision of Rs.10.00 crores has been made in Annual Plan 2001-2002 of Air India that is
 inadequate for actual aircraft induction.  As an interim measure, Air India is inducting A310-300 aircraft on dry lease
 for growth and fleet rationalisation.  Air India has signed an agreement with Singapore Airlines for the dry lease of two
 A310-300 aircraft and with M/s. General Electric Aviation Service (GECAS) of USA for the dry lease of two A310-
300 aircraft.  
15.       When asked whether non-procurement of aircraft would lead to under valuation of Air India since non-
availability of aircraft is resulting in non-utilisation of capacity of Air India, the Committee was informed that although
 Air India is not pursuing aircraft acquisition, it is adding capacity through dry leasing of aircraft and also through Code
 Share/Block Space Arrangements. Air India has been vigorously pursuing the conclusion of the Code Share/Block
 Space Arrangements with foreign airlines to supplement its own physical operations.  As on 31
st March 2000, Code
 Share/Block Space Arrangements implemented by Air India envisaged the deployment of 1128 seats per week in each
 direction.  Thereafter, Air India has finalised Code Share/Block Space Arrangements with the following airlines:-

Virgin Atlantic LON/DEL/LON 130

Thus the capacity deployment by Air India under the Code Share/Block Space Arrangements will reflect an increase of

16.       The Committee has also been informed that Air India has taken several steps to overcome the losses incurred
 during the last few years.  Some of these are as under:-
Several posts of India based officers abroad have been abolished;
Two voluntary schemes have been notified, viz. shorter working scheme and leave without pay and allowance scheme
 for a period of two years extendable upto five years;
Redeployment of employees from non-operational to operational areas;
Freeze on external recruitment in non-operational categories;
10% cut in daily outstanding allowance payable at all foreign stations and 25% at Indian Stations; and
(vi)            Introduction of route rationalization programme to optimise revenue involving curtailment of flights on
 marginal and loss making routes and the redeployment of this capacity to profit making routes. 
17.       The Committee notes that in view of the disinvestment proceedings, Air India has decided not to procure any
 new aircraft.  Instead Air India would be adding five more aircraft to their fleet on account of dry lease.  The
 Committee disapproves the idea of the Government to defer the acquisition of the aircraft by Air India pending
 disinvestment.  Not a single aircraft has been added to the fleet of Air India since long.  The Committee is of the view
 that non-acquisition of the aircraft would have certainly affected the valuation of Air India.  The Committee also notes
 the steps taken by Air India to minimise the losses and return to profitability and hopes that these steps would help the
 company in making a turnaround.

NEED FOR THE SATELLITE BASED NAVIGATION SYSTEM
 
55.       The Committee has been informed that at present navigation of the aircraft is carried out with the help of signals
 received by the aircraft from ground based navigational aids and landing aids which can be installed at places where
 proper terrain conditions are available and as such cannot be installed in forests, sea and other mountainous regions. 
 The aircraft are, therefore, perforce required to follow the routes where these aids have been installed.  ICAO has
 adopted satellite based CNS/ATM system for global implementation.  Adoption of this system would facilitate
 seamless navigation of aircraft across diverse airspace regions, increase airspace capacity, permit direct routes saving
 time and fuel and above all enhance air safety. 
56.            Airports Authority of India has been taking up the implementation of various elements of the CNS/ATM
 system.  One of the key elements of this new system is satellite-based navigation using the core satellite constellations
 like GPS of the USA and the GLONASS of the Russian Federation.  These satellite constellations continuously
 broadcast signals, which could be used for signals for determination of their position while in flight and thus use these
 signals for navigation between origin and destination. 
57.       The accuracy, integrity and availability of the signals from these satellites, however, do not meet the stringent
 requirements of aircraft navigation particularly in the critical phases of flight like precision approach and landing. 
 Therefore, there is a need for augmentation to enhance the accuracy, integrity and availability of these signals to meet
 the requirements of aircraft navigation in all phases of flight.  Space Based Augmentation System (SBAS), which could
 cover a large geographical area, is being developed as Regional Augmentation Systems by individual as well as group
 of countries.  The US WAAS, the European EGNOS and the Japan’s MSAS are the three front-runners in the field of
 SBAS.  The coverage of MSAS in the East and of EGNOS in the West leave a large air space in between and
 particularly over South Asia, including Indian air space uncovered. 
58.            Airports Authority of India is, therefore, planning to bridge this gap and provide coverage over this air space
 by putting its own SBAS.  It has been discussing for quite some time with the Department of Space (DOS), which has
 the necessary technology and expertise in this area.  A project Report has been prepared by the DOS for joint
 implementation of a Technology Demonstration System (TDS) as a proof of concept and a precursor to the full
 operation capability system with the cost of the system equally shared by Airports Authority of India and DOS.  While
 DOS would be the lead player in the implementation of TDS, Airports Authority of India will take over from there
 onwards and implement a full operational capability system with DOS continuing as a Technical Adviser. 
59.       The system, when in place, would not only provide coverage over the Indian airspace but has the potential to
 provide coverage over vast airspace much beyond with marginal additional cost.  In coordination with other
 neighbouring countries in fora like SAARC, this could finally evolve into a regional system bridging a gap between the
 EGNOS in the West and MSAS in the East. 
60.       After the implementation of SBAS to full operational capability, the system would run in parallel to ground

13.       The Committee was informed that in recognition of the need of funds for road infrastructure sector, Union

 programmes, the indigenous R&D organisations have made significant achievement and contribution in solving road
 engineering problems such as introduction of new materials like rubber/polymer modified bitumen, use of fly ash in
 road construction and anti-corrosive techniques, road user cost study to access effect of road condition on vehicle
 operating cost, pavement deterioration models, aesthetical and environment friendly road side furniture, reinforced
 earth technology, development of computer software for analysis and design of highway bridge superstructure,
 instrumentation of simply supported bridges and cantilever bridges.  These organisations generally make their best of
 efforts to produce results commensurate with the investment made in the Research Schemes.  But due to indigenously
 non-availability of modern equipments & instruments, inadequate interaction between Indian and International
 technical/scientific community and lack of adequate fiscal incentives to promote R & D efforts in highway sector; the
 indigenous research and development could not be made at par with international levels.  At present there are 39
 ongoing schemes on R &D.   
53.       The Committee is not satisfied with the pace of development in the    Research & Development activities in the
 Road sector.  Till date, the indigenous Research & Development is not able to match the international level.  The
 Committee understands that the Ministry earlier facing the problem of shortage of funds.  However, now the Ministry is
 well satisfied with the availability of funds and hopes that the Ministry will now concentrate upon R&D activities on
 road sector and provide sufficient funds therefor. 
 
* * * * * * 
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
HIGHER ALLOCATION FOR ROAD SECTOR
 
The Committee is happy to note that since 2000-2001 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has been getting
 sufficient funds as a result of which Ministry is now in a position to achieve the physical targets as initially envisaged
 for the Ninth Plan.  Earlier the Ministry has not been to exploit its potential due to paucity of funds.  Now there is no
 dearth of money for Road sector and so it is the turn of the Ministry to establish its expertise in the field of Road Sector.
(Para 12)
 
CENRTAL ROAD FUND 
The Committee is happy to note that with the setting up of the Central Road Fund, the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways has now been able to provide sufficient funds for the development and maintenance of State Highways and
 State Roads.  However, during the last year only an amount of Rs. 314.75 crores out of Rs.990 crores could be released
 to States for the purpose.  The Committee can understand this fact that within a short span of time, the States could not
 have been able to utilise whole amount of Rs. 990 crore allocated for the development of State Highways and State
 Roads.  The Committee hopes that in future the State Governments will be able to utilise the whole amount allocated to
 them in this regard.  However, the Committee wants the Ministry to impress upon the State Government that the State
 Highways and State roads should be developed in such a way that the entire State roads network would provide a feeder

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/51streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 system to the rail network thereby avoiding development of parallel road network.  The Committee is aware that there
 have been instances of diversion of funds and are not utilised for the purpose for which they are allocated. Therefore,
 Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should ensure proper and strict monitoring of
 the schemes for which the funds are allocated from the Central Road Funds so as to avoid cost escalation and time over
 run.
(Para 16)
 
CHECK POINTS & SPEED BREAKERS AT NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
 
The Committee is of the view that the check points on National Highways are illegal collection points for the local
 police and local bodies where traffic is stopped and harassed.  The Committee is also of the view that speed breakers on
 the National Highways are one of the reasons for accidents.  Therefore, it is much needed to remove all these speed
 breakers from National Highways.  The Committee is unable to understand why State Governments have not complied
 and implemented the directions of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways in this regard.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry should impose some financial penalty on those states who violate the
 guidelines and fail to remove check points and speed breakers from National Highways.
(Para 20) 
 
EXCISE DUTY ON MIXING OF CEMENT
 
The Committee agrees to the view put forth by the Ministry that proposed excise duty on mixing of cement is likely to
 increase the cost of construction of National Highways and open the new way of the harassment.  The Committee is
 unable to understand as to what has made the Ministry of Finance to treat the mixing of cement as production activity. 
 The Committee is of the view that Central Excise Department is finding new ways and means to earn revenue and to
 impose excise duties. The mixing of cement is one of such the examples.  The Committee therefore recommends that
 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter strongly with Ministry of Finance (Department
 of Revenue) to review the proposal.
(Para 22)
 
DEVELOPMENT OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS IN NORTH EASTERN REGION
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for development and
 improvement in the poor condition of the National Highways in the North East region.  The Committee hopes that
 allocated amount of Rs.282.15 crores will be fully utilised by the North Eastern States with the help of direct payment
 system as introduced by the Ministry. The Committee, however recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and
 Highways should frame some schemes for this region which will help the contractors or Public Works Departments of
 these states to procure hot mix plants, boilers and any other related thing which is needed in the construction of roads. 
                                                                                                                                                                (Para 25)
 
GUIDELINES FOR DECLEARING NEW NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Road Transport &Highways  has been declaring State roads as National
 Highways in violation of the guidelines prescribed in this regard, frequently.  It has increased the burden of the
 Government for maintenance of National Highways.  The Committee therefore recommends that the guidelines issued
 in this respect should be adhered to strictly.  The problems relating to the transferring of land to the Centre,
 rehabilitation and relocation in the case of road widening and four laning of National Highway, should be taken care of
 well in advance and if possible, it should be the part of the guidelines.  The Committee hopes that this will check the
 delays in execution of plans for development of newly declared National Highways.
(Para 32)
ROAD SAFETY
 
The Committee is worried about the number of road accidents in the country.  The Committee is of the view that most
 of the accidents occurs due to the driver’s negligence, unawareness of the road safety norms and non-implementation of
 the Rules and Regulations.  The efforts made for reducing the road accidents are not sufficient enough to reduce the

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/51streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 number of road accidents.  
The Committee thinks that refresher training programme for heavy vehicle drivers in the non-organised sector has not
 achieved the desired results.  The Ministry should not feel satisfied that the number of road accidents are decreasing as
 compare to previous year. However, they should make efforts to further decrease the number of road accidents that are
 taking lives of thousand of people every year.  Traffic sense in general is missing among the drivers.  Human aspects
 should be made important component for the training programme of drivers. The Committee recommends that drivers
 should be educated with regard to road safety rules and regulations, which will decrease the number of accidents. 
The Committee appreciates the introduction of ‘Smart Card’ by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. The
 concept of smart card is an innovative step and will definitely minimise the cases of issuance of fake licenses.
(Paras 38, 39 and 40)
 
GRANTS-IN-AID TO NON GOVERNMENT ORGANISATIONS
 
The Committee is surprised to note that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways does not have their own
 monitoring system to see how the Grants-in-aid given to Non-Government Organisation to undertake various types of
 road safety programmes are utilised.    The Committee is of the view that in the absence of proper monitoring system,
 funds are likely to be misused.  There is a possibility of the fake Non Government Organisation who can come forward
 to obtain grants with the purpose to undertake road safety programmes.  
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should set up its own
 monitoring system and should ensure that the grants, which have been allocated to Non Government Organisations,
 should be utilised for the purpose for which it is approved. The Ministry should also release the State-wise list of NGOs
 with their addresses for the information of general public. This will definitely increase the awareness of the public
 about the activities of Non Government Organisation which in turn will ensure proper utilisation of the allocated funds
 and reduce the chances of the corruption.
(Paras 44 and 45)
VEHICULAR POLLUTION
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the measures taken by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways to check and
 control the pollution of the vehicles.  Thanks to the vehicular pollution, Delhi is known as one of the most polluted city
 in the world.  The Committee hopes that with the enforcement of use of CNG in public vehicle will reduce the level of
 vehicular pollution in Delhi and similar steps will be taken in respect of other polluted cities of the country. The
 Committee however recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter of having
 more and more outlets in the country to provide CNG to vehicles to avoid wastage of time in standing in the long
 queues.
 
The Committee is aware of the fact that vehicle owners have to pay heavy charges for obtaining ‘Pollution under control
 Certificate’ for their vehicles. This has been proving as discouraging factor and public in general is less enthusiastic for
 having pollution check up of their vehicles.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road
 Transport and Highways should take up the matter with the concerned agencies to create an environment where the
 vehicle owners may offer voluntarily first for testing their vehicles.
(Paras 48 and 49)
 
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the pace of development in the    Research & Development activities in the Road
 sector.  Till date, the indigenous Research & Development is not able to match the international level.  The Committee
 understands that the Ministry earlier facing the problem of shortage of funds.  However, now the Ministry is well
 satisfied with the availability of funds and hopes that the Ministry will now concentrate upon R&D activities on road
 sector and provide sufficient funds therefor.
(Para 53)

CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE BUOY MOORING (SBM)
 
23.       The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism under took the study
 visit to Cochin and came to know the peculiar problem being faced by Cochin Port Trust by construction of Single
 Buoy Mooring (SBM).  In this connection the Committee held discussion with representatives of Cochin Port Trust and
 Kochi Refineries Ltd. 
24.       In his deposition before the Committee during the discussion, the representative of Kochi Refineries Ltd.
 informed that the present crude oil processing capacity of KRL is 7.5 million tonnes per annum.  The crude oil is
 received in tankers at specially constructed jetties in Cochin Port Trust and pumped to the Refineries’ Storage tanks
 through pipelines.  Since March 1998, Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) was in force and the cost incurred by
 the Refineries in receiving crude oil and processing it into products was reimbursed completely by the Oil Co-
ordination Committee (OCC).  Since April 1998, the APM has been dismantled and the entire cost has to be borne by

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/52ndreport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 individual Refineries.  In this de-regulated scenario, KRL has to face competition from Private Sector Refineries in
 India as well as for imports, it was proposed to expand the crude oil processing capacity to 13.5 million tonnes per
 annum, along with measures to achieve value addition and cost reduction.  The present transportation cost of crude oil
 which contributes more than 50% of the total operating cost excluding the cost of crude oil, was identified as the most
 important area for cost reduction.  The only way to reduce cost was to receive crude oil in large ships.  However,
 Cochin Port, being an inland Port, has limitations for receiving large oil tankers.  It was in this background KRL
 thought of setting up an off-shore (i.e. 12 kms. away from the sea-shore and 6 kms. away from the Port limits) Single
 Buoy Mooring (SBM) and connected facilities which would be the cheapest option for operating the Refineries even at
 the existing level of 7.5 million tonnes.  
25.       The Committee also heard the views of the representative of the Cochin Port Trust after the presentation of the
 Representatives of Kochi Refinery Ltd. on the crucial problem faced by Cochin Port Trust.  The Committee was
 informed that in the event of setting up of the SBM by the KRL in the open sea, there would be non-utilisation of the
 existing infrastructure created by the port exclusively for the Kochi Refineries Ltd. (KRL) for handling POL products
 for their Refineries. 
26.       Cochin Port Trust developed two tanker berths way back in the 1950’s.  The Port Trust also developed an
 exclusive Oil Terminal in 1984 for handling POL products for KRL.  Other allied infrastructure such as flotilla, fire
 float, fire fighting facilities and also especially skilled manpower was created by the Port Trust exclusively for the
 Refinery.  The channel, which was 9.75 meters depth, was also dredged to 12.9 meters for handling bigger size vessels
 with a draft of 11.7 meters at Cochin Oil Terminal, by expending around Rs. 50 crores.  The total investment on the
 entire infrastructure created for the KRL would come to Rs. 100 crores.  The present move of KRL will make the entire
 Port infrastructure created exclusively for the KRL infructuous.   Once the POL handling operations are shifted to the
 proposed SBM, it will jeopardise the very survival of the Port.  The Port has already suggested to KRL that the Port
 Trust is prepared to create additional infrastructure for handling crude oil products. 
27.       The Committee wanted to know as to why the KRL did not take the Cochin Port Trust into confidence before
 going ahead with setting up of the SBM Project, especially, when the Port Trust was serving the KRL for the last so
 many years for handling POL products for the Refineries.  The Committee wanted to know the action taken by the
 Cochin Port Trust on their part after knowing about setting up of the SBM Project by KRL. 
28.       In reply, the Committee was informed by the KRL representative that the service being provided by the Cochin
 Port Trust was not considered economical in the de-regulated scenario.  Moreover, once the SBM was set up, there
 would not be any recurring loss to KRL, and the Consultant appointed to make feasibility study for the purpose opined
 that the project should be taken up at the earliest for implementation.  Any delay in its implementation would entail cost
 escalation.  So they decided to go ahead with the project independently.  It was also felt that consulting another
 organisation might delay the process.  It was mentioned that the mechanical completion of the project would take 36
 months and after that another three months for commissioning.  The Environmental Clearance for KRL’s Capacity
 Expansion Project including the crude oil receipt facilities had been obtained from the Ministry of Environment &
 Forests.  KRL is against any alternative proposal which would attract recurring expenditure on account of dredging etc. 
 Any delay in timely completion of the Project will entail cost escalation by about 25% of the total estimate.  The
 Planning Commission is also vehemently against any delay in commissioning the Project. 
29.       While clarifying the points raised by the KRL, the representative of Cochin Port Trust Stated that despite
 repeated requests by Cochin Port Trust,  KRL was extremely reluctant to share any information about their plans of
 expansion including the setting up of the SBM.  However, based on information having obtained from informal sources
 about the SBM, Cochin Port Trust immediately made representation to the Ministry of Surface Transport and the

CUSTOMS RELATED DIFFICULTIES FACED BY USER AGENCIES WORKING AT THE PORTS 
 
33.       The Committee also came to know about the Custom related problems being faced by various using agencies
 working at the Ports which in turn affecting the functioning of the Ports.   In this connection Committee during its visits
 to Cochin had the opportunity to acquaint itself to situation particularly at the Cochin Port Trust and held discussion
 with the concerned agencies.  The details of the some of the problems, which were brought to notice of the Committee,
 have been given in succeeding paragraphs.   
(i)         Issue of passes to main line operators. 
34.       The representative of the Cochin Steamer Agent’s Association Stated that the Customs do not recognize the
 Main Line Operators (MLOs) as Steamer Agents as far as containerized cargo is concerned and insist for
 filling/amendment of manifests by feeder line operators only.  If one MLO delays the submission of the Imports
 manifest of one container to the feeder line operator, the filling of the entire vessel’s containers manifest would be
 delayed resulting in delay for onward movement of containers like ICD, House De-stuffing, CFS movements etc.  In
 fact, the custodian of the cargo is the MLO.  It was stated that mammoth carriers, viz. Evergreen, Mearsk, German
 Express etc are not in a position to call directly at the Port and they can only operate through feeder lines.  In the
 circumstance, it may be considered to recognise the MLOs as Steamer Agents to amend/file manifest separately for
 each of their container, which would save a lot of time in clearance of Cargo/containers and consequential financial loss
 to the trade. 
35.       The representative of Customs Cochin clarified that as per the Customs Act, 1962, the transaction i.e.
 entry/departure/clearance/loading and unloading of the cargo in the Customs area has to be performed by the Master of
 the vessel or his authorised Agents.  As per the Act, the responsibility to account for the cargo carried by the vessel
 rests on the Master of the vessel.  If the cargo is not satisfactorily accounted for, the Master of the vessel is liable for
 penal action.  The Act, hence does not recognise Main Line Operators or feeder line operators, and expects the Master
 of the vessel to be responsible for the cargo carried by him.  Hence manifest filed by the Master of the vessel cannot be
 amended by any person other than the authorised Steamer Agents without his concurrence.  As such, it would not be
 possible to permit either the MLOs or feeder line operators other than the authorised Steamer Agents from
 filing/amending the manifest as per the provisions of the Customs Act.  The Customs do not have any control or
 jurisdiction over the Main Line Operator who operates in a far off place.  The Customs has control only over the person
 who actually brings the cargo to the Port.   The Customs Act warrants proper accountability of the cargo being brought
 to India.  At present, the feeder line operator has to depend on the MLOs for all information’s relating to the cargo
 coming through containers, i.e. the feeder line operator need not always be aware of the contents of the container.  In
 the absence of proper accountability no one could be held responsible particularly so in case contraband goods,
 narcotics or explosives are carried in containers, even though Section 116 of he Customs Act envisages taking penal
 action against the person who brings unaccounted cargo to India.  In the circumstances, without amending the relevant
 provisions in the existed Customs Act, the Customs is not in position to issue passes to the MLOs.

UNIFORMITY IN PORTS TARIFF
 
43.       The Committee was informed that the regulation is considered essential wherever the provide of services
 factions in a monopoly or near monopoly situation.  The regulatory authority is considered necessary even when the
 monopoly service provides in the State. The Major Ports Trusts Act, 1963 was amended by Port Laws (Amendment)
 Act 1997 (15 of 1997) to provide for an independent Tariff Authority for Major Ports for fixing and revising the Port
 Tariff.  An independent authority i.e. tariff authority for Major Ports (TAMP) for the above purpose was set up on 10
th
 April, 1997.  TAMP has jurisdiction only on major port trusts which are administered under the Major Port Trusts Act
 1963. 
44.       Till very recently, Indian Ports faced no competition and in most cases lay down the law in their own without
 any fear of loosing customers and facing down turn in business.   Their main concern was how to reduce the time that
 ships spent outside the berths waiting for a chance to avail of their services.  However the developments of the last few
 years have changed all this drastically.  Where formerly ships had to wait for a chance to enter on over crowded Indian
 Port, they have new choices of using developing and fast coming new Ports i.e. Minor/State Ports. In the Mumbai itself,
 Mumbai Port, Jawaharlal Nehru Port, the privately owned and managed Pipavau Port or even the newly developed
 Mundra Port further north on the west coast.  Each of these Ports is competing with each other to woo customers by
 competitive tariffs and superior service. The traffic of minor Ports from 36 million tonnes in 1998-99 to about 80
 million tonnes this year and 100 MT approximately during 2001-02 is an important remarkable development in the port
 sector.
 
45.       The Committee is of the view that in the present age of liberlisation and decentarlisation of power, monopoly of
 the State is itself going out.  To boost the Indian business and make friendly competitive environment, there is need to
 eradicate red tapism, rules & regulations to the extent as to which it is possible.  In the present scenario, minor and
 State Ports are developing with the fast pace and challenging the status of the Major Ports.  Tariff authority for Major
 Ports which regularise only the tariff for the Major Ports does not have any authority /control over the tariff at minor
 and State Ports. This situation gives special benefit of lower tariff to Minor/State Ports as to attract comparatively more
 cargo. 
46.       It is not appreciable that while facing the new challenges, the Major Ports are to be regulated in case of port
 tariff by the extra statutory/constitutional authority.  Due to the regulation of port tariff of Major Ports, the level playing
 field between Major Ports and minor/State Ports does not exist since only Major Ports come under the jurisdiction of
 regulating authority while other Ports do not.  It is a clearly discrimination towards the Major Ports of the country.  The
 Committee therefore recommends that uniformity of tariff at Ports in the country is highly required among the major,
 minor and State Ports.  In the present scenario of modernisation and Corporatisation of Ports, it is very essential that our
 Major Ports should have liberty to fix port tariff at their own.  In such case, there is no need of regulatory authority over
 Ports i.e. Tariff authority for Major Ports.  The Ministry of Shipping should seriously analyse the situation and bring
 necessary legislation in this regard to ensure uniformity in the Tariff of all Ports in the country.

65.       The Committee was apprised that now a day Indian Shipping Sector is facing heavy taxation, which is
 obstructing its natural growth.  The Mudaliar Committee, constituted after independence to go into the question of
 recommendations on how to increase India’s Shipping strongly recommended that Independent India should have a
 strong merchant fleet.  Till 1975-76, Indian Shipping achieved the target of 5 MT.  After that it has not been able to
 achieve much increase in the rate of growth.  The Ninth Plan target is 9 MTs.  The Ministry is of the view that this
 target is hardly to achieve due to several reasons, which obstructs the growth of shipping sector. 
66.       The Committee further apprised that Indian Shipping Sector is yet to be provided a friendly and facilitator
 policy.  It is evident that the shipping industry does not grow with itself, as the automobile industry or any other
 industry.  Where there are a number of indigenous companies, which compete with each other.  Where as in India’s
 Shipping Sector all major concerns i.e. Shipping Corporation of India, Great Eastern or Chougule do not compete each
 other in the Indian market.  They compete with international market.  This type of situation is not favourable to India’s
 Shipping Sector. 
67.       The Committee also came to know that shipping fleets of the most of the countries are enjoying benefits of zero-
tax regimes i.e. Singapore, U.K. etc.  All of them introduced zero tax-regimes.  The rate of taxation is 1% at the most. 
 Whereas, in India, shipping sector have regular taxation, which costs from 35% to 38%.  Besides this, the five percent
 (5%) customs duty has also imposed on the import of ships, which has never been in the past.  There is no country in
 the international arena, which imposes tax on ships.  High rate of tax i.e. 25% on the interest payment of external

 will also definitely boost the traffic handling and increase the capacity of the Major Ports in the country.  The 9th plan
 working group had made a projection of traffic of 424 million tonnes by the end year of 9th Five Year Plan.  It is
 anticipated by the Ministry that traffic handling of Major Ports may be at the best reach to a level of 325 MT.  It is also
 assessed that the capacity addition during the 9th plan will be of the order of 157 MT. The Committee is unhappy on the
 failure of achievement of projected Cargo handling of 424 MT as projected by the 9th plan-working group.  During the
 year 2000-2001, the Ports have not been able to utilise their traffic handling capacity of 314 MT and only 283.80 MT of
 the traffic was handled during that year.  The Committee is also disappointed to note that against the capacity of 344
 MT the Ministry has projected traffic handling of 325 MT for this year.  The Committee hopes that the Major Ports will
 utilise the additional capacity to be created this year and will enhance their cargo handling efficiency.
(Paras 13 and 17)
 
DEVELOPMENT OF MINOR PORTS
The Committee appreciates the performance shown by these minor/captive Ports.  Minor Ports are serving as alternative
 of the Major Ports in some cases and minimising the extra burden on the Major Ports.  The Committee is happy to note
 that the Ministry of Shipping is giving attention to it and supporting the development of these Minor Ports.  The
 Committee is of the view that Major Ports of the country are in the process of Corporatisation and modernisation which
 will definitely enhance their Cargo handling efficiency.  There is a need to look after these minor Ports also.  Their
 modernisation is also much needed along with the modernisation of Major Ports. Minor Ports can play catalytic and
 proactive role in the development of Inland Water Transport System in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that Ministry of Shipping should frame such schemes for technical/financial support to the respective
 maritime States for modernisation and development of these minor Ports, inspite of the fact that these are monitored
 and maintained by the States. 
(Para 22)

The Committee is of the view that there has been total lack of interaction between Kochi Refineries Ltd. and Cochin
 Port Trust in the matter of construction of Single Buoy Mooring which is likely to make the entire Port infrastructure
 created exclusively for Kochi Refineries Ltd. at the cost of Rs.100.00 crores infructous as reported by the Cochin Port

 Shipping and Petroleum and Natural Gas should evolve an amicable solution in the matter.  The future of the Cochin

(Para 32)
 
CUSTOMS RELATED DIFFICULTIES FACED BY USER AGENCIES WORKING AT THE PORTS 
ISSUE OF PASSES TO MAIN LINE OPERATORS
 
The Committee is of the view that world over the cargo handling activities have undergone a lot of transformation.  If
 the Main Line Operators are allowed to file/amend the manifest treating them as Steamer Agents for their specific
 boxes, it will reduce the difficulties of Custom House Agents and also the duration of stay of imports loaded boxes at
 the Port.  The Committee feels that with the advancement of the containerization, there are multiple Steamer Agents for
 containers carried by a particular vessel and therefore recommends that the Main Line Operators should also be
 recognised as Steamer Agents. 
The Committee is also of the view that of late the definition of cargo has changed from a physical unit to one which
 assures responsibility.  World over container traffic has been growing in a fast pace.  In the changed scenario of
 containerization the responsibility of the cargo actually rests with the main line operators.  The Customs Act was
 enacted in 1962 at a time when the concept of containerization was not there.  Amendment to the existing custom is
 inevitable to cater the needs of the Custom House Agents.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of
 Shipping should look into the matter and approach concerned Ministry of the Government of India for suitable
 amendment in the Custom Act 1962.
(Paras 36 and 37)
 
CUSTOMS OVERTIME BOOKINGS 
The Committee is surprised to see the present system of engaging the custom officials on payment of overtime
 individually and separately for custom clearance on Sundays/holidays and after office hours which perhaps may be
 against the existing financial principles.  The Committee is unable to understand that why every Agent/Shipper is
 insisted to pay overtime to the custom officials.  The Committee is of the opinion that in the era of containerization of
 Cargoes, it is not an appreciable practice and recommends that Port Trusts should be allowed to pay overtime payments
 to the custom officials in case they handle the work on Sundays/holiday and after office hour.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should take initiative in the matter and should approach the Ministry of
 Finance to settle the matter.                                                                          
(Para 40) 
 
AMENDMENTS ON ORDERS RELATING TO CUSTOMS REGULATIONS/NOTIFICATIONS
 
The Committee seriously notes the delay in processing the claims in accordance with the amended regulations.  The
 Committee is unable to understand that why clarifications on the orders relating to customs regulations/notifications
 issued by the Ministry of Finance are not treated as amendments and implemented with immediate effect in Cochin
 Port, where as, in other Major Ports these are treated as amended and implemented immediately.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to resolve
 the issue/problem as early as possible to avoid delay in processing the claims at Ports in the country.
(Para 42)
 
UNIFORMITY IN PORTS TARIFF
