CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE BUOY MOORING (SBM)
39.       Kochi Refinery Ltd. (KRL) has proposal for augmenting their capacity from 7.5 MTPA to 13.5 MTPA and they have ­­­mooted a proposal for installing a Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) in the open sea outside the port limit for handling the crude oil without utilizing the Cochin Port Facilities.
 40.      Last year also the Committee had gone into the matter. The Committee desired to know the progress made therein. The Ministry of Shipping in a written note stated that no agreement has so far been reached between Cochin Port Trust and Kochi Refinery Ltd. in the matter.  The KRL have not consulted the Port Trust about their requirement for improved crude oil handling facilities.
41.       The Committee further informed that the KRL plans for SBM for VLCC tankers, for which investment required would be around Rs.800 crores.  In this context, it is pertinent to note that the capacity expansion proposal of KRL, is in peril in view of the presence of the private oil companies and for the present traffic of 7.5 million MTPA the crude oil handling through SBM is not likely to be economical in view of the following:-
1.         Extra quantities of inventories have to be kept because of the heavier parcel size received through VLCC.
2.         In the monsoon belt area, tankers handling at SBM are not a proven practice and therefore there is requirement of additional crude oil inventory for the coverage of down times.
3.         For the reliable operation of the refineries, keeping an alternative facility in an adjacent all weather Port is essential as is proposed in similar case of the East Coast Refinery under construction near Paradip Port.  This would call for extra expenditure.
 
42.       The SBM facility is a mono user system and is no way beneficial to any other agencies.  It has also the risk of oil spillage and marine pollution of the area, which has immense wealth of fishing grounds.
43.       The approach and inner channels are the main infrastructure of a Port.  In Port like Cochin, this main infrastructure is provided and maintained mainly at the cost of bulk commodities like crude oil etc. and the facility thus available are used by other industries, which does not have stand alone capacity to provide and maintain this system.  In case the support from KRL is not available for maintaining the channels, the vessels built/calling for repairs at Cochin Shipyard which requires wider channel would be in difficulty.  The industries like FACT, KOMINCO – Binami Zinc Ltd., Hindustan Paper Corpn. Ltd., etc which requires deeper draft for bringing their limited quantity of cargo economically will also be in trouble.  The presence of KRL for sharing the dredging cost of the channels would be a boost and encouraging factor for materializing the ambitious project of Vallarpadam Container Transshipment Terminal which would help economic development of the export and import business the Kerala in particular and of the nation in whole.
44.       Giving the details of the proposals in lieu of Single Buoy Mooring, the Ministry informed the Committee that it is possible to increase the draft at the Cochin Oil Terminal (COT) to an economic level of 14 m, which would enable brining LR-I and LR-II tankers with full load and Suez Max tankers with a load of about 1.2 lakhs tones.  Alternatively, the Port has proposed for developing an inshore terminal South of Puthuvypeen near the Cochin Gut with a tank farm facility at Puthuvypeen and linking the tank farm area to the existing pipeline at COT.  The Port has also suggested that in case the SBM requirement is unavoidable, considering the size of the tankers to be deployed for the economic transportation of crude oil it can be installed off Puthuvypeen with tank farm at Puthuvypeen and connecting pipeline to the COT.  The Port has sufficient land for tank farm construction at Puthuvypeen. The Port has other development proposals like Vallarpadam Container terminal, LNG Terminal Etc. which require about 16.5 meters which is also the draft required for bringing Suez-Max Tankers with full load.  As the channels and marine facilities required are common, the development project will become complementary for sharing the cost.  And hence it would be possible to reduce the oil handling cost further in future when these development projects are materialized.
45.       Apart from land at Puthuvypeen, the Port has land at Vallarpadam for tank farm construction. In case tank farm is located at Vallarpadam, tankers at COT can be emptied directly to the Vallarpadom tank farm and thereafter can be transferred to KRL at a low pumping rate through the existing pipeline, which has capacity limitations due to age. By this arrangement it would be possible to differ the renewal of the existing pipeline in as much as pumping even at very low rate of 2000 tonnes/hour would achieve a throughput of more than 13.5 MTPA per annum.
46.       The port is prepared to take up the development work for increasing the draft to 14m on cost sharing basis. With 14m drafts it would be possible to bring LR-I and LR-II tankers with full load and Suez-Max tankers with parcel of 1.2 Lakhs tonnes. The investment required for this is Rs. 76 Crores. The incremental annual cash out flow including the annualized capital cost is about Rs. 30 crores. Against this it is estimated that a freight saving of around Rs. 70 Crores per annum can be realized from the transportation of 7.5 million tones of crude oil from Gulf area to Cochin in LR-II and Suez-Max tankers. As such a net saving of Rs. 40 crores can be expected when the draft is increased to 14m. The port is also prepared to take up the renewal of the existing pipeline passing through the city up to the KSRTC bus station as a joint project of the CPT and KRL for improvement of the system.
47.       The Port has not received a positive response from KRL for the above alternative proposals stating one or other reasons and they are moving ahead for installation of SBM near Thuravoor.
48.       The Committee observes that despite of alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust, the Kochin Refineries Ltd. is adamant to go ahead with his plan for construction of Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) without giving a positive thought to the proposals. The Committee is of the opinion that both Public Sector undertakings are under administrative control of the Government of India and in absence of agreement, any loss incurred to the Cochin Port Trust will be the loss to the Nation. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 52nd report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) of the Ministry of Shipping and recommends that Ministries of Shipping and Petroleum and Natural Gas should evolve an amicable solution to the problem. Kochi Refinery Ltd. should consider, in the national interest, the alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust before taking up the construction of the Single Buoy Mooring.
 
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
49.       The Ministry of Shipping is responsible for the coordinated development of Inland Water Transport (IWT) in the country and in particular, for the declaration and development of National Waterways. Through Centrally Sponsored Schemes, the Central Government also makes available assistance to the States for developing Inland Waterways other than National Waterways.
50.       Inland Water Transport is generally accepted as a fuel efficient, economical and environment friendly mode of transport. However, the potential of this important mode of transport has not been fully exploited so far. In countries/regions such as USA, Europe, China etc., where IWT Sector was given due importance, IWT has substantial share in inland transport network. However, in India, this sector has not developed with desired pace. Inadequate infrastructural facilities like depth and width required for economic IWT operations, terminals for loading/unloading, navigational aids and IWT fleet are the constraints facing the inland waterways.
51.       The responsibility of development of these waterways rests with Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI). This authority along with Central Inland Water Transport Corporation (CIWTC) as the principle operator are the two Central agencies engaged in the development of inland water transport in the country. The efforts of these organisations are supplemented and supported by inland water organisations of various States and private operators.

INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR)
65.       The Government of India has specific direction to all the Ministries/Departments that the decision of public investment, in any project/scheme, is taken after considering a minimum Internal Rate of Return (IRR) of the proposed projects. Planning Commission insist on minimum 12 percent of Internal Rate of Return for any project/scheme.
66.       In his deposition before the Committee, the Secretary, Ministry of Shipping stated that of late, the cost of funds has gone down which is reflected by reduced rates of interest. With reduction in the cost of funds, there is a need to review the requirement of minimum IRR from its present base level, especially in the case of the Inland Water Transport Sector because of its greater social and economic benefits and the nascent stage of its development. India has navigable waterways aggregating 14,544 kms, of which 5200 kms of major rivers and 485 kms of canals are navigable for mechanized crafts. Inland Water Transport (IWT) has not been able to realize its full growth potential despite being an extremely energy efficient, environmentally clean and economical mode of transport.
67.       The Committee agrees to views of the Ministry of Shipping and is of the opinion that at present Inland Water Transport System in the country is at the initial stage of its development. The allocation of amount for any proposed scheme/project in the field of Inland water Transport Sector is for its infrastructure development. Therefore, there is very low scope for any Internal Rate of Return (IRR) from this Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its approach for Inland water Transport Sector and should not insist for 12% IRR of any scheme/project in this field. The concept of Internal Rate of Return may ever be dispensed with as the benefits from such projects are passed on to the trade and economy.

COASTAL SHIPPING IN INDIA
81.       The Committee informed that presently the cargo moved by Coastal Shipping, which is entirely received for Indian vessels, mainly comprises of coal, klinker, cement, crude oil, PoL and Iron ore. During Ninth five-year plan period, physical target of addition 75 vessels of 0.265 MMT, GRT was proposed in addition to 25 vessels as replacement. 79 vessels have been added to the Costal Fleet during the above period, which exceed the plan target of 75 vessels as “Additional tonnage” account.
82.       The Committee further apprised that although 79 vessels have been added to the coastal fleet the payload capacity in GRT Terms grew only marginally and is lower by almost 200% than the target. This is mainly because a large no. of tugs were added to the coastal fleet having almost no impact on the Cargo/passenger carrying capacity. The pressure on land-based modes, therefore, has not been reduced. Addition to these reasons, the Ship owners are also reluctant to acquire dedicated coastal vessels due to various impediments such as complex customs procedure, time consuming system of Post clearance, high manning scales at par with overseas Shipping, poor port infrastructure etc.
83.       The Committee further informed that for development of coastal shipping, following policy measures need to be considered: -
 
Continuation of cabotage law supported by suitable fiscal and financial incentives.
Earmarking exclusive route for Coastal Shipping along the Indian Coast.
Exclusive berths to be earmarked for coastal ships at all major parts.

OBSERVATION/CONCLUSION/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
APPRAISAL OF NINTH FIVE-YEAR PLAN AND PROJECTION FOR 10TH FIVE-YEAR PLAN
The Committee is not satisfied with the performance of the Ministry of Shipping during Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could utilise only Rs.4838.92 crores out of the approved outlay of Rs. 9428 crores in Port Sector. The Committee is of the view that the reasons given by the Ministry of Shipping for the heavy shortfall i.e. delays in sanctioning of the schemes, delays in tender finalization, award of contracts etc are not of such nature which were beyond the control of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its working and come out with specific remedial measures (predictive and preventive) to eliminate the delays leading to under-utilisation of allocated funds. Agencies/Individuals should be made accountable as and when lapses occur.
The Committee is also of the view that there has to be realistic approach while preparing any Five-Year plan. 44 Major Schemes of Ninth Five Year Plan are likely to spill over to the Tenth Five-year plan, which may affect the physical/financial targets of the Ministry fixed for the Tenth Plan. The funds proposed for Port Sector during Tenth Five Year Plan period are Rs.17416.40 crores. The Committee hopes that while preparing the Tenth Plan, the Ministry of Shipping would have visualized the possible problem and taken remedial action so that the approved plan outlay for the Tenth Five Year Plan are utilised optimally.
The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Shipping failed to achieve the target of  9 million tonnes for the Ninth Five Year Plan. The achievement of 6.84 MT is at par with the target achieved during the Eighth Plan. This shows that the tonnage acquisition was static during the Ninth Five Year Plan. The Ministry could not identify the problem of shipping industry during the full five years of Ninth Plan and did not take adequate steps to improve the situation.
The Committee is of the view that that Shipping Industry can play important role in the development of national economy. Therefore, it is necessary to provide conducive fiscal regime to Indian Shipping Sector so that it can become internationally competitive. The Committee notes with some satisfaction the fiscal concessions given to the Indian Shipping Sector and measures taken by the Government of India recently towards growth of Indian Tonnage.  The Committee, however, recommends that recommendations of the Rakesh Mohan Committee should be considered positively by the Government of India and further concessions necessary for the healthy Shipping Sector should be provided as early as possible. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation that Government of India should not levy heavy taxation on Shipping Sector. The Government should explore the possibility of Tonnage Tax régime in the country as early as possible.
(Paras 13, 14, 23 & 24)
DREDGING AT MAJOR PORTS
The Committee notes that Major Ports are spending large amount on the capital dredging either through their own resources or from the borrowed funds, which has definitely affected their financial performance.  It is also a fact that for the ports, it is difficult to raise borrowings for capital dredging because it may not result into commensurate incremental resources.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that capital dredging at all the Major Ports should be taken as national priority by the Government of India. The Government of India, as a matter of policy should provide adequate plan funds to all the Major Ports for carrying out Capital Dredging at the Ports.
The Committee strongly disapproves the procedure adopted by the Government of India in the matter of providing funds to Kolkata Port Trust for Capital Dredging. The Committee is surprised to note that on one side, the Government of India has, in principle, decided to fully reimburse the cost on items directly related to dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly as well as cost incurred on items directly related to maintenance dredging of Haldia Shipping Channel, where as, on other hand, the allocation for capital dredging has been reduced in a arbitrary manner. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be no constraint of funds for the Kolkata Port so far as dredging is concerned. Silting at Kolkata Port is problem of recurring nature therefore the actual requirement of fund for dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly and Haldia Shipping Channel be identified and provision be made at Budget Estimate stage itself.
In connection with dredging operation at the Kolkata Port Trust, the Committee would like to draw the attention of Ministry of Shipping to the comments made in the CAG report (Report No. 4 of 2002) which are reproduced below:-
“There was short fall of 19.28 million cubic metre (m.cu.m.) of dredging against the ad-hoc targets during 1996-2001 and targeted minimum depth was not achieved despite an expenditure of 1290.95 crore.”
The Committee would like to have clarification from the Ministry about navigability targets achieved vis-à-vis the contracts executed for dredging in Kolkata and Haldia Port. 
While appreciating the move, the Committee recommends that the proposed policy of long-term lease of land by Kolkata Port Trust be finalized at the earliest so as to enable the KoPT to moblise the resources to meet its urgent requirement.
(Paras 28, 34,35,36 & 38)
CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE BUOY MOORING (SBM)
The Committee observes that despite of alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust, the Kochin Refineries Ltd. is adamant to go ahead with his plan for construction of Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) without giving a positive thought to the proposals. The Committee is of the opinion that both Public Sector undertakings are under administrative control of the Government of India and in absence of agreement, any loss incurred to the Cochin Port Trust will be the loss to the Nation. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 52
nd report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) of the Ministry of Shipping and recommends that Ministries of Shipping and Petroleum and Natural Gas should evolve an amicable solution to the problem. Kochi Refinery Ltd. should consider, in the national interest, the alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust before taking up the construction of the Single Buoy Mooring.
(Para 48)
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
The Committee is unhappy to note that during the Ninth Five year plan, no progress have been made in Inland Water Transport Sector in terms of tonnage handled. The cargo handled at the beginning of Ninth Plan was 20 million tonnes and despite the investment of Rs. 150 crores during the Ninth Plan, cargo movement has remained at the same level.
The Ministry of Shipping has failed to provide adequate infrastructural facilities including night navigation for Inland Water Transport Sector during the Ninth Five Year Plan in the present three National Waterways. Now the Ministry has very ambitious programme for the Tenth Five Year Plan in IWT sector. An amount of Rs. 1710 crores has been proposed as budgetary support for this sector. Six new waterways in different States are going to be declared by the Ministry of Shipping as National Waterways. The Committee appreciates these steps but would like to be reassured that the existing waterways are strengthened with adequate infrastructure capacity as well as marketing drive so that the tonnage movement in the existing waterways get improve. The Committee also recommends that the Government should analyze the reasons as to why the Cargo movement did not improve despite the huge investment during the Ninth Plan. The Committee would like to be informed about the steps taken to improve the Cargo Movement and year-wise details of the target fixed in this regard. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should adopt road map towards optimum utilisation of plan outlay in Inland Water Transport Sector after thorough review of hindrances being faced by this sector. The Committee also recommends that Government should fix the specific year-
wise targets for the Tenth Plan for providing night navigation facilities in existing National Waterways and inform the Committee accordingly.
The Committee appreciates the steps and efforts taken by the Ministry of Shipping for revival of the Central Inland Water transport Corporation Ltd.  The Committee is of the view that expertise and facilities of ship repair and dry dock facilities at Rajabagan Dockyard should not go waste. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while taking steps for revival of Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd., the facilities of ship repair and Dry Dock available in Rajabagan Dockyard should be exploited fully so that assets and  manpower engaged in those activities are utilised optimally. The Committee also expect that the present ambiguity with regard to future manpower in the Rajabagan Dockyard should be removed and the manpower requirement in Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd. for the next five-years be firmed up and informed to all concerned including the Committee. 
The Committee agrees to views of the Ministry of Shipping and is of the opinion that at present Inland Water Transport System in the country is at the initial stage of its development. The allocation of amount for any proposed scheme/project in the field of Inland water Transport Sector is for its infrastructure development. Therefore, there is very low scope for any Internal Rate of Return (IRR) from this Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review its approach for Inland water Transport Sector and should not insist for 12% IRR of any scheme/project in this field. The concept of Internal Rate of Return may ever be dispensed with as the benefits from such projects are passed on to the trade and economy.     
(Paras 57, 58, 64 & 67)
 
MARITIME TRAINING IN INDIA
The Committee appreciates the proposal for establishment of an Indian Institute of Maritime Studies under Societies Registration Act, 1960 and placing the Government run Maritime Institutions within the domain of this Society. The move will certainly give a qualitative boost to the maritime training in the country. The Committee, however, recommends that the Government of India may consider to give the status to Indian Institute of Maritime Studies similar to that of IITs’ and introduce a central legislation accordingly at the earliest. 
(Para 72)
 
SHIPPING CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD.
The Committee is not satisfied with the attitude and approach of the Government of India is respect of Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. On one hand, the Government of India has taken decision to go for disinvestment in SCI, whereas on other side, Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. has expansion plan for acquisition of vessels during the year of 2002-03 involving an amount of Rs. 647.84 crores for investment.  The Committee fails to understand as to why the decision for disinvestment of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) has taken place when SCI is able to manage its activities through its own resources.
On enquiry from the Ministry regarding revaluation of assets of SCI, the Committee was informed that no revaluation has taken place, so far, since process of disinvestment started.        
The Committee fails to understand why the SCI has not revalued its assets as the matter of disinvestment of SCI has been under consideration for the last 3-4 years. Owner should be aware of its assets value when a major part of it is being disposed of.
(Paras 78,79 & 80)
COASTAL SHIPPING IN INDIA
The Committee is unhappy to note that during Ninth Five year plan no special attention was given on coastal shipping which is one of the most energy efficient, eco-friendly and cheap modes of transport for movement of bulk commodities over long distances. Considering the vast coastline and congestion on land routes, the costal shipping offers an effective alternative means of Transport. Despite this, no adequate policy measures have been taken by the Ministry. There are 184 minor/intermediate ports in the country along the 5560 kms coastline of India. Minor/intermediate ports can play important role in the coastal Shipping. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of Shipping should frame a comprehensive policy and prepare plans to promote the coastal shipping in the country. 
(Para 84)

 Kerala to Gulf Countries. Ministry of Civil Aviation have informed that Published fares on Internal routes are fixed

 fares quoted in the market are usually much lower than IATA fares.  In competitive markets, market forces play a

43.     The Airports Authority of India (AAI) aims at providing world class Airport services and facilities as are
 necessary for the sale and efficient operation of air transport services and to make available amenities for passengers
 and other users of the airports. 
44.     During the evidence, the attention of the Secretary (Civil Aviation) was drawn to a note internally circulated by
 the Airports Authority of India wherein it had been stated that the long-term leasing of the airports would not require
 any amendment of the AAI Act.  In this connection, the Committee sought the comments of the Ministry. In their reply,
 The Ministry of Civil Aviation have stated as under:-
"As per the legal advice furnished by Airports Authority of India's legal consultant (M/s Amarchand Mangaldas &
 Suresh Shorff, appointed in connection with the leasing of the airports), which was duly supported with the legal
 opinion given by Justice Bhagwati, Ex-Chief Justice of India, the proposed long term leasing could be accomplished
 within the provisions of the existing statute viz. the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 read with the Rules under the
 Aircraft Rules 1937.  Accordingly, in the background paper furnished earlier, it was indicated that it would not require
 any amendment of Airports Authority of India Act, which was shown as one of the advantages of opting for the route of
 'Long term leasing'.
However, subsequently, the Ministry of Law to whom the legal opinion was forwarded for vetting has advised that
 amendment by way of amplification of Section 12 of the Airports Authority of India Act for providing an enabling
 provision is a must. Hence the amendment Bill.
It may be seen that other routes of privatization like corporatisation, outright sale, etc. where the ownership of airports
 will also shift to the successful bidder, will involve large scale amendments, unlike the route of long term lease for
 which simple amendment by way of amplification of Section 12 of the Airports Authority of India Act is only
 required."

The Committee, in its 42
nd Report on Demands for Grants 2000-2001 of the Ministry of Civil Aviation, had expressed
 hope that the rationalization of fleet with less types of aircraft will help reduce the demand for investment and spares,
 maintenance facilities and simulators and will also result in better utilization of aircraft infrastructural facilities and
 technical manpower of pilots and maintenance engineers.  The Committee, however, notes that while an expert
 committee has been set up to assess Air India's long term fleet requirements but no time-frame has been given to the
 Committee within which it should submit its recommendations.  The aircraft are required to be acquired during the
 Tenth five Year Plan Period, that is, 2002-2007.  In fact, a decision on this should have been completed by now so that
 by the time the Tenth Plan commenced, the Air India had started acquisition of the type of aircraft it proposed to
 acquire during this period. The Committee, therefore, reiterates the recommendation made in its earlier report that the
 Air India decide in time bound manner and keep the Committee fully apprised as to what kind of fleet it should go in
 for so that necessary steps may be taken immediately to rationalise their fleet.

 and the fact that Air India has not only been able to curtails its losses in the year 2000-2001 but is also expected to
 make a marginal profit in 2001-2002.

 replies as promised by the Secretary during the meeting.  The Committee would like to be apprised of the hike in fare
 of Air India/Indian Airlines flights from Kerala to Gulf countries, during the last three years, alongwith brief reasons
 therefor.

It is evident from the statements given by the Secretary (Civil Aviation) that the Government's decision not to procure

 which, however, did not materialize for one reason or the other.   This had affected the market share, route network as
 well as the product upgradation programme of Air India and Indian Airlines to some extent.   Now that the Government
 has decided to acquire the aircraft, the Committee appreciates the decision of the Government.

 acquisition of aircraft, source of funding, lead period for procurement alongwith specific provisions of financial outlays

The Committee observes that both Air India and Indian Airlines have a very low equity base.  Indian Airlines has a paid
 up capital of Rs.105.19 crores against an authorized capital of Rs.500 crores.  Similarly, Air India has a paid up capital
 of Rs.153.84 crores and an authorized capital of Rs.500 crores.  This low equity base has resulted in curtailing their
 borrowing ability.  It is of immediate necessity to enhance the equity base of both the airlines to enable them to achieve
 a healthy debt-equity ratio, and also enable them to go in for further borrowings.  The Committee has been informed
 that a commitment has already been made by the Ministry of Finance to contribute to the equity of Indian Airlines
 linking it to the acquisition of aircraft.  The Committee recommends that similar dispensation would be necessary for
 Air India as well.  The Committee appreciates the decision of the Government to strengthen the airlines instead of
 going in for disinvestment as stated by the Secretary in his deposition before the Committee.  For this purpose, the

R E P O R T
 
INTRODUCTION
 
Demand No. 76 pertains to the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.  The Ministry of Surface Transport
 has been bifurcated into two Ministries i.e. Ministry of Road Transport and Highways and Ministry of Shipping.  The
 Department of Road Transport and Highways, which was part of the erstwhile Ministry of Surface Transport has been
 notified as a separate Ministry of Road Transport and Highways w.e.f. 7
th November 2000.
 
2.       The Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is responsible for development, formulation and implementation
 of policies relating to Road Transport, National Highways and Transport Research.  Its main function relates to road
 development and maintenance including Border Roads, Planning, Co-ordination and Road Transport.
 
3.       The Ministry is administratively divided into two wings namely Road Transport Wing and Highways Wing.
 
4.       Road Transport Wing is concerned with the formulation of broad policies relating to Road Transport, Road
 Safety, Motor Vehicles Act, legislation relating to Road Transport Corporations, besides making arrangements for

59th Report

 movement of motor vehicular traffic with the neighbouring countries.
 
5.       Highways Wing is mainly concerned with the matters relating to:-
 
(i)
           Advising Government on all general policy matters relating to road development;
 
(ii)
          Development & Maintenance of roads declared as National Highways;
 
(iii)
        Administration of Central Road Fund;
 
(iv)        Evaluation of standard of road and bridge and specification;
 
(v)          Performance of road research;
 
(vi)        National Highways Authority of India and National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers and
 
(vii)       Roads other than or National Highways in Union Territories.
 
Following are the autonomous bodies functioning under the administrative control of this Ministry:-
 
(a)
          National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) and
(b)         National Institute of Training of Highway Engineers (NITHE).
 
 
REVIEW OF NINTH FIVE-YEAR PLAN
 
6.         For the Ninth Five-Year Plan, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had proposed an outlay of Rs.
 23000 crores as worked out by the working group on roads.  However, the Planning Commission had approved an
 outlay of Rs. 8862.20 crores.  During 1999-2000 and 2000-2001, substantial additional funds were made available at
 R.E. stage and as a result of which the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways was allocated a plan outlay of 19700.82
 crores.  However, the Ministry could utilise only Rs.13929.11 crores only.  Resulting in a shortfall in utilisation of
 funds to the extent of Rs. 5771.71 crores.  Major reasons for the under-utilisation was that expenditure had been low in
 the beginning of 9
th Five Year Plan as only the feasibility studies were being done for NHDP and pace of expenditure
 increased after the works were awarded.  In respect of Special Repair Programme, shortfall was due to the fact that the
 funds were provided at the fag end during 1999-2000 and therefore these could not be utilised fully.
 
7.         For E & I works out of CRF, works costing about Rs. 231 crore were approved in principle but detailed estimate
 for all works not submitted by States/UTs.
 
8.         The Committee regrets to note that on one hand the Ministry had proposed an outlay of Rs. 23000 crores for the
 9
th Five Year Plan where as on other hand they could utilise only 13929.11 crores out of the approved plan outlay of
 Rs. 19700.82 crores during the 9 th Plan period leaving a shortfall of Rupees 5771.71 crores.  It appears that while
 proposing its plan outlay, the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways had not been realistic in its approach. The
 utilisation of remaining approved outlay could have improved the road scenario in the country.  In future, the Ministry
 should have realistic planning so that the approved outlay can be utilised fully.

NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
 
16.       National Highways being a Central Subject, the entire expenditure on its development and maintenance is met
 by the Government of India.  In addition, financial assistance is provided in the form of grants-in-aid for development
 of certain selected State roads/bridges.  Funds are also provided to State Govts. and Border Road Development Board

17.       The length of National Highways for which the Government of India is constitutionally responsible stood at
 57,737 km at the end of March 2001.  During the current year, a further length of 373 km. has been added to the NH
 Network and at present it stands at 58,112 kms.
 
18.       National Highways Authority of India is looking after 14000 kms of National Highways, the Border Roads
 Organisation has 4000 kms of National Highways and about 41000 kms of National Highways are being looked after
 by the Ministry directly.
 
19.       National Highways Development Project (NHDP) comprises 4/6 laning of Golden Quadrilateral connecting
 Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata and North-South and East-West corridors from Srinagar to Kanyakumari and
 Spur from Salem to Cochin with a total length of about 13151 Kms. The target date for completion of works for North-
South and East-West corridors is December, 2007 and for Golden Quadrilateral it is December, 2003 and it envisages
 total investment of Rs. 57000.00 crores.  Out of total 13151 km for NHDP, 1779 kms have already been 4-laned and
 4602 km is under implementation.
 
20.       Keeping in view the quantum of investment involved in the NHDP, the Committee desired to know whether the
 Government have any  standardise cost per km or whether the cost varied from  place to place.  In his reply, the
 Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways submitted as under:
 
“…… we prepare estimation on the basis of the schedule of roads. It comes to Rs. 4 to 4.5 crores/km on the
 average.... the standard cost per kilometer would be very difficult to arrive at. It depends on the soil condition
 and so many other factors. All things vary from place to place. When we say Rs. 4 to 4.5 crores, it is the average
 of all the areas....”
 
21.       The Ministry further informed the Committee that the designs of roads and bridges are based on the standards
 and specifications prescribed by Indian Roads Congress and the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways.
 Construction of roads includes embankment, pavement, culverts and bridges, ROB/RUBs etc. Also, the height of
 embankment, pavement thickness, design of culverts and bridges in one stretch of road are generally not identical with
 those in other stretch of the road.
 
22.       The cost of construction of roads is based on various parameters like specifications of construction, cost of
 construction materials, type of soil, type of terrain, cost of labour and cost of equipment. Though specifications of
 construction may be uniform, other factors vary and are different in different regions. Even in a region the factors such
 as terrain, soil characteristics, source of construction materials etc may vary significantly resulting in variation in cost
 of construction.  The estimate for construction cost of a particular stretch of road in a region is estimated based on
 construction specifications and standard schedule of rates applicable in that area. The rates for various items of work in
 the schedule of rate are the analysed rates considering the requirements of labour, material and their leads and
 equipment and their standard output. Thus, the schedule of rates gives standard rate per unit of quantity in a particular
 region. It is evident from above that the cost of construction of one km of road will depend on design features and the
 region of its location. It is therefore, difficult to standardize the cost of construction of roads in different regions
 because of variable parameters as noted above. An average cost of construction of roads may however be assessed for
 planning purposes.

25.       Giving in details of mechanism of distribution of funds out of Central Road Fund, the Secretary, 
 Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, informed the Committee as under: -
 
“.....We had framed guidelines to see that this money that is released for the construction of roads - it is State’s
 money; it is meant for utilization for improving the State highways and major district roads of the State. Very
 often, we had seen and it is our past experience that the money was not utilized for the very purpose for which it

 was given. Therefore, the guidelines that the Ministry framed indicate that one-third of the State’s share would
 be made available to the State right in the beginning. Therefore, the States would send proposals for the
 Ministry’s approval. They would first identify the stretches and send the proposals to the Ministry for approval.
 We do not scrutinize the estimates. We do not call for any details, but we would like to know which are the
 roads they propose to improve. We approve the lists. Thereafter, the States are free to call the tenders. As and
 when the money is spent by them, they send utilization certificates which are to be accompanied by the details of
 the expenditure incurred, the names of the projects on which the money has been spent. On receipt of the
 utilization certifications, we release that much money. The State should have one-third of the amount available

26.       The Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways drew the attention of the Committee towards problem
 faced by them in respect of utilisation of Central Road Fund and stated as under:-
 
“... I would briefly mention the other problems that we face. One such problem is utilization of CRF.  More
 cooperation is required from the States in the utilisation of the money; they should not divert the funds

 money that was made available to the Finance Department of the States would get diverted to other purposes
 and not to the roads; it may be because of so many problems of the States but this is the status. In this process,
 road construction activity has suffered. I must hasten to add that with the constant persuasion, many of the State
 Governments have woken up and, I think, utilisation would improve....”
 
“........ When we release the money in the month of April-May, the State is expected to rotate that money and get
 the works done by sending bills to us for further releases. They never do it. The road laying gets affected.
 Though I release Rs.20 crores to a State, unfortunately, the money is not available with the PWD. It is held up
 by the Finance Department. They don’t pay the contractors. Then they stop work. Once the work is stopped, the

 recommendations contained in its Fifty First Report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) of the Ministry which is as
 under:-
 
“However, the Committee wants the Ministry to impress upon the State Government that the State Highways and
 State roads should be developed in such a way that the entire State roads network would provide a feeder
 system to the rail network thereby avoiding development of parallel road network. The Committee is aware that
 there have been instances of diversion of funds and are not utilized for the purpose for which they are allocated.
 Therefore, Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should ensure proper and
 strict monitoring of the schemes for which the funds are allocated from the Central road Funds so as to avoid
 cost escalation and time over run.”
 
28.       The Committee is of the view that in the past, there were scarcity of funds for the development of roads and
 National Highways in the Country. Now with the constitution of dedicated Central Road Fund (CRF), the financial
 crunch of funds of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways and State Governments have been reduced to a large
 extent for the development & maintenance of all categories of roads. The Committee regrets to note that the utilisation
 by the States is not commensurate with allocation of funds.  The Committee is of the view that non-utilisation and
 diversion of funds, if any, will defeat the very purpose of the constitution of Central Road Fund.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter of proper
 utilisation of funds from Central Road Fund at every possible stage/level with State Governments. For this purpose, a
 Monitoring Cell may also be set up to oversee the progress of projects of National Highways in different states. The
 State Governments should be informed about the lack of progress in the National Highways Projects. This should be a
 continuous process through out the year for overseeing the proper utilisation of Central Road Fund in different states.

 Rs.1.14 crore for schemes/ programmes in North-Eastern States and the remaining Rs. 10.35 crores for schemes the rest
 of India).  The proposed allocation is Rs. 30.00 crore in the Annual Plan 2002-03.  The Ministry while furnishing the
 reasons for non-utilisation of funds during the 9th plan stated that the some of the projects were dropped on the
 direction of the Planning Commission, due to poor response from the State Governments.  Some projects were not
 found feasible also.  The meetings of National Road Safety Council and Road Safety Programme Implementation
 Committee could not be held during first three years of the plan period and therefore administrative expenses could not
 be incurred.
 
31.       The Committee expresses its anguish over non-utilisation of plan outlay approved for Road Transport Sector
 during 9
th plan period.  The Committee is of the view that Road Transport Sector is not less important and its ignorance
 will defeat the very purpose of having good quality of roads.  The Committee is surprised to note that meetings of
 National Road Safety Council and Road Safety Programme Implementation Committee could not be held during first
 three years of the plan period.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that due attention should be given to transport
 sector and ensure that plan outlay approved for transport activities are utilise fully.
 
PROBLEM OF OVERLOADING
 
32.       Taking up discussion on Road Transport Sector, the Committee drew  the attention of the Ministry of Road
 Transport and Highways to the expanded chassis and size of truck as result of which there are instances of overloading
 upto 100 per cent.  The Committee desired to know the precaution being taken and the provisions of the law in this
 regard.
 
33.       In their reply, the Ministry of Road  Transport and Highways informed the Committee that under section 113 of
 Motor Vehicles Act, 1988 prohibits plying of over loaded vehicles. Section 114 of the Act empowers officers of the
 Transport Department or officers authorised by the State Government to direct any vehicles, if suspected of overloaded,
 to the nearest way bridge enroute or nearest destination. If weighment establishes overloading, excess load has to be
 off-loaded. Section 194 lays down penalty for overloading, in addition of off- loading of the excess load. The power
 and responsibility to enforce these provisions rests with the States. These instructions have been reiterated to the States
 on number of occasions. The Ministry of Finance has also been approached to provide suitable fiscal incentive by way
 of lower excise duty on multi-axle trucks to encourage increasing use of these road friendly vehicles and to reduce
 instance of overloading.
 
34.       For design of roads, the overloading of vehicles is measures in terms of Vehicle Damage Factor (VDF). The
 VDF is a multiplier to convert the number of commercial vehicles of different axle loads and axle configuration to the
 number of standard axle repetitions. It is defined as equivalent number of standard axles per commercial vehicles. The
 VDF is very high on our roads.
 
35.       Overloading of vehicles has been contributing to the premature failure of several road stretches. Studies have
 revealed that with 10% over loading over the permissible axle load limit, the pavement life gets reduced by about 35%
 and with 30% over loading pavement life gets reduced by about 65%. To illustrate this, if strengthening of pavement
 for a 200 km long section, to meet the needs of 10.2 tonnes axle load, requires an investment of Rs. 100 crore for a
 design life of 10 years and with 30% over-load (5tonnes more pay load), it would last for only 3.5 years, implying
 further investments of the order of Rs.100 crore at accelerated intervals. In spite of provisions of designs, premature

59th Report
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/59threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:58:16]
 failure of pavement cannot be ruled out because of continued overloading of vehicles, which goes unchecked, both in
 weight as well as repetitions.
 
36.       The Committee feels that overloading of trucks is a serious problem, which requires closer attention by Ministry
 of Road Transport and Highways alongwith State Governments. The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry
 of Road Transport and Highways should strongly take up this serious issue and a meeting at the minister level with all
 State Governments should be called at the earliest to devise means for curbing this problem. The Committee also
 recommends that the Ministry of Finance should provide fiscal incentives by way of lower excise duty on multi axle
 trucks to encourage increasing use of these road friendly vehicles and to reduce instance of over loading.
 
37.       The Committee also recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should have co-ordination with
 the Ministry of Industry and other concerned agencies involved in manufacturing of heavy Motor vehicles so that there
 can be a check on manufacturing of expanded chassis.  The Committee is of the view that this step can check
 overloading to a great extent.
 
38.       The Committee is also of the view that there is lack of Public awareness in respect of this problem. The Ministry
 of Road Transport and Highways has failed on the front of publicity efforts, which were to be taken in this regard. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry Road Transport and Highways should come up with publicity
 efforts, at large scale, addressing to the truck drivers and transport agencies engaged in transportation business
 including general public.
COMPUTERISATION IN ROAD TRANSPORT SECTOR
39.       With a view to induct information technology in road transport sector, back-end and front end computerization is
 being introduced. Back-end computerization envisages incorporation of details of existing driving licenses &
 registration certificates on common software at RTO level and then linking it up at State level. Front-end operation
 involves issue of smart card-based driving licenses and Registration Certificates of motor vehicles, based on common
 ISO 7816 specifications. This would ensure that documents issued by one state could be read in other States as well.
 
40.       The Committee enquired about the present status of computerization and any time frame for it. In their reply, the
 Ministry stated that Standardized software for both front-end and back-end computerization has been made available to
 all the States/UTs. As per information available, back-end computerization has been operationalised in about more than
 fifty RTOs in the country. For front-end computerization, Government of Gujarat has gone ahead in respect of both
 driving license and registration certificates. The back-end computerization envisages incorporation of various details in
 respect of driving license, registration certificates and permits for commercial vehicles, at the RTO level in a standard
 computerized format. The front-end operation envisages issue of smart card based driving license and registration
 certificates at the RTO level.
 
41.       The data available from some of the RTOs where back-end computerization has been done establishes that
 substantial increase in revenue has accrued to the States. The State/UTs have been urged to expedite the
 computerization process, however no realistic time frame for completion of the activities on part of Government of
 States/UTs can be indicated at this juncture.
 
42.       The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in respect of
 computerization in Road Transport Sector. The Committee feels that computerization is very essential in the field of
 Road Transport Sector. The Committee is of the view that without any time limit/frame for any scheme, the Ministry of
 Road Transport and Highways will not achieve its set targets.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry
 of Road Transport and Highways should frame the time limit for computerization in Road Transport Sector and
 completes it as early as possible.

REPORT
 
Tourism has emerged as one of the world's most important economic activities.  It is not only a major social
 phenomenon of the modern society with enormous economic consequences but also the world's largest export industry.
 According to the World Tourism Organisation (WTO), about 698 million tourists travelled internationally in 2000 and
 spent about US$ 476 billion.  The importance of tourism as an instrument for economic development and employment
 generation, particularly in remote and backward areas, has been now well recognized the world over.
 
2.       India is a country of continental dimensions with a fascinating kaleidoscope of diverse races, languages, religions,
 customs and traditions.  Tourism has emerged as a major industry of the Indian economy contributing substantially to
 foreign exchange earnings and also as potential generator of employment opportunities.  The spillover effect of tourism
 by creation of employment opportunities in related services sectors is tremendous.  According to a World Tourism and
 Travel Council (WTTC) study, the travel and tourism economy in India employed 17.7 million people in the year 2000,
 which is 5.6 percent of the country's total employment for that year.  Tourism is presently India's third largest export
 industry after readymade garments and gem and jewellery.  The international tourist traffic was only 16,829 in 1951. 
 During the last 50 years, the international tourist arrivals have gone upto 2649378 during the year 2000, which reflects
 a compounded annual growth rate of about     11 percent.  The foreign exchange earnings from tourism in the country

3.       The Department of Tourism, Ministry of Tourism and Culture, is the nodal agency for the formulation of national
 policies and programmes and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government Agencies, State
 Governments/Union Territories and the Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country. 
 The role of the Department of Tourism has been to coordinate and supplement the efforts of the State/U.T.
 Governments in development of tourism through Central financial assistance, to catalyse private investment, strengthen
 promotional and marketing efforts and to provide trained manpower resources. 
         
4.       Tourism industry in India enjoys bright prospects as the country possesses a rich cultural heritage and tourist spots
 which offer a diversity of attractions and places of historical and archaeological importance.  The Committee is of the
 view that although tourism is an important foreign exchange earner and its employment potential is vast, its virtues
 have not been exploited optimally and have largely remained untapped.  Realising the multiple spin-off effects of
 tourism for the Indian economy, the Committee took up the subject "Development of Tourism in the Country" for

 the development of tourism in the respective States and the problems/hurdles faced in promoting development of
 tourism in the country.

21.     Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands are among the world's most spectacular islands.  The precious
 heritage of ecology and culture of these islands is supported by an extremely fragile ecosystem.  Andaman & Nicobar
 consist of 572 emerald islands, islets and rocks out of which 36 islands are inhabited.  The lands are covered with dense
 forest and endless variety of exotic flowers and birds.  The rare flora and fauna, under-water marine life and corals,
 with crystal clear water and mangrove-lined creeks offer a dream view of the rare gifts of nature.  The coral islands of
 Lakshadweep consists of 36 islands of which 11 are inhabited and have become very popular tourist destinations in the
 recent years.  Considering the limited infrastructure, the administration of these islands propose to promote low volume
 high value tourist inflow to these islands because of the fragile eco-system of the rain forest and under water corals.
 
22.     The Committee's discussion with the administrations of the Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands

 islands.  The mode of connectivity to these islands is by air and sea.  Port Blair is connected with Chennai and Calcutta

 major stumbling block before the inter-state tourism is poor connectivity.  Domestic Tourism cannot be promoted

CONCLUSION
 
33.     The Committee is of the view that tourism industry in India enjoys bright prospects as the country has some of the
 finest beaches, hill resorts, historical places, heritage property, pilgrim centres and wildlife backwater spots which offer
 a diversity of attractions.  The diverse cultural heritage, festivals, art forms, cuisines can form a fine blend of tourism
 products.  Tourism serves as a potent, positive force to stimulate economic development, improve ecology and foster
 national integration through mutual understanding.  Tourism transcends territorial boundaries and concerted efforts are
 needed to promote tourism for economic development.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tourism
 industry should be properly planned, developed and managed at all levels of government in participation with the
 private sector.  It will certainly strengthen the country's cultural structure and natural heritage and lead to positive
 economic results including enhanced employment and income opportunities in rural areas.

The Committee agrees that the security considerations of the country cannot be compromised.  However, it must also be
 admitted that granting visa-on-arrival to the foreign tourists at the airports can certainly give a boost to the foreign
 tourist arrivals in the country.  The Committee is of the view that a step in this direction can be taken by initially
 introducing visa-on-arrival for tourists from friendly countries, countries which do not pose a security threat to our
 country and are tourism generating markets.  Later, if the scheme is successful and helps in foreign tourist influx to the
 country, it can be extended to other countries too on a case-to-case basis.
(Para 11)
 
SPECIAL TOURIST POLICE FORCE
 
The Committee feels that the issue relating to the safety and security of the tourists, especially foreign tourists is very
 important and needs to be looked into seriously.  The Committee is of the view that incidents of harassment of foreign
 tourists bring a bad name to the country and have an adverse effect on the foreign tourist arrival.  Deployment of
 Special Tourism Police Force can be an effective tool for ensuring safety and security of the tourists.  The Committee
 appreciates the creation of the Special Tourism Police Force by some of the states.  The Committee also suggests that

SIXTIETH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/60threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:59:17]
 the police personnel of the States should also be provided special 'tourist-oriented' training.  Such form of official
 protection to international and domestic tourists would certainly instil confidence amongst the tourists visiting these
 territories.  A successful implementation of such measures will definitely encourage the other State Governments in
 implementing similar schemes for the promotion of tourism in their respective States.
(Para 13)
RATIONALISATION OF TAXES ON THE TOURISM INDUSTRY
 
The Committee feels that the hotel industry is the backbone of tourism.  The major share of tourism revenue to the
 government is contributed by this sector.  However, there are a lot of taxes and sometimes duplication of taxes at both
 Central and State levels on the hotel sector.  The multiple taxes have imposed a heavy financial burden on the hotel
 industry.  The Committee observes that taxes on hotel rooms and food levied by both the Centre and the States add upto
 over 45 percent, making the industry grossly uncompetitive.  The Committee is of the view that there ought to be
 coordination and synergy between the Centre and the State Governments on the tax front and that there is an urgent
 need to rationalize both Central and State taxes on tourism.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Central
 Government/State Governments must come forward with rationalisation of taxes and provide concessions for the hotel
 industry to give a fillip to the arrival of the tourists in the States.  Further there should be uniformity in the rate of
 various taxes levied by the State Governments on the hotel industry.
(Para 19)
 
The Committee observes that there is a lack of uniformity in taxes, laws and regulation across the States.  While the
 State Governments are taking steps to develop tourism in their respective states, the lack of coordination among them
 and the higher rates of road tax/disparity in the taxes in the states, especially southern States have had negative effect
 on the growth of tourism in these states.  These factors also result in hardships for the tourists as also increase the cost
 of travel for the tourists.  The Committee therefore, recommends that there should be a composite transport permit for
 tourist vehicles.  The Committee also recommends that the Central and the State Governments should take immediate
 steps to create uniformity between the local vehicles and the visiting vehicles.  Steps should also be taken to facilitate
 easy travel and free inter-State movement for tourist vehicles.
(Para 20)
 
TOURISM DEVELOPMENT IN ANDAMAN & NICOBAR AND LAKSHADWEEP ISLANDS
 
The Committee feels that Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands have the potential of growing into top
 destinations for beach tourism and water sports.  But for the constraint of transportation of tourists from the mainland,
 these islands would have attracted a still larger number of tourists, earning revenue and generating employment for the
 local islanders.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the work on the extension of runway at Port Blair may be
 completed at the earliest and the frequency of flights may also be increased so that more and more tourists are able to
 land there.  The Committee welcomes the decision of DGCA to permit the foreign tourist charter flights to land at Port
 Blair and recommends that this fact may be given wide publicity amongst national as well as international tour
 operators.  Similarly, round the year air services, well connected with other important centres like Kochi,
 Thiruvananthapuram and Goa may be introduced to give a boost to the development and promotion of tourism in the
 Lakshadweep Islands. Further, clearance to the proposals for construction of airfields at Kavarati, Minicoy, Andrott,
 Kadmat and Kiltan Islands should be expedited.  The Committee also feels that creating eco-friendly tourist
 infrastructure and water sports facility involves huge expenditure.  Due to the limited resources available to these two
 Union Territories, it may not be possible for the administration of these islands to create infrastructure and other
 facilities in the islands.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the administration of these islands should create
 conducive atmosphere for private investment and, thereafter, invite private sector participation in developing the
 necessary infrastructure, accommodation and high quality eco-friendly tourists/resorts.
(Para 24)
 
PERMIT SYSTEM FOR THE TOURISTS
 
The Committee is of the view that foreign tourists constitute an important component of tourists who wish to visit the
 Andaman & Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands.  The restrictions on foreigners to stay beyond permitted period in the
 Islands and visiting only selected islands has discouraged the foreigners from visiting these islands.  The Committee,

SIXTIETH REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/60threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:59:17]
 therefore, recommends that in order to optimally exploit the potential of tourism in these islands, the restrictions on the
 foreigners on visiting the islands may be removed and they may be permitted to stay/enjoy the beauty of the islands for
 longer periods.  The Committee also feels that opening up new islands for foreigners also needs to be given priority and
 recommends that the Central Department of Tourism should take up with the Ministry of Home Affairs the proposal
 regarding opening up of more islands for the foreign tourists.
(Para 26)
 
The Committee appreciates the Government for having opened some areas of Nagaland for foreign tourists and hopes
 that this step will certainly have a positive effect on the growth of tourism in that area.  However, the Committee is of
 the view that the levying of U.S. Dollars 30 from the foreigners who wished to visit Sikkim will discourage the foreign
 tourists from visiting Sikkim.  The Committee recommends that the government should consider abolishing the permit
 system for foreign tourists, as has been done in the case of Assam and Meghalaya.  The Committee hopes that it will
 definitely help in boosting foreign tourist arrivals in the state.
(Para 28)
 
CONSTRAINTS OF COASTAL REGULATION ZONE ACT
 
The Committee is of the view that the impact of tourism on the environment and ecology requires serious
 consideration.  There is no doubt that unplanned tourism not only degrades the environment physically and otherwise
 but also carries the seeds of its own destruction.  However, the Committee feels that the provisions of CRZ Act do not
 take into account the unique features of the coastal lines of various States in the country, particularly of Andaman &
 Nicobar and Lakshadweep Islands and Kerala.  India has many beautiful beaches, which can be developed from
 tourism point of view.  The Committee recommends that the Government should, therefore, seriously consider relaxing
 the provisions of the Costal Regulation Zone Act.  The Ministry of Environment and Forests should also take a liberal
 view and consider positively the proposals seeking relaxation of CRZ restrictions for tourism projects.
(Para 30)
 
LACK OF CONNECTIVITY
 
The Committee feels that there exists a fairly large domestic tourist movement in the country.  However, one major
 stumbling block before the inter-state tourism is poor connectivity.  Domestic Tourism cannot be promoted unless the
 air, rail and road links across the various states and places of tourist interest in the country are improved.  In absence of
 a comfortable access to the places of tourist interest, the tourist cannot be encouraged to visit such places.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends, that the tourist destinations in the country should be well connected by rail, road
 and air with the urban centres/cities of the region to ensure easy accessibility.  Also the movement of the trains should
 be regularised and speeded up.  The Committee also feels that tourism is closely interlinked with the Civil Aviation
 Sector.  Air linking of the various tourist places in the country as well as places abroad from where tourist arrival is
 expected is essential for development of tourism in the country.  The Committee also recommends that efforts should
 be made to explore the possibility of upgrading the Veer Sarvarkar Airport at Port Blair and Bogdogra Airport into
 international airports so that these places could find a place on the international tourist map.  Also, The Ministries of
 Civil Aviation and Railways should take steps for providing the necessary infrastructure and improve air and rail
 connectivity to the various states in the country.
(Para 32)
 
CONCLUSION
 
33.       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the tourism industry should be properly planned, developed and
 managed at all levels of government in participation with the private sector.  It will certainly strengthen the country's
 cultural structure and natural heritage and lead to positive economic results including enhanced employment and
 income opportunities in rural areas.

 The Airports Authority of India (Amendment) Bill, 2000 seeks to enable the Airports Authority of India with
 the prior approval of the Central Government, to lease the airport premises to private investors as well as the State
 Governments and to assign the required functions to such lessees. 
           
2.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states any money payable by such lessees on this account will
 accrue to the Airports Authority of India to undertake the development of other airports.  The lessee shall have all the
 powers of the Authority necessary for the performance of such functions in terms of the lease.  This has been proposed
 to be done through insertion of a new section 12A in the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994. The Airports Authority
 of India (AAI), the apex statutory organisation under the administrative control of the Government of India, Ministry of
 Civil Aviation, at present manages 94 civilian airports and 28 civil enclaves at Defence airports in the country.
 
3.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill further states that there is a general feeling of perceptible lack
 of standard of services and facilities at the airports which is not at par with international standards.  The need is,
 therefore, for the infusion of private sector investments as also for restructuring of airports.  The Government feels that
 this will go a long way in speeding up airport infrastructure development, improving managerial efficiency, increasing
 local responsiveness and improving service levels.  It will, in turn, generally stimulate the economy by boosting tourism
 and trade.  Accordingly, it has been decided to undertake the task of restructuring the airports of Airports Authority of
 India through a long-term lease.  Since the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 does not explicitly provide for long-
term lease of the airports, it has been proposed to amend the Act.
 
4.         In their background note furnished to the Committee giving the reasons for the introduction of the Bill, the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation have brought out the following points:-
4.a       Where do our airports stand
4.a.1    International Air Transport Association (IATA) conducts passenger surveys on an ongoing basis and results are
 published in the IATA Global Airports Monitor annually.  The report published by Global Airport Monitor measures
 passenger satisfaction through 60000 interviews at 57 major airports worldwide, for a wide range of customer service
 attributes.  For most airports, the sample sizes are typically between several hundred respondents and several thousand. 
 The IATA surveys include 19 service elements for airports like overall satisfaction with airport, wash rooms, signages,
 availability of baggage carts, government passport/customs inspections, baggage delivery surveys, parking facilities,
 sense of security, ambience of the airport, etc.
 
4.a.2    The results of the survey for the year 1999, reveals that Mumbai and Delhi ranked amongst the three least
 favourable airports in the Asia Pacific region for all 19 service elements.  According to the Survey, these airports
 continue to offer the lowest service levels in terms of overall satisfaction with the airport and the rating for Mumbai and
 Delhi were 2.3 and 2.6, respectively on a scale of 1 (='very poor') to 5 (='excellent').  These results ought to be seen in
 the context of an average of 3.5 for airports in Asia Pacific region and 3.8 for world airports.  Copenhagen, Singapore's
 Changi and Helsinki rank top for overall passenger satisfactions amongst the 57 airports covered in the 1999 survey
 with a rating about 4.3 to 4.4. In case of duty free sales, the average sale per passenger at Delhi and Mumbai is 3.06 and
 1.46 USD, respectively against the average of 8.67 USD for Asian airports and 17.97 USD for world airports. In respect
 of number of employees per million passengers also, Mumbai airport has 273 employees per million passengers, Delhi
 289, Chennai 365 and Kolkata 545 as compared to Kuala Lumpur airport having 105 employees per million passengers,
 Beijing 84, Brisbane 11, Perth 19.  However, a large number of services have been contracted out in case of Brisbane
 and Perth.
 
4.a.3    As such, there is an ample scope for improvement in the service levels of our airports as well as their overall
 standing not only in the Asia Pacific, but also in the world at large.  Given the critical role of the aviation industry for
 the national development, there is an imperative need to improve the standings of our airports vis-à-vis the best in the
 world.  There is a paramount need to augment service performance of airports by evolving vital interlinkages between
 aviation industry and other allied sectors.  Modern quality management systems not only require continuous monitoring
 of users' satisfaction levels to maintain appreciable standards and to identify areas for improvement, but also a bench
 mark to put the service performance in context.  Airport managements need to position themselves in the global market
 in terms of customers' satisfaction and to learn from the world's leading airports how to improve satisfaction levels for

SIXTY-FIRST REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/61streport.htm[28-08-2018 13:00:17]
 their customers, if the airports are to meet the ever-widening expectations of the users in the years to come.
4.b       Present Management Structure
4.b.1    At present, Airports Authority of India, undertakes the management of 94 airports and 28 civil enclaves at
 Defence airfields and provides air traffic services over the entire Indian airspace and adjoining oceanic areas.  However,
 various airlines are operating through 61 airports only.  Fifty two percent of entire traffic of about 39 million is handled
 at just two international airports in Delhi and Mumbai.  
 
4.b.2    The Ministry have brought out that the present system of management of all airports by a public sector entity
 such as the Airports Authority of India has several inbuilt lacunae.  Some of which are as follows:
(i)
                  The service conditions of employees are governed by the general directions of Department of Public
 Enterprises and it is very difficult to reward/punish the staff leading to lack of professionalism and poor
 service standards.
(ii)
                Being a public sector, every aspect of their functioning is open to scrutiny under an elaborate institutional
 system, which may at times focus on procedural formalities  rather than  substantive results, leading to
 following a  very cautious attitude on the part of management. Invariably, such attitude stifles initiatives and
 risk innovation.  This also leads to delay in decision making and further results in the airports' functioning
 uncompetitive in the fiercely competitive world of today. 
(iii)
               Because of inherent service conditions, there is relative lack of sensitivity about needs and aspirations of
 the passengers and other users, leading to poor service standards despite heavy investments in the facilities,
 notwithstanding.
(iv)
              Lack of professionalism and initiative create an ambience not conducive to quick and total absorption of
 new technology as well as new management techniques.
(v)                Being a public sector, the Airports Authority of India has to go through the lengthy procedures involving
 the Ministry, Public Investment Board and Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs etc. for clearance of
 their major investments.  This leads to delayed or over/under investment. 
4.c       Resource Gap
4.c.1    Investment in airports being capital intensive, has to be planned well in advance to meet demand requirements. 
 The Airports Authority of India had an investment plan of Rs.3421.87 crores under the 9
th Five Year Plan to meet the
 future growth demand of air traffic, overcome current congestion at specific airports and to upgrade existing facilities
 including communication and air traffic facilities.  About two-third's of the total five-year investment plan amounting to
 Rs.2037.29 crores was to be financed from internal resources of the Airports Authority of India and Rs.283.37 crores
 from the Central Government budgetary resources.  The resource gap of Rs.1101.21 crores was expected to be financed
 by borrowing funds from the domestic capital markets and by increasing airport charges.
           
4.c.2    About 65 per cent of the total five-year investment plan, generated from the Airports Authority of India's internal
 resources, is for expansion, modernisation and construction of new terminal buildings mainly located at Delhi, Mumbai
 and Thiruvananthapuram.  An additional 28 per cent  has been allocated for upgrading navigational aids and cargo
 warehouses.  In addition to the planned outlays, preliminary feasibility studies and proposals were being reviewed by
 the state governments and the private sector.  "Other" initiatives, not included in the Airports Authority of India's plan,
 are in the range of about Rs.19,100 crores.  These investments are contemplated for new airports - Mumbai, Bangalore,
 Goa and Hyderabad amounting to about Rs.14,600 crores, terminal buildings at various airport locations amounting to
 Rs.2,400 crores, related supporting airport infrastructure of Rs.1,500 crores and cargo facilities of Rs.600 crores.  If all
 these investments proposals were to be realised, the total investment gap would increase significantly from the original
 estimate of Rs.1101 crores to Rs.20,201 crores.
           
4.c.3    The Ministry's brief further states that the Airports Authority of India's 9
th Five Year Plan is, on the one hand,
 unrealistic when compared to its past investment performance and, on the other, unambitious  in relation to investment
 being undertaken/contemplated in other countries.  Besides, it is doubtful that the proposed investments levels will help
 upgrade the principal international gateway airports to world-class standards.

4.d       Financial Performance of the Airports Authority of India
4.d.1    The financial performance of the Airports Authority of India during the last five financial years is as under :-

1995-96 Rs.276.05
