4.d.2    It has also been brought out by the Ministry that while there has been modest increase in revenues by 68 per cent
 from Rs.1003.33 crores in 1995-96 to Rs.1691.28 crores in 1999-00, costs (mainly staff) have increased significantly
 by 185 per cent from Rs.727.28 crores in 1995-96 to Rs.1346.55 crores in 1999-2000.
 
4.d.3    As regards the Airports Authority of India's performance against plan investment is concerned, during 8
th five-
year plan, the planned investment outlay was Rs.1950 crores, while the actual expenditure was only Rs.1496 crores. 
 Similarly in the 9 th five-year plan, the anticipated achievement is likely to be Rs.2120 crores against the planned
 investment of Rs.3421.87 crores, which is about 60 per cent only.  Some of the reasons for these delays can be
 attributed to the inefficiencies in the construction industry, long bureaucratic delays for approval of contracts, delay in
 Government approval for projects and complex public procurement procedures. Some of these inefficiencies are
 endemic in the present management structure of airports, Airports Authority of India and the Government.  In fact, it is
 evident that the limited investments, which are so very unambitious, are also not being optimally utilised.
 
4.e       Need for change in the structure
4.e.1    In view of the foregoing, the Ministry feels that Indian airports face formidable challenges both internally and
 externally.  The internal challenges stem from ownership and management related issues, lack of commercial
 orientation, undeveloped revenue sources, inefficient provision of services, distorted pricing schedules, the absence of
 underlying regulatory structures, and insufficient investment to achieve world class standards.  Historically, the Airport
 Authority was able to manage despite these internal weaknesses, since there were few compelling reasons to alter the
 status-quo.  However, external challenges resulting from capacity, efficiency, and resource constraints and changes in
 market access necessitate a review, revision and restructuring the existing ownership, management and regulatory
 structures.
 
4.e.2    On the demand side, Indian airports are faced with growing capacity constraints due to increase in air traffic
 growth, the globalisation of industry, and the global trend towards deregulation and liberalization of the airline
 industry. At the very least, strains on capacity will necessitate upgradation of air traffic control services to reduce
 congestion and ensure the safe movement of aircraft.  With the progressive liberalization of Indian economy and
 globalisation, international trade is poised to enhance the importance of air cargo transport.  International Civil Aviation
 Organisation (ICAO) estimates that a           1 per cent increase in exports has a concomitant 1.5 per cent increase in the
 demand for air cargo.  The growth in air cargo operations has several important implications for airports, including
 operations and handling, dedicated investments and facilities, and inter-modal connections.
 
4.e.3    Another external challenge facing our airports is the rapid changes taking place in the airline industry.  In the
 domestic aviation market, new domestic carriers have entered the market which also need to be provided fair and equal
 access to terminals and passenger facilities.  In the international market, strategic alliances among airlines have altered
 the traditional nature of traffic flows, requiring a proactive promotion of airlines to airport destinations.  Besides, the
 development of large aircraft will require new taxiways, aprons, gates, runways and terminal facilities.
 
4.e.4    With anticipated changes in the airline industry to meet future growth capacities, environmental concerns will

SIXTY-FIRST REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/61streport.htm[28-08-2018 13:00:17]
 come into sharp focus, commending airport authorities to evolve airport development strategies especially the
 construction of new airports and the extension of existing facilities.  Several vital issues such as human habitat around
 airports excessive noise pollution, waste disposal, air emissions, and water pollution will need to engage undivided
 attention to facilitate smooth supply of airport services.
 
4.e.5    To meet the growing challenges of growth in air traffic resulting from the globalisation of aviation industry, low
 levels of investments, spectacular advances made in the field of technology to improve safety and communication
 standards and limited public funds to keep pace with the investment priorities urgently call for initiating farsighted
 programmes to impart strength and dynamism to aviation industry to remain technologically contemporaneous and
 qualitatively top class.
 
4.f        Action Taken by the Government
4.f.1     Against this background, there are no two views that massive investments are required to create world-class
 airports and to bring services at par with the international standards. For this, there is a compelling need to create
 favourable investment climate and also to restructure the existing management structure of major airports.  In January
 1999, the Government decided to achieve the same through corporatisation of the major airports at Delhi, Mumbai,
 Chennai and Calcutta.  The idea was that the corporatisation would bring about effective changes in the management,
 contribute to an overall productivity growth and attract investments in order to improve the standards of service and
 facilities.
 
4.f.2     Later, it was realized that the objective of having world-class international airports would be better achieved by
 restructuring through long-term lease instead of corporatisation.  The restructuring of the management structure would
 be achieved in a shorter time-span and more effectively by dispensing with the intermediate step of corporatisation. 
 Since the idea behind corporatisation was ultimate private sector participation in the ownership and management of
 airports, it would have to be followed by disinvestment of the newly created corporations.  Restructuring through long-
term lease is undoubtedly a more direct approach.  Moreover, in this process the ownership of the airports would remain
 with the Airports Authority of India and the lease income would accrue to the Authority, thus enabling it to undertake
 the development of rest of the airports without depending upon budgetary support.  With this rationale, it was decided
 in January 2000 to restructure the airports through long-term lease route.  It was also noted by the Government that the
 retention of lease rentals by the Airports Authority of India would have to be subject to a clear definition of the
 respective obligations of Airports Authority of India and the lessee airports and of Airports Authority of India in respect
 of all other airports, including the non remunerative ones, without gross budgetary support, as far as possible. 
 
4.g       The need for amendment in Airports Authority of India Act, 1994
4.g.1    The Ministry have further stated that the issue as to whether Airports Authority of India has the power under the
 Airports Authority of India Act, 1994, to transfer the airports on long-term lease to private investors was examined
 from the legal point of view.  According to the legal opinion*, "the provisions of the Act make it clear that the airport-
assets have been vested in the Authority for better management of the airports by it and for the discharge of its functions
 under the Act, the Authority may enter into contracts.  In this light of the matter, it can be said that that the Authority
 can lease out assets vested in it for efficiently discharging its functions/duties under the Act, but the Authority cannot
 divest itself of its responsibilities under the Act.  It would do violence to the whole intent and purpose behind
 enactment of the Act if the functions/duties of the Authority are privatized."  Therefore, it was opined that for carrying
 out the proposal of the Administrative Ministry, suitable amendment in the Act would be required.  Hence, the Airports
 Authority of India (Amendment) Bill, 2000 was introduced in the Parliament.

 mechanism for fixation of charges/fees also. There will be a well-defined formula for levying of aeronautical charges.
 The initial rate will be same as the existing rates being charged by Airports Authority of India.  Subsequent maximum
 increase permissible will be based on the index of inflation.  Full effects of inflation will not be passed to the lessee. 
 There will be a factor for improving the efficiency of operations.  So the lessee will be encouraged to improve the
 services to enable him to earn profits.  No free hand will be given in this respect.  Detailed formulations were being
 formalized in consultation with the legal and financial consultant which will be incorporated in the lease agreement
 which will be finally placed before the Cabinet for approval.  These formulations will be subject to a periodic review in
 accordance with well laid out procedures.   Accepting the need for a regulatory authority, the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 added that the constitution of a regulatory authority was under contemplation.  The question whether it requires a
 separate legislation or it can be done under the existing rules is being examined. 
 
19.3     To another query on the subject, the Committee was further informed by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that a
 proposal is separately under consideration for setting up an Airport Economic Regulatory Authority to provide an
 appropriate regulatory regime for all airports, keeping in view the service standards also.
 
19.4     The Committee is concerned about the absence of any regulatory mechanism in the Bill for regulation of
 fees/charges/levying of aeronautical charges by the private operator.  The Committee is of the view that the present
 legislation should contain a mechanism about a regulatory body for fixing and checking the parameters defined for the
 investments made and improvement in the performance of the airports.  The Committee appreciates that a proposal is
 separately under consideration for setting up an Airport Economic Regulatory Authority to provide an appropriate
 regulatory regime for all airports.  The Committee recommends that a regulatory authority must be in place before the

 Bill is passed by the Parliament and that a suitable clause regarding regulation of tariff etc. by the said authority should
 be incorporated in the Bill. 
 
20.       While discussing the various provisions of the Bill, the Committee was also concerned about certain other issues
 which have not been covered in the Bill i.e., inclusion of aims and objectives in the Bill, protection to the interests of
 the employees of the Airports Authority of India, Ministry going ahead with the leasing process without final approval
 of the Parliament and the direction of the Ministry of Civil Aviation to AAI in respect of ongoing and new projects at
 the airports.
 
21.       Attention of the Committee was also drawn to the proposal forwarded by the Government of Karnataka to the
 Ministry of Civil Aviation requesting for amendments to the Airports Authority of India Act, 1994 to facilitate
 finalizing the agreement with foreign partners for Bangalore International Airport.  The Committee recommends that
 the Government needs to take a firm view in the matter and amend the Airports Authority of India Act accordingly.
 
22.       
Inclusion of aims and objectives in the Bill
22.1     The Committee observed that the aims and objectives of the Bill had not been specifically mentioned in the Bill. 
 The Committee suggested to the Ministry of Civil Aviation that since the Bill aims at improvement in services and
 bringing in more investments at the airports, the terms 'infusion of private sector investments' and 'improve service
 levels' should be reflected in the Bill itself.  In response, the Ministry of Civil Aviation informed that generally the aims
 and objectives are written in the beginning of the main Act, which are already written in the main Airports Authority of
 India Act.  With each amendment, a Statement of Objects and Reasons is enclosed.  The same has been done.  The
 interpretation of every clause is done within the broad contours of objects and reasons.  Therefore, it is generally not
 felt necessary to mention the aim and object in the beginning of every clause.  Moreover, the amended clause, inter
 alia, states "in the interest of administration and generally for carrying out any or all of its functions under Section 12". 
 Section 12(4) of the main Act already states that "In the discharge of its functions…., the Authority shall have due
 regard to the development of air transport service and to the efficiency, economy and safety of such service." In view of
 the above, it was not felt necessary to include further in section 12A "for improvement in services and for bringing in
 more investment" as it is already provided in the main Act and is the constant endeavour of the Authority and the
 Government.
 
22.2    The Committee brought to the notice of the Ministry of Civil Aviation that the two objectives of the Bill, namely
 'improvement in services' and 'bringing in more investment' at the airports did not form part of the original AAI Act,
 1994.  Ministry of Civil Aviation was of the opinion that infusion of private sector investment and improvement of
 service levels through world-class technology and managerial expertise is inherent in the philosophy of privatization. It
 was, therefore, not considered necessary to mention this specifically.  However, Ministry of Civil Aviation have
 further stated that they have no objection prime-facie to include this in the Bill, but as per the laid down procedure this
 will have to be considered and approved by the Cabinet.
 
22.3     The Committee recommends that the basic objectives of the Bill i.e. 'infusion of private sector investments' and
 'improve service levels' should be incorporated in the text of the Bill in a suitable form.
 
23.       Protection to the interests of the employees of the Airports Authority of India
 
23.1     The Committee was also concerned about the interests of the employees of the Airports Authority of India
 working at the four metro airports. The representatives of the employees Unions of the Airports Authority of India had
 also expressed apprehension about the safety and security of their jobs after the leasing of the airports.  The Committee
 enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation as to what would be the fate of the employees of the Airports Authority of
 India working at the airports proposed to be leased out.  In reply the Ministry of Civil Aviation stated that in order to
 prevent any misgivings amongst the employees of the Authority working at the airports, appropriate provisions will be
 incorporated in the service regulations for deputation of employees, so as to ensure that the rights of the employees are
 in no manner compromised or put in peril. The details were being worked out in accordance with the different laws in
 consultation with legal and financial consultants.

23.2     During the evidence of the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation on the 26 th June 2002, the
 Committee suggested to the Ministry that the terms and conditions of the proposed lease agreement should clearly
 indicate that the rights of the employees working under the new dispensation would not be tinkered with even after the
 lease agreement.  The Chairman, Airports Authority of India, while briefing the Committee on the issue stated as under.
"…….Sir, the interest of the employees are fully protected through a lease agreement. The employees will be
 on deputation with the new operator or the lessee, for a period of three years. The employees will have the
 option to come back to the Airports Authority of India if they do not want to be absorbed, under the terms
 and conditions of the new operator.  After three years, if they come back, they would be absorbed in the
 Airports Authority of India, on the same terms and conditions that they are enjoying. If they want to get
 absorbed in the new dispensation, under the new operator, with new terms and conditions, they can very
 well do so."
           
23.3     The Committee takes note of the fact that there has been vehement opposition to the Bill from the employees
 unions of the Airports Authority of India.  The Committee is of the view that the exercise of leasing of airports cannot
 succeed without the participation of the employees of the Authority.  The Committee feels that a more transparent
 interaction should be held with the representatives of the employees.  The Committee recommends that the interest of
 the employees should be taken care of and that the existing terms and conditions of the employees of the authority
 should not be altered at all after the leasing of the airports.   Further the thinking of the Ministry with respect to
 protecting the interests of the employees should come out in concrete terms in the Bill so as eliminate any doubts in the
 minds of the employees.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a provision for protecting the interests of the
 employees should also be incorporated in the Bill itself on the same lines as appearing in Sub-clause (5) of Clause
 111(C) of the Major Port Trusts (Amendment) Bill, 2001.
 
24.       Ministry going ahead with the leasing process without final approval of the Parliament
24.1     The Committee took note of the fact that the Ministry of Civil Aviation had been going ahead with the process
 of long term leasing of the airports without waiting for the final approval of the Parliament.  On being enquired from
 the Ministry of Civil Aviation about the reasons for going ahead with the leasing process when the Bill on the subject
 was under consideration of the Parliament, the Ministry replied that the privatization of four metro airports through
 long term leasing  is an ongoing process and a commitment has been made to complete the process during the year
 2002-03 in the Budget document. Moreover, the leasing exercise which has been approved, in principle, by the Cabinet
 involves complex strategic issues which require substantial preparatory work including Opportunity Briefing meetings
 (as a marketing strategy), drafting of lengthy bid documents which have legal implications, two stage global bid and
 evaluation process etc. This exercise is a considerable time consuming one and in order to adhere to the time frame, it is
 imperative that the preparatory work is simultaneously taken up for effective implementation of the project at the final
 stage.  The work connected with leasing was preparatory work in this context.  Neither any firm commitment had been
 made in this regard, nor any final decisions taken. It was further informed that it would be useful to continue with this
 work so that required decision can be taken at an appropriate time, and there is no delay for want of prior preparatory
 work.
 
24.2     The Committee is not satisfied with the reply furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and took a serious note
 of the fact that Ministry of Civil Aviation did not wait for the approval of the Parliament and went ahead with even
 drawing the various schedules of the leasing process and taking action thereon.
 
25.       Direction to AAI in respect of ongoing and new contracts
25.1     The Committee also came to know that the Ministry of Civil Aviation had directed the Airports Authority of
 India to put on hold major construction works at the four metro airports, pending the finalisation of the decision
 regarding the long-term lease of the airports.  When the Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation
 whether any such instructions had been issued to the Airports Authority of India and if so, how the developmental
 programmes at the airports had been affected, it was informed that in the backdrop of Government's decision to lease
 the four metro Airports to private operators in order to improve management and upgrade facilities at these airports to
 world-class standards, Ministry of Civil Aviation had initiated preparatory steps. Accordingly, consultants had been

SIXTY-FIRST REPORT

 appointed, who in turn had completed the due diligence work in relation to these airports. Based on the parameters and
 principles identified by the consultants, capital works are required to be undertaken by the prospective operators on
 leasing.
25.2     In the first three years of the lease period, the private operator shall be mandated to complete all the ongoing
 capital works. In addition, Airports Authority will identify certain works to create a visible impact from the users
 perspective, which shall also be undertaken by the private operator. The private operators shall prepare a long term
 Master Plan incorporating major capital works and facilities to be created in the long term, taking into consideration the
 future traffic growth.         
25.3     In view of the above, Ministry of Civil Aviation had issued a directive to the Airports Authority of India to put
 on hold major construction projects, in which work had not commenced yet. The directive was also made applicable to
 major contracts of commercial nature. The basic objective behind issuing this directive was to ensure that the value
 realization to the Airports Authority of India is not adversely affected on account of leasing and also that the projects
 are not taken up in adhoc manner. Besides such a decision would also allow operational flexibility to the private
 operator to draw up a comprehensive plan of action for incorporating their vision.
25.4     Ministry of Civil Aviation have further stated that the aforesaid directive has not resulted in any delay and
 consequent cost and time overrun for any ongoing project. Further, Airports Authority has the freedom to approach the
 Ministry with any specific proposal for approval with necessary justification keeping in mind the operational
 requirements at Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata airports.  It is felt, on the other had, that there is a need for re-
prioritization of projects to be taken up at these four airports in the light of the due diligence work undertaken by the
 consultant. Hence there was the need for vetting by the Ministry.
 
25.5     The Committee is not in agreement with the replies furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation and is of the
 view that developmental activities at the airports should not be brought to a halt pending the leasing process.  The
 Committee recommends that the developmental projects which have been already sanctioned by the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation be allowed to continue and not made to suffer due to the leasing of airports.
 
26.       General Observation
The Committee is of the view the objectives behind the Bill i.e. "speed up airport infrastructure development,
 improve managerial efficiency, increase local responsiveness and improve service levels" are commendable but the
 legislation introduced for the purpose falls short of many essential requirements.  It appears that no proper thinking has
 gone into the preparation of the Bill and that it has been very hastily drafted.  The Bill in its present form even fails to
 mention the basic aims and objectives behind the Bill.  The Bill does not address to a number of important functional
 and economic issues that would arise as a result of the leasing of the airports to the private operators.   The term 'person'
 used in Clause (1) of Section 12A of the Bill has not been clearly specified.  The Bill also does not contain any
 provision with regard to tariff regulation mechanism and only now the Government is considering the setting up of an
 Airport Economic Regulatory Authority.  The Ministry have admitted that certain functions such as security and Air
 Traffic Control will, in no case, will be transferred to the private operator, but the Bill does not clearly specify as to
 which functions of the Airports Authority of India would be handed over to the private operators and which functions,
 in no case, will be transferred to the private operators.  The Committee strongly feels that the Government has come up
 with a piecemeal legislation.  The Committee, in the interest of the nation, is not in favour of proceeding ahead with the
 Bill in its present form.  The Committee urges upon the Government to carefully consider all the points mentioned
 above and recommends that the Government should come up with a comprehensive legislation incorporating all the
 suggestions made in the preceding paragraphs in the Report.

            The Major Port Trust Act, 1963 provides for constitution of Board of Trustees of all the major ports in the
 country and vests the administration, control and management of these ports and for matters connected therewith in
 such authorities.  11 major ports are governed under this Act.
 
2.         The Major Port Trusts (Amendment) Bill, 2001 seeks to enable corporatisation of the existing major ports in the
 country.  Corporatisation of major ports would involve abolition of the present system of trustees by de-notification of
 major port from the purview of Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, and after sorting out several related aspects convert the
 Port Trusts into a company under the Companies Act, 1956.  At present, the major ports in the country function under
 the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. 
 
3.         The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill inter-alia states that the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, needs to
 be amended to provide for vesting undertaking of the major ports in successor companies; define scope of transfer of
 assets and liabilities, protect the rights of successor companies in relation to the licenses, etc., granted to the erstwhile
 Major Port Trusts, vest the land and waterfront in the Central Government, provide consideration for transfer of assets
 and liabilities; protect the guarantees enjoyed by the port trusts and lay down the terms and conditions of leasing the
 land and waterfront to the companies.  Certain consequential amendments are required to the Indian Port Act, 1908.

4.         The Ministry of Shipping *cited the following reasons for corporatisation of major ports and introduction of the
 Bill: - 
 
REASONS FOR CORPORATISATION
 
4.1       11 major ports in India are autonomous bodies under the Ministry set up under Major Port Trusts Act, 1963. 
 These ports have made constant endeavour to improve the conditions and facilities provided by them.  In the fiercely
 competitive world of today, ports face new challenges and can no longer afford to be complacent.   A structural change
 is therefore required for improvement of functioning of the ports. 
 
4.2       The Ministry further felt that the provisions of the Act do not allow operation of services by the ports on
 commercial lines as approval of the Central Government is required in a majority of decisions. A number of measures
 taken by the Central Government in the recent past have resulted in improving the operational efficiency at major ports
 to some extent. However, under the restrictive ambit of the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963 the major ports are unable to
 operate in market-oriented situations and obtain flexibility of commercial operations. Even after delegating more
 powers and making some amendments to the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, from time to time, the basic objective of
 offering efficient and satisfactory services to the port users has not been achieved fully.   A structural reorganization of
 Major Port Trusts is called for to: (i) provide the necessary independence of authority and decision-making; (ii)
 coagulate investment; (iii) execute projects speedily; and (iv) manage operations with professional finesse.
 Accordingly, the required structural re-organization of the major ports is sought to be achieved through their
 corporatisation.
 
______________________________________________________________________
*Background note furnished vide
 their O.M. No. PW/12011/3/2000-PO.1 dated 23.10.2001.
 
4.3       A profit oriented commercial organization operating in a competitive environment will strive to minimize costs
 and improve services. These are necessary measures if the organization is to retain and expand its operations while
 earning a satisfactory return on the investment, without compromising on the goal to improve efficiency and thereby,
 reap the benefits of lower cost and improved services for importers and exporters. The other advantages expected from
 commercial activities to be carried out by corporate bodies are operational freedom and flexibility enjoyed by the
 management in taking commercial and investment decisions and their quick response to the market conditions or the
 need of the trade. At present, as Major Port Trusts all that they are required is to prepare annual statement of income
 and expenditure, which merely shows operating surplus. They do not maintain accounts on commercial lines; nor do
 they maintain profit and loss accounts. Corporatisation of major ports would make profit and loss statements mandatory
 and will lead to establishment of commercial accounting practices, creation of profit centers and drawing up of balance
 sheets.  The Ministry feels that this would enable correct valuation of the assets of the ports in the long term, corporate
 bodies would eventually contribute revenue to the Government in the form of corporate tax. Further, formation of
 corporate bodies will increasingly compel their management to tap capital market to raise funds like any other
 corporate entity. This will also make it possible for the Government to measure their performance in terms of the return
 on investment and eventually enable divestment of Government holding.
 
4.4       The Ministry has further stated that certain consequential amendments were required to the Indian Ports Act,
 1908. The Indian Ports Act, 1908, was applicable to major ports. However, certain sections of this Act such as Sections
 6(1)(j), 6(1)(jja), 6(1)(kk), 33(1), 33(3), 34,35,46 and 47 were not made applicable to the major ports. The corporatised

 procedures.  It will establish strong linkages with intelligence agencies for assessment/revaluation of threat perceptions.

 that the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security has assessed to scope of the activities and services to be rendered by the new
 Aviation Security Training Academy.  The scope of activity of this Training Academy will be to conduct and certify
 specialized training in aviation security at basic and advance level as also to train the trainers for carrying out refresher
 courses in their respective organizations.  Other activities include maintaining an institutional framework for national
 and international exchange programmes in aviation security, arranging seminars and conferences on the subject,
 encouraging research and sharing databases on the various aspects of aviation security including the technical database
 on security related equipments.
 
100.     Since CISF, which is Central Police Force is already a trained force in security functions, the proposed institute
 is required to train and sensitise the force mainly in aspects relating to airport security.  Similarly, it is proposed to train
 the staff of airlines and other related agencies mainly on security aspects.  The scope of the Institute/Academy will now
 be a specialized one.
 
101.     The Committee also enquired regarding the present status with respect to preparing the revised project for the
 proposed Aviation Security Training Academy and its estimated cost.  The Committee was informed by the Ministry
 vide their O.M. dated the 23
rd December 2002 that BCAS has prepared a project report which was discussed at a
 meeting taken by Secretary (Civil Aviation). In the light of the discussions, it is being revised.  The revision will take a
 few more days to complete.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
102.   The Committee understands that the dimensions of aviation security have changed significantly during the last
 year and so.  The Committee recommends that the revised project for the proposed Aviation Security Training
 Academy should be prepared and a final view in the matter should be taken at the earliest so that the project could take
 a final shape.

4.         On scrutiny of the said Action Taken Replies, the Committee  has made observations on each item of Action
 taken/proposed to be taken by the Ministry.  The recommendations of the Committee contained in the Fifty-seventh
 Report, action taken thereon by the Government, and recommendations/observations of the Committee on each item of
 action taken has been given in the succeeding paragraphs.
 
APPRAISAL OF 9TH FIVE-YEAR PLAN AND PROJECTION FOR 10TH FIVE-YEAR PLAN
 
RECOMMENDATION (Paras 13 & 14)
 
5.         The Committee is not satisfied with the performance of the Ministry of Shipping during 9
th Five Year Plan. The
 Ministry could utilise only Rs.4838.92 crores out of the approved outlay of Rs. 9428 crores in Port Sector. The
 Committee is of the view that the reasons given by the Ministry of Shipping for the heavy shortfall i.e. delays in
 sanctioning of the schemes, delays in tender finalization, award of contracts etc are not of such nature which were
 beyond the control of the Ministry. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should review
 its working and come out with specific remedial measures (predictive and preventive) to eliminate the delays leading to
 under-utilisation of allocated funds. Agencies/Individuals should be made accountable as and when lapses occur.
 
6.         The Committee is also of the view that there has to be realistic approach while preparing any Five-Year Plan. 44
 Major Schemes of 9
th Five Year Plan are likely to spill over to the 10 th Five-Year Plan, which may affect the
 physical/financial targets of the Ministry fixed for the 10 th Plan. The funds proposed for Port Sector during 10 th Five
 Year Plan period are Rs.17416.40 crores. The Committee hopes that while preparing the 10 th Plan, the Ministry of
 Shipping would have visualized the possible problem and taken remedial action so that the approved plan outlay for the
 10th Five Year Plan are utilised optimally.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
7.         The observations of the Committee have been noted.  It is however submitted that the allocation of Rs.9428
 crores for the Ninth Plan (1997-2002) is only indicative, to be operationalised subject to availability of resources,
 through the successive Annual Plan allocations for the Ninth Plan period.  The aggregate of the 5 Annual Plan outlays
 during the period was Rs.6963.92 crores.  Against this, expenditure incurred during the Ninth Plan period was
 Rs.4816.46 crores.  It is also pertinent to point out that the overall port capacity achieved in the major ports as on
 31.3.2002 is 343.95 million tones per annum, whereas the traffic handled by these ports during 2001-02 was 287.57
 MT.  Thus, the major ports have now reached the stage where the capacities available exceed the traffic.  There has also

TONNAGE ACQUISITION PROGRAMME DURING TENTH PLAN
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 23)
 
10.       The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Shipping failed to achieve the target of 9 million tonnes
 for the 9
th Five Year Plan. The achievement of 6.84 MT is at par with the target achieved during the 8 th Plan. This
 shows that the tonnage acquisition was static during the 9 th Five Year Plan. The Ministry could not identify the
 problem of shipping industry during the full five years of Ninth Plan and did not take adequate steps to improve the
 situation.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
11.       It is not true that the Ministry did not take adequate steps to improve the situation.  Ministry of Shipping has
 been taking steps from time to time to facilitate the growth of Indian tonnage.  The following fiscal measures have been
 taken by the Government at the initiative of this Ministry.
 
a. Restoration of Section 33AC of the Income Tax Act from 50% to 100% tax relief on amounts earmarked for
 vessel acquisition in separate account;
b. Increase in depreciation rate on ships from 20% to 25%.
c. Necessary amendments in EXIM policy to rectify the anomaly which had necessitated procuring of special import
 license for the purpose;
d. Ministry of Shipping convinced Ministry of Finance to roll back imposition of 5% customs duty on acquisition of
 ocean going ships from abroad;
e. Expanding the scope of Section 33AC to stimulate Indian Ship owners to earmark higher funds for acquisition of
 tonnage.  Further, to make this section more attractive for Indian ship owners, Government has decided to allow
 deduction of funds transferred under Section 33AC while computing book profits for the purpose of Minimum
 Alternate Tax.
f. The Government has allowed private sector participation in providing training to seafarers, which would help in
 producing a higher number of quality seafarers to man Indian flag tonnage.
 
12.       In addition to the above, this Ministry constituted an Expert Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri Rakesh
 Mohan, Adviser to Finance Minister to review the Indian Shipping and suggest measures to address its problems.  The
 Committee in its report recommended introduction of tonnage tax as is followed by the leading Maritime Nations of the
 world.  The report of the Committee and recommendations thereon have been accepted by this Ministry and referred to
 Ministry of Finance for implementation.
 
13.       As regards the tonnage remaining static during 9
th Plan, while lack of conductive fiscal environment was the
 main reason, the fact that the Shipping Industry faced recession during the first half of the 9 th Plan period also did not
 help the cause of Indian Shipping.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
14.       The Committee notes the reply of the Government.  The Committee takes exception to the use of the word “it is
 not true” by the Ministry in their replies and directs that the Ministry should refrain from using such wording in future.

 economy. Therefore, it is necessary to provide conducive fiscal regime to Indian Shipping Sector so that it can become
 internationally competitive. The Committee notes with some satisfaction the fiscal concessions given to the Indian

DREDGING AT MAJOR PORTS
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 28)
 
18.       The Committee notes that Major Ports are spending large amount on the capital dredging either through their
 own resources or from the borrowed funds, which has definitely affected their financial performance.  It is also a fact
 that for the ports, it is difficult to raise borrowings for capital dredging because it may not result into commensurate
 incremental resources.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that capital dredging at all the Major Ports should be
 taken as national priority by the Government of India. The Government of India, as a matter of policy should provide
 adequate plan funds to all the Major Ports for carrying out Capital Dredging at the Ports.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
19.       In the matter of capital dredging, the Government has already approved the River Regulatory Scheme of Kolkata
 Port Trust involving an outlay of Rs.350.84 crores, which will be financed entirely through budgetary support. 
 Budgetary support has also been earmarked for ‘Deepening of the Channel’ scheme of Paradip Port Trust.  A proposal
 for budgetary support for capital dredging for the Cochin channel for the proposed Vallarpadam Container Terminal
 and LNG Terminal at Cochin Port has also been taken up with the Planning Commission.  Further, a proposal for
 Japanese funding of the project ‘Deepening and Widening of Channel at Jawaharlal Nehru Port’ has been taken up with
 the Ministry of Finance (Department of Enonomic Affairs) and a token provision for budgetary support to this project
 has also been made in the Tenth Plan outlay.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
20.       While noting the reply of the Government, the Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Shipping
 should identify channels in other remaining Major Ports for capital dredging and Government of India should provide
 budgetary support for the same.

21.       The Committee strongly disapproves the procedure adopted by the Government of India in the matter of
 providing funds to Kolkata Port Trust for Capital Dredging. The Committee is surprised to note that on one side, the
 Government of India has, in principle, decided to fully reimburse the cost on items directly related to dredging and
 maintenance of River Hooghly as well as cost incurred on items directly related to maintenance dredging of Haldia
 Shipping Channel, where as, on other hand, the allocation for capital dredging has been reduced in a arbitrary manner.
 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that there should be no constraint of funds for the Kolkata Port so far
 as dredging is concerned. Silting at Kolkata Port is problem of recurring nature therefore the actual requirement of fund
 for dredging and maintenance of River Hooghly and Haldia Shipping Channel be identified and provision be made at
 Budget Estimate stage itself.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
22.       Since the Budget Estimates for 2002-03 had already been finalized, the matter for full reimbursement of the
 expenditure  incurred by the Port Trust based on audit certificates will be taken up with the Ministry of Finance during
 Revised Estimates stage.  However, the matter will be pursued with the Ministry of Finance for allocation of the entire
 requirement based on audit certificates, at Budget Estimates stage itself during 2003-04 and onwards.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
23.       The Committee was further informed by the Ministry of Shipping vide O.M. No.PD-11013/5/2002-US(I) dated
 4.12.2002 that Capital Dredging Project under the scheme “River Regulatory Measures” for improvement of the
 draught in the Hooghly estuary of Kolkata Port Trust was sanctioned by the Government of India in November, 2001. 
 The project envisages cutting a channel of approximately 10 kms. of length for a width of 200 mtrs. (at bottom) upto a
 depth of 4.5 mtrs.  below chart Datum by Capital Dredging through Jiggerkhali Flat along an alignment favourable to
 the flow of the river in this region.
 
24.       Tender for the major component of the work (capital dredging) was issued on five occasions but could not be
 finalized because of unwillingness of intending bidders to accept maintenance dredging for one year in the newly
 dredge cut channel, apprehension of bidders that they would not be able to guarantee the required depth within the
 estimated limit of quantity of dredging as well as possibility of failure to dredge and sustain the channel within the
 proposed alignment etc.  Due to its inability in freezing the techno-commercial deviations put forward by the bidders,
 Kolkata Port Trust has engaged National Institute of Ocean Technology (NIOT), Chennai as consultant to review/refine
 the project in the light of present hydro-dynamic conditions of Hooghly estuary as well as to revise the technical part of
 the tender document after finalizing the recommendations.  NIOT have already started the work of reviewing the
 scheme and their report is expected by the end of December 2002.
 
25.       The Committee was further informed that Ministry of Shipping had a budgetary allocation of Rs.175 crores this
 year.  Unfortunately, on account of technical snag, Rs.175 crores has been surrendered at the R.E. stage.  The next
 meeting on Revised Estimate and Budget Estimate will take place after seven days.  The Ministry of Shipping have
 given proposal for about Rs.200 crores for raising the capital next year.  If the NIOT report comes, hopefully, by the
 end of December on schedule an entire technical tendering process would be facilitated.  Then there will be about 2-3
 months time when the operation can start.  Now, if the operations take about three months to start, then, probably the
 next financial year will come and, by that time, hopefully, the funds will not be problem. 
 
26.       The Committee is constrained to note that the Ministry of Shipping was unable to spend Rs.105 crores during
 this financial year and surrendered the said amount at Revised Estimate stage.  The Committee is of the opinion that
 capital dredging at Kolkata Port is a very important matter and needs time bound action plan.  Earlier, there was
 scarcity of the amount for the capital dredging at port, but now the Ministry is unable to spend the amount allocated for
 capital dredging, inspite of budgetary support from the Government of India.  The Committee, therefore, further
 recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should spend the allocated budgetary fund in a time bound manner and get
 prepared the action plan for capital dredging.

RECOMMENDATION (Para 48)
 
37.       The Committee observes that despite of alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust, the Kochi
 Refineries Ltd. is adamant to go ahead with its plan for construction of Single Buoy Mooring (SBM) without giving a
 positive thought to the proposals. The Committee is of the opinion that both Public Sector undertakings are under
 administrative control of the Government of India and in absence of agreement, any loss incurred to the Cochin Port
 Trust will be the loss to the Nation. The Committee, therefore, reiterates its earlier recommendation made in its 52
nd
 report on Demands for Grants (2001-02) of the Ministry of Shipping and recommends that Ministries of Shipping and
 Petroleum and Natural Gas should evolve an amicable solution to the problem. Kochi Refinery Ltd. should consider, in
 the national interest, the alternative proposals suggested by the Cochin Port Trust before taking up the construction of
 the Single Buoy Mooring.

 constituted to interact with the officials of Kochi Refineries Limited to study and work out a feasible alternative
 logistics solution.  In response, Kochi Refineries Limited has also constituted a high level Committee to interact with
 the port officials.  Based on the deliberations so far, Cochin Port Trust has expressed the hope that they would be able
 to arrive at a mutually acceptable solution.

CENTRAL INLAND WATER TRANSPORT CORPORATION LTD. (CIWTC)
 
RAJABAGAN DOCKYAR (RBD)
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 64)
 
52.       The Committee appreciates the steps and efforts taken by the Ministry of Shipping for revival of the Central
 Inland Water transport Corporation Ltd.  The Committee is of the view that expertise and facilities of ship repair and
 dry dock facilities at Rajabagan Dockyard should not go waste. The Committee, therefore, recommends that while
 taking steps for revival of Central Inland Water Transport Corporation Ltd., the facilities of ship repair and Dry Dock
 available in Rajabagan Dockyard should be exploited fully so that assets and manpower engaged in those activities are
 utilised optimally. The Committee also expect that the present ambiguity with regard to future manpower in the
 Rajabagan Dockyard should be removed and the manpower requirement in Central Inland Water Transport Corporation
 Ltd. for the next five-years be firmed up and informed to all concerned including the Committee. 
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
53.       In the light of the Cabinet decision in June 2001, steps have been initiated for disposal of assets of Rajabagan
 Dockyard along with its land, buildings, plant, machineries and offering the advantage of its manpower resources.  The
 decision to close Rajabagan Dockyard of CIWTC was taken after considering various aspects and recommendations,
 including the report submitted by the consultant.  The idea is to ensure that the Corporation concentrates on its core
 activity of cargo movement.  The Government is fully aware that the productive assets of the Corporation have to be
 utilized to the optimum level.  Action has been initiated for disposal of land which is not directly relevant for the core
 activity of the Corporation.  With a view to rationalizing the manpower, a voluntary retirement scheme has been
 introduced in the Corporation and it is expected that 241 employees during 2001-02 and 2002-03 each and 168
 employees during 2003-04 will opt for VRS.  Even if Rajabagan Dockyard is sold, the manpower is likely to be utilized
 by the new owner.  A large number of employees of CIWTC including Rajabagan Dockyard have opted for the
 voluntary retirement scheme.  A rational assessment of the manpower requirement of the Corporation has been made
 and the VRS is expected to take care of the surplus manpower.

INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR)
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 67)
 
55.       The Committee agrees to views of the Ministry of Shipping and is of the opinion that at present Inland Water
 Transport System in the country is at the initial stage of its development. The allocation of amount for any proposed
 scheme/project in the field of Inland water Transport Sector is for its infrastructure development. Therefore, there is
 very low scope for any Internal Rate of Return (IRR) from this Sector. The Committee therefore, recommends that the
 Government of India should review its approach for Inland water Transport Sector and should not insist for 12% IRR of
 any scheme/project in this field. The concept of Internal Rate of Return may ever be dispensed with as the benefits
 from such projects are passed on to the trade and economy.     
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
56.       Acting on this recommendation of the Committee all concerned agencies like Planning Commission and
 Ministry of Finance will be informed about the recommendation while seeking approval to the schemes/projects of the
 IWT sector.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
57.       The Committee notes the reply of the Government.
 
MARITIME TRAINING IN INDIA
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 72)
 
58.       The Committee appreciates the proposal for establishment of an Indian Institute of Maritime Studies under
 Societies Registration Act, 1960 and placing the Government run Maritime Institutions within the domain of this
 Society. The move will certainly give a qualitative boost to the maritime training in the country. The Committee,
 however, recommends that the Government of India may consider to give the status to Indian Institute of Maritime
 Studies similar to that of IITs’ and introduce a central legislation accordingly at the earliest. 
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
59.            Necessary action to register the Indian Institute of Maritime Studies (IIMS) Mumbai as a Society under the
 Societies Registration Act, 1860 has been taken by the Government and the Directorate General of Shipping, Mumbai,
 has filed necessary papers in the office of Registrar.
 
60.       IITs are conceived as Institutes of National importance with a special role assigned to the President of India,
 whereas the IIMS to begin with is being established as a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860
 and not under a separate Act of Parliament as in the case of IITs.  It is expected that once the Society starts functioning,
 it will soon be on its own and can gradually move towards a situation where conversion to a ‘deemed University’ or a
 ‘University’ or separate status under a special Act can be considered.  Thus, IIMS is seen as foreunner to its being
 converted to a higher status.
 
61.            However, many of the provisions of IIMS have similarities with the provisions of IITs.
 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
62.       The Committee notes the reply of the Government.

RECOMMENDATION (Para 78)
 
63.       The Committee is not satisfied with the attitude and approach of the Government of India is respect of Shipping
 Corporation of India Ltd. On one hand, the Government of India has taken decision to go for disinvestment in SCI,
 whereas on other side, Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. has expansion plan for acquisition of vessels during the year
 of 2002-03 involving an amount of Rs. 647.84 crores for investment.  The Committee fails to understand as to why the
 decision for disinvestment of Shipping Corporation of India (SCI) has taken place when SCI is able to manage its
 activities through its own resources.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
64.            Disinvestment of Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. (SCI) is in accordance with the Government’s overall
 policy to disinvest its stake in non-strategic Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs).  Regular business plans, including
 acquisition of assets, are normally not put on hold pending disinvestment.  It is part of the SCI’s corporate plan, which
 has been approved by the Planning Commission as well.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
65.       The Committee notes the reply of the Government.
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 79 and 80)
 
66.       On enquiry from the Ministry regarding revaluation of assets of SCI, the Committee was informed that no
 revaluation has taken place, so far, since process of disinvestment started.
 
67.       The Committee fails to understand why the SCI has not revalued its assets as the matter of disinvestment of SCI
 has been under consideration for the last 3-4 years. Owner should be aware of its assets value when a major part of it is
 being disposed of.
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
68.       As per the prevailing practice, the assets of a going concern like SCI, are not required to be revalued
 periodically.  Such revaluation is generally undertaken at the time of merger/acquisitions involving change of
 ownership or change in management control.  In the case of SCI, no such revaluation has been done so far.  In the
 context of the proposed disinvestment however, a detailed asset valuation exercise is being carried out, which will be
 kept in view while fixing the reserve price for strategic sale of SCI.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
69.       The Ministry in its further reply vide O.M. No.SD-11018/4/2002-MD dated 5.12.2002 informed the Committee
 that presently, Government equity in SCI is 80.12%.  Government has now decided to disinvest 51% of the equity share
 capital of SCI to a strategic partner along with Management control.  Action is in progress by the Ministry of

70.       The Committee is not satisfied with the reply of the Government.  The Committee is surprised to note that on
 one side Government of India are prepared to sell Shipping Corporation of India (SCI), where as, on other side SCI
 does not know about the value of its assets.  The Committee is unable to understand the reasons for not doing the

 recommendation that Shipping Corporation of India should make revaluation of its assets.
 
COASTAL SHIPPING IN INDIA
 
RECOMMENDATION (Para 84)
 
71.       The Committee is unhappy to note that during 9
th Five year plan no special attention was given on coastal
 shipping which is one of the most energy efficient, eco-friendly and cheap modes of transport for movement of bulk
 commodities over long distances. Considering the vast coastline and congestion on land routes, the costal shipping
 offers an effective alternative means of Transport. Despite this, no adequate policy measures have been taken by the
 Ministry. There are 184 minor/intermediate ports in the country along the 5560 kms coastline of India.
 Minor/intermediate ports can play important role in the coastal Shipping. The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 Ministry of Shipping should frame a comprehensive policy and prepare plans to promote the coastal shipping in the
 country. 
 
ACTION TAKEN/PROPOSED TO BE TAKEN
 
72.       The Government has taken various measures to develop coastal shipping in the country.  As a measure to
 encourage its development, coastal ships and sailing vessels have been exempted from payment of lightdues. 
 Instructions have been issued to all Major Ports (except Calcutta Port Trust who has provided a separate birth for
 coastal ships) to grant priority berthing to coastal ships without priority berthing charges.  The Central Board of
 Exercise and Customs have issued instructions permitting sanction of drawback as the port of loading after shipment of
 goods.  The Coastal fleet in the country has increased.  It stood at 329 ships with GRT of 7,31,367 as on 31.12.2001.  A
 proposal to declare coastal shipping as an infrastructure industry was also taken up with the Ministry of Finance, but the
 same was not agreed to.
 
73.       It has since been decided by the Government to conduct a combined study on development of coastal shipping
 and minor ports.  The proposed study will identify cargo that can be diverted to coastal shipping from other modes of
 transport, evaluate future traffic potential for coastal movement in the next 10 years and explore the possibility of
 developing new routes to meet the existing and potential demands.  The study will identify minor ports for use by
 coastal shipping, keeping in view the rail/road connectivity and recommend the infrastructure needed at such ports.  It
 will also examine the possibility of establishing an integrated transport system between coastal ships and Inland Water
 Transport.  It will prepare a plan of action and give broad coast estimates thereof.  The proposal for award of the study
 is under process.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION/OBSERVATION OF THE COMMITTEE
 
74.
              While noting the reply of the Government, the Committee takes serious view over refusal by the Ministry of
 Finance to declare coastal shipping as an infrastructure industry.  The Committee is of the view that the
 coastal shipping is, at present, in the initial stage and requires comprehensive policy.  To declare, coastal
 shipping as an infrastructure industry is a first step towards its promotion.  The Committee, therefore,
 further recommends that the coastal shipping should be declared as an infrastructure industry.   The
 Committee further recommends that proposal for award of combined study on development of coastal
 shipping and minor ports be processed, expeditiously.

R E P O R T
 
            The Hotel Corporation of India Limited (HCI), a public limited company wholly owned by Air India Limited
 and was incorporated on July 8, 1971, under the Companies Act, 1956.  It was established when Air India decided to
 enter the hotel industry in keeping with the then prevalent trend among world airlines.  Its main objective was to offer
 to the passengers a better product, both at the international airports and at other places of tourist interest, thereby also
 increasing tourism in India.  Air India also aimed to cater to the requirement of in-flight catering as well as to provide
 quality hotel accommodation to the passengers and crew.  Since then Hotel Corporation of India was operating four
 hotels, in Mumbai (two), Delhi (one) and Srinagar (one), one Hotel at Rajgir and two flight catering units in Mumbai
 and Delhi.
           
2.         The Annual Report 2001-2002 of Ministry of Civil Aviation contains a chapter on Hotel Corporation of India. 
 While highlighting the main functions/achievements of HCI, the chapter gives the following details with regard to the
 Centaur Hotel Mumbai Airport, Mumbai :-
 
            “The first hotel of the Company, namely the Centaur Hotel Bombay Airport was commissioned in
 May 1975.  The Hotel at Mumbai Airport has 288 rooms including 4 Deluxe Suites, a 24 hour Coffee
 Shop, 2 Speciality Restaurants, Bar, Shopping Arcade, Health Club, Swimming Pool, Beauty Parlour,
 Banquet and Conference facilities for the transit passengers etc.  The hotel right from its inception, was
 well received by the airlines, travel agents and business travellers and has had a high occupancy, the
 hotel is extremely popular and has a reputation for excellent food.  60 Guest Rooms alongwith its
 connected Shafts and corridors were renovated in December, 2000.
 
Additional 60 guest rooms alongwith its connected shafts and corridors are now under renovation
 and expected to be completed by the end of February, 2002.”
           
3.         During October 2002, there were reports in the electronic/print media that Centaur Hotel Mumbai Airport
 (CHMA), sold by the Government to Batra Hospitalities for Rs.83 crores had been later resold by the latter to the
 Sahara Group for Rs.115 crores.  Almost all national dailies and magazines covered articles in this regard.  The issue
 was also raised in the Parliament and a marathon debate on the subject was held in the Parliament during its Winter
 Session in the year 2002 wherein replying to a query on the subject, the Minister of Disinvestment, Shri Arun Shourie,

 Airports Authority of India.  The Committee brought to the notice of Ministry of Civil Aviation that turnover levy
 payable to Airports Authority of India was reduced from 6 per cent to 2 per cent on the direction of the Ministry of
 Disinvestment with a plea that such remission will fetch attractive price of the property even when Ministry of Civil
 Aviation was not in favour of such decision.  The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation as to what
 was the impact of such reduction to the revenue of Airports Authority of India and how the loss of such revenue of

 first round not many bidders submitted their financial bids.  There will be reduction in revenue to Airports Authority of

20.       As regards refixing of the reserve price, the Committee was informed that J.P. Morgan (India) Private Limited
 (formerly Jardine Fleming India Securities Limited) had submitted separate valuation reports before and after reduction
 of the levy.  The valuation reports for CHMA were submitted to Ministry of Disinvestment on November 5, 2001 and
 January 18, 2002 before the submission of first and second round of financial bids for CHMA.  The lease rentals were
 reduced from 6 per cent to 2 per cent of the turnover prior to the invitation of the second round of financial bids.  This
 was the only parameter that was altered between the first and second valuation reports and the valuations were modified
 accordingly.  These reports are available with the Ministry of Disinvestment.  On both occasions, the reserve price was
 determined by the Valuation Committee constituted by Government of India and the valuation reports formed a part of
 consideration for determination of the reserve price.  Reserve price with 6 per cent turnover levy was Rs.76.2 crores
 and with 2 per cent, turnover levy Rs.78.3 crores. 
 
21.       The Committee observes that the reduction of turnover levy from 6 per cent to 2 per cent which entails the
 reduction of revenue of Airports Authority of India, has been aimed to ensure better price of CHMA.  To get a better
 price for the benefit of AI, the Government has taken a route which leads to a loss of revenue to another Government
 company.  The loss to AAI for this reduction of rate of turnover levy from 6 per cent to 2 per cent has been reported to
 be approximately Rs.17 crores.  Applying the Net Present Value method (with IRR factor 7 per cent which was higher
 than the bank rate), the loss comes to Rs.5.58 crores.   To compensate such a loss the reserve price has been increased
 by Rs.2.1 crores only from Rs.76.2 crores to Rs.78.3 crores.  The Committee is of the view that the issue required
 further clarification and investigation.

TRANSFER OF THE PETROL PUMP
 
30.       The Committee also took note of a controversy that arose over the actual ownership of a petrol pump, which was
 located in the premises of Centaur Hotel Mumbai Airport.  The Committee enquired from the Ministry of Civil
 Aviation regarding the details of the assets considered for physical valuation and whether the petrol pump was also
 included in the valuation.
 
31.       The Ministry of Civil Aviation replied that all the assets of HCI were valued by the Asset Valuer.  The petrol
 pump and its equipments did not belong to HCI which only had dealership of the petrol pump. Therefore, the Asset
 Valuer did not value the petrol pump.  The revenue from the petrol pump dealership was taken into account by the
 Advisors for determining the value of CHMA under different methods.
 
32.       However, the Committee noted that in the status note furnished vide  their O.M. No.13/2/2002-F.I dated the 18
th
 December, the Ministry of Civil Aviation stated that at the time of transfer of business of Centaur Hotel Mumbai
 Airport on 5.6.2002, the petrol pump, which was also a part of the transaction, was transferred to M/s Batra Hospitality
 Pvt. Ltd. (BHPL) on ‘as is where is’ basis.  The Joint Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation  (Shri Sanat Kaul) requested
 the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas for transferring of the dealership of I.O.C. for the said petrol pump to M/s.
 Batra Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.  The petrol pump was operated by M/s BHPL till 4.10.2002 when IOC informed HCI vide
 letter No.MSO/R/4340 dated 27.9.2002 that the dealership agreement dated 16.3.1975 executed between HCI and IOC
 stands terminated with immediate effect.  Since HCI had already effected the physical transfer of the petrol pump
 alongwith the hotel w.e.f. 5.6.2002, BHPL were requested to take up the matter with India Oil Corporation. 
 
33.       From the position furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, it is quite clear that the petrol pump was owned
 by the IOC, another PSU under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.  The Committee is unable to understand as
 to how the Ministry of Civil Aviation could get the valuation done and also proceed to transfer the ownership of the
 petrol pump without the consent of the concerned PSU and the Ministry.  The Committee is of the view that neither the
 Ministry of Disinvestment nor the Hotel Corporation of India had the right to transfer the petrol pump to M/s. Batra
 Hospitalities Pvt. Ltd. since neither of them were the owners of the petrol pump.  This clearly reflects that no proper
 thought was given to the selling process by the Government before inviting the Expression of Interest for the properties
 of HCI.

 dated the 18
th December 2002 informed the Committee that in response to a query of Ministry of Disinvestment, Shri
 A.L. Batra informed on 18 th October 2002 that 100 per cent shares of CHMA had been transferred to Sahara Group.

 Agreement nor any benefits or burdens under this Agreement shall be assigned by either Party without the prior written
 consent of the other Party”.  The Committee, therefore, enquired from the Ministry whether the transfer of 100 per cent
 shareholding of BHPL to Sahara Group was an assignment in disguise, the legality of the transfer of shareholding to the

 the Attorney General of India (copy at Annexure-6) on the matter which inter-alia brings out that there was no
 obligation on BHPL to obtain any prior consent as contemplated by Article 13.4 of the Agreement to Sell and hence,
 there has been no breach of the Lease Agreement.

 Lease Agreement with regard to the re-sale of CHMA.  However, keeping in view the experience and to stop such
 quick change of hands at a premium, necessary provisions may be incorporated in the Agreement to Sell in respect of

 brought out with regard to the selection criteria, reduction of turnover levy, rebidding process and the transfer of petrol

REDUCTION OF TURNOVER LEVY
The Committee observes that the reduction of turnover levy from 6 per cent to 2 per cent which entails the reduction of
 revenue of Airports Authority of India, has been aimed to ensure better price of CHMA.  To get a better price for the
 benefit of AI, the Government has taken a route which leads to a loss of revenue to another Government company.  The
 loss to AAI for this reduction of rate of turnover levy from 6 per cent to 2 per cent has been reported to be

REBIDDING PROCESS
 
The Committee is not convinced with the reply furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation that “Unless the shortlisting
 criteria were changed, it was unlikely that any new bidder would have shown interest”.  It may be pointed out that
 initially there were 17 parties who were short listed out of 19 parties who submitted EOI and subsequently 4 parties
 have participated in due diligence.  Hence, there was a qualitative change in the offer by reducing the turnover levy
 from 6 per cent to 2 per cent.  The contention of the Ministry of Civil Aviation that it was unlikely that any new bidder
 would have shown interest is, therefore, not tenable.
(Para 27)
 
The Committee is of the view that the idea of reduction in turnover levy was to go for re-bidding by exploring ways and
 means to secure better response for re-invited bid.  But, by restricting the invitation of the 2
nd round bid among the four
 parties only, the very purpose of reduction in turnover levy was defeated as only one bidder, that too the same for the
 earlier bid, remained in picture. Also, no thought was given to the views expressed by Shri R. C. Aggarwal.  The
 second round of bidding was, therefore, clearly a case of considering a ‘single bid’.
(Para 28)
 
The Committee feels that the ground rules for participating in the bidding process, as prescribed in the original
 advertisement inviting EOI for the properties of HCI, were framed in such a restrictive manner that it allowed hoteliers
 only in the bidding process.  As a result, the market for the properties of HCI could not be fully explored and several
 other interested parties, who were interested in offering better prices for the properties of HCI, could not enter the
 bidding process.  The Committee also feels that the 100 per cent shareholding of BHPL, which took over CHMA has
 been acquired by Sahara Group with the sole intention of taking over the business of CHMA within a short span of just
 6 months of taking over of CHMA by Shri A. L. Batra.  This clearly shows that there were interested parties for CHMA
 which were not properly explored, disproving the contention of the Ministry of Civil Aviation that it was unlikely that a
 new bidder would have shown interest.  The Committee feels that the reason why only a single bid was considered even
 after reducing the turnover levy, needs to be investigated.

TRANSFER OF THE PETROL PUMP
 
33.       From the position furnished by the Ministry of Civil Aviation, it is quite clear that the petrol pump was owned
 by the IOC, another PSU under the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas.  The Committee is unable to understand as
 to how the Ministry of Civil Aviation could get the valuation done and also proceed to transfer the ownership of the
 petrol pump without the consent of the concerned PSU and the Ministry.  The Committee is of the view that neither the
 Ministry of Disinvestment nor the Hotel Corporation of India had the right to transfer the petrol pump to M/s. Batra
 Hospitalities Pvt. Ltd. since neither of them were the owners of the petrol pump.  This clearly reflects that no proper
 thought was given to the selling process by the Government before inviting the Expression of Interest for the properties

1                    INTRODUCTION
 
1.1      Hotel Corporation of India Limited ("HCI") is a wholly owned subsidiary of Air India. Air India entered the hotel
 business in order to promote tourism in the country and to cater to the requirement of in-flight catering as well as to
 provide quality hotel accommodation to the passengers and crew. HCI was incorporated on July 8, 1971 with the
 objective of carrying on business of operating hotels and flight kitchens. HCI was operating four hotels, in Mumbai
 (two), Delhi (one) and Sringar (one), one hotel at Rajgir and two flight-catering units in Mumbai and Delhi.
2          RECOMMENDATION OF DISINVESTMENT COMMISSION
2.1      The Disinvestment Commission, in its 6
th Report published in December 1997, presented its recommendations in
 respect of disinvestment of Hotel Corporation of India (HCI).  It recommended that hotels at Mumbai and Delhi be sold
 as separate units through a transparent and competitive bidding process after undertaking a proper valuation through a
 Financial Adviser.
2.2      For hotel at Srinagar, the management of Air India may initiate dialogue with J&K Government in order to exit
 from its ownership. It was suggested that since lands on which the two airport hotels at Mumbai and Delhi are located
 belong to the AAI, Air India would need to negotiate and settle the terms of transfer with AAI prior to the sale.
2.3      It further suggested that Air India may decide whether the flight catering services should continue to be provided
 by HCI or whether it should be sold as independent units through a transparent competitive bidding process like the
 process of sale of Hotels.
2.4      The Commission in its 5
th Report had clarified that disinvestment in a subsidiary company of a PSU should be
 decided by the Board of Management of the concerned PSU.
 
3.         Follow-up Action on the Recommendations of Disinvestment Commission:
3.1      Air-India in its Board Meeting held in July 1998 considered the recommendation of the Disinvestment
 Commission and decided to accept in principle the dis-investment in HCI. However, the actual modalities of
 disinvestment were to be decided on the receipt of the report of a Consultant which was to be appointed by the Air
 India Board. The Department of Disinvestment, in its note dated 12.2.2000 regarding disinvestment of Government
 equity in Air India inter-alia, sought the approval of the Cabinet Committee on Disinvestment (CCD) so that the
 revenue realized accrues to Air India. The CCD, in its meeting held on 26.5.2000 took note of the proposal.
3.2      It was also decided to sort out the long pending issues of settlement of lease terms for the lease of AAI land at
 Mumbai and Delhi Airports for which there were no formal agreements. Shri Sanat Kaul, Joint Secretary, Ministry of
 Civil Aviation was appointed as sole Arbitrator in September, 1999 and after going through the records and hearing
 both AAI and AI/HCI gave his award in end November 1999 and suggested for execution of fresh lease deeds for a
 period of about 30 years. In the said award, he suggested that HCI should settle the dues with AAI and also pay the
 turnover levy of 2% for the years HCI made profits (for the past) and AAI should also agree for sub-letting in view of
 the disinvestment of these properties to the prospective buyers or entering into fresh lease on the terms like the case of
 Radisson in Delhi and Leela hotels in Mumbai on market terms.

REPORT
 
The Department of Tourism is the nodal agency for the formulation of national policies and programmes on
 Tourism and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government agencies, State Governments/UTs and the
 Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The Department of Tourism plays a
 crucial role in coordinating and supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territory Governments catalyzing
 investment, strengthening promotional and marketing efforts and private in providing training manpower resources.
 The main activities of the Department are: -
 
i)
                  Policy formulation and planning
ii)                Co-ordination
iii)               Regulation
iv)              Infrastructure and Product development
v)                Human Resource Development
vi)              Publicity, Marketing and Facilitation
vii)             Research, Analysis, Monitoring and Evaluation
viii)           International Co-operation and External Assistance
ix)              Parliament work
x)                Management of Public Sector Undertakings and Autonomous bodies
 
2.         The Department of Tourism is headed by a Secretary.  The post of Director General (Tourism) has been merged
 with the post of Secretary (T) who is assisted by the Joint Secretary and the Additional Director General. In addition to
 the Headquarters Organisation at New Delhi, the Directorate General of Tourism has 21 India tourism Offices in India
 (including 5 Regional Offices), situated at Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai, Kolkata, Agra, Bhubaneshwar, Aurangabad,
 Bangalore, Cochin, Guwahati, Hyderabad, Imphal, Jaipur, Khajuraho, Naharlagun, Panaji (Goa), Patna, Port Blair,
 Shillong, Varanasi and Thiruvananthapuram.  There are 13 India tourism Offices Overseas, which include 5 Regional
 offices at Sydney, New York, Tokyo, Frankfurt and Dubai.  The other India tourism Offices are located at Los Angeles,
 London, Toronto, Paris, Amsterdam, Milan, Singapore and Johannesburg.

13.       A tourist circuit is defined as a route on which at least three major tourists destinations are located in such a
 manner that none of these are in the same town, village or city.  At the same time they are not ­­­­separated by a large
 distance  so that a tourist would not like to cover them in a sequence.  The scheme is basically a merger of all the

 employment. India’s share of global domestic tourism is much higher (around 4.6% of estimated global domestic

th Five Year Plan, the Department of Tourism sanctioned

 put forth by the Department of Tourism for delay i.e. lack of coordination between the State Government and different
 other Ministries in the implementation of projects, besides low level of monitoring and review of progress.  The
 Committee is of the opinion that involvement of Members of Parliament in identification, development and monitoring
 of tourist destinations in their respective state, can avoid delay and cost overrun in execution of tourism projects. In this
 connection, the committee reiterates its earlier recommendation made in 55
th Report, which is reproduced below;
 
“The Committee recommends that the Department of Tourism should involve the Members of Parliament in
 the identification and development of places of tourist interest in their respective states.  The Committee is of
 the view that, as elected representatives of the people, Members of Parliament can also help the Department in
 identifying tourism sports in their states and inform the Department of Tourism which can take steps to
 develop such tourism areas.  The Committee also recommends that the Department of Tourism should, by
 way of taking the initiative, request the Members of Parliament to identify places, which can be developed as
 tourist spots.  The Members of Parliament should also be kept informed of the status of the tourism projects in
 their respective states.”

 Parliament in identification, development and monitoring process of tourists destinations/circuits in their respective
 states and have a task force which will coordinate between different Ministries as well as State Governments and
 respective Members of Parliament in that state for monitoring the progress of physical targets every quarter or so.
